a2001: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Organizing Bookmarks by Path: a Starter Project Lesson 20.1 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Import bookmarks with their original hierarchy Normalize links and explain duplicate groups Rank topics and assemble a reading path Export an editable collection and progress file Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 1 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : TypeScript. Why: Typed local transformations and portable browser interfaces run with Node standard libraries. In plain words first The idea in one line Make a useful reading path from saved links. The problem In plain words first A browser's bookmark export is a tree of folders, often years deep, with the same page saved twice under slightly different addresses. This project turns that pile into a reading path you can act on. It does four things in order: flattens the tree without forgetting which folders each link lived in; decides when two links are really the same page; ranks the pages against topics you name; and writes an HTML page plus a progress file you can edit and feed back in. The habit it teaches: never throw information away while cleaning. The original URL, the folder path and the reason two links were merged all stay in the output, so a person can check every decision. Help a reader recover a useful collection from an exported bookmark pile. Normalize URLs conservatively, merge exact duplicates, score user-defined topics from saved titles and notes, and export an editable reading path as HTML and JSON. You build a standalone reading-path page and bookmarks.json with retained original URLs. Step 1 · Import bookmarks with their original hierarchy Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript What you build. Flatten a folder tree while keeping original URLs and every ancestor folder. Public contract. Copy Input is an array of folders {title,children} or bookmarks {id,title,url,notes?} . Return {id,title,url,notes,folders:string[]} . IDs must be unique; notes default to an empty string. Validate absolute HTTP(S) URLs without credentials. Limit folder nesting to 32. Stage 1 may validate URLs directly; normalizeURL is introduced in stage 2. Worked example. A folder Maps / Basics containing bookmark a produces folders:["Maps","Basics"] ; the original https://EXAMPLE.invalid/#intro remains verbatim. An empty input returns [] . Failure cases and hints. Reject duplicate IDs, missing titles, non-string notes and unsafe protocols. Recurse with a copied ancestor array, not one shared array. Use your result. After stage four, pass a JSON file of your own through the same entry point: Copy A standalone reading-path page and bookmarks.json with retained original URLs. Open output/report.html and inspect the machine-readable companion files. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.mjs (61 lines) Copy Step 2 · Normalize links and explain duplicate groups Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript What you build. Explain exactly why two saved links point at the same document. Public contract. Copy Use the WHATWG URL representation: lowercase host, remove default port and remove fragment. Retain the query and its order, path case and trailing slash. Return groups {url,items,reason} in first-seen order with copied original records. Worked example. https://EXAMPLE.invalid:443/maps#intro and https://example.invalid/maps#scale normalize to https://example.invalid/maps . ?view=print remains a separate group. The sample imports 12 saved records into 11 document groups. Failure cases and hints. A tracking-looking query may change a page. Do not remove query parameters or merge HTTP with HTTPS. Reject credentials. Use your result. Copy Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.mjs (55 lines) Copy Worked example Which links are the same page? https://EXAMPLE.invalid:443/maps#intro : the host is lower-cased to example.invalid , the default HTTPS port :443 is dropped, and the fragment #intro is removed (it only scrolls within the page). Result: https://example.invalid/maps . https://example.invalid/maps#scale normalizes to the same string, so the two bookmarks form one group, with the reason recorded. https://example.invalid/maps?view=print keeps its query: a query can change what the server returns, so it stays a separate document. http://example.invalid/maps stays separate too: a different scheme is a different request, and the project never guesses that they match. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Removing the fragment is safe for "same document" because the server never sees it. ✗ Dropping every query parameter is a safe way to merge tracking links. Some parameters change the page ( ?view=print , ?page=2 ); removing them silently merges different documents. ✓ Each group keeps the original records, so the exported page can still show the address the user saved. ✗ Scoring a duplicate group once per saved copy is fair because the user saved it twice. The project scores each keyword once per group, so duplicates do not push a page up the list. Step 3 · Rank topics and assemble a reading path Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript What you build. Rank a reading collection with visible keyword evidence. Public contract. Copy Match lowercase Unicode word tokens. Each unique keyword scores 3 if any group title contains it and 1 if any notes contain it; duplicate bookmarks do not multiply scores. Sum topic scores, sort descending then by id. Return {id,title,url,originals,folders,topics,score,evidence} using the first saved record as identity. Topic keywords must be nonempty strings and are intended as single tokens. Worked example. For topic Mapping:["map"] , title Map basics adds 3; notes Read this map first adds 1. Total is 4. A duplicate save of the same title contributes zero additional points. Mapping guide does not contain token map . Failure cases and hints. Test a keyword in notes only and a word embedded inside another word. Preserve unmatched records at score zero. Use your result. Copy Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.mjs (41 lines) Copy Step 4 · Export an editable collection and progress file Step 4 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript What you build. Carry reading order and completion between a browser review and the next command. Public contract. Copy Progress is {schemaVersion:1,order:string[],completed:string[]} . Order is a full permutation of current IDs; completed contains unique known IDs. The browser provides Move up/down, Read checkboxes and a JSON download. All visible text is escaped or assigned with textContent. Worked example. If current IDs are ["a","b"] , review {schemaVersion:1,order:["b","a"],completed:["a"]} renders b before a and checks a as read. ["a","a"] is not a permutation and must fail. Failure cases and hints. Reject stale progress rather than silently dropping unknown IDs. Escape closing-script text in embedded JSON. Use your result. Copy A standalone reading-path page and bookmarks.json with retained original URLs. Open output/report.html and inspect the machine-readable companion files. Pass downloaded progress back with node cli.ts sample.json resumed-output progress.json ; compare the new progress.json and the displayed order. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.mjs (73 lines) Copy Run the finished project Predict before you run The sample holds 12 saved bookmarks, and two of them are the maps page saved with different fragments. How many documents should the importer report, and which two ids should appear as a duplicate group? The finished reference runs with one command, from its solution/ folder: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output imported: 12 and documents: 11 match the prediction: one pair, map-1 and map-2 , collapsed into a single document. order is the reading path: pages sorted by topic score, highest first, ties broken by id, so the same input always gives the same order. later-6 ("Publish a map", notes "Sharing a community map") and map-1 ("Map basics", notes about coordinates) earn the same score, so the tie rule decides: ids sort alphabetically and later-6 comes first. That is the point of a stated tie rule: the order is reproducible, even if it is not the order a person would pick. The HTML page and progress.json sit in output/ : reorder or tick items in the browser, save the progress file, and the next run applies it. Code solution/cli.ts (62 lines) Copy Code solution/main.ts (203 lines) Copy Code solution/sample.json (96 lines) Copy Where the project stops The importer consumes the documented JSON folder tree, not arbitrary browser HTML. URL equality is document-oriented because fragments are removed; query strings remain significant. Ranking uses lexical tokens, not a remote model. Links are never fetched. Break it on purpose A first version merges https://shop.invalid/item?id=7 and https://shop.invalid/item?id=9 into one group, and the reading path silently loses a page. Which normalization step went too far? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this project Flatten trees but keep every ancestor folder and the original URL. Normalize conservatively: lower-case the host, drop default ports and fragments, keep the query. Record why links were merged, so a person can audit the grouping. Score each keyword once per group, and break ties by id for a stable order. Round-trip state through a small, validated progress file. Exercises Add an import adapter for one browser export format while keeping this typed boundary. (step 1) Add an explicit user-approved tracking-parameter policy with its own receipt. (step 2) Support user-specified prerequisite edges before ranking independent topics. (step 3) Merge progress across revised collections with an explicit conflict report. (step 4) Solutions Solution A browser import adapter Read the browser's own export (for example the Netscape bookmark HTML format) in a separate function that produces exactly the same folder tree the importer already accepts. Validation, URL checks and folder limits stay in one place, and the adapter can be tested on its own fixture. Solution A tracking-parameter policy Let the user list parameter names to drop (for example utm_source ). Apply the list during normalization, and add a receipt to each group: "merged because utm_source was removed by your rule". Without the explicit list, keep today's behaviour. Solution Prerequisite edges Treat "read A before B" as a directed graph, check it has no cycles, then sort topologically. Among pages that are ready at the same time, keep the current score order. A cycle is an error that names the pages involved. Solution Merging progress after the collection changes Match old progress to new items by id. Ids that vanished go into a "removed" list, new ids are appended unread, and a completed item whose URL changed is reported as a conflict for the user to decide, never resolved silently. Solution B1 · Two products merged The normalizer removed the query string. Queries can select different content, so they must stay part of the document identity; only the fragment, the default port and the host's case are safe to normalize. a2002: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects A Workbench for Repairing Broken CSV Files Lesson 20.2 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Profile columns and retain original cells Propose explicit normalization rules Preview changes and review ambiguous values Export a reusable repair recipe and cleaned table Before you start Needs : Python 3.10+; lists, dictionaries and functions Type : Project, level 1 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Python. In plain words first The idea in one line Fix messy tables without losing the original cells. The problem In plain words first A spreadsheet that people typed by hand has the same garden written three ways and dates in two orders. Cleaning it is easy. Cleaning it so that someone can trust the result is harder: every change has to be visible, every guess has to be refused, and the same recipe has to give the same table next month. The project builds that in four steps: profile each column while keeping the original cells; write the fixes as an explicit, ordered recipe; preview every changed cell and park the ambiguous ones for a person; then replay the recipe and record each human decision in a ledger. Help a spreadsheet owner repair inconsistent labels, dates and missing values through an explicit sequence of transformations. Preview every changed cell, keep ambiguous cases for review, and export a cleaned CSV with a reusable transformation recipe and HTML comparison. The implementation uses Python 3.10+ and standard libraries. Samples are original teaching data. Read API.md for exact input, output and error contracts. What you will build: cleaned.csv, recipe.json and a cell-level HTML before/after report Step 1 · Profile columns and retain original cells Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Retain exact source cells while counting missing and distinct values. Build the mechanism. The sample has North Garden, north garden and N. Garden. Keep their original spelling and row numbers before changing anything. Exact contract. Implement profile(text): rows preserve strings and profile counts whitespace-only cells as missing. Read API.md , including return fields and failure behavior. The first starter supplies file I/O and HTML presentation; implement the domain functions in main.py . Keep earlier functions passing because later stages compose them. Verify it. The stage tests include held-out inputs independent of the demo, boundaries, malformed data and an adversarial case. Inspect the failing assertion before changing a rule. Failure boundary and extension. Quoted commas belong inside one cell. Reject duplicate headers and rows with a different width. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_1.py (21 lines) Copy Step 2 · Propose explicit normalization rules Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Build an explicit ordered recipe from supplied policy. Build the mechanism. Trim happens before alias lookup, so " North Garden " can map to the canonical North Garden. No guessed synonym is applied. Exact contract. Implement propose(table, aliases=None, date_columns=None). Each rule is an explicit trim, alias or date operation. Failure boundary and extension. An unknown column is an error. Missing values remain missing; an imputation policy is a possible extension. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_2.py (27 lines) Copy Step 3 · Preview changes and review ambiguous values Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Show every changed cell and quarantine uncertain dates. Build the mechanism. 14/03/2026 becomes 2026-03-14. Both 03/04/2026 and 04/03/2026 remain pending because either ordering is plausible. Exact contract. Implement preview(table, recipe), returning rows, changes, pending and a SHA-256 review fingerprint. Failure boundary and extension. A date like 31/02/2026 is invalid, not merely ambiguous. Keep it visible instead of coercing it. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_3.py (34 lines) Copy Worked example Why `03/04/2026` waits for a person 14/03/2026 has a day of 14. No month is 14, so the only reading is 14 March: it becomes 2026-03-14 automatically. 03/04/2026 could be 3 April (day first) or 4 March (month first). Both are real dates, so the tool refuses to pick. 04/03/2026 has the same problem the other way round. 31/02/2026 is different: neither reading gives a real date, so it is invalid , not ambiguous, and it is reported as an error. The preview carries a SHA-256 fingerprint of the input and the recipe. A person's decision is accepted only for the exact table and recipe they reviewed. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Trimming before the alias lookup lets " North Garden " match the alias for North Garden . ✗ The tool may map N. Garden to North Garden because they look alike. Only aliases you supply are applied; nothing is guessed from spelling. ✓ A decision recorded for one input is rejected when the input changes, because the fingerprint no longer matches. ✗ An empty volunteers cell should be filled with 0. A blank is "unknown", not zero; the tool counts it as missing and leaves it. Step 4 · Export a reusable repair recipe and cleaned table Step 4 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Replay the recipe and validate human cell decisions. Build the mechanism. A decision for row 2 date=2026-04-03 is accepted only for the matching input and recipe fingerprint. Every accepted edit enters the change ledger. Exact contract. The JSON input contains csv text, aliases and date_columns. Outputs are cleaned.csv, recipe.json, receipt.json and review.html. Download decisions.json from the HTML, add {row,column,value} entries to cells, and run the same command with --decisions decisions.json. Replay the exported recipe on another compatible table with --recipe recipe.json. Read cleaned.csv with csv.DictReader as the downstream consumer. Failure boundary and extension. Only slash dates and ISO dates are recognized. Reviews resolve pending date cells; no locale or semantic inference is claimed. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_4.py (48 lines) Copy Run the finished project Predict before you run The sample has three rows: North Garden , north garden and N. Garden , with dates 14/03/2026 , 03/04/2026 and 04/03/2026 . The aliases map the two variants to North Garden . How many cells will change, and how many will wait for review? Garden ) became North Garden , and 14/03/2026 became 2026-03-14 . pending: 2 : the two dates whose day and month could swap. Everything else is in demo-output/ : cleaned.csv , the replayable recipe.json , a receipt.json with fingerprints, and review.html , which shows each cell before and after and lets you record decisions for the pending dates. The next file comes from a US office. What goes wrong, and how does this project's design prevent it? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this project Keep original cells and row numbers; never edit in place. Write cleaning as an explicit, ordered recipe you can replay. Apply only supplied aliases; refuse guesses. Ambiguous is not invalid: queue the first, reject the second. Bind human decisions to a fingerprint of the input and the recipe. Build it on your machine Each step above is meant to be built, not only read. The source repository ships a starter and the checks for every step, and its test runner grades your own folder step by step: Copy Write the step, run its checks, then move to the next step. The checks for each step are also shown above, under that step, so you can see what is expected before you start. Exercises Questions to test what you built. Try each one before you open the solutions. Add a rule that splits Name (Role) into two columns. Where in the recipe does it go, and what must the preview show? A reviewer accepts 03/04/2026 as 3 April. Next week the same file arrives with one extra row. Should the decision still apply? How would you report a column where 40 percent of cells are blank? Solutions Solution A split rule Add it as a new rule type that runs after trimming and before aliases, so the alias lookup sees the cleaned name. The preview must show both new cells and the source cell for every row, and the receipt must list the rule, so replaying the recipe produces the same columns. Solution A decision on a changed file No. The fingerprint covers the whole input, so the decision is refused and the date goes back to pending. That is deliberate: the tool cannot know whether the new row changes what the reviewer meant. A per-row fingerprint would let unchanged rows keep their decisions, at the cost of more bookkeeping. Solution A mostly blank column Report the count and the share of missing cells in the profile, without filling anything. Whether to fill, drop or keep the column is a decision for the data owner, and it belongs in the recipe as an explicit rule if they choose one. Solution B1 · Day-first everywhere 03/04/2026 from a US office means 4 March (month first), so the date silently moves a month. The project prevents this by never choosing an order for ambiguous dates: they wait for a person, and the decision is tied to the exact file it was made for. a2003: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Auditing Train/Test Dataset Splits for Leakage Lesson 20.3 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Fingerprint normalized records Audit duplicate and group leakage Split groups with stable hashing Report split size and leakage together Before you start Needs : Python 3.10+, lists, sets, dictionaries, Unicode normalization and hash functions Type : Project, level 1 (Starter). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Python. Why: The standard library makes parsing, scoring, and failure handling visible without hiding the mechanism behind a framework. In plain words first The idea in one line A dataset gate that names the records responsible for content and incident leakage. The problem In plain words first A test set is supposed to be questions the model has never seen. Two things quietly break that. The same text can sit in both train and test under different ids, perhaps with different spacing or capitals. And two different records can come from the same incident, so a model that learned one already knows the answer to the other. This project builds a gate that catches both kinds of leak and names the exact records responsible: fingerprint the text after normalizing it, check which fingerprints and which groups appear on both sides, split by group instead of by row, and report sizes and leaks together. A dataset gate that names the records responsible for content and incident leakage. Python 3.10+; lists, sets, dictionaries, Unicode normalization and hash functions. The core uses standard libraries. The grader checks your selected workspace; it never fills in missing behavior from the reference. Where it stops: Pass {train,test} records to the CLI, or {records} with --split 0.25 --seed experiment-1. Add --check in CI to return exit2 when the split is unusable. Step 1 · Fingerprint normalized records Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Create stable SHA-256 fingerprints for text after NFKC normalization, case folding, and whitespace collapse. What changes. A random split can place the same example in both train and test under different ids. Normalize Unicode, whitespace, and case before hashing the content. Keep ids separate from content fingerprints so renamed records still collide. Normalization is an explicit policy. It detects exact normalized duplicates, not paraphrases, images, or semantically equivalent code. Hashing does not make content anonymous when the input space is guessable. Work through one concrete case. The strings "Ｒetry NOW" and "retry now" normalize to the same text under NFKC, case folding and whitespace collapse. Their record ids may differ, but their content fingerprints must agree. Change the lab inputs and calculate the result before reading its metrics. The figure computes from those inputs; the implementation tests below remain the source of completion evidence. Implement the contract. Implement fingerprint against the stated contract. Use the public API contract and the typed starter signatures. Return values from core functions and let the supplied driver own file input, argument parsing and presentation. Apply normalization before UTF-8 encoding and hashing. Never hash a dictionary representation, whose ordering and incidental metadata change independently of content. Verify and inspect. A fresh workspace should fail until you implement the contract. After every stage is complete, run your actual artifact from the supplied sample: Investigate the failure boundary. Try "retry now!". Punctuation remains meaningful, so this contract should not claim that it matches "retry now". Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_01.py (21 lines) Copy See it drawn Two spellings, one fingerprint Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The first two strings differ only in case and surrounding spaces, so after normalization they hash to the same value: that is a content leak if one is in train and the other in test. The third has a hyphen, which normalization deliberately does not remove, so it gets a different fingerprint. Normalization is a policy: it catches exact duplicates up to case, spacing and Unicode form, not paraphrases. Step 2 · Audit duplicate and group leakage Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Validate ids, text, and groups, then report intersections across train and test. What changes. Content leakage and group leakage are different. Two distinct support messages from the same incident can leak the answer even when their text differs. Track both normalized content hashes and group ids across partitions. Return the colliding hashes and group names, not just a percentage. The reviewer needs to locate the records. Reject duplicate record ids because they make that evidence ambiguous. Work through one concrete case. train-a and test-a share normalized text across different incidents. train-a and test-b have different text but share incident-1. The report keeps two independent evidence lists with the exact record ids involved. Implement the contract. Implement audit against the stated contract. Build value-to-record-id indexes for both sides, then intersect keys. The hash alone proves a collision but does not tell a beginner which source rows to inspect. Investigate the failure boundary. Give two records the same id. Reject before constructing evidence because the resulting location would be ambiguous. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_02.py (33 lines) Copy Step 3 · Split groups with stable hashing Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Return train and test arrays with no group overlap. What changes. Partition groups, not rows. Hash the seed and group id into a stable fraction and compare it with the requested test fraction. Every row in a group follows the same decision, regardless of input order. Hash partitioning gives an expected fraction rather than an exact row count. Small datasets may have an empty partition. Report that honestly instead of moving one row and breaking group isolation. Work through one concrete case. If incident-A contains nine messages and incident-B contains one, a50 percent group split can yield nine train rows and one test row. Moving one message to balance counts would reintroduce incident leakage. Implement the contract. Implement split_groups against the stated contract. Derive the partition decision from seed plus group, never input row order. Reversing the input list may change row order but must preserve each id's partition membership. Investigate the failure boundary. Generate 20 groups with different sizes, change the seed and compare group isolation and row balance separately. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_03.py (30 lines) Copy Worked example Splitting by group Each group id (an incident, a user, a document) is hashed together with the seed into a number between 0 and 1. If that number is below the test fraction, the whole group goes to test; otherwise it goes to train. Every row of incident-1 therefore lands on the same side, in any input order. The cost: the split hits the requested fraction only on average. With three groups and a fraction of 0.3, the test side may get zero groups, one or two, and the report says so instead of pretending. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Two different texts from the same incident are a leak even though their fingerprints differ. ✗ A random row-level split prevents group leakage if the dataset is large enough. Rows of one group scatter across both sides at any size; only splitting by group prevents it. ✓ The same seed and group ids always produce the same split. ✗ "No leaks found" means the split is usable. An empty test side has no leaks too; the report checks both partitions are non-empty. Step 4 · Report split size and leakage together Step 4 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Produce a JSON audit with partition sizes, group counts, and a usable flag requiring both nonempty partitions and no leakage. What changes. A clean split can still be useless when nearly all records land in training. Report row counts, group counts, and leakage in one artifact. Keeping these numbers together prevents a clean-leakage claim from hiding an empty test set. The checker does not certify statistical representativeness. Time-dependent tasks often need a chronological split, which this project deliberately leaves as a later extension. Work through one concrete case. A report with zero leaks and test_rows=0 is unusable. The supplied dirty fixture has both partitions but still fails because content and group evidence remain. These are distinct reasons for the same gate outcome. Implement the contract. Implement summarize against the stated contract. The CLI composes summarize with provenance indexes and optionally returns exit 2. A CI job should retain the JSON artifact even when the gate fails so a reviewer can locate the problem. Investigate the failure boundary. Create an authored clean pair, run --check and confirm exit 0. Add a normalized copy under a new id and confirm exit 2 with both original ids in the artifact. Normalization finds exact normalized copies, not paraphrases. Stable group hashing does not guarantee balanced classes or time-aware evaluation. Source text remains present in exported partitions. Recap What to keep from this project Content leaks and group leaks are different; check both. Fingerprint text after a stated normalization policy. Split by group with a seeded hash, so every row of a group stays together. Name the records responsible, not just a percentage. Report sizes with leaks: an empty test set is also unusable. The source repository ships a starter and the checks for every step, and its test runner grades your own folder step by step: Copy Write the step, run its checks, then move to the next step. The checks for each step are also shown above, under that step, so you can see what is expected before you start. Exercises Questions to test what you built. Try each one before you open the solutions. Why must the fingerprint ignore the record id? Your groups are users, and one user has half the data. What happens to a 20 percent test split? How would you extend the gate to catch near-duplicates such as paraphrases? Solutions Solution Why ignore the id The same text often enters a dataset twice under different ids (an export ran twice, a record was copied). Including the id would make every copy unique and hide the leak. Solution One huge group That user goes wholly to one side. If it lands in test, test is about half the data; if in train, test holds the rest. Group splits trade exact proportions for honesty; report the realized sizes, and consider stratifying the remaining groups or treating the giant group separately. Solution Near-duplicates Add a second, separate check: embed or shingle the texts and flag cross-split pairs above a similarity threshold for review. Keep it as a report, not an automatic block, because similarity thresholds produce false positives that a person must judge. Solution B1 · Reworded tickets Exact string matching misses case and spacing differences, which the normalized fingerprint would catch. Group leakage (tickets from the same incident) is what really broke the result, and the group check catches it. Neither check catches a paraphrase from a different incident; that needs a similarity check. The problem In plain words first A downloads folder fills up with copies, renamed copies and files whose names say nothing. The problem In plain words first You reword a prompt to fix one complaint, and something else quietly breaks: the answer stops being valid JSON, or starts leaking a secret. In plain words first The idea in one line Build a bounded coding loop that applies exact patches to a disposable workspace and runs its real tests through an allowlisted tool contract. The problem In plain words first A coding agent is a loop: look at the code, propose a change, run the tests, repeat. The dangerous parts are the tools. A file tool that follows ../ or a symlink can touch files outside the project. A patch that overwrites blindly destroys someone else's edit. A "test" tool that runs whatever command the model writes is a shell for the model. And a loop that trusts the model's "done" claims success without evidence. This project builds each tool with a hard contract, then a loop that stops only on real evidence (the tests pass) or on a budget. The planner is a recorded list of actions, so the whole run is repeatable and inspectable. A repair agent that exposes the patch/test evidence trail and refuses unsupported success claims. Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Rust. In plain words first The idea in one line Account for usage and budgets with integer arithmetic. The problem In plain words first Model calls are billed per token, at different rates for input, cached input and output. Before a call you can only estimate the cost; after it, the provider reports what was actually used. A budget needs both: a cautious quote to decide whether to start, and the real usage to settle the account. This project does that accounting in Rust with whole numbers only (nano-dollars), so no rounding can drift the total. It estimates tokens from characters, validates the provider's usage record, prices it with overflow checks, and keeps a ledger that refuses work it cannot afford. This is a baseline for preflight planning; actual provider counts can differ by language, punctuation and tokenizer. Where it stops: Rates are explicit fixture inputs in integer nano-dollars per token, not current provider prices. In plain words first The idea in one line Build suggestions that explain which words they learned from. The problem In plain words first Autocomplete is the oldest language model there is: count which words follow which, and suggest the most common next word. Before neural networks, this was how phones predicted text. This project builds one you can fully inspect: it counts single words and one- or two-word histories from a small corpus, suggests completions for what you are typing, and shows for each suggestion how often it was seen and in which source text. In plain words first The idea in one line Check that an API tutorial still works from its first request to its final result. The problem In plain words first API tutorials go stale. A field gets renamed, and step 2 of the tutorial now describes a response that no longer exists, but nobody notices until a reader is stuck. This project turns a tutorial into a test: it pulls out request blocks that the author marked as executable, threads values from one step into the next (create a loan, then read it by its new id), runs the requests against a local test service with timeouts, and exports results a CI system understands, pointing at the exact line of the tutorial that broke. It never edits the tutorial itself. It drafts a correction and waits for a person to accept it. Help a documentation author verify a sequence of HTTP examples. Type : Project, level 2 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Explain why two environments resolve the same setting differently. The problem In plain words first "It works on staging but not in production." Often the code is the same and the configuration differs: a timeout set in a defaults file and overridden by an environment variable, or a secret that changed. Finding which layer won, and why, is tedious by hand. This project explains configuration drift. It loads named layers in order (defaults, then files, then environment), resolves each key while keeping the full history of which layer set what, compares the expected values with what a running system actually reports, and exports a report that is safe to hand to a CI job or an AI assistant because secret values are redacted. Help a developer compare declared defaults, environment overrides and observed JSON configuration. Preserve precedence and redaction rules, expose shadowed values, and attach every explanation to its source file or variable name. Export a drift report that an assistant can consume without receiving secret values. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go implementations are exercised by the grader. In plain words first The idea in one line Turn location-tagged observations into a map another tool can use. The problem In plain words first A team walks a park and records observations on their phones: "broken bench here", "good shade there", each with GPS coordinates, a time and maybe a photo. It validates each observation, computes real distances on the globe, proposes groups of nearby notes with the distance evidence kept, lets a reviewer keep or split each group without deleting anything, and exports both GeoJSON and an offline HTML map. In plain words first The idea in one line Turn exported email into an evidence-backed review queue and unsent reply drafts. The problem In plain words first An assistant that "handles your email" is easy to imagine and risky to build: it might group unrelated messages because they share a subject line, label a request as information, or send a reply that promises something you never agreed to. This project builds the careful offline version. It reads exported messages with a proper MIME parser, threads them by their message-ID headers rather than subjects, triages each one with explicit phrases and shows the phrase that matched, and writes reply drafts that quote the source and leave a marked gap for your answer. Nothing is ever sent. Turn exported email into an evidence-backed review queue and unsent reply drafts. You build an HTML review desk, triage.json, and downloadable unsent .eml drafts. Inputs: A directory of exported .eml messages. Only plain-text bodies are classified; HTML-only messages remain visible for manual review. Where it stops: A directory of exported .eml messages. Only plain-text bodies are classified; HTML-only messages remain visible for manual review. Step 1 · Read MIME without losing message identity Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Parse exported messages and preserve their exact plain-text evidence. What you are building. An email is a structured message, not a body obtained by splitting at the first blank line. MIME can contain multiple alternatives, attachments and transfer encodings. Use BytesParser with an explicit policy, then select the plain-text body. Keep the sender, subject, message ID, reference IDs and body status beside the text. Work through an example. A message with From: Ada ada@example.invalid , Message-ID: a@example.invalid , and the body Please reserve a chair produces sender ada@example.invalid and the exact body text. A second HTML alternative must not replace that text. If Message-ID is absent, a digest of the original bytes supplies stable local identity. Before coding, write down the returned fields for that example and one input that should fail. Keep the expected result beside your implementation so you can distinguish a contract change from a bug. Implement the contract. parse_message(raw: bytes) -> dict Return keys id, sender, subject, text, references and body_status. Reject empty input, input larger than 1,000,000 bytes, and missing sender addresses. Collapse whitespace in the subject but preserve body line breaks. Deduplicate reference IDs. An HTML-only body becomes empty text with no-plain-body status. Hints and failure cases. Start with one plain message, then construct multipart/alternative. Prefer the parser's get_body over traversing every text part: an attached text file is not the email body. Test fallback IDs by parsing the same bytes twice. Run your stage. The starter deliberately raises an implementation error. Later initialization preserves your source rather than replacing it. A passing result requires every selected test to run; a skipped test is not completion evidence. Check your reasoning. Why must two messages with the same subject still keep separate identities? What information would be lost if HTML were silently converted to plain text? Connect it to the finished artifact. An HTML review desk, triage.json, and downloadable unsent .eml drafts. The default classifier uses explicit phrase rules, not an LLM. It handles a folder of exported messages and never connects to your mailbox or sends replies. Keep attachments separate from text used for triage. Three messages a, b referencing a, and c referencing b belong to one thread. A fourth message with the same subject and no reference stays separate. For triage, Please confirm matches action. For your information matches information. A body containing both is uncertain, because choosing a single winning rule would hide the conflict. Implement the contract. group_threads(messages: list[dict]) -> list[dict] triage(message: dict, rules: dict | None = None) -> dict Return stable thread IDs and messages sorted by ID. Identical duplicates collapse; conflicting records with the same ID raise ValueError. Rule categories are action and information; unmatched or conflicting categories become uncertain. The problem In plain words first A postmortem tells the story of an incident, and stories drift toward a cause: "the deploy broke latency". Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Python. In plain words first The idea in one line Explain replacements, unknown values and dependencies before an infrastructure change. The problem In plain words first Infrastructure tools such as Terraform show a plan before they change anything: create this, update that, replace the database. Reviewers skim long plans and miss the line that matters, usually a replacement (delete and recreate) hiding among updates, or a value that will only be known after the change. This project turns a saved plan into a short change brief. It loads the plan while masking sensitive values, classifies each action and singles out replacements, traces which resources depend on which (even through values that are still unknown), and exports a Markdown brief and a JSON impact graph, each item linked by its exact resource address. Read a saved Terraform plan JSON for a developer reviewing a proposed change. Preserve unknown and sensitive-value markers, separate replacement from in-place updates, and trace declared dependencies. Produce a review brief whose explanations link to exact plan addresses; never apply the plan. The implementation uses Python 3.10+ and standard libraries. Samples are original teaching data. Read API.md for exact input, output and error contracts. A live recorder additionally needs an already-running loopback OpenAI-compatible model server Type : Project, level 2 (Builder). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Python. Why: The standard library makes parsing, scoring, and failure handling visible without hiding the mechanism behind a framework. In plain words first The idea in one line A reproducible local-model recording and comparison artifact with visible coverage and confidence error. The problem In plain words first "The local model got 67 percent" is not an evaluation. Which model revision, which prompt, which hardware? Did it answer every question? When it was confident, was it right? How long did it take? This project builds a scorecard that answers those questions from recorded predictions, so the numbers can be reproduced and compared. It validates each prediction record, measures exact-answer accuracy together with coverage, measures calibration (whether confidence matches correctness), and publishes accuracy beside latency percentiles, with a manifest of exactly what was measured. A reproducible local-model recording and comparison artifact with visible coverage and confidence error. Python 3.10+; JSON, ratios, sorting, percentiles and basic HTTP. A live recorder additionally needs an already-running loopback OpenAI-compatible model server. The core uses standard libraries. The grader checks your selected workspace; it never fills in missing behavior from the reference. Where it stops: record.py writes the same {manifest,source,labels,records} contract consumed by cli.py. --baseline compares only identical label fingerprints; --min-accuracy supplies a local CI gate. Step 1 · Validate prediction records Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Validate unique ids, string answers, confidence in [0,1], and nonnegative latency_ms. What changes. A prediction record is evidence: id, answer, confidence, and measured latency. Require unique ids and finite numbers. NaN can otherwise slip past comparisons and turn a failure into an apparently valid report. The harness consumes recordings so every metric test runs without a model. To evaluate a real local model, record its responses in the same contract and keep the execution environment beside the resulting JSON. Work through one concrete case. Two records with idcase-a make joining to labels ambiguous, so validation rejects them even if their answers agree. Confidence must be finite and within 0..1; NaN must fail before any comparisons or averages. Change the lab inputs and calculate the result before reading its metrics. The figure computes from those inputs; the implementation tests below remain the source of completion evidence. Implement the contract. Implement validate against the stated contract. Use the public API contract and the typed starter signatures. Return values from core functions and let the supplied driver own file input, argument parsing and presentation. A boolean is an integer subclass in Python but is not a latency measurement. Preserve answer, confidence, latency and id together so later metrics cannot accidentally align by array position. Verify and inspect. A fresh workspace should fail until you implement the contract. After every stage is complete, run your actual artifact from the supplied sample: Investigate the failure boundary. Reorder prediction rows and prove the score stays the same. Then duplicate one id and confirm that the run fails instead of double-counting it. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_01.py (27 lines) Copy Step 2 · Measure normalized exact-answer accuracy Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Return correct, total, accuracy, and coverage against a complete label mapping. What changes. Exact-answer matching is appropriate for constrained outputs such as labels and short reference answers. Normalize case and whitespace only; do not remove facts or punctuation to inflate a score. Require one prediction per labeled item and reject unknown ids. Missing predictions count as incorrect in the denominator. The coverage metric reveals how much of the dataset was actually attempted. Work through one concrete case. With ten labels, six correct predictions, two wrong predictions and two missing predictions, accuracy is6/10 and coverage is8/10. Dividing by eight would reward a system for avoiding difficult cases. Implement the contract. Implement accuracy against the stated contract. Normalize only case and repeated whitespace for this task. Keep punctuation and facts intact. Reject prediction ids absent from the expected label map. Investigate the failure boundary. Record only one easy correct answer from a ten-case dataset. Predict accuracy 0.1 and coverage 0.1 before running the scorer. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_02.py (24 lines) Copy Step 3 · Measure confidence calibration Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Compute fixed-width bin ECE weighted by bin count, retaining per-bin evidence. What changes. A model that is wrong with 99 percent confidence is more dangerous to an automated router than a model that admits uncertainty. Expected calibration error groups predictions by confidence and compares average confidence with actual correctness. ECE depends on bin choice and sample count. Report every nonempty bin, its size, and its gap. A tiny sample or an apparently low ECE does not establish calibrated probabilities on new tasks. Work through one concrete case. Four predictions at confidence 0.9 contain three correct answers. Their observed accuracy is0.75 and their single-bin gap is0.15. A second bin with one confident wrong answer must be weighted by one sample, not equally with the four-sample bin. Implement the contract. Implement calibration against the stated contract. Place confidence 1.0 in the final bin with min(index,bins-1). Report nonempty bin counts beside ECE so the average cannot conceal tiny evidence. Investigate the failure boundary. Split the same records into five and ten bins. Explain why the ECE changes even though the model answers did not. Try each one before you open the solutions. Why keep per-bin evidence instead of just the ECE number? Two runs of the same model give 0.67 and 0.70 accuracy on 30 questions. Is that a difference? How would you compare two models fairly on latency? Solutions Solution Per-bin evidence One number hides where the problem is. A model can be well calibrated at low confidence and badly over-confident at 0.9, which is exactly where an automated router trusts it most. The bins show that. a2030: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Log Volume Reduction Lesson 20.30 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Parse and bound log records Group repeated templates with source locators Compare sampling policies on rare events Export compact context and coverage Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 2 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Rust, Python. In plain words first The idea in one line Shrink a noisy log stream while keeping evidence of rare failures. The problem In plain words first Logs are cheap to write and expensive to keep and to read. A common fix is sampling: keep one line in ten. It works for the noise and fails for the one line that mattered, because the rare "disk full" error is exactly the line a uniform sample is likely to drop. This project compares two ways of shrinking a log. Rust parses lines into located records and groups repeated messages into templates (numbers replaced by a placeholder). Two samplers spend the same budget: uniform sampling picks evenly spaced lines, rarity sampling keeps one example of every template first. Python then checks which rare templates survived. Help an engineer build compact log context for an assistant. Learn bounded template grouping, counts and representative examples, then compare uniform and rarity-aware sampling on authored failure fixtures. Export compressed JSONL and a coverage report showing which important events were lost. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Rust, Python implementations are exercised by the grader. What you will build: Compact log context JSONL and rare-event coverage comparison Step 1 · Parse and bound log records Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Rust Turn each line into a validated, located record. What you build. Rust parses a UTF-8 file with one LEVEL, tab and message per line. Levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR. Preserve the one-based source line. The bounded contract accepts at most one MiB, 10,000 records and 4096 bytes per line. Worked example. WARN retry request 42 after 50ms becomes line 1, level WARN, original message, and template retry request # after #ms . Only ASCII digit runs are replaced; non-ASCII text remains intact. Implement the contract. parse_logs(&str) -> Result<Vec<Record>,String> ; Record{line:usize,level:String,message:String,template:String} . template(&str)->String replaces maximal ASCII digit runs with #. Reject blank messages, invalid severity and control characters. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.rs (33 lines) Copy Step 2 · Group repeated templates with source locators Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · Rust Count repetition without discarding its source range. What you build. Group by the pair (level, template). A group contains total count, first and last source line, and the first encountered original message. Sorted group keys make serialization stable. Digit normalization is a heuristic, not semantic equivalence. Worked example. The 200-line burst contains 199 WARN retries and one ERROR disk-full message at line 138. Its retry group spans lines 1 through 200. The disk group has firstLine=lastLine=138. Implement the contract. group(&[Record])->Vec<Group> ; Group{level,template,count,first,last,example} . Return groups in lexical level/template order. Source ranges include gaps; they are not a claim that every intervening line belongs to the group. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.rs (34 lines) Copy See it drawn Templates by replacing digits Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Two retries with different request ids collapse into one template, and so do the two "served N requests" lines. The error stays its own template with a count of 1, which is what makes it "rare". Digit replacement is a heuristic: it would also merge "error code 404" and "error code 500" into one template, losing a distinction you might need. Step 3 · Compare sampling policies on rare events Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Rust Spend a fixed record budget on common or rare templates. What you build. Uniform sampling chooses indices floor(i*N/budget). Rarity sampling sorts by template frequency and then source line, selects one representative of each template first, and fills any remaining budget from that sorted order. No random seed or model is needed. Worked example. With 200 records and budget 8, uniform chooses indices 0,25,50,75,100,125,150,175 and misses disk-full at index 137. Rarity selects that one-off template first. Both return at most eight records. Implement the contract. sample(records:&[Record],budget:usize,policy:&str)->Result<Vec<Record>,String> . Policy is exactly uniform or rarity. Zero budget and empty input return an empty vector; a budget beyond the input returns every record once. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.rs (36 lines) Copy Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ With a budget of 8 from 200 lines, uniform sampling keeps lines 0, 25, 50 and so on, whatever they say. ✗ Rarity sampling is always better than uniform sampling. It wins on this fixture; if the rare line happened to fall on a uniform index, both would keep it. One example proves nothing general. ✓ Each retained template keeps its count from the full stream. ✗ Keeping fewer rows always means fewer bytes. One long line can outweigh several short ones; measure bytes separately. Step 4 · Export compact context and coverage Step 4 of 4 · about 2 hours · rust+python Measure which diagnostic templates survive compression. What you build. Rust compact output emits one JSON object per retained template, with counts from the full source stream. Python validates the exported groups against the source and calculates rare-template coverage. The context can be read by any JSONL consumer. Worked example. Uniform output retains one template and represents 199 source records; rareCoverage is 0. Rarity output retains two templates representing all 200 records; rareCoverage is 1. This measures templates, not token savings or causal understanding. Implement the contract. Rust compact(&[Record],&[Record])->String ; JSONL fields schemaVersion,level,template,count,firstLine,lastLine,example . Python coverage(source:str,compact:str,rare_max:int=2)->dict rejects unknown groups, duplicates, count mismatches and invalid locators. The shipped demo does not run as it stands here (it expects a fixture file the repository does not include), so the recorded run is shown instead. What you should see Copy Reading this output Uniform sampling selected 8 lines, all of the common template: 1 of 2 templates retained, 199 records represented, rare coverage 0.0, and lostRare names the disk-full error. Rarity sampling selected 8 lines including one example of each template: both templates retained, all 200 records represented, rare coverage 1.0. The <tmp> paths are temporary output files; the recording came from the source project's own run. Read the finished code The complete reference, file by file. Open a file to read it; the stages above say which part each function belongs to. Code solution/demo.py (14 lines) Copy Code solution/main.py (45 lines) Copy Code solution/main.rs (175 lines) Copy Break it on purpose An on-call engineer searches the sampled logs for the 03:12 outage and finds only "served N requests" lines. The full logs, deleted after a week, had a single "connection pool exhausted" error at 03:11. What would rarity sampling have kept, and what would it still have lost? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this project Parse lines into located, bounded records. Group by (level, template) and keep counts and first and last lines. Uniform sampling spends the budget on common lines; rarity sampling keeps one of each template first. Measure rare-template coverage, and bytes separately. One fixture shows a mechanism, not a general winner. Build it on your machine Each step above is meant to be built, not only read. The source repository ships a starter and the checks for every step, and its test runner grades your own folder step by step: Copy Write the step, run its checks, then move to the next step. The checks for each step are also shown above, under that step, so you can see what is expected before you start. Exercises Try a Unicode digit. Explain why a wider numeric normalization might merge identifiers unexpectedly. (step 1) Create two different messages that collapse to the same digit template and discuss the diagnostic evidence this loses. (step 2) Move the rare event onto a uniform index. The demonstration advantage should disappear for this fixture, which illustrates why one example cannot establish universal superiority. (step 3) Change rare_max and compare recall. Add a byte-size metric separately; a long example can make fewer rows larger than expected. Rust collections and Python JSON . (step 4) Solutions Solution Unicode digits Python's \d matches digits from other scripts (Arabic-Indic, Devanagari). A wider rule might merge identifiers that differ only in such digits, or treat a version string as a number. Decide which digits count and test both kinds. Solution Two messages, one template "user 12 deleted file 7" and "user 7 deleted file 12" both become "user deleted file ". The template keeps one example message and a count, so who deleted what is lost unless you keep the original lines. Solution Rare event on a uniform index Put the error at line 0 or 25. Uniform sampling now keeps it too, and both policies report coverage 1.0. The fixture's result depended on where the rare line sat. Solution Changing rare_max A larger rare_max counts more templates as rare, so coverage is computed over more templates and may drop if the budget is too small to keep them all. Report the byte size of the output beside the row count, because one long message can make a "smaller" output larger. Solution B1 · The missing error Rarity sampling would have kept one example of the "connection pool exhausted" template, with its count and source line, so the search would have found it. It would still have lost the other lines around it (what led up to the error), which is why keeping context windows around rare events is a common next step. a2031: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Turning Meeting Notes into Action Items Lesson 20.31 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Parse explicit action records with line provenance Validate owners and calendar dates Deduplicate exact commitments without losing citations Publish an escaped HTML checklist and summary Before you start Needs : Python 3.10+, line-oriented parsing, dictionaries, ISO dates, escaping and JSON files Type : Project, level 2 (Builder). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Python. Why: The standard library makes parsing, scoring, and failure handling visible without hiding the mechanism behind a framework. In plain words first The idea in one line A source-linked commitment inbox whose export requires an explicit review decision. The problem In plain words first After a meeting, someone writes "Alex to publish release notes by Friday" and the rest of the notes are prose. Turning that into a task list is where assistants invent things: an owner from a name mentioned nearby, a date from "next week", a commitment from a suggestion. This project starts strictly. Only lines in an explicit format, ACTION owner | date | task , become actions, each with its line number. Missing owners and impossible dates become visible review flags instead of crashes or guesses. Exact duplicates merge but keep every source line. Prose that looks like a commitment can be proposed, but is labelled as a proposal. Nothing is exported until a person decides. A source-linked commitment inbox whose export requires an explicit review decision. Python 3.10+; line-oriented parsing, dictionaries, ISO dates, escaping and JSON files. The core uses standard libraries. The grader checks your selected workspace; it never fills in missing behavior from the reference. Where it stops: Use the schema_version1 actions.json receipt with stable action ids and original source lines. CSV columns are id, owner, due and task, and contain approved actions only. Step 1 · Parse explicit action records with line provenance Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Python Parse ACTION lines, keep source line numbers, and reject malformed marked lines. What changes. Natural meeting prose contains suggestions, decisions, and commitments. Start with an explicit format: ACTION owner | YYYY-MM-DD | task. The problem In plain words first "Rewrite this in plain language" is a common request to a model, and a risky one: a shorter sentence can drop a number, change it, or lose the definition of a term the reader needs. This project builds a rewrite desk where every change is checked against what must not change. It splits the text into paragraphs and records the facts in each (numbers, protected terms). It produces a candidate rewrite per paragraph and says where the candidate came from (a recorded model proposal, or visible phrase substitutions). It compares readability and facts, flagging changed numbers and missing definitions. Only proposals a person accepts are applied; everything else keeps the original text. Help a technical author revise dense prose using visible sentence and vocabulary measures, protected terms and an optional real rewriting provider. Compare original and proposed paragraphs, surface changed numbers and missing definitions, and export only the author's accepted revisions with a Markdown change record. In plain words first The idea in one line Turn a question and a pile of documents into a report where every sentence can be checked. The problem In plain words first A research agent takes a question, searches documents, and writes a report. The failure everyone has seen is a fluent report whose citations do not support its sentences. This project builds an agent where every sentence is checked. It uses three languages, each for what it does well: a BM25 search engine in Rust, the pipeline in Python, and a report viewer in TypeScript. The pipeline splits the question into facets, extracts exact sentences as citable snippets, writes only from those snippets, has a critic check every sentence against its cited snippet and drop unsupported ones, and publishes a report with a machine-readable trace. A final step scores the agent on public test questions. Level 2, Builder. About 20 hours. Rust, Python and TypeScript standard libraries. Runs offline. Requires Python 3.10+, rustc and Node 22.18+. Turn a question and a folder of documents into a report where every sentence can be checked. You build the pipeline that deep research tools run: search, snippet extraction, planning, cited writing, claim verification, publishing and evaluation. Rust owns ranking, Python owns evidence and orchestration, and TypeScript owns publication. Both language boundaries use inspectable JSON. The replay model keeps tests deterministic; a live model is optional. What you will build: An evidence ledger for technical decisions showing how source updates change published claims. Where it stops: Prepare a technical decision memo whose claims link to the supporting source passages. Compare reports after source documents change and inspect which claims need revision. Step 1 · Search the corpus Step 1 of 7 · about 5 hours · rust+python Retrieval decides which evidence the rest of the system can use. What you build. Implement search/main.rs : a standard-library-only Rust engine that loads markdown documents, builds a BM25 index and handles one JSON request per line. Python's report_agent/search.py compiles and invokes that engine; it does not implement a second ranking algorithm. Rust fits the indexing work because ownership makes the index lifetime explicit and native loops handle term counts efficiently. Python remains a small orchestration layer. A language boundary is useful only when both sides have a clear contract and tests that exercise the real process. Parse the corpus. Each document starts with three header lines, a blank line and original explanatory text: Copy The fixture corpus contains 12 original notes on isolation concepts. Source links identify supporting official specifications or documentation; these notes are teaching fixtures, not copied product documentation. Missing header fields are errors. Keep the body separate from metadata, and sort file paths before loading them so tests do not depend on directory enumeration order. Build the index. Tokenize the title and body, lowercase ASCII letters, keep digits, and remove the provided stopwords. Count how often each term occurs in each document and in how many documents it occurs. Document frequency counts documents, not occurrences. Copy With k1=1.5 , repeating a word helps less as its frequency grows. With b=0.75 , long documents receive a length correction. A rare term such as interceptor contributes more than kernel . Sum the contribution of query terms and sort by descending score, then ascending document id. An empty query or an unknown word returns no results. Define the process contract. A request has an operation and typed fields. The engine flushes each response line and exits when stdin reaches EOF. It writes diagnostics to stderr so stdout remains parseable JSON. Copy Copy The second request returns exactly {"tokens":["kernel","vm"]} . The protocol also supports idf , docs , doc and score . Invalid JSON or wrong field types return an error object. The supplied codec handles strings and escapes according to RFC 8259 , including Unicode surrogate pairs. A fractional result limit is invalid; zero is a valid empty result request. Implement engine_binary() to return a pathlib.Path to the compiled executable named search . Compile once per process in a fresh private temporary directory with the prefix rra-private-build- and mode 0700 ; reuse that path within the process and register cleanup on exit. Never trust a predictable shared executable cache. Each index writes its input documents to a private temporary directory. Use an argument list with subprocess.run , a timeout, and explicit return-code checks. Never put a question into a shell command. Your task. A finished sentence looks like this: Copy Why it matters. The most common failure in generated reports is a fluent sentence with no source, or a source attached to a sentence it does not support. The fix is structural, not a better prompt: define a citation format, then reject any output that breaks it. Strong report systems enforce grounding in code, for example by making the writer work only from extracted, numbered evidence. Weak ones ask the model nicely and hope. (step 7) Solutions Solution Term and document frequency Term frequency counts occurrences inside one document, so repeats raise it. Document frequency counts how many documents contain the term at all; a document counts once however often the term appears in it. Solution An edited source If text is inserted before the snippet's start offset, the stored offsets now point at the wrong characters. Store the document's hash with each snippet, and re-extract (or mark the snippet stale) when the hash changes. Solution A failed live model The trace must say a live model was attempted and failed, and whether the run fell back to the offline planner. Labelling it "verified offline run" would misreport what actually produced the report. Solution Run-local ids S1 is a display label assigned in order within one run. Another run with different search results assigns S1 to whatever snippet comes first. Compare runs by document and offsets, not by display id. Solution Before acting on a recommendation An independent check outside the corpus: a test deployment, a second source, or a person with the domain knowledge. Lexical support shows the sentence matches its snippet, not that the snippet is right for your situation. Solution Changed claim or changed evidence Compare both the sentence text and the cited snippet's hash between runs. Same words with a different snippet hash means the evidence changed under an unchanged claim, which needs a fresh look. Solution Generalizing beyond the fixtures Held-out questions and documents the agent was never tuned on, scored with the same metrics, with enough items that a few questions do not decide the result. Solution B1 · Citations that do not support Step 5, the critic: it scores each sentence against its cited snippet and drops (and records) sentences without support. Step 4's rule, that the writer arranges only snippet text, prevents most of them in the first place. In plain words first The idea in one line Measure ranking quality with precision, recall, reciprocal rank, and discounted gain while exposing duplicates and missing judgments. The problem In plain words first You change a search system and the average score goes up. Ship it? It validates rankings and graded judgments (how useful each document is for each query), computes precision and recall at a cutoff, rewards useful results near the top with reciprocal rank and NDCG, and compares two systems query by query, listing which documents moved. In plain words first The idea in one line Remove bounded sensitive-text patterns before records enter a model pipeline. The problem In plain words first Before support tickets or notes go to a model, emails, IP addresses and internal case numbers should come out. A redaction step sounds simple: find them and replace them. The details are where data leaks: two matches that overlap, a receipt that stores the very value it removed, offsets that drift after the first replacement. This project builds a bounded redaction gate. It detects a small, stated set of patterns (emails, valid IPv4 addresses, literal strings you supply) as character spans, merges overlapping spans into one, replaces each with [REDACTED] using offsets from the original text, and writes a receipt that records where and what kind, but never the value. In plain words first The idea in one line Find a service's owner and runbook with evidence for every answer. The problem In plain words first An alert fires on a file path at 2 a.m. Who owns that code, and where is the runbook? The problem In plain words first Translating subtitles is not just translating sentences. The problem In plain words first An agent that runs many model calls needs a budget it cannot overrun. Adding up children's durations double-counts steps that ran in parallel. And a step that retried after an error can burn tokens without changing the total time at all. This project builds a trace debugger. It reads spans (named steps with start, end, parent, tokens and status) from a JSONL file, validates the parent tree, computes each span's own time by subtracting the union of its children's intervals, and renders a timeline plus a before-and-after comparison of time, tokens and errors. In plain words first The idea in one line A static inspector that reads ELF, PE/COFF, and Mach-O files you compiled and reports their layout, names, links, and function starts. The problem In plain words first An executable file is not a mystery box; it has a documented layout. Linux uses ELF, Windows uses PE/COFF, macOS uses Mach-O, and each says where the code is, which parts are writable, which functions it calls from shared libraries and where execution starts. This project builds a static inspector for all three, written defensively because binary files are untrusted input. It is a bridge from phase 13's reverse-engineering lessons to a working tool: read headers; list sections with permissions and entropy; resolve symbols and demangle C++ names; read imports, exports, relocations and macOS chained fixups; recover strings and function starts even from stripped binaries; and publish a JSON report, an HTML byte map and a diff between two builds. A static inspector that reads ELF, PE/COFF, and Mach-O files you compiled and reports their layout, names, links, and function starts. You give it an ELF64 object, a COFF object, a PE32+ image, or a Mach-O 64 file. It reports the format, the architecture, and the sections and segments with permissions and entropy. It also reports symbols with demangled C++ names, imports, exports, relocations, Mach-O chained fixups, strings with their section, and function starts. With the unstripped build of the same source, it scores each function start method with precision and recall. It writes a JSON report, a standalone HTML report with a byte map, and a diff between two builds. Python 3.10 or later and the standard library only. The grader also uses Python. The fixtures are already built, so you need clang only to rebuild them. Where it stops: Check the contents of a build before a release: which sections are writable and executable, which libraries it imports, and which names strip removed. Compare two builds of your own program and see which sections grew, which symbols moved, and which strings changed. Step 1 · Detect the format and parse the header Step 1 of 6 · about 1.5 hours · Python Read the magic bytes and identify ELF64, a COFF object, a PE32+ image, or Mach-O 64. Parse the file header of each into one shape: format, architecture, kind, entry point, and the raw fields. Read the Mach-O load commands in sequence. Refuse 32-bit, big-endian, universal, and truncated files with a FormatError that names the reason. Read the project README first. This stage applies the ELF header reader of lesson 32 . It adds COFF, PE32+, and Mach-O with the tables of lesson 40 . What you build. You write three functions in the formats module: detect_format(data) reads the first bytes and returns "elf64" , "coff" , "pe" , or "macho64" . parse_header(data) returns one dictionary shape for all four formats. load_commands(data) returns the Mach-O load commands in file order. Every later stage calls parse_header first. If the header is wrong, every section, symbol, and fixup after it is wrong too. Why it matters. A file extension does not identify a binary. A .o file from clang can be ELF or Mach-O. A .obj file is a COFF object and has no magic number at all. The inspector must decide from the bytes, and it must refuse a file it cannot read correctly. A tool that guesses and continues prints tables that look correct and are not. All four formats in this project are little-endian. The supplied unpack(fmt, data, offset) helper reads one record with struct.unpack_from and raises FormatError when the record runs past the end of the file. Use it for every read, so a truncated file always fails with a message that names the offset. Work through one concrete case. The first 32 bytes of the stripped arm64 build are: Copy Read them as eight little-endian 32-bit fields ( <IiiIIIII ): Field Bytes Value Meaning magic cf fa ed fe 0xfeedfacf Mach-O 64, little-endian cputype 0c 00 00 01 0x0100000c arm64 ( CPU_TYPE_ARM with the 64-bit flag) filetype 02 00 00 00 2 MH_EXECUTE , so kind is "executable" ncmds 12 00 00 00 18 18 load commands follow sizeofcmds a8 05 00 00 1448 they occupy bytes 32 to 1480 flags 85 00 20 00 0x00200085 MH_NOUNDEFS , MH_DYLDLINK , MH_TWOLEVEL , MH_PIE The load commands start at offset 32. Each starts with cmd and cmdsize . The first is LC_SEGMENT_64 ( 0x19 ). The next starts at 32 plus its cmdsize . One of the 18 is LC_MAIN ( 0x80000028 ), whose entryoff is 0x5e8 . The __TEXT segment starts at virtual address 0x100000000 , so the entry point is 0x1000005e8 . That is the address of _main in the unstripped build. The other formats follow the same pattern: ELF: 7f 45 4c 46 , then EI_CLASS 2 (64-bit) and EI_DATA 1 (little-endian). e_type 1 is relocatable. e_machine 62 ( 0x3e ) is x86-64. The tally object has e_shnum 13 and e_shstrndx 1. COFF object: no magic. Bytes 64 86 are machine 0x8664 , then 0a 00 is 10 sections. SizeOfOptionalHeader is 0, which is what makes it an object. PE image: MZ at offset 0, e_lfanew at 0x3c is 0x40 , and PE\0\0 is at 0x40 . The optional header starts at 0x58 with magic 0x20b (PE32+). Return "elf64" . MZ : read e_lfanew at 0x3c and require PE\0\0 there. Return "pe" . 0xfeedfacf read as a little-endian word: return "macho64" . Raise for 0xfeedface ("32-bit") and for ca fe ba be ("universal"). Otherwise, if the first 20 bytes parse as a COFF file header with a machine in COFF_MACHINES , SizeOfOptionalHeader 0, and 1 to 96 sections, return "coff" .
