This stage uses the section header table from lesson 32 and the segment and section tables of the three formats from lesson 40 . What you build. You write five functions in the layout module: shannon_entropy(data) returns bits per byte, rounded to 4 decimal places. sections(data) lists every section with a permission string and the entropy of its bytes. segments(data) lists ELF program headers and Mach-O segments. section_at_offset(section_list, offset) and section_at_address(section_list, address) find the owner of a file offset or a virtual address. Stages 4, 5, and 6 use them. Why it matters. Sections tell you what the link editor made. Segments tell you what the loader maps and with which permissions. A section that is writable and executable, or a data section with entropy near 8, is a fact a reviewer must see before a release. Entropy measures how evenly the byte values spread. The maximum is 8 bits per byte, when all 256 values occur equally often, and zero padding is 0. In the fixtures, the code sections measure from 5.5 to 5.9 and the string sections from 4.0 to 4.7. The padding between segments measures 0.0. Compressed or encrypted data comes close to 8. Each format stores permissions in a different place: Format Where Bits ELF section sh_flags SHF_WRITE 0x1 , SHF_ALLOC 0x2 , SHF_EXECINSTR 0x4 ELF segment p_flags PF_X 0x1 , PF_W 0x2 , PF_R 0x4 COFF and PE section Characteristics MEM_EXECUTE 0x20000000 , MEM_READ 0x40000000 , MEM_WRITE 0x80000000 Mach-O segment initprot , maxprot VM_PROT_READ 1 , VM_PROT_WRITE 2 , VM_PROT_EXECUTE 4 An ELF section without SHF_ALLOC is not loaded, so its string is "---" . A Mach-O section has no permission bits of its own. It takes initprot of the segment with the same name. In a Mach-O object the only segment has an empty name, so use the instruction attributes ( 0x80000400 ) for "r-x" and the table MACHO_SEGMENT_PERMS for the rest. Work through one concrete case. Its size is 4, but it holds no bytes in the file. So file_size is 0 and its entropy is 0.0. Now compute entropy for the 15-byte string tally report v3 . On the arm64 executable, __TEXT,__text is 768 bytes with entropy 5.8595, __TEXT,__cstring is 4.6413, and __DATA,__common is zerofill with file_size 0. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_02.py (135 lines) Copy See it drawn Entropy in bits per byte Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Entropy measures how unpredictable the bytes are, from 0 (all identical) to 8 (every byte value equally likely). Zero padding scores 0, this repetitive text about 3, and random bytes about 7.2: close to the maximum of 8, which only very long random inputs reach, since 256 bytes cannot contain all 256 values evenly. Compiled code usually lands around 5 to 6.5, and compressed or encrypted data near 8, which is why a high-entropy section in an ordinary program is worth a second look. You write three functions in the symbols module: read_cstring(data, offset, end=None) reads one NUL-terminated name and refuses a name that has no terminator before end . demangle(name) turns a supported Itanium C++ name into its source form, or returns None . symbols(data) returns every symbol of the file in one shape. Why it matters. Symbols are the names a reviewer reads first: which functions a build defines, which ones it needs from elsewhere, and what strip removed. All three formats store names as offsets into a string table. A name offset that points outside its table is the most common corruption in a damaged file. A reader that does not check it prints text from some other table. Why it matters. The bytes of a call or a pointer in an object file are often zero. The relocation record says what the link editor writes there. In a linked image, the loader fills import slots before the program runs. On current macOS, the fixup information sits inside the pointer slots themselves, as chained 64-bit words. A disassembler that reads one of those slots without decoding it reports a pointer to an address that does not exist. Lesson 20.40 opens with that exact mistake. Solutions Solution Refusing unsupported formats Parsing them with assumptions made for little-endian 64-bit files would produce plausible but wrong numbers. A clear refusal tells the user what to do (extract one architecture first) instead of misleading them. Solution Prologues at -O2 Optimizing compilers skip frame setup in small leaf functions and interleave instructions, so the familiar "save registers, set frame pointer" pattern is often missing. At -O0 nearly every function has it. Solution A new dependency New imports (library and symbol names), likely growth in __text and __stubs , new strings, and new function starts, each listed in the diff with sizes. Solution B1 · An unchecked size Python would silently return a short slice (or a huge allocation in other languages), and later code would misread it as the section's content. a2049: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Exploring Decision Tradeoffs Lesson 20.49 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Declare options and evidence Compute comparable scores Explore sensitivity and dominance Export the chosen scenario Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 3 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : TypeScript. In plain words first The idea in one line Show when a different priority changes the preferred option. The problem In plain words first A weighted scoring table ("accessibility 50 %, setup time 30 %, visitor flow 20 %") makes a decision look objective. It can hide three things: an option whose data is missing, a hard limit one option breaks, and how close the result is, so that a small change in priorities flips the winner. This project builds a decision board that shows all three. Options and criteria are declared with fixed ranges and a source note for every value. Scores are normalized honestly, with missing values and broken limits making an option ineligible rather than quietly scoring zero. A sensitivity sweep shows when changing one weight reverses the ranking. The board exports the chosen scenario as a reusable decision record. Help a community team compare practical project options using a user-supplied criteria table and supporting notes. Apply explicit constraints, weighted scores and sensitivity analysis, keep missing values visible, and export an interactive HTML decision board and a reusable decision record. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. TypeScript implementations are exercised by the grader. What you will build: An interactive tradeoff board, criteria.csv and decision-record.json Step 1 · Declare options and evidence Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript Make ranges, constraints and uncertainty explicit. What you build. Create a table of criteria and options. Every criterion declares a fixed min/max range, cost or benefit direction and a nonnegative weight. Every option supplies a numeric value or null plus a source note for every criterion. Null means not measured, never zero. Worked example. Open gallery has access 9, setup 8 and flow 8. Exhibition pods has 6,2,7. The archive layout has unknown flow and stays visible but ineligible. All three fixtures are authored teaching data. Implement the contract. parse(text:string):Decision . Criteria: {id,label,weight,direction,min,max,limit?} . Options: {id,label,values:{criterion:number|null},notes:{criterion:string}} . Reject duplicate IDs, missing notes, out-of-range numbers, unknown criterion keys and zero or nonfinite total weight and nonfinite range widths. At most 30 criteria, 200 options and one MiB. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.ts (74 lines) Copy Step 2 · Compute comparable scores Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript Normalize units without hiding missing values or hard constraints. What you build. Benefit normalization is (value-min)/(max-min); cost normalization is (max-value)/(max-min). Normalize the active weights to sum to one. A cost limit is a maximum; a benefit limit is a minimum. Any missing value or limit violation makes the aggregate score null. Worked example. Open gallery normalizes to access .9, setup .2, flow .8. At weights .5,.3,.2 the score is .67. Pods scores .68 and ranks first. An unknown archive flow produces null rather than a renormalized score. Implement the contract. normalize(c:Criterion,v:number):number ; score(data,weights={}):Row[] sorted by descending score then ID. A row has {id,label,score,missing,violations,normalized} . Weight overrides are raw nonnegative magnitudes; invalid, overflowed or all-zero weights throw. Read weight overrides only from own properties; criterion IDs such as constructor are valid data. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.ts (80 lines) Copy Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ For a cost criterion such as setup hours, a lower value normalizes to a higher score. ✗ An option with a missing value can be scored as 0 on that criterion. That penalizes "unknown" as if it were "worst"; the option is ineligible until measured. ✓ Ranges are fixed in advance, so adding an irrelevant option cannot change the others' scores. ✗ A higher weighted score means the option is objectively better. In plain words first The idea in one line Turn workload events into a timeline with the exact objects behind each clue. The problem In plain words first When a Kubernetes rollout goes wrong, the clues are events: "Failed", "BackOff", "Started", repeated dozens of times across pods with generated names. Reading raw event lists is slow, and asking an assistant to read them risks leaking configuration and drawing conclusions from event reasons alone. This project turns exported events and workloads into a timeline. Go parses the export while keeping when each event happened separate from when the export was taken, merges repeated snapshots of the same event, connects each event to the workload revision that produced the pod by following owner references (never by guessing from names), and exports a redacted context pack. TypeScript renders the timeline from that pack. Help an on-call engineer inspect exported Kubernetes events and workload snapshots. Group repeated events, distinguish observation time from occurrence time, and link each suggested investigation to object identity and rollout revision. Export an HTML timeline and a redacted JSON context pack for an assistant. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go, TypeScript implementations are exercised by the grader. a2052: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects An LLM Gateway with Fallbacks Lesson 20.52 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Validate provider endpoints Classify failures without retrying everything Send one bounded HTTP request Route with a total-attempt budget Before you start Needs : Structured outputs Type : Project, level 3 (Engineer). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Route a bounded request through providers with explicit failure semantics. The problem In plain words first Calling one model provider is a single point of failure. A gateway that falls back to a second provider helps, if it knows when to fall back. Retrying a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx) on another provider makes sense. Retrying a malformed request (400) everywhere just multiplies the failure. Following a redirect could send your API key somewhere you never configured. This project builds a small HTTP gateway in Go with explicit failure rules: validated provider URLs, a status classifier with three outcomes, one bounded attempt (size and time limits, no redirects), and a router that walks providers in order under a total attempt budget and one overall deadline, keeping each provider's credentials to itself. Build a local non-streaming HTTP proxy with real provider fallback, per-provider environment credentials, response limits, and one overall deadline. Verify the complete wire path with loopback servers. Go 1.22 or later, standard library only. Four stages, about eight hours. You need structs, slices, callbacks, errors and basic JSON; the stage prerequisites link to the relevant curriculum. Start with the offline example before connecting a provider. Where it stops: Connect an existing chat-completions client to a local fallback endpoint Trace provider outages without forwarding caller credentials Step 1 · Validate provider endpoints Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Treat the provider list as trusted configuration. What you build. Implement Endpoints(values) before opening a connection. Allow HTTPS, plus HTTP on exactly localhost , 127.0.0.1 or ::1 for local services. Reject userinfo, fragments, queries, line breaks, missing hosts and other schemes. Remove exact duplicates while preserving provider order. In plain words first The idea in one line Build a content-addressed document index with deletion tracking, version checks, and freshness-aware retrieval. The problem In plain words first A RAG system answers from an index of documents. a2057: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Retry Storms: a Lab Lesson 20.57 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Model concurrent failures with a deterministic clock Compare bounded backoff and jitter Enforce shared retry budgets and server delays Replay against a local HTTP service Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 3 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go, TypeScript. In plain words first The idea in one line Watch many reasonable retries combine into an overloaded service. The problem In plain words first One client retrying a failed request is sensible. Twenty clients retrying the same overloaded service at the same moment is a retry storm: each retry adds load exactly when the service can least take it, and a short outage turns into a long one. This project makes the storm visible. A deterministic replay simulates many clients against a failing service on a virtual clock. Bounded exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries out. A shared retry budget caps the total number of retries across clients, and server hints such as Retry-After are honoured. Finally the same policy runs against a local HTTP service, and the counters are checked independently. Help SDK authors choose retry behavior when many clients fail together. Replay concurrent clients against a deterministic service model, compare bounded backoff and jitter with a shared retry budget, then run the same policy against a local HTTP fixture. Export amplification and recovery timelines with a reusable client policy. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go, TypeScript implementations are exercised by the grader. What you build. Replay clients that all begin at time zero. The service returns 503 before failUntil or when the count at the exact millisecond exceeds capacity. Sort scheduled attempts by time then client ID. Success ends that client. The supplied fixed Delay scaffold supports this stage; richer backoff comes next. Worked example. Three clients, capacity 2 and failUntil=0 produce two initial successes and one 503. With one allowed attempt, the report has three calls and two successes. Initial calls are never counted as retries. Implement the contract. Replay(clients,failUntil,capacity int,p Policy,budget int)(Report,error) . Policy fields are BaseMS, MaxMS, Attempts, Jitter, Seed. Version-1 report has mode, clients, calls, successes, retries and timeline. Limits: 0..1000 clients, 1..10 attempts, positive capacity, nonnegative time and budget. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. What you build. Backoff before retry n starts at BaseMS and doubles until MaxMS. Jitter selects a deterministic integer in [0,cap] from the client, attempt and seed. This arithmetic sequence is an educational reproducibility device, not a cryptographic random generator. Worked example. Base 10 and cap 25 produce 10,20,25,25 without jitter. With jitter enabled, each client can schedule a different delay. A zero delay is valid full jitter and may amplify the same time bucket. Implement the contract. Delay(p Policy,client,attempt int) int , with attempt numbered from 1 for the first retry wait. Mix ((client+1) 1103515245 + attempt 12345 + seed) using uint64: xor with x>>16, multiply by 2246822519, xor with x>>13, then take modulo (cap+1). Validate rejects invalid bounds. With "full jitter" (a random wait between 0 and the backoff), the same 60 retries spread across dozens of windows and the busiest holds only a few. The seed is per client, so the run is reproducible; real conclusions need several seeds, as the exercises say. Step 3 · Enforce shared retry budgets and server delays Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Bound aggregate attempts across clients, not just each individual request. What you build. Add a shared cap on scheduled retries to Replay. A mutex-protected Budget uses Take to admit at most the declared number across live goroutines. Parse Retry-After as nonnegative integer seconds or an HTTP date. A past HTTP date yields zero delay. Worked example. Twenty clients may each allow four attempts, but a shared budget of 12 bounds the simulation at 32 total calls. Admission is deterministic by schedule order in simulation and depends on goroutine order in live mode. Implement the contract. NewBudget(n int)*Budget ; (*Budget).Take()bool ; ServerDelay(value string,now time.Time)(time.Duration,error) . Invalid values fail. A live server delay above MaxMS stops the request rather than retrying earlier than instructed. It limits one process; a fleet needs a shared admission service. In plain words first The idea in one line Reconnect a streamed answer without duplicating text or hiding an incomplete result. The problem In plain words first Chat answers arrive as a stream, token by token. Connections drop. This project builds stream recovery for server-sent events (SSE). It decodes bytes incrementally so characters and events survive any chunk boundary, applies events by stable id so a repeated event changes nothing, reconnects with the id of the last accepted event, keeps a cancelled answer as a draft, and exports a trace that can rebuild the answer exactly. A tool contract specifies required parameters, property types, and validation keywords like enum , minimum , and maximum . A valid call provides the required parameters matching their declared types. The problem In plain words first Agent jobs (write a report, summarize an incident) take time, and workers crash. The problem In plain words first Most requests are fast, but a few are very slow, and in a system that makes many calls, those few dominate how slow it feels. Hedging is a classic remedy: if the first request has not answered after a short delay, send a second copy to another replica and take whichever answers first. It works, and it costs extra requests. This project measures both sides. It summarizes latency with nearest-rank percentiles, launches a duplicate only when the delay expires, lets only a valid response win (a fast error is not a winner), records the losing request even after cancellation, and exports latency and extra work side by side. The problem In plain words first "Run the agent's code in a sandbox" covers a wide ladder of protections: a separate process, a restricted filesystem, a container with its own network rules, a micro virtual machine with its own kernel. a2073: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects An Inbox for Signed Webhooks Lesson 20.73 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Preserve raw bytes and delivery identity Verify signatures and timestamp bounds Deduplicate retries with a durable inbox Replay accepted deliveries with processing receipts Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 4 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Accept a delivery once and retain the evidence needed to replay it safely. The problem In plain words first Services tell each other about events through webhooks: an HTTP POST saying "this report was uploaded". The receiver must check that the POST really came from the sender (a signature), that it is not an old message replayed by someone else (a timestamp window), and that a retry of the same delivery is processed once. And when processing has a bug, you want to replay accepted deliveries later, deliberately, without re-accepting them as new. This project builds such a receiver in Go: it keeps the raw request bytes, verifies an HMAC signature over the delivery id, timestamp and body, stores each accepted delivery durably before acknowledging it, answers retries as duplicates, and replays stored deliveries through an explicit command that writes processing receipts. Help developers feed external events into an agent workflow without losing retries or accepting altered payloads. Verify an authored signature scheme over the raw body, enforce timestamp bounds, and store stable delivery identities before dispatch. Export an HTTP receiver and a replay CLI that distinguishes a transport retry from a new business event. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go implementations are exercised by the grader. What you will build: Local webhook receiver, delivery ledger and explicit replay CLI Step 1 · Preserve raw bytes and delivery identity Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Read the exact authenticated body before decoding business data. What you build. Read POST requests with X-Delivery-ID, X-Timestamp and X-Signature. Preserve raw bytes exactly. JSON whitespace is part of the signed content; decoding then reserializing would alter the authenticated message. Worked example. The fixture body ends with a newline on disk. Signing that file includes its newline. Removing the final byte changes the signature even though the JSON object represents the same data. The transport delivery ID is distinct from business eventId inside the body. Implement the contract. ReadDelivery(*http.Request)(Delivery,error) returns ID, Timestamp, Signature, Body. Require POST, canonical int64 decimal timestamp, ID matching [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}, and 1..65536 raw bytes. JSON validity is a processing-stage concern. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage_test.go (52 lines) Copy Step 2 · Verify signatures and timestamp bounds Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Authenticate identity, timestamp and raw bytes under an explicit teaching scheme. What you build. The authored signature is v1= followed by lowercase HMAC-SHA256 hex over decimalTimestamp + dot + deliveryID + dot + rawBody. The shared secret comes from an environment variable and is never written to the inbox. Verify with hmac.Equal and bound accepted timestamps. Worked example. At now=1770000000 and a 300-second window, now-300 and now+300 are accepted. now-301 is stale. Altering a single body byte or delivery ID fails authentication even inside the time window. Implement the contract. Sign(key []byte,id string,timestamp int64,body []byte)string ; Verify(Delivery,key,now,skew)error . Keys require at least 16 bytes; skew must be 0..1 hour. Receiver uses five minutes. This format is original and not compatible with a named webhook provider. Parsing the JSON and serializing it again produces the same data with different whitespace, and the signature no longer matches. That is why the receiver keeps and verifies the raw bytes before decoding anything. compare_digest compares in constant time, so the check does not leak how many characters matched. Step 3 · Deduplicate retries with a durable inbox Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Persist accepted identity and body before acknowledging delivery. What you build. Write a mode-0600 temporary file, sync its content, and publish it through an atomic no-overwrite hard link. Sync the directory before acknowledging success. Delivery filenames are SHA-256 digests of IDs, preventing path traversal. Existing IDs with identical raw bytes are transport retries; changed bytes are conflicts. Worked example. The first signed delivery returns HTTP 202. The same ID and bytes return 200 without replacing the original acceptedAt. The same ID with a newly valid signature but a different body returns 409. A changed body under the old signature returns 401 before storage. Implement the contract. Accept(dir,id,body,now)(Entry,created,error) ; LoadEntry(dir,id)(Entry,error) . Entry stores schemaVersion, deliveryId, base64 body, sha256 and acceptedAt. ErrConflict identifies reused delivery IDs. Corrupt stored records fail closed. Replay starts a new, explicitly named processing run; transport deduplication is unchanged. Step 4 · Replay accepted deliveries with processing receipts Step 4 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Make a new processing run explicit while keeping transport deduplication intact. What you build. Replay reads only accepted inbox entries. The authored local processor extracts eventId and data from JSON and writes a processing receipt keyed by delivery ID plus explicit run ID. Repeating the same run returns its existing receipt; a different run is a deliberate replay. Worked example. Delivery delivery-1 carries business-42. Replay run review-1 creates one receipt; repeating review-1 creates none. A new delivery-2 may carry business-42 and is a distinct transport identity. Business-level deduplication is a downstream policy. Implement the contract. Replay(dir,id,run,now)(Processing,created,error) ; fields schemaVersion, deliveryId, runId, businessEventId, bodySHA256, processedAt and payload. The first replay under run id review-1 created a processing receipt (with the body's SHA-256, the business event id and the payload); the second replay with the same run id did not ( sameRunCreatedAgain: false ). One receipt in total, and nothing about the transport side changed. Read the finished code The complete reference, file by file. Exercises Send the same JSON with different whitespace and compare its raw SHA-256 digest. Do not use semantic JSON equality at the signature boundary. (step 1) Add a provider adapter only after implementing and testing its published raw-byte signing rules. Do not assume a different service uses this concatenation order. Go HMAC and Go SHA-256 . (step 2) Kill a process between writing and linking. Unlinked .pending files can remain but are never accepted deliveries. This local-filesystem design requires hard-link and fsync support; do not claim equivalent behavior on arbitrary network filesystems. (step 3) Feed receipt.payload to a downstream queue with an idempotency key. External exactly-once effects require a separate transactional design; a local processing receipt cannot establish that guarantee. (step 4) Solutions Solution Whitespace and digests The raw SHA-256 changes with any whitespace change, even though the JSON means the same. Signatures are over bytes, so the receiver must hash and verify the bytes it received, never a re-serialization. Solution Another provider's scheme Each provider defines its own concatenation, header names and encoding. Implement its published rules exactly, with its test vectors, in a separate adapter; reusing this scheme would reject all their real deliveries, or worse, accept forged ones. Solution A crash before linking The .pending file stays on disk, but only linked entries count as accepted deliveries. The sender's retry is then accepted normally. The design relies on hard links and fsync, so it should not be claimed for filesystems without them. Solution Downstream effects Send receipt.payload to the next queue with the run id plus delivery id as the idempotency key. Exactly-once effects in other systems still need those systems to honour the key; a local receipt cannot guarantee it. Solution B1 · Re-serializing before verifying Preserve and verify the raw bytes first. Any change to how JSON is written changes the bytes, so verifying a re-serialization fails legitimate deliveries. a2074: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects A Streaming Agent Shell in Rust Lesson 20.74 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Parse a deliberately small action language Confine file tools to a bounded root Track budgets and terminal state Stream bounded JSON events through real stdin Before you start Needs : Data management , Tool schema design Type : Project, level 4 (Systems). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Rust. In plain words first The idea in one line Build a real stdin/stdout Rust action loop with bounded reads, an explicit command grammar, path containment, and streamed JSON events. The problem In plain words first Coding agents need to look at a repository: list files, read one, search for a string. Giving them a real shell does that and much more, which is the problem. This project builds a tiny observation shell in Rust that any agent can drive over stdin and stdout, and that can do only what it says. It parses a deliberately small command language (help, pwd, list, read, literal search, quit) and rejects everything else, shell syntax included. File tools resolve paths inside one root and refuse anything that escapes it. Every request uses one slot of a budget, and quit is final. Input lines are size-limited before they are read, and every reply is a JSON event with a sequence number and the request's id. An inspectable repository-observation process usable by different coding agents. The Rust process accepts a deliberately small tool language. Its Python adapter accepts JSONL with caller ids and tool arguments, then translates only known commands. No argument becomes an operating-system shell command. Where it stops: JSONL requests use caller ids and explicit tool argument objects. Step 1 · Parse a deliberately small action language Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Rust Define an action enum for help, pwd, list, read, literal search and quit. Unknown commands are rejected, including shell-like instructions. Search separates its pattern and path with a tab so spaces remain valid inside either argument. a2077: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Coordinating a Distributed Eval Farm Lesson 20.77 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Partition stable case identities Fence each shard lease Accept idempotent completion receipts Run a bounded local worker pool Before you start Needs : Go 1.22 or later on Linux or macOS, Python 3.10 or later for the grader, Go structs, pointers, errors and JSON files, Goroutines, channels and context cancellation Type : Project, level 5 (Frontier). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Partition cases, lease shards and aggregate bounded concurrent workers. The problem In plain words first A large evaluation is split across many workers. Some crash mid-run, some are slow and finish after their work was given to someone else. The final score must still count each test case exactly once, from the right result. This project coordinates an evaluation farm in Go. Cases are assigned to shards by a stable hash of their ids, so a restart knows which cases belong where. A shard is leased with a version that survives process death, and a new worker advances that version (fencing) when it takes over. A result is accepted only from the current lease, once. Finally a pool of real worker processes runs the farm, with a crash injected to prove recovery. Turn a file of recorded model predictions into a resumable evaluation run. Separate worker processes acquire persisted shards, compare answers and publish fenced receipts. Kill a worker after its claim, restart the run and prove an old worker cannot overwrite the replacement's result. Go fits the coordinator because the same dependency-free binary can launch child workers, bound concurrency and coordinate filesystem state. This implementation distributes work across processes on one Linux or macOS host. It does not provide a multi-machine transport or perform model inference. Four stages take about 8 hours. Solutions Solution Hashing ids Chunks depend on file order and length: adding or reordering one case moves many others to different shards, which breaks resumption. A hash of each id gives a placement that never changes for that case. Solution A repeatedly failing shard Count attempts per shard and stop retrying after a limit, marking it failed with the last error. Retrying forever hides a case that crashes every worker. Solution Several machines Replace the local file lease with a shared coordinator that supports compare-and-swap (a database row, etcd, or similar), keep the same versioned fencing, and store receipts there too. Solution B1 · Double-counted shard The second result for shard 7: only one receipt per shard is accepted, and only from the current lease version. In plain words first The idea in one line A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset that turns functions in an object you compiled into structured C, then proves the output. The problem In plain words first A decompiler turns machine code back into readable source. Commercial tools do it for whole programs; this project does it for a handful of small C functions compiled to x86-64, entirely from scratch in Python, and then proves its output is right. It is the deepest build in the course and follows phase 13's reverse-engineering lessons step by step: read the ELF object and its relocations; decode the instructions the fixtures use; recover control flow, including a jump table; lift to an intermediate form and SSA; simplify compiler idioms (such as division by a constant done with multiplication); recover the function signature and types; structure the graph into if, while and switch; and finally recompile the emitted C and check it matches the original byte for byte, with relocations masked. A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset. It reads an ELF relocatable object that you compiled, turns each function into structured C, and then proves the output: it recompiles the C, compares relocation-masked bytes, runs the original and the decompiled version side by side over an input grid, and writes an evidence report that lists every unknown. The core uses the Python standard library only. clang is optional: it enables the recompile and differential legs of stage 8. The grader checks your selected workspace; it never fills in missing behavior from the reference. Analyze only programs that you compiled from source. The fixtures are small C functions written for this project. What you will build: A decompiler that turns the functions of an x86-64 relocatable object you compiled into one C file, and an evidence report that says what was proved and what stays unknown. Where it stops: Run python3 -m minidec verify on your own object and its source. The command writes decompiled.c, recompiled.o and report.json; a CI job can fail on status fail or unknown. Step 1 · Read an ELF relocatable object Step 1 of 8 · about 2 hours · Python Validate the ELF64 header, read section headers, the symbol table and every RELA record, and cut each function out of .text with its relocations and its alignment padding. A PC-relative record points at S + A + (end of instruction - P), so a target is resolved only with the end of the instruction that holds the field. Read the project prerequisites first. This stage applies An ELF Binary Reader from Scratch: Program Anatomy and the relocation part of Disassembly and Control Flow . What you build. You build the loader that every later stage reads from. It accepts the bytes of one ELF64 little-endian x86-64 relocatable object ( ET_REL ), and it gives back: the section headers, each with its name and its bytes, the symbol table, with name, value, size, type, binding and section name, every RELA record, grouped by the section it patches and sorted by offset, one function at a time: its bytes, the relocations inside it, and the alignment padding after it. It also resolves a relocation to the place it points at after linking. Why it matters. A relocatable object is the output of clang -c . The link editor has not run yet, so every address that refers to another section is a field of zero bytes plus a RELA record. The jump table of band , the lookup table at -O1 , and every call to another function are visible only through those records. If the loader drops them, stage 3 cannot find the jump table, stage 7 cannot name the lookup table, and stage 8 compares bytes that the link editor will overwrite. A function symbol gives the start and the size. The bytes between the end of one function and the start of the next are alignment padding. Stage 3 decodes the padding with a linear sweep to show where the sweep and the recursive descent disagree, so the loader reports it separately. Work through one concrete case. Build the fixture yourself, or use the committed objects. The objects were built with: Copy The header of samples-x86_64-O1.o starts with 7f 45 4c 46 02 01 : the magic, ELFCLASS64 (2) and little-endian (1). At offset 16, e_type is 1 ( ET_REL ) and e_machine is 62 ( EM_X86_64 ). The section header table is at e_shoff , each entry is 64 bytes, and the first five section names are the empty null section, .strtab , .text , .rela.text and .rodata . .text is 0xb2 bytes long. The five function symbols, in address order, with their sizes: name value size next start padding tenths_and_fifths 0x0 0x23 0x30 13 thirds 0x30 0x1a 0x50 6 band 0x50 0x17 0x70 9 fold 0x70 0x26 0xa0 10 record 0xa0 0x12 0xb2 0 band holds one relocation. The record in .rela.text has r_offset 0x5f, type 2 ( R_X86_64_PC32 ), the .rodata section symbol, and addend -4. Inside the function the offset is 0x5f - 0x50 = 0xf. The field belongs to leaq (%rip), %rcx , which starts at 0x5c and ends at 0x63. The psABI says the link editor stores S + A - P in a PC-relative field, where S is the symbol value, A is the addend and P is the field address. The processor adds the field to the address of the next instruction. So the operand reaches: Copy The table starts at .rodata+0x0 . Its first eight bytes are 05 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 : the values 5 and 8 of the switch in band . At -O0 , .rodata itself has six relocations, one per jump table entry. Each is a PC-relative record against .text whose target, resolved with the table base as the end, is 0x78, 0x81, 0x8a, 0x93, 0x9c and 0xa5. These are the six case blocks of band . Change the addend, the field offset and the instruction length in the lab. The target moves by the same amount as the distance from the field to the end of the instruction, which is why relocation_target refuses a PC-relative record without that end. Implement the contract. Read every section header; SHT_NOBITS has no bytes. Name sections from e_shstrndx . Then set self.symbols and self.relocations . Any table outside the file raises ElfError . ElfObject._read_symbols() -> list[Symbol] Every 24-byte Elf64_Sym of every SHT_SYMTAB , named through the string table at sh_link . Type is st_info & 0xf , binding is st_info >> 4 . ElfObject._read_relocations() -> dict[str, list[Relocation]] Every 24-byte Elf64_Rela of every SHT_RELA , keyed by the name of section sh_info , sorted by offset. A symbol index past the table raises ElfError . ElfObject.function_extent(name, section=".text") -> (start, end, padding_end) From the function symbol: start is the value, end is start + size , padding_end is the next function start or the section size. Unknown names raise ElfError . ElfObject.function(name, section=".text") -> FunctionBytes The bytes in [start, end) and the relocations inside that range, with offsets relative to start . relocation_target(relocation, field_end=None) -> Target Absolute: S + A . PC-relative ( R_X86_64_PC32 , R_X86_64_PLT32 ): S + A + (field_end - P) . A PC-relative record with no field_end raises ValueError . A section symbol has S = 0. The CLI is supplied. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_01.py (115 lines) Copy Step 2 · Decode the x86-64 subset Step 2 of 8 · about 3 hours · Python Decode legacy prefixes, REX, one and two byte opcodes, ModRM, SIB, displacements and immediates for the instructions the fixtures use. Record where the displacement and immediate fields sit so relocations can be matched to operands. Every instruction must agree with the captured disassembler listing by address, bytes and AT&T text. This stage applies Disassembly and Control Flow , sections "The Instruction Format Has One Rule Per Field" and "Linear Sweep". What you build. You build a decoder for the part of x86-64 that clang emits for the fixtures at -O0 and -O1 . decode(code, address) reads one instruction and returns an Instruction with its bytes, a normalized operation, its operands, its operand width, its control-flow kind and its branch target. It also records where the displacement field and the immediate field sit inside the instruction. linear_sweep decodes a byte range in address order and lists every byte that it cannot decode. The decoder is checked against a disassembler listing. For every instruction of the four committed objects, your address, your bytes and your AT&T text must equal the captured listing. Why it matters. Every later stage trusts the decoder. A wrong operand width changes a 32-bit value into a 64-bit value, and the recompiled C then differs from the original. A wrong field offset makes stage 3 miss the relocation on the lea that holds the jump table base. The listing gives you an oracle with no judgment in it. You do not decide that your decode looks right. You compare it. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_02.py (144 lines) Copy Step 3 · Recover control flow Step 3 of 8 · about 2 hours · Python Follow control flow by recursive descent, resolve the position-independent jump table from its relocations and bounds check, split basic blocks, then compute dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops. An indirect jump with no matching idiom stays unresolved and is reported. This stage applies Disassembly and Control Flow , sections "Recursive Descent", "Basic Blocks", "Dominators With the Iterative Algorithm" and "The Jump Table in grade at -O0", and Compiler Idioms and Optimization for the bounds-check idiom. What you build. You build the control-flow graph of one function: recursive_descent decodes only the bytes that control flow reaches from the entry. A jump table resolver turns jmpq *%rax into a list of targets, with the table found through its relocation and its length taken from the bounds check. ControlFlowGraph splits the instructions into basic blocks with typed edges: jump , taken , fallthrough and table . The graph computes reverse postorder, immediate dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops. Why it matters. A linear sweep decodes alignment padding as if it were code. Recursive descent decodes only what can run, but it stops at an indirect jump unless something tells it where the jump goes. For the fixtures that something is the relocation on the lea that loads the table base and the relocations inside the table. Dominators are the input of everything after this stage. SSA places phis on dominance frontiers (stage 4). A back edge is an edge to a block that dominates its source, and every loop that stage 7 emits starts from one. The immediate post-dominator of a branch is the place where its two arms join again, and stage 7 uses it to close an if . Work through one concrete case. band at -O0 occupies 0x50 to 0xba, with 6 bytes of padding up to 0xc0. Without a resolver, recursive descent from 0x50 decodes 16 instructions. It follows the ja at 0x62 to the default block at 0xae, falls through to 0x64, and stops at jmpq *%rax at 0x76. That jump is listed in unresolved , and the six case blocks are never reached. What you build. You build two things. The lifter turns each decoded instruction into IR statements. The IR has assignments, stores, branches, jumps, a switch through a recovered table and returns. Its expressions are constants, variables with a width, binary operations, casts, loads, flag records and section addresses. Registers become variables named by their 64-bit family ( eax writes rax at width 32). The flags register is an ordinary variable named flags . Frame bookkeeping ( push , pop , mov %rsp, %rbp , stack adjustments) produces no statements, and a slot at a constant offset from %rbp becomes a local variable such as local_8 . The SSA builder gives every definition its own version. It places phi statements on the iterated dominance frontier of each variable's definition sites, renames uses over the dominator tree, and inserts a cast where a use has a different width than the definition it reads. Why it matters. x86-64 instructions do several things at once. subl %edi, %esi writes %esi and six flags. A later jle reads two of those flags. SSA makes every later question local. "Which value does this use read?" has one answer, the single definition with that version. What you build. You build signature recovery for the optimized SSA function: Parameters. The System V psABI passes the first six INTEGER arguments in %rdi , %rsi , %rdx , %rcx , %r8 and %r9 . A register read at version 0 is read before any write. The highest such argument register fixes the count, so a function that reads only %rsi still has two parameters. Union-find joins them, and each web gets one name: param_N for an argument, local_8 for a stack slot, eax_1 for a register value. Types. The widest definition in a web gives int or long . A web used as the base of a scaled element access becomes a pointer to the element. A web used as the base of constant offsets becomes a pointer to a struct with one field per offset. Pointer types spread along copies and phis. Signedness. Arithmetic shifts, signed division, signed compares and sign extension say signed. Logical shifts and unsigned division say unsigned. A lone unsigned compare is the range-check idiom of a switch , and it does not make the value unsigned. Return type. The width of the value in %rax at each return. If no path writes %rax , the result is void , and that guess is listed as an unknown. Every decision carries the instructions that support it. Why it matters. The machine code has no types. A wrong parameter count changes the call in the stage 8 driver. A wrong width truncates a long . A wrong signedness flips the result of a compare for negative inputs. In plain words first The idea in one line Improve an explicit routing skill from labeled development errors, then require a separate evaluation gate before promotion. The problem In plain words first "Self-improving" agents are an attractive idea and an easy way to fool yourself: an agent that edits its own rules until its test score goes up has simply learned its test. This project builds a self-improving skill with the limits that make it honest. The skill is a transparent router: an ordered list of word rules mapping support messages to a team. Labelled cases are split into development and holdout sets by a hash of their ids, with the split audited for leaks. New rules are proposed only from mistakes on the development set, and only for words that point to one label. A candidate is promoted only if it improves the untouched holdout without breaking a case that used to be right, and even then promotion waits for a person. a2102: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems HTTP 400 on Long Answers: max_tokens over the Limit Lesson 21.2 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 1 (Screen). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : screen, debugging. Roles : applied AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer, inference engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : the shared second L4 of a two-GPU node, with another user's processes on it The situation In plain words first A request fails with HTTP 400 before any token is generated, and the ticket asks to "turn off the limit". This case trains a habit interviewers look for: when a server refuses a request, read the numbers in the error and work out who owns each one. Here one number belongs to the client (how many tokens it asked for) and one to the server (the longest request it was configured for). A product team runs Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B on one vLLM server for an internal writing tool. A support ticket arrives: "the API rejects long answers". The client sets max_tokens to 50000 so that the model never cuts an answer short, and every such request comes back as HTTP 400 at once, before any token streams. Shorter requests work. The ticket asks the platform team to "turn off the limit". You pick it up with the error body, the startup log of the server and the manual. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The answer the client got Copy The pool and the maximum length of that server at startup Copy A request that the server cut at its own cap Copy The troubleshooting entry for this status code Copy The four choices when the pool holds too few users Copy Questions to answer first Read the error body. Which two numbers does it compare, and which parameter does it name? Where does the server get the second number, and what does it have to do with the KV pool? The ticket asks to turn off the limit. What are the two honest fixes, and who makes each change? A second ticket reports the same status code, but the message names the prompt length. What is different, and what is the fix? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A 400 that arrives before any token streams means the request was rejected during validation, not during generation. ✗ Setting max_tokens very high is a harmless way to avoid cut-off answers. It must fit the server's maximum length; the right fix is a realistic value plus checking the finish reason. ✓ A finish reason of length tells the client the answer was cut. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the body. The message says that max_tokens=50000 cannot be greater than max_model_len=40960 , and the param field names max_tokens . The server checks the numbers of a request before it schedules anything, so the 400 arrives at once and no token is generated. The client asked for more output than one request may hold. Read the startup lines. The server derived a longest request of 40,960 tokens from the model config, and it sized its pool at 84,480 tokens from 9.02 GiB of KV cache memory. The second line says that 2.06 requests at the full length fit at once. The maximum length is a budget for one request, and the pool is the budget for everyone. A request for 50,000 output tokens would exceed the first budget on an empty server. Read what a cut answer looks like. In the same check session a request with max_tokens of 64 ran, and the server stopped it with the finish reason length . That is how a client learns that an answer was cut: the stream ends with length instead of stop . A huge max_tokens is not the way to avoid a cut; the finish reason is the way to see one. Read the two shapes of the error. The troubleshooting entry gives both. When the prompt tokens plus max_tokens exceed the limit, the message names the model's maximum context length and gives the counts. When max_tokens alone is above the limit, the message is the one in this ticket. The fix is the same pair in both cases: a shorter prompt or a smaller max_tokens on the client, or a larger maximum length on the server if the pool allows it. Read the order of server-side choices. The manual lists four moves when the pool holds too few users, in order of cost, and the first is to lower the maximum length to the longest context that users send. The direction of this ticket is the opposite: raising the limit lets one request take a larger share of the pool. The startup line already said that about two full-length requests fit. A larger limit means fewer users at full length, so it is a measured decision, not a ticket closure. What actually happened The limit is a budget, not a bug. The client asked for 50,000 output tokens on a server whose longest request is 40,960 tokens, and the server refused before any work. The client fix is a max_tokens that the product needs, far below the limit, and a check of the finish reason so that a cut answer is visible to the user. That is what the 64-token check shows: the server reports length when it cuts. The server fix exists, and it is conditional. Raise --max-model-len only after you measured the longest prompt plus answer that users send, and only if one request at that length still fits the pool next to the other users. On a pool of 84,480 tokens, each step up in the limit lowers the count of full-length requests that fit, from the 2.06 of the startup line. The startup check enforces the same rule from the other side: a server whose one full-length request does not fit refuses to start, as the shared-GPU start in the manual did at 2,928 tokens when only 2,912 fit. Wrong turns "Turn off the limit on the server." The maximum length is the KV cache that one request may take, and the pool sizes it. Without it one request can claim most of the pool and starve every other user. "Set max_tokens to exactly the limit." Then the prompt plus the answer exceeds the context, and the server returns the other shape of the same 400, the one that names the prompt tokens. "Raise the maximum length until the ticket stops." A longer limit means fewer requests fit at once. Measure the longest real request first, and check that it fits the pool. "Retry the request." A 400 is a check on the numbers in the request, and the same request gets the same answer. The lesson to carry A 400 from a model server is usually a budget that the operator set on purpose. Read the two numbers in the message, find which side owns each one, and change the side that is wrong: the client's request, or the server's measured limit. Never remove a limit to close a ticket, and teach clients to read the finish reason instead of asking for an unbounded answer. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual lists this status code in the troubleshooting page , orders the server-side choices in the memory counting page and shows the same budget at startup in the out-of-memory page . Recap What to keep from this case Read both numbers in the error and assign each to its owner. Ask for the output length the product needs, not the maximum imaginable. Check the finish reason so cut answers are visible. Raise a server limit only after measuring real prompt plus answer lengths. a2103: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems OOM with the KV Cache Pool at 5 Percent Lesson 21.3 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 1 (Screen). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : screen, debugging. Roles : applied AI engineer, inference engineer, AI developer relations engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 with the MLX backend Model : mlx-community/Qwen3-0.6B-4bit Hardware : a laptop with unified memory, shared with the other programs of a desktop session The situation In plain words first A laptop server dies with "Insufficient Memory" at 32 concurrent requests, while its own log says the token cache was only 5 percent used. The obvious conclusion ("the laptop is too small") is wrong. The case trains you to notice when the memory a component reports is not the memory that ran out: here, an automatic setting reserved most of the free memory for a cache, leaving nothing for the computation itself. A developer advocate prepares a workshop demo on a laptop. The server runs a small quantized model on the MLX backend, started with the model path and nothing about memory. Single requests work, and a few people at once work. To show what the laptop can do, the advocate runs the benchmark client with 32 requests in flight at once. The whole server dies. The log ends with a Metal error, Insufficient Memory , and the process tree is gone. The decode lines right before the crash show 32 running requests, with token usage at 0.05. The advocate concludes that the laptop cannot serve 32 users and plans to show the demo at four. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The pool line of the first start Copy The pool lines of the second start, minutes later Copy The benchmark at a concurrency of 32, and the crash Copy Why the two starts sized the pool differently Copy How the manual reads the crash Copy The pool line of the kit's server, with an explicit fraction Copy The same benchmark against the kit's server Copy Questions to answer first The pool was almost empty when the server died. Where was the memory, if not in the pool? Two starts of the same command gave two pool sizes. What changed between them? What rule produced the fraction, and what does that rule assume about the machine? Which flag fixes this, what value did the capture kit use, and what did the pool look like after? What proves the fix: a startup line or a benchmark result? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A cache that is nearly empty when the process dies points to memory used somewhere the cache does not count. ✗ Automatic memory fractions are always safe on a laptop. They are computed from a snapshot of free memory; other programs and activations can need more later. ✓ Setting the cache's share explicitly let the same benchmark finish 128 of 128 requests at concurrency 32. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the decode lines before the error. Thirty-two requests held 16,095 tokens, which is 5 percent of a pool of 312,581 tokens. The pool had reserved 33 GB and used under 2 GB of it. The next prefill needed activation memory outside the pool, but the operating system had none left to give. One failed command buffer took down the scheduler, the parent received a SIGQUIT, and it killed the process tree. The server did not run out of KV cache. It ran out of everything else. Compare the two startup lines. The first start saw 27.81 GB of available system memory and gave the pool a budget of 24.25 GB, for 227,022 tokens. The second start, minutes later, saw 38.29 GB and gave 33.39 GB, for 312,581 tokens. Nothing changed in SGLang. Other programs on the laptop used less memory at the second start, so the snapshot of free memory was larger and the pool grew with it. Read the rule. Both budgets are 87.2 percent of the free memory, because the automatic fraction resolved to 0.872. On this backend the rule takes the smaller of two numbers, a fraction of the Metal working set and a fraction of the system memory available right now, and the second one is the snapshot that moved. The rule assumes that the machine belongs to SGLang for the life of the server. A laptop with a browser and an editor open is not that machine. Read the fix in the kit's start. The capture kit passes --mem-fraction-static 0.4 . Its startup line shows a snapshot of 48.49 GB and a budget of 19.39 GB, which is 0.4 of the snapshot, for a pool of 181,574 tokens. That pool still holds far more than 32 requests of 640 tokens need, so the smaller pool cost nothing in this workload. Prove it with the same load. Against the kit's server, the benchmark at a concurrency of 32 finished all 128 requests in 64.83 seconds. The startup line shows the split. The benchmark result shows that the server survived the load that killed it before. What actually happened The laptop was never the limit. The automatic fraction took 87 percent of the free memory for a pool that the workload used at 5 percent, and left the activations of the next prefill with nothing. With --mem-fraction-static 0.4 the pool shrank to 181,574 tokens and the same benchmark completed 128 of 128 requests at a concurrency of 32. The demo now starts with the fraction set, and the advocate reads two lines after every change: the kv_budget on the pool line and max_total_num_tokens on the settings line. On this backend the cache memory metric reads 0.0, because the MLX pool is allocated outside the accounting that the metric reads, so the pool log line is the number to trust. Wrong turns "The laptop cannot serve 32 users." The pool held 312,581 tokens and 32 requests used 5 percent of it. The memory ran out outside the pool, where the fraction left too little. "Raise the fraction so the pool is bigger." The pool was the cause. It took 87 percent of the free memory and starved the activations. Lower it. "Restart the server, the second start had more memory." The snapshot changes with the other programs on the machine, and the next start can find less. Set the fraction so the pool does not depend on the snapshot. "Set the fraction to 0.95 to be safe." A fraction of 0.95 leaves 5 percent for activations, and issue #39675 in the manual reports exactly that failure on the first prefill. The lesson to carry A pool that is almost empty when the process dies tells you the memory went somewhere the pool does not count. On a machine that runs anything else, a fraction computed from a snapshot of free memory is a bet on how the rest of the machine behaves for the life of the server. Set the share yourself, read the two startup lines that show the result, and prove a memory fix with the load that broke it, not with a start that succeeded. How this connects Where this is taught The memory page of SGLang 101 records the crash and the fix in the crash we recorded and our position: set the fraction yourself on any shared machine . Recap What to keep from this case An almost empty pool at the crash means the memory went elsewhere. Set memory shares yourself on machines that run anything else. Read the pool size and the maximum token count after every change. Do not shrink the demo before understanding the crash. a2104: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Published Port That Answered on One Loopback (IPv4 vs IPv6) Lesson 21.4 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 1 (Screen). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : screen, debugging. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : sbx v0.47.0 Model : none; shell commands inside the sandbox Hardware : one Mac with the microVM runtime The situation In plain words first A page works in the browser but a test harness on the same machine cannot connect, and the developer starts editing the server inside the sandbox. The cause sits outside it: the port was published on the IPv4 loopback only, and the harness tried the IPv6 one ( ::1 ). The case trains a quick, general check: compare the addresses each client used before touching the service. A developer serves a static site from inside a sandbox on port 8080 and publishes it to the host with sbx ports m101-demo --publish 18081:8080 . A browser on the host opens the page. A test harness on the same host reports that it could not connect, and its log shows that it tried ::1 . The developer suspects that the server inside the sandbox listens on one interface only and starts editing its configuration. You have the publish command and its listing, the same URL fetched on both loopback addresses, the listing in sbx ls , a second publish with a protocol named, and the unpublish calls. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. A port published without a protocol, and the listing Copy The same URL on the two loopback addresses Copy The binding in the PORTS column of sbx ls Copy A publish with the protocol named, and the JSON listing Copy Two unpublish calls and the empty listing Copy Questions to answer first Which side refused the connection, the server in the sandbox or the host binding? What in the listing says so? What does a publish without a protocol bind, and since which release? How do you publish so that both loopbacks answer? The -p flag on sbx run did not help on a re-attach. Why? How do you remove a binding, and how do you check that it is gone? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ localhost can resolve to 127.0.0.1 or ::1 , depending on the client. ✗ If one client connects, the service must be listening on every address. A port mapping has its own address family; here it bound tcp4 only. ✓ Fetching the same URL on both loopback addresses separates the two hypotheses in one minute. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the protocol column. The publish answered Published 127.0.0.1:18081 -> 8080/tcp4 , and the listing shows one row with the host address 127.0.0.1 and the protocol tcp4 . The host binding is IPv4 only. The server inside was never asked. Confirm with the two fetches. 127.0.0.1:18081 returns 200. [::1]:18081 fails to connect and curl exits 7. The failing side is the host loopback where nothing listens. Name the rule. Without a protocol, publishing uses tcp4 , so the host side is 127.0.0.1 alone. The manual dates the change to v0.42.0: a published port no longer listens on ::1 unless you name the protocol. The 2025 plugin bound both loopbacks, which conflict C39 records. sbx ls shows the same binding in its PORTS column. Publish for both families. --publish 8080/tcp binds 127.0.0.1 and [::1] on ephemeral host ports, and sbx ports --json lists three records: the first tcp4 binding and two tcp ones, one per address. Name a host port in the spec when the harness needs a fixed one. Remove what you no longer need. --unpublish 18081:8080 and --unpublish <port>:8080/tcp each remove their mapping, and the JSON listing ends empty. -p on sbx run applies at creation only, so later changes go through sbx ports . What actually happened The server was fine. The host binding was tcp4 , so only 127.0.0.1 listened, and the harness's connection to ::1 found no listener. Publishing 8080/tcp with a fixed host port gives both loopbacks a binding, and the harness connects. The edits inside the sandbox are reverted. Wrong turns "Bind the server inside the sandbox to all interfaces." The guest side already answered through the IPv4 mapping. The missing listener was on the host loopback. "Pass -p 18081:8080/tcp on the next sbx run." On an existing sandbox the flag is ignored. Use sbx ports. "Turn off IPv6 in the test harness." It works, and it hides a binding rule that the next harness will hit again. The lesson to carry When one client reaches a service and another does not, compare the addresses each one used before you touch the service. A port mapping has its own address family, and a listing that prints it saves an hour of edits in the wrong place. How this connects Where this is taught The ports page gives the tcp4 rule and the protocol table, and the conflicts register records the change as C39. Recap What to keep from this case When one client works and another does not, compare the addresses they used. A port mapping has an address family; read it in the listing. Test both loopbacks before editing the service. Revert edits made on a wrong hypothesis. Level 1 (Screen). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : screen, debugging. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first A training run stops at start with a TypeError about None right after experiment tracking was turned on. One teammate wants to remove tracking forever; another wants to paste an API key into the command line. Neither is needed: one required flag was missing. The case trains two habits: compare your command with the documented one when a startup fails on None , and keep secrets out of command lines. A team has read its first runs from the log with grep . For the first long run they want a dashboard, so they add --use-wandb --wandb-mode offline --wandb-project miles-lab to the run's extra arguments. The run stops at start with a TypeError about NoneType and str . No step line was written. One teammate blames the image and wants the tracker removed for good. Another wants to paste the team's API key into the extra arguments to force an online run, because "offline mode is what broke it". The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The run with the tracker on and no group name Copy The same run with a group name Copy The same run with the other tracker Copy The tracker flags the manual uses, and the rule about the group Copy Where the key for an online run goes Copy The flags for the other tracker Copy Questions to answer first What kind of bug produces this TypeError , and what does it tell you about the GPU, the engine and the image? Which flag was missing, and which two log signs show that the tracker then worked? The teammate wants to paste the API key into the run arguments. Name two places where that key would then appear. Which tracker needs no account and no network, and what does it need instead? The team now has a dashboard. What do they keep as well, and why? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A None where a string was expected at startup usually means a setting was never given. ✗ Offline tracking mode caused the crash. The missing --wandb-group flag did; offline mode works once it is set. ✓ API keys belong in a private file read into the environment, not in arguments a launcher prints. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the error. TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'str' is Python adding a string to a value that is None . A setting that nobody gave is being joined into a name. Nothing in that line concerns the GPU, the engine or the weights. The run never reached its first step, so the tracker setup is the only code that ran. Read the run that worked. The same recipe with --wandb-group plain logged step 0 and step 1 . The log printed W&B offline mode enabled. Data will be saved locally. , and the tracker folder holds offline-run- folders next to its debug logs. The manual names the rule: keep --wandb-group , because without it a run ends at startup with exactly this error. Read the other tracker. The same recipe with -e TENSORBOARD_DIR=/root/lab/runs/plain/tb and --use-tensorboard logged Saving tensorboard log to /root/lab/runs/plain/tb. and wrote two event files. This tracker needs a folder and one flag, and neither an account nor a network, and you read it on the host with tensorboard --logdir . Read the key rule. For an online run, leave out --wandb-mode offline . Keep the key out of the command line, because commands go to the shell history and the process list, and the launcher prints the full command in the log. Put WANDB_API_KEY=<your key> in a file with mode 600 and pass it with --env-file . The extra arguments are the one place the key must never go. What actually happened The crash came from one missing flag, --wandb-group . Add it, keep offline mode until an account and a network are wanted, and check the two signs: the W&B offline mode enabled line and the offline-run- folder. The run then reaches step 0 and step 1 as the check did. For a team with no tracker account, use TensorBoard with a folder and one flag, and open the folder on the host. Keep the log in any case. The manual read every number in it from the log, and the log is where the first exception of a broken run sits. Wrong turns "The image is broken, drop the tracker." The same image ran the same recipe to step 1 with one more flag. The error names a missing value, not a missing library. "Paste the API key into the extra arguments to force online mode." Offline mode was not the cause, and the launcher prints the full command into the log, so the key would sit in the log, the shell history and the process list. "A dashboard replaces the log." The dashboard shows the metrics. The log holds the startup lines, the engine lines and the first exception when a run breaks. The lesson to carry A type error on a None at startup is a missing setting, and the fastest check is the documented command next to yours. Secrets go in a file that only you can read and reach the process through the environment, never through arguments that a launcher echoes. A dashboard adds a view, and the log stays the record. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual gives the tracker commands, the group rule and the key rule in the read the run page . Recap What to keep from this case A type error on None at start is usually a missing setting. Compare your command with the documented one. Never pass secrets as command-line arguments. Keep the plain log even when a dashboard is added. a2106: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems The Sandbox That Stopped Itself: Idle Timeouts Lesson 21.6 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 1 (Screen). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : screen, debugging. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : sbx v0.47.0 Model : none; shell commands inside the sandbox Hardware : one Mac with the microVM runtime The situation In plain words first A long install inside a sandbox is gone after an hour and the sandbox shows "stopped". The developer suspects a crash and wants to rebuild everything. In fact the daemon stopped the sandbox on purpose, after the last session closed and a grace period passed, and said so in its log. The case trains a basic question: did the thing stop, fail, or get deleted, and what does the component that owns its lifecycle say? A developer opens a shell sandbox on a repository, starts a long dependency install, and closes the terminal to go to a meeting. An hour later sbx ls shows the sandbox with the status stopped . The install did not finish, and no error was printed anywhere the developer looked. They conclude that the daemon crashed or that someone removed the sandbox, and they want to recreate it from scratch. You have the two listings, the daemon log lines for that sandbox, and the output of an explicit stop and a prune from another day. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. Sbx ls before and after the last session closed Copy The two auto-stop lines of the daemon log for m101-demo Copy An explicit stop, a prune, and the list after it Copy Questions to answer first Did the sandbox crash, get removed, or stop? Which listing settles it? What do the two daemon log lines say happened, and at what level? What survives a stop, and what does not? How do you get back into this sandbox, and what would prune have done? How do you keep a job running after you disconnect? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ "Stopped" is a state, not an error; it says nothing about a crash. ✗ No error on screen means nothing was logged. The daemon logged the stop at INFO level, in its own log. ✓ Starting long jobs detached keeps the sandbox from stopping when the terminal closes. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the status. The first listing shows running and the second stopped . A removed sandbox is not listed. A crashed daemon could not answer sbx ls . The sandbox stopped. Read the daemon log. Both lines are INFO , not errors. The first says that the auto-stop grace period expired and the runtime is stopping. The second says that the runtime was auto-stopped after the last session disconnected. The trigger was the closed terminal: it was the last session. Each line carries the daemon version, so you know which release did it. Know what a stop keeps. The explicit stop prints state preserved and the restart command. The manual lists what persists across a stop and a restart: installed packages, Docker images, configuration changes, command history, and workspace files not on a mount. A running process is not on that list, so the install died with the microVM. Come back the right way. sbx run --name m101-demo reattaches and starts the stopped sandbox. sbx prune would have deleted it: in the capture it removed both stopped sandboxes and left an empty list, and rm and prune also delete the secrets scoped to the sandbox. Keep it running on purpose. sbx run -d against an existing sandbox keeps it running after the sessions disconnect, until you stop or remove it. A kit can declare the long-running@1 capability for the same effect. The manual's ledger marks the auto-stop as observed and not documented, so expect no page to warn you. What actually happened The daemon stopped the sandbox on purpose after the last session closed and a grace period passed, and its log says so at the INFO level. Nothing crashed and nothing was removed. The developer reattaches with sbx run --name , finds the packages that had finished installing still there, and starts the install again. For the next long job they start the sandbox detached, so no session is the last one. Prune stays out of the runbook until a sandbox is wanted gone. Wrong turns "Run sbx prune to clean up, then create the sandbox again." Prune removes every stopped sandbox, with its state and its secrets. The sandbox you want back is exactly a stopped one. "The daemon crashed." It wrote two INFO lines and answered the listing. A crash would have left no second listing. "Create a new sandbox with the same name." The name belongs to the stopped one, and a new sandbox would lose the installed state. Reattach instead. The lesson to carry When a thing you started is gone, ask whether it stopped, failed, or was deleted, and read the log of the component that owns its lifecycle before you rebuild anything. A platform that stops idle work on its own will do so again. Find the flag or the capability that marks work as long-running and use it on purpose. How this connects Where this is taught The lifecycle page records the auto-stop and what a stop keeps, and the claims ledger gives the behaviour the verdict observed, with no vendor page behind it. Recap What to keep from this case Distinguish stopped, failed and deleted. Read the log of the component that owns the lifecycle. Reattach before rebuilding; work may still be there. Run long jobs detached.
