a2107: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems The Trainer That Rejected an Attention Backend Name Lesson 21.7 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 1 (Screen). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : screen, debugging. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first An engineer sets the trainer's attention implementation to triton because the inference engine uses a backend of that name, hoping the two will produce matching numbers. The trainer refuses the name at once. The case trains the idea that two components using the same word do not mean the same thing: each validates settings against its own list, and the error that prints that list is the fastest documentation. An engineer wants to shrink the log probability gap between the rollout engine and the trainer. The engine runs its Triton attention backend, so she sets the trainer's attention implementation to triton as well, with a name she copied from an example. The idea is that two sides with one kernel name agree on more numbers. The run ends about a minute after the launcher's first line. The trainer prints a ValueError , and a line from the fault-tolerance layer says that the trainer's init failed. She asks whether the image is broken and whether to pull another tag. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The launcher line, the trainer error and the failed init Copy The troubleshooting entry for this error Copy Where the flag value came from, and the one pair that both sides accept Copy The true on-policy contract: the models, the kernel and the two checks Copy Questions to answer first Which process raised the error, and which list does the error print? How does this failure differ from a rollout engine that dies at start? Why does a name that the engine accepts not reach the trainer as a valid name? Is there a pair of settings that gives both sides one kernel on this machine? What do you change, and which line in the next log shows that the run is healthy? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ The engine's backend names and the trainer's implementation names are separate lists. ✗ Using the same kernel name on both sides makes their log probabilities match. Matching numbers needs a specific supported pairing (here, only on Hopper GPUs), not matching names. ✓ An error message that lists valid values is the quickest reference. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the error. The trainer raised ValueError: Specified attn_implementation="triton" is not supported , and it printed the names it accepts: eager , flash_attention_2 , flash_attention_3 , flash_attention_4 , sdpa , flex_attention , and their paged forms. The next line, from the trainer controller, reads phase=fail for fn=init after 0.7 s. The trainer never came up, and the job said so and stopped. The launcher line and the fail line are one minute apart. A dead rollout engine, by contrast, leaves the job running for an hour with HTTP 503 errors. Match the manual entry. The troubleshooting page has this symptom: a trainer attention name that the installed transformers library does not accept, such as triton . The check is a ValueError that lists the accepted implementations, and the fix is to pick one from that list. The manual's runs left the trainer setting at its default. See where the name came from. The engine and the trainer keep two different lists. In the FSDP actor, a bridge to the engine's Triton attention turns on only when the build reports an AMD GPU. On an NVIDIA GPU the value goes straight to the transformers library, which has no attention named triton . The example that the engineer copied was for the other kind of GPU. Read the contract. Miles has one pairing where both sides run one kernel: the engine on its fa3 backend and the trainer on flash_attention_3 , for the dense Qwen3 models in the contract, and that kernel accepts GPUs with compute capability 8.0 to 9.0. The GB10 is outside that range, so on this machine no setting puts one kernel on the two sides. The manual's advice outside the contract is to watch the gap and lower its sampler part. What actually happened Remove the attention flag on the trainer side, or set it to a name from the error's own list. Leave the engine on its backend. The two lists are different, and the only pairing that makes both sides bit-exact needs a Hopper GPU, which this machine is not. The healthy run then shows a rollout 0 line within minutes, and a step-0 gap inside the range of the healthy runs on this machine, 0.0136 to 0.0164 for this model without top-p or top-k. Wrong turns "The image is broken, pull another tag." The error is a value check in the trainer library against its own list of names. The manual's runs used this image with the default name and completed. "Give the engine the same name as the trainer, so the names match." The engine accepts triton and the trainer does not. Matching names does not give matching kernels, and the trainer still refuses to start. "Use the contract pair, FlashAttention 3 on both sides." The engine's FA3 backend refuses the GB10 at start, because of its compute capability range, and the job then runs for an hour against a dead engine. The lesson to carry Two components that read the same word do not read the same thing. Each one checks a setting against its own list, and an error that prints the list is the fastest fix you will get. Read the list, pick from it, and do not expect a shared name to buy shared numerics. Bit-exact agreement between a server and a trainer is a contract with a model list and a hardware range, not a flag. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual lists this error in its symptom table and the contract that both sides must meet in the true on-policy limits page , and the SGLang manual shows the same run and where the flag value came from in its RL rollout engine page . Recap What to keep from this case The same word can mean different things to different components. Read the valid values the error prints. Change one side at a time and measure the gap. Know which hardware a claimed property needs. a2108: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Five-Minute Cold Start: Weight Loading on the GB10 Lesson 21.8 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, forward deployed AI engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 in its release container Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first New replicas take over five minutes to answer, so the autoscaler declares them unhealthy and starts more, and the spike is over before they help. Before changing flags, the case asks you to read the timing of each startup phase. Almost all of the time is copying the model's weights, which no serving flag shortens. The fix is to change the design around that fact. A team serves Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 from a pool of GB10 machines behind an autoscaler. At a traffic spike the autoscaler starts new replicas. Each new replica takes more than five minutes before it answers its first request, so the autoscaler counts it as unhealthy and starts more. By the time the replicas are up, the spike is over, and the team pays for machines that served nothing. The first guess is the image pull or the network. The logs rule both out: the container image was already on each machine, and the weights were on the local NVMe drive. The second guess is that the model is simply too large for the machine, but each replica serves well once it is up. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The settings of the server that started Copy The end of the weight load Copy The compile and the warmup Copy The graph capture and the KV cache sizing Copy The memory accounting line at the end of startup Copy Questions to answer first Read the startup lines in order. Where did the five minutes go, and how much of that was the copy of the weights? On this machine the weights and the GPU allocation live in one memory. Why does the load still take minutes? Which lines prove that the server sized itself as planned, and what do they say about a fraction of 0.75 on this machine? What can a second start of the same image on the same machine skip, and what must it pay again? A field report cut a cold start of another engine from 695 s to 88 s and then to 9.6 s. Which cost did each step remove, and which of those steps apply here? How does this change the autoscaling design? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Reading phase timings before changing settings shows which phase dominates. ✗ A faster image pull would fix the cold start. The weight copy took 325 of 330 seconds; the image was not the problem. ✓ Keeping replicas warm and weights on local NVMe avoids paying the load at every spike. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the log as a timeline. The weight loader finished after 325.26 seconds, and the model loading line reports 56.93 GiB of memory and 330.542793 seconds. The compile took 18.67 s in total and the warmup 0.40 s. The graph capture finished in 39 secs and took 1.17 GiB. So the weights are almost all of the start, and the compile and the graphs together are about one minute of it. The second question is why a copy inside one memory takes so long. The loader copies each tensor from the memory-mapped safetensors file into the GPU allocation, one tensor at a time. On the GB10, a copy from a file-backed page is slow. An open issue in the engine's tracker measured about 1.7 ms for each tensor copied from the file view, against about 0.2 ms for a copy that started in host memory. The 0.31.0 release made a different part of the load faster, an indexed lookup of expert names that saves about 25 s on this machine, and the cost of each tensor copy stays. The fix is not in a flag. The sizing lines show that the memory plan held. The settings line asked for a fraction of 0.75 and an override of 14,685 blocks. The server found 31.32 GiB available for the KV cache, overrode its own count of 21,381 blocks with the 14,685 that the sweep wanted, and reported a pool of 234,960 tokens, enough for 28.68 concurrent requests of 8,192 tokens. The accounting line at the end gives the whole split: 114.94 of 121.69 GiB free at startup, a desired share of 91.27 GiB at 0.75, and an actual use of 58.16 GiB for the weights and other memory, 1.78 GiB for the peak activation and 0.31 GiB for the graphs, with 31.32 GiB of cache in use. On unified memory the fraction is a share of the whole machine, and the rest stays free for the OS and its page cache. A second start on the same machine pays the weights again. The compile is different: the log shows the engine saving its compiled function to a cache directory, so the next start loads it instead of compiling. The graph capture repeats. The field report in the SGLang manual, from an engineer blog of April 2026 about an eight-GPU server, timed the same phases on the other engine: 695 s cold, with 531 s of it the weight load. Kernel caches kept between runs brought a warm start to 88 s, and a process checkpoint with the weights staged in host memory brought it to 9.6 s. The first step is the cache mount that applies here. The last step needs host memory that the weights can wait in, which this machine shares with the GPU. What actually happened The cold start is the weight copy, 325.26 s of a 330 s load, and no serving flag shortens it. The team changes the design around that fact. Each replica starts once and stays up, because a restart pays the full load again. The weights stay on the local NVMe drive and never on a network mount. The compile cache directory is on a volume that survives the container, so the second start skips the 18.67 s compile. The autoscaler changes in two ways. Its readiness check waits for the application startup line and one short request, and a replica that is still loading counts as starting, not as unhealthy, so the autoscaler stops adding replicas on top of replicas that are about to come up. And the scaling signal moves from the current queue to a forecast with a lead time longer than the six minutes that a start takes, or the pool keeps warm standby replicas that are already loaded. On this machine the fraction of 0.75 left 31.32 GiB for the cache. The block override capped the pool at 234,960 tokens, and without the override the same memory holds about 342,000 tokens at 96 KiB per token, so a standby replica can take a large share of a spike by itself. Wrong turns "The image pull is slow, cache the image." The image was local. The log puts 325.26 s in the weight loader after the container had started. "Add replicas faster when the queue grows." Every replica pays the same five minutes, and the spike lasts less than that. More replicas that arrive late cost more and serve nothing. "Lower the memory fraction so the server starts sooner." The fraction decides the cache size, not the copy speed. The weights take 56.93 GiB and 325.26 s at any fraction. "Turn off the compile and the graphs to save a minute." Together they cost about one minute of a five-minute start, the compile is cached after the first start, and both pay back on every decode step for the life of the replica. The lesson to carry When a start is slow, read the phase timings before you change anything, because the largest phase is usually one that no flag controls. Then move the design to fit it: start rarely, keep what a restart can reuse on storage that survives, and give the autoscaler a signal with more lead time than the start takes. A replica that is loading is not unhealthy, and a probe that cannot tell the difference will scale a fleet into the ground. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual reads this startup log in the DGX Spark page , weighs compile and graph capture in the compile page and names the image and the driver in the version pins , and the SGLang manual gives the cache directories and the field report in its operating page . Recap What to keep from this case Read phase timings before changing anything. The largest phase is often one no flag controls. Design around it: warm replicas, local weights, persistent caches. Make health checks tolerate a known start time. a2109: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Request ID That Broke Prefix Caching Lesson 21.9 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.6 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer, agentic AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory, and a GB10 as the second machine The situation In plain words first Every reply takes about two seconds to start, even for a repeated question, although the 3,000-token system prompt never changes. A relay adds a new request id as the first line of that prompt. Prefix caching only reuses work for an identical beginning, so a changing first line makes every request a cache miss. Moving the id fixed it: in the measurement, from 2,161 ms to 98 ms. An agent product sends every request through a relay. For tracing, the relay puts a new first line in the system prompt, in the form Request id <hex>. , with a new value on each call. The system prompt itself is 2,999 tokens long and never changes. The team serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B with SGLang on an L4, with --enable-cache-report on. Users report that the first token takes about two seconds on every turn, even when they repeat a question. The team doubles the memory fraction, tries a different eviction policy and turns on hierarchical caching. The wait does not move. The metrics endpoint reports a cache hit rate near zero. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. Five requests whose system prompt starts with a request id Copy The same five requests with a stable system prompt Copy The same request id moved to the end of the system prompt Copy The scheduler log while the three forms went through Copy The summary of the same experiment on a GB10 with a larger model Copy Questions to answer first The first listing shows five requests. What does the cached token count tell you about where the match stopped? How does the radix tree match a prompt, and why can nothing after the first difference match? In the third listing the id comes last in the prompt. Predict the cached token count before you read it, then explain the difference. Which three places can confirm a hit or a miss on a running server, from the closest to the request to the most general? The team tuned the cache tiers and the eviction policy first. Why did none of those settings help, and in which order do you change prompts and server flags? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A prefix cache can reuse only the part of the prompt that is identical from the very first token. ✗ More cache memory or a different eviction policy would have helped. Nothing was cacheable; the first line changed on every request. ✓ Stable content first, per-session content next, per-request content last. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the first listing one field at a time. Each request sends about 3,030 prompt tokens and the server reports cached_tokens of 3 or 6. The first token takes 2,159.2 to 2,171.2 ms on every round. So each request pays the full prefill of the system prompt, and the only tokens that the cache found are the few that come before the random hex digits. The second listing is the control. The same question after a stable system prompt reports 2,998 cached tokens of 2,999 from the second round on, and the first token arrives in 80.7 to 85.1 ms. The first round shows 3 cached tokens and 2,143.9 ms, because it filled the cache. So the server and the model can serve this prompt about twenty-five times faster when the prompt matches. The third listing moves the same random id to the end of the system prompt. The count rises to 2,983 to 2,987 cached tokens. The first token takes 93.1 to 99.7 ms. The tokens are almost the same in all three forms. Only their order differs. The radix tree compares tokens from the first one and stops at the first difference. Nothing after a difference can match, because the attention values of every later token depend on every earlier token. A cache that reused the later tokens would return wrong answers. The scheduler log shows the same story from the server side. The stable rounds log #cached-token: 2998 with one new token. Then five prefill batches log about 3,025 to 3,029 new tokens with 3 or 6 cached. Then the id-at-end rounds log 45 to 50 new tokens with 2,983 to 2,987 cached. The last listing repeats the experiment on a GB10 with a mixture-of-experts model. The times are different, 632.2 ms against 44.75 ms, and the cached token counts are the same: 6 against 2,998. What actually happened The relay put a changing value at the start of the only part of the prompt that every request shares. One edit fixed it. Move the trace id out of the system prompt and send it as request metadata, or put it at the end. In our measurement on the L4 the median first token fell from 2,161.4 ms with the id at the start to 98.2 ms with the id at the end, and the median cached token count rose from 6 to 2,986 of about 3,030. Prove the fix from three places. Start the server with --enable-cache-report and read cached_tokens in the usage block of each response. Read #cached-token on each Prefill batch line of the scheduler log. Read sglang:cache_hit_rate from /metrics . On vLLM, read vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total and vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total . The cache settings that the team changed first were not the problem, because no eviction policy or host tier can match tokens that differ from the start. Wrong turns "Raise the memory fraction so the cache holds more." The pool was not full. The misses came from the prompt order, so a larger pool holds more blocks that nothing matches. "Turn on hierarchical caching." A host tier keeps evicted prefixes, and nothing was evicted. The prefix never matched in the first place. "The hit rate is low because the questions differ." The question is about 30 tokens at the end of a prompt of 2,999 tokens. A changing question costs about 30 tokens of prefill, not 2,999. "Hash the system prompt and route by it." Routing matters when several servers split the traffic, but this was one server, and the prompt differed on every request before routing could help. The lesson to carry Treat the prompt layout as part of the serving system. Put the content that never changes first, the content that changes per session next, and the content that changes per request last. Keep ids, timestamps, hashes and random seeds out of the system prompt, and keep tool definitions and JSON keys in a fixed order. Before you change any cache flag, read the cached token count on your real requests. A prompt fix can recover a hit rate that no server flag can. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual measures the three prompt forms in the prefix-friendly prompts page and explains the tree in the RadixCache page , the vLLM manual gives the same rule in its prefix cache page , and the RadixAttention lesson builds the mechanism from scratch. Recap What to keep from this case Prompt layout is part of the serving system. Never put a changing value at the start of a shared prefix. Send trace ids as metadata. Check the cache hit rate before tuning memory. a2110: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Health Probes That Added Load: Liveness vs Readiness Lesson 21.10 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.23 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, forward deployed AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 against vLLM 0.31.0 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory The situation In plain words first Pods restart in a loop exactly during traffic spikes. The liveness probe generated a token on every check, so it waited in the same queue as the users, timed out under load, and killed the busiest pod, which pushed its users onto the next one. The case trains the idea that a probe is a client: if it shares the users' queue, it fails exactly when restarting hurts most. A platform team runs SGLang pods on Kubernetes. The liveness probe asks /health every few seconds with a short timeout, and a failed probe restarts the pod. During a traffic spike the busiest pods restart in a loop. A probe times out, the pod is killed in the middle of its answers, its users move to the other pods, and the next busiest pod fails its probe. The service recovers only when the spike passes. The scheduler log of a restarted pod shows the probes themselves, as prefill batches of one token between the user requests. The ticket proposes two changes: a longer probe timeout and a higher memory limit for the pod. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The health probe around the ready line of our L4 server Copy The three health endpoints and the two settings behind them Copy What the code claims and what two incidents showed Copy The routes of a vLLM server with an API key, with and without the key Copy The first health check of a vLLM server after startup Copy Questions to answer first Read the log around the ready line. What did the server do when the probe asked for its health, and what does that cost under load? Name the three endpoints and the question that each one answers. The code says that the probe costs nothing when the server is busy. Why is that true for the work and false for the timing? Design the probes: readiness, liveness and a deep check. Give the endpoint, the setting, the timeout and what happens on a failure. The other engine answers its health route without generating. What does that change for a deep check there? A restart in the middle of answers also needs a clean stop. Which signal, to which process, and how long do you wait? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A liveness probe that does real work competes with user requests. ✗ A shorter probe timeout makes failure detection safer. Under load it makes healthy-but-busy pods fail the probe and restart. ✓ Readiness decides whether a pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether it is restarted. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the eight log lines in order. At 14:43:37 the probe asked /health and got a 503, because the server was still starting. The server then sent itself one request to /generate , froze the garbage collector, and printed the ready line. Two seconds later the scheduler logged a prefill batch of one new token, and right after it the probe got its 200. Nothing else was running. That one-token batch was the probe. By default /health does not only answer, it sends a request through the model and waits for the result. The second listing names the three endpoints. /ready returns 200 when the tokenizer manager is ready, and it sends nothing to the model. /health and /health_generate share one handler: they return 503 while the server starts or shuts down, and otherwise they send a one-token request with max_new_tokens of 1 and wait for any output from the detokenizer. SGLANG_ENABLE_HEALTH_ENDPOINT_GENERATION defaults to true, so a plain /health generates too. The wait is SGLANG_HEALTH_CHECK_TIMEOUT , 20 s by default, after which the handler marks the server unhealthy and returns 503. The third listing is the subtle part. The docstring is right about the work: any output from the scheduler counts as proof of life, so a busy server does not need to finish the probe's token. It is wrong about the timing. The probe request waits in the same queue as the users, and when the first token of anyone takes longer than the probe timeout, the probe fails. The two incidents show both halves. One report saw the health check fail with no response from the detokenizer for 20 seconds, on a large model under high load. A second found that a timed-out probe left its request in the scheduler, so failed probes accumulated. Under a spike, the probe is a user who gives up after 20 s and tells the orchestrator to kill the server. The last two listings are the other engine. Its /health , /ping and /load routes answer 200 without an API key, and its first health check after startup is followed by the model list, not by a prefill batch. The manual says why: that health route answers 200 when the engine runs and does not generate a token, so a 200 does not prove that a request completes. On that engine the health route is a liveness check by design, and a deep check means one short request. What actually happened The probes were the incident. The liveness probe generated a token on every call, waited in the user queue, timed out under load and killed the busiest pod, which moved its load to the next pod. Set /ready as the readiness probe, so a pod joins the service when it can accept requests. For liveness, set SGLANG_ENABLE_HEALTH_ENDPOINT_GENERATION=false , after which /health returns 200 without a request to the scheduler, and keep that probe on the pod. Move /health_generate to a slower deep check that alerts a person and restarts nothing. The probe timeout then stops mattering under load, and the memory limit was never the problem. On the other engine, use /health for liveness as it is, and make the deep check one short request. Then fix the stop. Only a SIGTERM to the main process drains the running requests: the server returns 503 on /health during the drain, logs the remaining requests every 5 s, and exits when none remain. A signal to the whole process group or a forced exit stops work in progress. Set the termination grace period longer than the longest request at the output cap, and cap max_tokens first, or a drain can never finish in time. Wrong turns "Raise the probe timeout to a minute." The probe still waits in the user queue, and a timed-out probe left its request in the scheduler in one report. A longer timeout hides the overload for longer and then kills the pod anyway. "Raise the memory limit of the pod." The pods did not run out of memory. They were killed by the orchestrator after a probe waited too long. "Use the generating endpoint for liveness, because it proves that the model works." A deep check that restarts the busiest pod under load is the incident. A deep check should alert a person. "Kill the pod fast so the others take over." A signal to the process group killed the scheduler child first and failed every running request. Only a SIGTERM to the main process drains. The lesson to carry A probe is a client, and a client that waits in the same queue as the users will fail exactly when the users wait, which is when a restart hurts most. Separate the questions: can the process accept requests, is the process alive, and can the model produce a token. Give each question its own endpoint, its own schedule and its own consequence, and never let the slow question trigger a restart. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual shows the probe in the log in the health page and gives the probe settings, the incidents and the drain in the operating page , the vLLM manual explains its health route in its health page and the production probes in the production page , and the SRE for AI lesson covers runbooks for this class of loop. Recap What to keep from this case A probe is a client; do not put it in the user queue. Use a cheap readiness check for traffic decisions. Make liveness check that the process is alive, not that it can generate. Restarting a busy pod moves its load to the next pod. a2111: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Startup OOM on a Shared GPU: Max Model Length Lesson 21.11 15 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 15 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, screen. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : the shared second L4 of a two-GPU node, with another team's processes on it The situation In plain words first On a GPU shared with another team, a server stops at start with an error naming a maximum length of 40,960 tokens. A colleague's first fix lowers the memory fraction too. The error itself points to the real lever: the server tried to reserve room for the longest possible request, and the service never sends anything close. The case trains reading a startup failure as a question about your traffic. An on-call engineer deploys Qwen/Qwen3-8B with vLLM on the second L4 of a node. Another team runs its pods on that GPU and holds part of its memory. The server stops before it prints the KV cache size line, and the log ends with a ValueError that names a maximum of 40,960 tokens. A colleague has seen the error before and sets two flags: --gpu-memory-utilization 0.83 , to stay under the memory that the other team uses, and --max-model-len 2928 , which matches the pool of 2,928 tokens that they want for a test. The server fails again, with almost the same message. The engineer now wants to raise the memory fraction to 0.95 and try once more. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The first start, with the default maximum model length Copy The second start, with the maximum length set to the pool size Copy A start on the same shared GPU that reached the pool line Copy The three startup failures and the flag for each Copy Questions to answer first The error names 40,960 tokens. Where does that number come from, and why does one request at that length decide whether the server starts? The second attempt set the maximum length to the pool size and missed by 16 tokens. Explain the arithmetic that the error line shows. On a shared GPU, what does the memory fraction describe, and why is raising it the wrong first move? Which startup line proves that a fix worked, and what do you compare it with? Put the three flags in the order you would change them, and name the log text that points to each. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ The maximum model length decides how much cache memory the server must reserve. ✗ Lowering the memory fraction is always the first fix on a shared GPU. It leaves less room for the cache; lowering the maximum length to real request sizes is the first lever. ✓ The limit should be the longest request the service really sends, with some margin. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the first error from the end. vLLM must be able to serve at least one request at the model's maximum sequence length. For this model that length is 40,960 tokens, taken from the model config when nobody sets --max-model-len . One request of that length needs 5.62 GiB of KV cache, and after the weights and the startup profile only 1.01 GiB was free on this shared card. The message even computes the answer: the estimated maximum model length is 7,360 tokens. The server did not fail because the GPU is too small for the model. It failed because the default length is far longer than any request the service will send. The second error is the same check with a different margin. The settings line shows max_model_len at 2,928, the fraction at 0.83 and a block override of 183 blocks of 16 tokens, which is 2,928 tokens. The check compares one request of the maximum length with the KV cache memory that the profile left, and that memory holds only 2,912 tokens. Both sides print as 0.4 GiB, so the check failed by a hair. A length equal to the pool that you want does not help when the profile leaves less memory than that pool. The third listing is what success looks like on the same card. A smaller model started with a fraction of 0.5, loaded 1.12 GiB of weights, and printed the two lines that matter: Available KV cache memory: 9.02 GiB and GPU KV cache size: 84,480 tokens , with the maximum concurrency for the default length at 2.06 times. Those two lines are the proof that a start reached the pool. The last listing maps the three errors to three flags. An error about the maximum sequence length points at --max-model-len . An error that the free memory is below the desired utilization points at --gpu-memory-utilization , or at the other process. A CUDA out of memory during the profile or the graph capture points at the batch limits or the graph capture size. What actually happened The fix was one flag, read from the error. We set --max-model-len 2048 , which covers our 640-token requests, and the server started. Later we raised it to 2,304 tokens so that tests with 2,048-token prefixes fit. On a shared GPU the fraction and the maximum length work together, and the maximum length is the one to lower first, down to the longest request that the service really sends. Raising the fraction to 0.95 would have been wrong twice over. The fraction is a limit for one vLLM instance on the whole GPU memory, not a share of what is free when the server starts, so a higher fraction on a shared card claims memory that another tenant already holds. And the first error asked for 5.62 GiB for a length that no request needs. When two instances must share one GPU with a known pool each, set the cache in bytes with --kv-cache-memory-bytes instead. After every change, start the server with tee on the log and grep for GPU KV cache size , then compare the pool with the count from the memory page. Wrong turns "Raise the memory fraction until it starts." The fraction is a share of the whole GPU, not of the free memory. On a shared card a higher fraction claims memory that another process holds, and the start can fail later in the profile or the other team's job can fail instead. "The GPU is too small for an 8B model." The weights loaded. The check that failed was for one request of 40,960 tokens, and the message said that 7,360 tokens would fit. "Set the maximum length equal to the pool." The second start did that and missed by 16 tokens. The pool is counted in blocks of 16, and the length check needs a little margin. "Use the blocks override in production to force the pool." The override does not check that the memory exists. It is a test flag, and on a shared card it fails at the first request that needs the memory. The lesson to carry A startup check that fails on a limit is a question about your traffic, not about your hardware. Read the number in the error, ask which setting put it there and what the real requests need, and change that setting first. On any shared machine, a fraction of total memory is a promise that the other tenants did not make, so prefer limits that name the exact bytes you want. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual matches each startup error to one flag in the startup out of memory page , counts the pool in the memory page and reads the startup lines in the health page , and the SGLang manual shows the same startup sizing in its memory fraction page . Recap What to keep from this case Read the number in the error and find which setting produced it. Lower the maximum length to real traffic first. On a shared GPU, memory fraction and maximum length work together. Raise limits later only with measurements. a2112: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Bigger Prefill Chunk That Would Not Start: CUDA Graph Capture Lesson 21.12 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4, the first GPU of a two-GPU node The situation In plain words first Doubling the prefill chunk size should halve the scheduler turns for long prompts, but the server never starts, and the log ends with a PyTorch "INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED". It looks like a framework bug. It is an out-of-memory error during graph capture, surfacing as a confusing assert. The case trains you to look for the first resource failure behind a strange error, and to keep a control run with the default. An engineer wants long prompts to get their first token sooner on an L4 server that runs Qwen/Qwen3-8B . The idea is simple: a prefill chunk twice as large means half as many scheduler turns for a long prompt. They start the server with --chunked-prefill-size 8192 and leave every other flag at its default. The server never becomes ready. The log ends with a RuntimeError from PyTorch that reads INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED and asks the reader to report a bug to PyTorch. The engineer opens a bug report with the PyTorch project and proposes to pin an older PyTorch for the whole fleet. The same server with no chunk flag has served every benchmark run on this card. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The engine, the model, the card and the one changed flag Copy The last six lines of the failed start Copy The same server with the default chunk Copy The default start on the same card: the pool, the free memory and the prefill capture Copy The settings line of the default start Copy The default chunk and the largest decode batch, by GPU memory Copy How the manual reads the failed start Copy Questions to answer first The last line asks for a PyTorch bug report. Which line holds the real error, and how do you tell a cause from a consequence in this log? The pool is the same size in the failed start and in the sweep. Where did the memory go? Which startup step runs after the pool and needs memory outside it? How does the chunk size change what that step needs? The default start captured the same step on the same card. How much memory did its first captured shape use, and how much was left when it began? If the team still wants a chunk of 8192 here, which flag makes room and which flag should they not touch? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A capture interrupted by running out of memory can end in an unrelated-looking assert. ✗ An INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED always means a bug to report upstream. Here it was a symptom; the cause was memory for the 8192-token prefill graph. ✓ The default chunk of 4096 started and served every run on the same card: that is the control. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read upward from the assert and stop at the first error. Two lines above the PyTorch assert is torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: out of memory . The assert, markCaptureEnd called with no captures in progress , is what the allocator says after a graph capture was cut short by that error. The scheduler then received a SIGQUIT from its child. The manual reads it the same way: the real error is the out-of-memory line, and the assert is the consequence. Check what the pool took. The failed start allocated a pool of 24,094 tokens, with 1.65 GB each for K and V, the same pool that the sweep servers on this card had. After the pool, 2.90 GB was free. So the pool did not grow with the chunk, and the memory that ran out was memory outside the pool. Find the step that failed. The line Capturing prefill shape (num_tokens=8192 avail_mem=2.33 GB) names it. Since the breakable graph for prefill arrived in the CUDA builds, startup captures a prefill graph for each shape up to the chunk size. The largest shape is the chunk itself. A capture of 8192 tokens holds the activations of an 8192-token prefill, and that needed more than the 2.33 GB that was left. Compare with a start that worked. The default start on this card shows the same sequence with a smaller shape. Its pool held 22,939 tokens that day, 2.86 GB was free after the pool, and the first captured shape was num_tokens=4096 with 2.28 GB available. That capture ended after 48.33 s with 0.83 GB used and 1.45 GB still free. Twice the tokens in the capture asked for more than the whole remainder. Read where the default comes from. The table in the CUDA graphs page gives a chunk of 4096 for a card of 20 to 35 GB, and 8192 only from 60 GB upward. The default is sized to the memory that a capture can expect on that card. The scheduler page measured chunk changes on the GB10 and found no gain at 1 and 2 requests each second, and a loss at 0.5 with a smaller chunk. On the L4 the larger chunk never started, so there is no measurement of its gain. What actually happened Close the PyTorch report. The assert is a symptom of a capture that an out-of-memory error interrupted, and the cause is the prefill graph for 8192 tokens on a card with 2.33 GB left after the pool. The team kept the default chunk of 4096, and that server, on that card, started and served every run, which is the control that the incident record states. If a larger chunk is still wanted on this card, make room for the capture instead of removing it. Lower --mem-fraction-static by one step, so the pool shrinks and the capture has more than 2.33 GB, then read the Capture target prefill CUDA graph end line for the memory the capture used. The CUDA graphs page gives the order: fix capture memory with a smaller graph batch size or a lower fraction, and keep graphs on. Then measure the first token at the team's prompt lengths with both chunks before the change ships, because the manual found no gain from a chunk change on the machine where it could run both. Wrong turns "Pin an older PyTorch, the assert says to report a bug." The assert reports an interrupted capture. The out-of-memory line two lines above it is the cause, and an older PyTorch changes nothing about free memory. "Raise the memory fraction so the capture gets more memory." The fraction gives memory to the weights and the pool. Raising it shrinks what is left for the capture. Lower it. "Turn CUDA graphs off and keep the big chunk." A server without decode graphs pays launch time on every token for every user. Fix the capture memory and keep the graphs. "A bigger chunk always makes prefill faster, so it is worth the memory." The manual measured chunk sizes on the GB10 and found the three settings inside the seed spread of each other at 1 and 2 requests per second. Measure before you pay. The lesson to carry When a startup log ends in an assert from a library, read upward to the first error, because the library is often the second victim. Then ask which step the error fell in and what that step's memory depends on. A flag that changes a shape, such as a chunk size or a graph batch size, changes the memory of the capture that uses that shape, and the pool that the fraction sized does not move to make room. On a small card, the default chunk is a memory decision, not a speed decision. How this connects Where this is taught The scheduler page of SGLang 101 records the failed start in its chunked prefill part , the graph capture section states the default chunk by GPU memory and the rule for capture memory , and the memory page explains how the fraction splits memory between the pool and everything else . Recap What to keep from this case Look behind strange errors for the first resource failure. Larger chunks need larger captured graphs and more memory. Keep the default as a control run. Change one setting at a time. Mark complete and continue Mark as not done Previous 21.11 · Startup OOM on a Shared GPU: Max Model Length Next 21.13 · Three Refusals from a Local Container Registry
a2113: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Three Refusals from a Local Container Registry Lesson 21.13 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : sbx v0.47.0 Model : none; shell commands inside the sandbox Hardware : one Mac with the microVM runtime The situation In plain words first Three different commands fail in a row while publishing a sandbox kit, and it is tempting to blame one broken release. They are three separate causes: a validation command for older kit versions, a build driver that cannot export the required image format, and a registry missing from the allowlist. The case trains splitting a chain of failures into independent questions instead of looking for one villain. A platform team writes its first v3 kit, a shell workload with one allowed host, and pushes it to the team's own registry. In the capture a local registry at localhost:15000 stands in for it. Three commands then fail in a row. sbx kit inspect on the pushed reference says the kit cannot be installed because its source is not in the allowlist. sbx kit inspect on the source directory tries to build it and stops with an exporter error. sbx kit validate on the same directory says the kit is a v3 source kit and the load path has no kit builder. An engineer concludes that v3 kits do not work in this release and proposes to rewrite the kit as a v2 mixin. You have the three failures, the build logs of two pushes made with two different builders, and the validate output for a v2 mixin from the same tree. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The two settings that the refused inspect suggests, and its exit code Copy Sbx kit inspect on the v3 source directory Copy The start of the build with a docker-container builder Copy The export and push steps of the docker-container build Copy The same build with the default driver of the host daemon Copy Sbx kit validate on the v3 source kit Copy Sbx kit validate on the v2 mixin Copy Questions to answer first Three failures, one conclusion. Group the failures by the component that produced each message before you read the build logs. Which sbx kit commands accept a v3 kit, and which do not? The two builds used different drivers. What did each export, and which result is a kit? What does the allowlist refusal protect, and which of the two suggested settings would you apply? How does the kit reach a sandbox once the three causes are fixed, and what does the manual admit it did not capture? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Three errors in a row can have three causes. ✗ If validate rejects a kit, the kit is malformed. The command targets older kit versions; on a v3 kit it is simply the wrong tool. ✓ An install refused because the source is not allowlisted is a policy decision, not a broken artifact. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Separate the generations. sbx kit validate passes the v2 mixin with VALID and refuses the v3 directory as a v3 source kit with no builder. The manual's ruling on conflict C13 is that validate , pack , push and pull are v1 and v2 tooling. A v3 kit is an OCI image, built and pushed with Docker tooling. So the validate failure is not a defect: the command was never meant for this kit. Read the two build logs for the driver. The build that worked ran on a docker-container builder. Its export step wrote layers, a manifest, a config, an attestation manifest and a manifest list, then pushed the manifest. The other build ran on the docker driver of the host daemon; its export wrote an image, named it, and pushed it with docker, with no manifest list and no attestation. The manual read the registry afterwards: the default driver pushed a Docker schema 2 manifest with no annotations, and an image without the descriptor annotation is not a kit to any consumer. The second push looked successful and produced something no sandbox can use. Read the source inspect failure in that light. sbx kit inspect on the directory tried to build the kit with the host daemon, and the OCI exporter is not supported for the docker driver. The fix is the same as in step 2: a docker-container builder, or the containerd image store that the error names. Read the admission rule. The refusal of the pushed reference comes from kit.allowedSources , which defaults to docker.io/ since v0.34.0, as conflict C40 records. The error suggests two values. Add the registry prefix localhost:15000/m101/ , and do not set * : the error itself says that allowing any remote source is not recommended. The descriptor line of the good build names the frontend 3.0.0-m.8 , a milestone, so the pinned frontend version belongs in the ticket too. Run it by reference. A v3 workload is consumed by sbx run or sbx create with the reference in place of the agent name, and a sandbox cannot mix v3 kits with v1 or v2 kits. The manual says plainly that no capture shows sbx running a v3 kit, because the capture kit never changes sbx settings . Say so when you report. What actually happened Three causes, and none of them is a broken release. The sbx kit artifact commands are v1 and v2 tooling, so validate on a v3 directory is the wrong command. The default docker build driver cannot export an OCI image, so the push it made is not a kit, and the source inspect fails for the same reason; a docker-container builder exported the manifest list with the descriptor annotations. The daemon admits kits only from the prefixes in kit.allowedSources , which is docker.io/ by default, so the team's registry prefix must be added. With the builder changed and the prefix added, the kit runs by reference. The rewrite to a v2 mixin is withdrawn, and the team records that its own run of the kit is the first measurement, because the manual has none. Wrong turns "Set kit.allowedSources to * so every registry works." The error names that option and advises against it. The allowlist is the only check between a typed reference and a kit that configures a sandbox. "The push with the default driver succeeded, so the registry copy is fine." It pushed an image with no descriptor annotation. A consumer sees an ordinary image, not a kit. "Rewrite the kit as a v2 mixin because validate passes on that." The v2 tooling passed because that kit was v2. The v3 kit needs Buildx, not a different format. "Create the kit builder sandbox and run validate again." In the capture the source build ran in the host daemon, and the builder status read not created after it. The validate path still names only v1 and v2 artifacts. The lesson to carry When one new thing fails three ways, name the component behind each message before you judge the thing. A format check, a build exporter and an admission list are three systems, and each has its own fix. A push that returns success is not proof that the artifact has the shape its consumer needs. Read the manifest back. How this connects Where this is taught The descriptor page records the two builds and the allowlist refusal, the kit commands page gives the v2 tooling and the kit settings, and the conflicts register rules on C13 and C40. Recap What to keep from this case Split a chain of failures into separate questions. Check that each command supports the format you use. Check the build driver can export what you need. Allowlists are policy; change them deliberately. a2114: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Resumed Run That Silently Restarted at Step 0 Lesson 21.14 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first A long training run dies at night and is restarted from the newest checkpoint folder. In the morning the reward curve starts from the beginning again: the resume silently did not happen. The checkpoint was pointed at the wrong level of the folder tree, and the trainer starts fresh without a message when it finds nothing to load. The case trains checking that a resume really resumed, from the log, before walking away. A long GRPO run saves a checkpoint every 20 steps into a host folder that is mounted into the container. One night the run dies. The on-call engineer starts the same command again at once. To be safe, she points --load at the newest iter_ folder inside the checkpoint folder, and she keeps the same > runs/plain.log redirect, because the dashboard reads that file. In the morning the reward curve of the new run begins where the first run began days ago. The first step line in the new log reads step 0 . The team splits: one side says the checkpoints are corrupt, the other says the resume feature does not work on this trainer. Nobody can say why the first run died, because the old log is gone. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The two runs of the restart check Copy The first run: its save line, and its silence about the empty folder Copy The second run: what a real resume prints Copy What the checkpoint folder holds after both runs Copy The manual's rule for the load flag and the log file Copy The lines a resumed run must show, and the test before a long run Copy The files that the checkpoint converter wrote Copy Questions to answer first The new log starts at step 0 . Which lines must appear above it when a resume works, and what does their absence prove? How loudly does Miles complain when the folder it loads from holds no checkpoint? What does that mean for the runbook? The flag named the newest iter_ folder. Why is that the wrong path, and which file does Miles read to find the last step? The restart also destroyed something that the team now misses. What, and how do you restart so that it survives? Write the test that every long run passes before it starts, with the step numbers you expect to see. The team wants to serve the model from a saved step. Which tool does that, and what does it need besides the checkpoint? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A trainer may start from step 0 without an error if it finds no step to load. ✗ Pointing at the newest iter_ folder is the safest choice. The tracker file lives in the parent checkpoint folder; that is what --load needs. ✓ Writing the resumed run to a new log file keeps the old evidence intact. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the shape of the check. The manual ran two short runs with the same flags: --save /ckpt/run-a --save-interval 20 --load /ckpt/run-a . The first ran 2 steps on an empty folder. The second ran 4 steps on the folder the first one left. This is the smallest test of a resume, and it is what the team should have run before the long run. Read the first run. It wrote [FSDP] Saved checkpoint to /ckpt/run-a/iter_0000002 , because Miles always saves after the last step. The count of lines that mention a missing tracker or a missing folder is 0. The load folder was empty and Miles said nothing about it. That silence is the whole incident: a run that finds nothing to load looks exactly like a run that was never asked to load. Read the second run. It printed three Loaded lines, for the model, the optimizer and the LR scheduler, each with the folder of the step. Its first step line is step 2 , not step 0 , and it saved iter_0000004 at its end. These three lines and that first step number are the proof of a resume. The team's log has none of them, so the new run started fresh. Read the folder. It holds iter_0000002 , iter_0000004 , a rollout folder and one file, latest_checkpointed_iteration.txt . That file is the tracker. It sits in the parent folder, not inside an iter_ folder. Apply the rule for the flag. --load names the parent folder, never one iter_ folder inside it, because Miles reads the tracker file there to find the last saved step. The engineer pointed the flag at a folder with no tracker, so Miles had no step to resume, which is the same case as an empty folder, and the manual's test shows that this case prints nothing. Apply the rule for the log. The manual asks for a new log file on a restart, such as > runs/plain-resume.log , because the redirect empties the old log and the old log is where the cause of the failure is. The team lost the cause of the night's crash with the same keystroke that lost the resume. Read the converter output. The FSDP trainer writes distributed checkpoints that other tools cannot load. The converter turned the step 2 checkpoint into a model folder with the weights, the configuration and the tokenizer files, given the base model folder for the configuration and the tokenizer. What actually happened The checkpoints were fine. The resume did not happen because --load named an iter_ folder, which holds no tracker file, and Miles starts fresh without a message when it finds no step to load. Point --load at the parent folder, /ckpt/run-a , start again with a new log file, and read the three Loaded lines and the first step number before you walk away. The run then continues from the last saved step, as the check run did from step 2 . Make the check part of the runbook. Before a long run, run the command with MILES_NUM_ROLLOUT=2 , then again with MILES_NUM_ROLLOUT=4 , and require step 2 as the first step line of the second run. Choose --save-interval from the step time, so that a crash costs less than you accept: with a step of five minutes, an interval of 12 loses at most one hour. To serve a saved step, run the converter inside the container with the step folder, an output folder and the base model folder. Wrong turns "The checkpoints are corrupt." The folder holds the step folders and the tracker file, and the manual's second run loaded the model, the optimizer and the LR scheduler from the same kind of folder. Nothing in the new log says that a load failed, because no load was attempted. "The resume feature does not work on the FSDP trainer." The check run resumed at step 2 on the FSDP trainer and saved iter_0000004 . The feature needs the parent folder, and it got a step folder. "Point the flag at the step folder to be sure it loads the right step." The tracker file in the parent folder names the last step. A step folder has no tracker, so the flag loads nothing. "Keep the same log file so the dashboard does not break." The redirect empties the old log and destroys the only record of the crash. Use a new file for each restart and point the dashboard at a folder. The lesson to carry A feature that fails silently must be verified by its positive signal, never by the absence of an error. For every resume, every cache load and every state restore, know the log lines that prove it happened and the first value that must differ from a cold start, and test the whole restart path on a short run before you rely on it. Never let a restart overwrite the evidence of the failure that caused it. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual gives the checkpoint flags, the resume lines, the two-step test and the converter in the failures page . Recap What to keep from this case Check the loaded step in the log before trusting a resume. Point resume options at the level the tool expects. Never overwrite the previous run's log. Silent fallbacks deserve explicit checks. a2115: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Reward Module Import Error That Hung RL Training Lesson 21.15 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first A training job ran for two hours, completed zero steps and was killed at its time limit. The custom reward function could not be imported by the worker processes, the first rollout failed, and the run never exited. The case trains two habits: test an import in the exact environment that will use it, and treat a job that hangs after an error as a separate problem from the error itself. A team adds its own reward function to a GRPO run. The function lives in a file in the lab folder on the host, and the run names it with --custom-rm-path my_rewards.custom_rm . A run queue starts the job at night. In the morning the queue shows that the job reached its time limit and came back with code 124, and that it completed zero steps. The container had been up for about two hours. The host also runs the watchdog from an earlier incident, the script that stops a run whose rollout engine died. It did not fire. A teammate reads that as proof that the engine was healthy, blames a slow GPU, and proposes to double the time limit and start the job again. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. What the run queue recorded for this run Copy The first and the last timestamped line, and the size of the log Copy Every minute of the log that held a 503 line Copy The exception from the rollout executor Copy The summary that the capture kit wrote for this run Copy The counting rule of the watchdog Copy Questions to answer first The exit code is 124 and the step count is zero. What does that pair tell you before you open the log? The log holds 183,248 lines. Is this a hang, a crash, or something else? Where in the log do you read first? Count the 503 lines per minute and apply the watchdog rule by hand. Was the watchdog wrong not to stop this run? Read the exception. Which process raised it, and why does one missing environment variable reach that process? Miles kept running after the error. Which second guard would have caught this run, and what does it watch? What do you run before the next attempt, and which log line proves that the fix worked? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Code importable on the host may be invisible to worker processes in a container. ✗ A job that reaches its time limit was just slow. Zero completed steps after two hours points to a failure the job never exited from. ✓ A one-line import test in the container would have shown the problem in seconds. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the queue record. The queue started the job at 00:19:01 and recorded RC 124 at 02:17:10 with steps=0 . Code 124 is what the queue writes when its own time limit stops a job. So the run did not end by itself, and it did not finish a step in two hours. More time would not have changed the count. Read the span and the size. The first timestamped line is at 00:19:02 and the last at 02:17:06, and the file holds 183,248 lines. A run that writes a log of that size for two hours is not asleep. It is busy with something that is not training. The reason is near the start, not at the end. Run the watchdog arithmetic yourself. The log holds 44 lines of 503 Service Unavailable , 40 of them in the minute of 00:24 and 4 in the minute of 00:25. The watchdog reads the last 60 s every 30 s and adds a strike only if the count is above 100. It needs 10 strikes in a row. This run never gave it one strike. The watchdog was correct. The rollout engine did not die, and a short burst like this can come from a healthy engine. Read the exception. At 00:21:09 the rollout executor logged that a rollout task raised ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'my_rewards' . The scoring of answers runs in the Ray workers, and that is where the import failed. After this line no rollout 0 line ever appears, because no answer can be scored. The 503 burst three minutes later is noise next to this line. Find what the run did not pass. The kit summary says it: the run passed --custom-rm-path my_rewards.custom_rm and not -e PYTHONPATH=/root/lab . The container sees the lab folder as /root/lab , but Python does not search that folder unless the variable names it. The launcher passes the variable on to the Ray workers, so the one setting fixes the import in the process that needs it. See why nothing stopped the run. The manual records the same test: after this error the job stayed up for two hours with no rollout step, and the watchdog did not stop it because the engine wrote only 44 error lines. The watchdog watches for one failure shape, a dead engine. A run that cannot score its answers has a different shape, almost no errors and no progress. What actually happened The run failed at its first rollout because the reward module was not on the Python path of the Ray workers. Stop the container, add -e PYTHONPATH=/root/lab next to MILES_EXTRA_ARGS , and start again. Before that, test the import in the container with the one-line command from the manual, which scores one answer and should print 1.0 , and run the function on ten answers that you scored by hand, including an empty answer and an answer cut at the length limit. The line that proves the fix is the first rollout 0 line, which shows a rollout/raw_reward that your function computed. Then give the queue two rules. Treat a time-limit exit with steps=0 as a failure, not as a slow run. Stop a run that shows no rollout 0 line within ten minutes of its start, which is the manual's sign that the engine or the trainer did not start. Wrong turns "The watchdog missed a dead engine, so lower its limit." The run wrote 44 error lines in two hours, all inside two minutes. A healthy run with 16 answers per prompt wrote 2,209 in one minute. A limit low enough to catch 44 fires on every healthy burst, and still misses this run, which went quiet for the rest of the two hours. "Double the time limit and start it again." The log grew to 183,248 lines with no finished step. More time buys more lines and the same count. "Rebuild the image with the reward file inside." That works until the next change to the reward. The launcher already passes PYTHONPATH to the Ray workers, so one variable on the run command is the fix. "Write the reward as a plain function so the import gets simpler." The import failed on the module name, before any function ran. A plain function fails later and in a different way, because Miles awaits the result. The lesson to carry A job that cannot start its work and does not stop is the most expensive failure, because it spends its whole time limit and gives no signal. Every guard watches for one failure shape. The dead-engine guard counts errors, and an import error produces almost none. Add a guard for progress, such as a first step by a deadline, read the exit code of the queue as data, and read a log from its start, where the first exception sits. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual gives the two settings for a custom reward and records this hang in the custom reward page , lists the symptom in the troubleshooting page , builds the error-count rule in the watchdog page , and names the ten-minute rule for a missing first step in the first ten steps page . Recap What to keep from this case Test imports in the environment that will run them. Set the module path for workers explicitly. Score a few known answers before a long run. A hang after an error needs its own fix. a2116: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Rolling Update That Dropped Every Streamed Answer: SIGTERM Handling Lesson 21.16 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.23 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, forward deployed AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 on its MLX path Model : mlx-community/Qwen3-0.6B-4bit Hardware : one laptop with unified memory, which captures no CUDA graphs The situation In plain words first Every deploy breaks the answers that were being streamed, and each stopped server logs a crash. The orchestrator sent one polite stop signal; a wrapper script forwarded it to every process in the group, killing the scheduler before the server could drain its requests. The case trains following a signal from the orchestrator to the process that should receive it. A platform team deploys SGLang pods with a rolling update. The container starts the server through a small wrapper script. When the orchestrator asks the pod to stop, the wrapper forwards the signal it receives to its whole process group. Every deploy produces a burst of failed requests. The users who were in the middle of an answer get a broken stream, and the pod log of each stopped server reports a crash, although nothing was wrong with the model. The on-call engineer reads the end of one log and finds the crash in it. The team has two proposals: raise the grace period for termination from 30 s to five minutes, and add a retry in the gateway for the broken streams. You review the evidence before either change ships. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The end of a stopped server's log, as the team read it Copy What the server does on a SIGTERM to its main process Copy A SIGTERM to the main process only, with one request running Copy The request completes and the server exits Copy What the client saw across the drain Copy The two exits that skip the drain, and the grace period rule Copy Questions to answer first The log says that a subprocess crashed with exit code -15. What is that exit code, and who sent it? Read the drain description. Which process must receive the signal, and what happens to the health endpoint while the drain runs? The second capture sends the signal to one process while a request runs. Trace the request from the signal to the exit code. A longer grace period was proposed. What decides the right value, and why does the output cap come first? Name the two ways a server skips the drain, and the environment variable trap at this version. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A graceful stop needs the stop signal to reach the server's main process, which then drains. ✗ Forwarding the signal to the whole process group makes shutdown more reliable. It killed the child processes first, so the server could not finish its answers. ✓ exec in the wrapper makes the server the container's main process. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the exit code. A negative exit code is a signal number, and 15 is SIGTERM. In the first listing the parent logs that it received SIGTERM and starts to drain, and in the same second its scheduler child dies of the same signal. Two processes do not receive one signal at the same instant unless the sender addressed the group. The wrapper did that. The scheduler died first, the parent found a dead child, took the crash path, slept 5 seconds for diagnostics and killed the tree. Every running request died with the scheduler. The crash in the log is the symptom of the wrapper, not a fault in the server. Read who owns the drain. The manual describes the path. On SIGTERM the HTTP server sets gracefully_exit , and /health begins to answer 503. A watchdog in the tokenizer manager checks the flag every 5 s and logs the remaining requests every 5 s until none remain. Then it sends ShutdownReq to the schedulers and gives them 15 s to exit before it kills them. The drain lives in the main process. A scheduler that gets the signal itself never gets the shutdown request, so the drain cannot begin. Read the clean stop. In the second capture, the probe sent SIGTERM to the server process alone while one request for 3000 tokens ran. The decode batches continue after the signal line, and one second later the log says that a health check arrived during shutdown and returned 503. That 503 is what the orchestrator needs: stop sending traffic here, the pod is on its way out. Ten seconds later the request returns 200, the watchdog logs zero remaining requests, and the server process finishes. Read what the client saw. Health 200 before the signal, 503 during the drain, the request complete with all 3000 tokens and the finish reason length after 14.2 s, and an exit code of 0. Nothing was lost, and the server was gone about thirteen seconds after the signal. Read the two exits that skip the drain. A server that is already UnHealthy exits at once, and so does a server with SGL_FORCE_SHUTDOWN set. The environment module declares the new name SGLANG_FORCE_SHUTDOWN , and its compatibility code copies old names to new names only, so the watchdog at this version still reads the old name. Setting only the new name does nothing. The manual read this in the code, did not run it, and calls it a likely bug. The same listing gives the rule for the grace period: longer than one request at the output cap, and a 32K-token answer at 30 tokens per second needs more than 18 minutes. What actually happened The wrapper was the incident. It turned one SIGTERM into a signal for every process, the scheduler died before the parent could drain, and the parent reported a crash it did not cause. The fix is to make sglang serve the main process of the container, with exec in the script or as the entrypoint, so that the orchestrator's signal reaches the server alone. The capture is the proof: with the signal sent to one process, the request for 3000 tokens finished, /health returned 503 during the drain, and the exit code was 0. Then size the stop. Cap max_tokens first, and set the grace period longer than one request at that cap. A five-minute grace period with no output cap still cuts every answer that runs longer than five minutes. For a forced stop in a test environment, set SGL_FORCE_SHUTDOWN=1 , never only the new name. The gateway retry stays out: a drain finishes the answer on the pod that holds its cache, and a retry starts the answer again from its first token on another pod. Wrong turns "Raise the grace period to five minutes." The signal reached the scheduler child directly, so the drain never began. No grace period helps a drain that does not start, and a grace period shorter than one answer at the output cap still cuts answers. "Retry the broken streams at the gateway." A retry pays for the prompt and the generated tokens a second time on another pod. The drain finishes the answer where it runs. "Set SGLANG_FORCE_SHUTDOWN=1 for a fast stop in staging." At this version the watchdog reads SGL_FORCE_SHUTDOWN, so the new name does nothing, and a forced stop skips the drain, which is the incident. "The scheduler crashed, so file a bug against the engine." Exit code -15 is a signal, not a fault. The log says who died first and who sent the signal. The lesson to carry A graceful stop is a protocol between one sender and one receiver. Know which process holds the drain, make sure only that process gets the signal, and size the time you give it from the longest work you allow. Then test the stop with a request in flight and read the exit code, because a stop that works on an idle server proves nothing. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual records both stops and the variable name trap in the shutdown part of the operating page , and the SRE for AI lesson gives the runbook shape that turns this reading into a repeatable check. Recap What to keep from this case Follow a signal from the orchestrator to the process that should handle it. Make the server the main process ( exec ). Graceful shutdown means draining in-flight requests. A crash log can be a symptom of how the process was stopped.
