a2117: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Cancel Retries That Never Ended: Terminal Task States Lesson 21.17 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : A2A 1.0.1 with the manual's capture kit (the test-runner, code-reviewer and deployer agents) Model : no model; the agents are deterministic fixtures Hardware : one machine, localhost, no network The situation In plain words first A supervisor retries CancelTask all night for two tasks that keep answering with an error. Its rule, "an error means try again", treats a permanent state as a temporary one: the tasks had already finished, and a finished task cannot be cancelled. The case trains reading what an error means before deciding to retry, and checking the task's state instead of repeating the call. A supervisor service drives a fleet of remote agents. At the end of a run it lists every task it started and sends CancelTask to each one. Its rule for every call is simple: an error means "not yet", so the call goes out again until it returns a task. Last night the shutdown never finished. Two tasks on the test-runner agent answered an error on every attempt, for the whole night. The on-call engineer reads the supervisor log. One of the two tasks had been stopped by an operator earlier in the run, by hand, through the same agent. After the shutdown routine failed to cancel it, the engineer sent it the message "Try again" to wake it up, and got a second kind of error. The ticket says that the agent is stuck and asks for a restart of the agent. You have the four exchanges that the capture kit recorded for the same sequence of calls. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The send that started the suite, and the state it came back in Copy The reply to the first CancelTask Copy The second CancelTask on the same id, status and code Copy The detail inside the second cancel error Copy A message sent to the canceled task, and the code it got Copy The detail inside the error for the message Copy What the specification and the implementations say about a repeated cancel Copy Questions to answer first What did the first cancel return, and what did the task still carry? The second cancel and the later message got two different codes. What do their details have in common? Is a repeated cancel an error or a no-op? What does the specification say, and what do the kit and the reference implementation do? Which call tells the supervisor whether to keep going, and what are its three possible outcomes? How does the supervisor continue the work that the canceled task was doing? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Cancelling a task that already completed is an error that will never go away. ✗ Retrying until success is a safe default for remote calls. It is only safe for transient errors; permanent states need a different branch. ✓ Calling GetTask once after the error shows the terminal state that closes the entry. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the send. The planner asked for the full suite with returnImmediately set, and the task came back in TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED . The task exists and runs while the client is away. Read the first cancel. The reply is the task itself, now in TASK_STATE_CANCELED , with the status message "Canceled at the client's request." The history holds the request and the agent's progress message, and the artifacts hold the two log chunks the suite had written. A cancel is a request that the server may refuse, and this one succeeded. Read the second cancel. The HTTP status is 200, because JSON-RPC errors travel in a 200. The body has an error with code -32002 and the message "Task cannot be canceled". The detail gives the reason TASK_NOT_CANCELABLE and, in metadata , the state TASK_STATE_CANCELED . The error does not say "try later". It says that the task already ended, and how. Read the message. The "Try again" message carries the task id and the context id of the canceled task. The code is -32004 and the reason is UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION . The metadata names the same state. A terminal task refuses a message, a cancel and a subscription. Only GetTask still answers. Read the rule. One section of the specification lists TaskNotCancelableError for a finished task, and another calls cancel idempotent. Both this server and the reference SDK return -32002, and a cancel on a deleted task may return not found. A client cannot know which server it meets, so after a cancel that errors it calls GetTask . Canceled means an earlier cancel worked. Another terminal state means the task ended first. Running means the server could not stop it. Check the stop set. Four states are terminal: completed, failed, canceled and rejected. A loop that waits for "a task" as its success condition never ends on a task that is already in one of them. What actually happened Nothing was stuck. The supervisor's retry rule treated a permanent state as a transient error, and the engineer's "Try again" repeated the same mistake with a message. The fix is in the client. When CancelTask returns an error, the supervisor calls GetTask once and reads the state. A terminal state closes the entry. The code -32004 is read with its metadata, because the same code also covers a card without streaming and a card without an extended card. To continue the work, the supervisor starts a new task in the same context and names the finished task in referenceTaskIds . It never sends a message to a terminal task. In the capture, every call after the cancel is one request and one definitive answer, which is what the shutdown now takes: one pass over the list. Wrong turns "Retry the cancel until it returns the task." The second cancel answers -32002 every time, and its metadata already names the final state. The retry can only stop when the client stops it. "Message the task to restart it." A terminal task never changes again. The message gets -32004. New work is a new task, with the old id in referenceTaskIds . "Read -32004 as 'this server does not support cancel'." The code covers three cases: no streaming, no extended card, and a terminal task. The message and the metadata, or a GetTask , tell them apart. "Stop the loop on completed, failed and canceled." Rejected is terminal too. A loop that forgets it polls a refused task forever. "Restart the agent." The agent answered every call at once with a correct error. A restart would throw away the task store and turn the next lookup into a not found. The lesson to carry An error from a mutation is not a reason to repeat the mutation. Read the state that the error names, or fetch it, and decide from the state. Separate the errors that time will change from the ones that no later call can change, and let the terminal set of your state machine end every loop, including the states you did not expect. How this connects Where this is taught The cancel page of A2A 101 walks through these four exchanges, the state table gives the client's next step for every state, the errors page explains why one code covers three cases, and the failure modes lesson describes the cascade that starts when a client cannot tell "I failed" from "this cannot be done". Recap What to keep from this case Classify errors as transient or permanent before retrying. After a failed cancel, read the task's state. Terminal states close the bookkeeping. Bound every retry loop. a2118: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Thermal Throttling That Voided an A/B Test Lesson 21.18 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.22 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory, in a node whose second L4 ran other tenants The situation In plain words first An A/B test of CUDA graphs shows no difference, and the team plans to turn graphs off. The GPU was overheating and throttled to 360 MHz, its clock was not recorded, and the two runs did not share conditions. The comparison measured heat, not graphs. The case trains recording the conditions an experiment depends on, and calling a result void when they changed. A team wants to know whether CUDA graphs help their Qwen/Qwen3-8B server on an L4. They run the concurrency sweep with graphs on, then the same sweep with graphs off, one after the other on the same afternoon, three seeds each. The two tables agree within a few percent, and at several points the run with graphs off reads a little faster. They conclude that graphs do nothing on this card and plan to turn them off in production to start faster and save memory. One teammate mentions that the fans of the node were loud all afternoon, and that the other L4 in the node was running another team's test pods and an FP8 sweep at the same time. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The first comparison of CUDA graphs on and off, as the team read it Copy The state of both GPUs in the node during that sweep Copy The start of each run in the repeated sweep, with the wait before it Copy The same comparison on a cooled card, both servers on one day Copy The same mistake in a speculative decoding test on the other engine Copy Questions to answer first The two sweeps agree within a few percent. Why is that agreement not evidence that graphs do nothing? Read the GPU state line. Which slowdown flag is set, what clock does the card run at, and what share of its maximum is that? What does a slow clock do to a launch-bound step and to a memory-bound step, and why does that hide a graph effect in particular? Design the protocol that makes an A/B pair comparable on this card. Give the start condition, the repeat rule and what you record. With that protocol, what did graphs change on this card, and where did the result surprise us? The same mistake appeared in a speculative decoding test on another engine. What was the clock gap there, and what did the team do with those runs? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A thermally throttled GPU can hide or invert a performance difference. ✗ Running the two arms one after the other on the same afternoon controls for the hardware. The card's clock changed with temperature; it must be recorded and matched. ✓ The repaired comparison found graphs saved about 1 % per decode step on this model. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Start with the first table. The default server and the server without graphs sit within a few percent at every concurrency, and the seed ranges overlap. At one user the ranges are 10.0 to 14.9 and 10.2 to 12.3 tokens per second, which is wide for a point that should be stable. The sweep had no GPU telemetry, so nothing in the table says what the card was doing. The GPU state line says it. The first GPU, the one that ran the sweep, was at 87 C, its SM clock was 360 MHz against a maximum of 2,040, and the software thermal slowdown flag was active while the card reported 100 percent utilization. The second GPU, at 81 C, held 2,025 MHz while it ran the other tenants' pods. The card under test was running at about a sixth of its clock for a reason that has nothing to do with the server flags. A CUDA graph removes the launch time of the kernels in one decode step. On this card and model that saving is about half a millisecond of a step of 60 to 70 ms, and a throttled GPU is slow on every step, so the saving disappears in the noise. At the same time the throttle moves with temperature and with the neighbour's load, so two sweeps that ran one after the other did not run at the same speed. Agreement within a few percent on a card whose clock wandered is no evidence at all. The team removed those numbers. The third listing shows the repaired method. Every run of the repeated sweep started at 72 C or below, and the kit waited for that temperature before each start, from 116 to 287 s. A run whose median SM clock fell under 1,000 MHz was set aside and repeated, up to three times. Both servers ran on one day, one after the other, with the same pool of 24,094 tokens, and a sampler recorded the clock and the temperature every second. The same-day pair is the result. Up to 16 users the graphs saved 0.5 to 0.7 ms of a step, about 1 percent, 60.15 against 60.64 ms at one user. Throughput was within 1.2 percent from 2 users up. At 16 and 32 users the server without graphs had the lower P99 ITL, 73 against 80 ms and 87 against 103 ms, with no seed overlap, and the manual reports that gap without a mechanism for it. At 64 users batches above 48 ran eager on both servers, so that row does not measure graphs at all. The last listing is the other engine. Its first speculative decoding runs had no clock lock. At one user the run with no speculation ran at 210 MHz and the run with speculation at about 1,400 MHz. A gap that large hides any effect of the feature, so the team set those runs aside and locked the clock at 900 MHz before it compared again. What actually happened The first A/B was void. The card ran at 360 MHz with the thermal slowdown active, the clock was not recorded, and the two sweeps did not share a clock. Any conclusion about graphs from those tables is a conclusion about heat. The repaired comparison kept graphs on. They saved about 1 percent of each decode step on this dense model, the throughput tie held within 1.2 percent, and the unexplained lower tail without graphs at 16 and 32 users is a reason to measure the tail on your model, not a reason to turn graphs off for memory. Size the graphs to your traffic instead. The method is the real fix: record clocks.sm and the temperature every second during every benchmark, start each run at a temperature that the card can hold, repeat any run whose median clock falls under your floor, and compare two runs only at similar clocks. The lab notes of the vLLM manual name four L4 sessions for the same reason, and compare numbers only inside one session. Wrong turns "Both configs ran on the same hot card, so the heat cancels out." The throttle moved with the temperature and with the neighbour's load. Two runs an hour apart did not share a clock, and a card at a sixth of its clock hides a half-millisecond effect in any case. "Lock the clock at the maximum and the problem is gone." A lock sets the highest clock, and a GPU at a high temperature still slows below it. We locked at 900 MHz, a value that the card could hold, and still set aside runs that fell under it. "Run the two configs in the other order." The second run still inherits the heat of the first. Alternate the configs, cool the card to the same temperature before each run, and record the clock. "Wait one minute between runs." The repeated sweep needed 116 to 287 s to reach 72 C before a start. Wait for a temperature, not for a time. The lesson to carry Every A/B on hardware needs a control for the hardware. A clock that changes with heat or with a neighbour is a hidden variable that moves every number by the same factor, and that factor swallows small effects and invents large ones. Record the clock with every measurement, hold the start condition fixed, and treat two numbers from different clocks as two numbers from different machines. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual records the first sweep and the repaired pair in the CUDA graphs page and sets the clock rule in its benchmark page , the vLLM manual tells the speculative decoding version in the EAGLE3 page and names the sessions in the lab notes , and the load testing lesson covers what a client cannot see. Recap What to keep from this case Record the conditions a benchmark depends on, such as clocks and temperature. Interleave arms or repeat them to spread drift. Declare a result void when conditions changed. Small effects need careful measurement. a2119: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A GPU Memory Share of 0.02 and Six-Times-Slower Rollouts Lesson 21.19 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first To leave room for the trainer, someone set the inference engine's memory share to 0.02. The run still worked and the reward looked normal, but each step took six times longer. The tiny cache forced the engine to process answers in many more rounds. The case trains checking speed as well as correctness after a configuration change, and knowing what a memory share actually buys. A team trains with GRPO on one GB10. The week before, a larger model was stopped by a memory kill, and the team learned to fear the node total. Someone sets the engine memory share, --sglang-mem-fraction-static , to 0.02 for the next runs, to leave the trainer as much room as possible. The launcher default is 0.4. The next morning a one-step check run has finished, with a reward in the usual range. The step took far longer than the day before. Nobody saw an error. One engineer blames the heat guard, another blames a slow disk, and a third says the engine must have fallen back to a slow kernel. You get the log of the check run, the log of the same check at 0.25, and the log of a normal run at 0.4. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The pool size, the rollout time and the reward of three runs Copy The KV cache line of the slow run at startup Copy The one flag that differed between the runs Copy The default run settings of the manual Copy How the engine turns the fraction into a pool Copy The troubleshooting entry for the engine memory fraction Copy Questions to answer first Three rollout times, three pool sizes. Which number moved with the time, and which did not? The reward of the slow run is normal. Why does that not clear the run? The KV cache line prints before the first step. What in it tells you the step will be slow, and how slow is the GPU? Count the sequences that one step must generate and the longest answer. What can a pool of this size hold at once? Which direction do you change the share, by how much per try, and what do you read after each try? The engine did not run out of memory and did not crash. Why is the low direction of this flag harder to notice than the high direction? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A correct result can hide a large slowdown. ✗ Giving the engine as little memory as possible is a safe way to avoid memory kills. Below a point the cache cannot hold enough work, and every step slows down. ✓ At 0.25 the rollout took 61 s against 386 s at 0.02. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Line up the three runs. Read perf/rollout_time on each line. The run with the low share took 386 s for one rollout. The run at 0.25 took 61 s, and the normal run at 0.4 took about a minute as well. The rewards were 0.61328125, 0.66015625 and 0.625. The reward did not follow the setting. The time did, by about six times. Read the pool sizes on the same lines. The slow run had max_total_num_tokens=3082 . The other two had 211,813 and 347,841. The pool is the number of tokens that the engine can hold in its KV cache at one time. The rollout time moved with the pool, and nothing else in the three lines differed. Read the engine line that came first. At startup the slow engine printed KV Cache is allocated with 3082 tokens, and a K size and a V size of 0.16 GB each. This line appears before any step runs. A reader who knows the normal value for the machine sees the problem here, minutes before the first slow step ends. Count the work of one step. The manual's defaults are 32 prompts per step, 8 answers per prompt and an answer limit of 1,024 tokens. One step generates 256 answers. A pool of 3082 tokens holds three answers at the length limit at once, and fewer with their prompts. The engine must run the step as a long series of small batches. Nothing is broken. The GPU is almost idle while it waits for room. Follow the flag to the pool. The share names the memory for the model weights plus the KV pool together. After the weights load, the engine measures free memory again and gives the pool what is left of the share. At 0.02 of the memory, the weights of even a small model take most of the share, and the pool gets the remainder. Use the manual's entry. The troubleshooting page lists both failures of this flag. A share that is too high leaves no room for activations and CUDA graphs, so CUDA reports that it is out of memory. A share that is too low does not always stop the engine, so the check is to read #tokens in the KV cache line. The fix for the low case is to raise the share by 0.05 or 0.1 at a time. What actually happened The engine share of 0.02 left a pool of 3082 tokens, and the rollout of one step took 386 s against 61 s at 0.25 and about a minute at the default of 0.4. The reward stayed in range because the answers were the same work, only in many more rounds. The fix is to put the share back to 0.4, or to 0.25 when the trainer needs more room, and never below the point where the pool stops holding a full step. The proving measurement is the pair of numbers at startup and after the first step: the #tokens in the KV cache line and perf/rollout_time . At 0.25 the pool held 211,813 tokens and the rollout took 61 s. Record both for every new setting of the flag, and change the share by 0.05 or 0.1 at a time. The memory kill of the week before was a trainer problem, and a smaller engine share did not prevent it, as the Ray incident shows. Wrong turns "The reward is fine, so the run is fine." The reward measures what the model learned, not what the step cost. At six times the rollout time, the same training takes six times the GPU hours. "The heat guard paused the run." A pause adds wall-clock time to a step, but the pool line of 3082 tokens explains the time without any pause, and the run at 0.25 on the same day took 61 s. "Raise the number of running requests." The engine admits requests only while the pool has room for their tokens. With 3082 tokens the pool, not the request cap, sets the batch. "Lower the share further, the trainer is what matters." The trainer kill of the week before happened at 0.4 and again at 0.2, so the share was not the cause there. Below 0.25 the trainer gains little and the rollout loses a lot. The lesson to carry A setting can be wrong in both directions, and the two failures look different. Too much memory for one component crashes it, which everyone sees. Too little makes it slow, which nobody sees until the bill arrives. Know the normal value of the sizing line that each component prints at startup, read it before the first step, and when you change a share, move it in small steps and record the size and the time together. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual names the two ways an engine share goes wrong in its symptom table , shows that a smaller share did not save the trainer in the Ray page , gives the run defaults in the lab notes , and the SGLang manual explains how the share becomes a pool in its memory sizing page . Recap What to keep from this case Check step time as well as reward after changes. Know the cache size each memory share gives. Fix the memory fear with measurements, not extremes. Keep the default unless you know why not. a2120: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems An Hour Polling a Task in Input-Required State Lesson 21.20 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : A2A 1.0.1 with the manual's capture kit (the test-runner, code-reviewer and deployer agents) Model : no model; the agents are deterministic fixtures Hardware : one machine, localhost, no network The situation In plain words first A planner polls a code-review task for an hour and times out, while the reviewer was waiting for the planner to answer a question. The wait loop only knew three stop states (completed, failed, canceled), so "input required" looked like "still running". The case trains listing every state a remote task can be in, and giving each one a branch. A planner sends a diff of payments-api to the code-reviewer agent and waits for the findings. Its wait loop is the one it uses for every remote agent: send the message, then call GetTask every few seconds until the state is completed, failed or canceled. Last night a review never came back. The planner polled the same task for an hour, then its own run timed out, and the release waited for a human reviewer in the morning. The on-call engineer pulls the first reply that the reviewer sent. It was not a failure, and the agent never went quiet. The planner knew the branch the diff was cut from, because it had checked the code out itself. You have the two exchanges of the review from the capture kit, a polling exchange on another agent for comparison, and the log of the kit's own planner, which handled the same question in its run. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The reply to the review request Copy A GetTask on a task that is still running, from another capture Copy The message that answers the question Copy The reply to the answer Copy How the kit's planner handled the same question Copy The nine states, their class, and the client's next step Copy Why the answer carries both ids Copy Questions to answer first What state did the first reply carry, and who wrote the message inside it? How does a task that waits for input differ from one that is working, when you look at two polls? Where does the planner's answer go, and which fields must it carry? Which states must a wait loop stop on, and what is the next step for each of them? The planner had the branch name in its own context. Why did the loop never use it? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A task can stop and wait for input without being finished. ✗ Anything that is not completed, failed or canceled means "still working". Interrupted states, such as input required, also stop progress. ✓ Answering an input-required task means sending a new message with the same task id. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the first reply. The state is TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED . The status message has the role ROLE_AGENT and asks which base branch the diff should be compared against. A blocking send returns at a terminal or an interrupted state, so the question was in the planner's hands from the first reply, before the first poll. Compare with a working task. In the polling capture the state is TASK_STATE_WORKING , the status message reports progress, and the artifact grows between polls. A parked task does none of that. Its state is the agent saying "your turn", and no number of polls changes it. Read the answer. It is an ordinary SendMessage . The message has a fresh messageId , the role ROLE_USER , the text main , and both the contextId and the taskId copied from the task. The reference SDK does not infer the context from the task and stamps a fresh one, so a client sends both ids. Read the second reply. The same task id comes back in TASK_STATE_COMPLETED with the status message 2 findings . The history now holds the question and the answer, and the review.json artifact names main as the base and lists the two findings with their lines. The task never left its id or its context. Read the planner log. The kit's planner sees the interrupted state, reads the question, answers from its own context with main , and reports the review one call later. The interrupted state is a branch in its loop, not a reason to wait. Read the state table. Nine states fall in three classes. Two are interrupted, and each has a different next step: answer on the same task for input, or pass the request to an approver and keep watching for authorization. Four are terminal, and the fourth, rejected, is the one most loops forget. What actually happened The loop had the wrong stop set. It waited for three terminal states and treated everything else as "still running", so an interrupted task looked like a slow one. The fix adds the two interrupted states to the stop set and gives each a branch. For TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED , the planner reads the status message and answers with a new message that carries the task id and the context id of the parked task. For TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED , it hands the request to whoever approves and subscribes or polls. For TASK_STATE_REJECTED , it stops and follows the message. The capture proves the path: the reviewer finished one call after the answer and returned the review artifact, and the kit's planner log shows the same handling end to end. Wrong turns "Poll faster, the reviewer is slow." The state says that the agent waits for the client. The poll rate does not move it. "Abandon the task and send a new request with the branch in it." It works, and it leaves a parked task behind on the agent, resends the diff, and loses the history. The protocol's path is a new message on the same task. "Answer with the taskId only; the server knows the context." The reference SDK stamps a fresh context on such a message. Copy both ids. "Treat an interrupted state as a failure and report it." The task kept its id, its history and its artifacts. Nothing failed, and the answer finishes it. "Send the answer as ROLE_AGENT, because the planner is an agent." The role is the direction of the message, not the kind of party. The client side is ROLE_USER , and the kit refuses the other role with -32602. The lesson to carry A wait loop must know every state the other side can enter, and it must stop on each state that asks something of the caller, not only on the states that end the work. When a remote system pauses with a question, the answer is often already in the caller's context, and the loop is the only thing that stands between the two. How this connects Where this is taught The interrupted states page of A2A 101 follows this review from the question to the answer, the task state page and the state table classify the nine states, the message page gives the id rules, and the failure modes lesson names context loss as one of the five ways an agent loop breaks. Recap What to keep from this case List every state a remote task can be in. Give interrupted states their own branch. Read the status message; it says what is needed. Time out loops that cannot see progress. a2121: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems An Implicit Deny in the Egress Proxy That Looked Like an Outage Lesson 21.21 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : sbx v0.47.0 Model : none; shell commands inside the sandbox Hardware : one Mac with the microVM runtime The situation In plain words first An agent in a sandbox reports that "the network is down" and asks for a repair. The fetch was answered within a second: a policy proxy denied the request by default, because the host was not on the sandbox's allow list, and replied with a 403 and an explanation. The case trains distinguishing a refused request from a broken network, and reading a tool's message instead of the agent's summary of it. A shell agent in a sandbox is asked to fetch a page from example.com as the first step of a larger task. It reports back that the network is down inside the sandbox and asks the operator to repair the connection. The operator pastes the agent's command into sbx exec and gets a reply within a second, so nothing timed out. The sandbox was created with the balanced preset and no rule of its own. The team's first guess is a broken proxy, because the reply holds two status lines that disagree. The second guess is a DNS failure. You have the two requests the operator ran, the policy check for that host, the policy log, and the commands that changed the rules afterwards. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. A HEAD request and a GET request to example.com from inside m101-policy Copy The decision for example.com from sbx policy check network Copy The policy log of m101-policy Copy A sandbox-scoped allow rule and the policy list after it Copy The HEAD request after the allow rule Copy The GET request after a deny rule replaced the allow Copy A deny rule added while the allow rule still exists Copy Questions to answer first The HEAD request printed two status lines and exited 0. Which component sent each line, and why is the exit code 0? The check says implicit and names no rule. What decided the request? The log shows two allowed hosts with different proxy paths. What does forward-bypass tell you? After the allow rule, what changed in the first status line of the same request? An explicit deny gives a different body. How do you tell the two denials apart from inside the sandbox and from the host? Why was the deny rule refused the first time, and what is the right order of operations? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A fast, explicit refusal is not an outage. ✗ If the agent says the network is down, the network is down. Agents summarize failures badly; the proxy's 403 said why the request was blocked. ✓ A sandbox-scoped allow rule turned the same request into a 200. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the HEAD request line by line. HTTP/1.1 200 OK is the forward proxy accepting the CONNECT . The HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden below it arrived inside the TLS session, with a 90 byte plain text body, under a certificate the sandbox trusts. curl printed both and exited 0 because it received a complete reply. The GET shows the body: an approval is required for example.com:443 . Nothing was slow and nothing was unreachable. A proxy answered with a decision. Ask the authorizer. sbx policy check network runs the same authorizer as the proxy, without sending anything. For this host in the sandbox context it returns allowed: false , deny_kind: implicit , the reason No matching allow rule (default deny) , and no rule. The balanced preset lists 194 hosts, and example.com is not one of them. The request matched nothing and was denied by default. Read the log. The blocked row names the host, the proxy path forward , the rule text no applicable policies for op(...) and the same reason. Two allowed rows show what the preset admits: a package host over forward , and a download host over forward-bypass , a tunnel that the proxy does not inspect. The log says what passed, and the check says why. Add the narrow rule. sbx policy allow network --sandbox m101-policy example.com adds a rule in the local scope for that one sandbox, and policy ls then counts 195 hosts. The same HEAD request now begins with HTTP/1.0 200 Connection established , and the origin's HTTP/2 200 follows. The proxy tunnels the connection and no longer speaks. Compare the two denials. With a deny rule in place of the allow, the GET body reads Blocked by local rule for example.com:443 . The implicit one asks for an approval. On the host, the check reports deny_kind: explicit with the rule id for the second case, and implicit for the first. Mind the order. The deny for example.com was refused while the allow for the same host existed in the same scope, and the error named the allow rule. Remove the allow first, then add the deny. Deny wins at evaluation time, but the CLI does not store the pair. What actually happened There was no outage. example.com is not on the allow list of the balanced preset, which has 194 hosts. The proxy denied the connection as an implicit default and answered inside TLS with a 403 and an approval message. A sandbox-scoped allow rule turned the same request into a tunnelled 200 from the origin. The agent's report was wrong in the way the lesson on failure modes predicts: it read one status code and reported a cause it had not checked. Fixes: Change the agent's instructions so that a 403 with an approval body is reported as a policy decision, with the host and the port, so the operator can add a rule. Run sbx policy check network --sandbox NAME host:port --json before you touch the network, and read deny_kind and rule . Add rules with --sandbox for one agent, and keep the global policy for hosts every agent needs. Before you add a deny in a scope, remove any allow for that host in that scope. Wrong turns "Restart the daemon, the proxy returns two different codes." Both lines are the proxy doing its job: the first accepts the tunnel, the second refuses the host. A restart changes no rule. "It is DNS, because example.com does not resolve." The request reached the proxy with the host name, and the proxy denied the host by policy. The body, the check and the log all name the host and the port. "Allow example.com globally so this stops." A global rule admits the host for every sandbox. The local scope exists for one agent's need. "Add a deny rule now so the agent cannot try again." The deny conflicts with the allow in the same scope and is refused, and the agent's task needed the host. Fix the report, not the host. The lesson to carry An agent that reports a failure gives you a claim, not a diagnosis. Reproduce the call outside the agent, read the whole reply and not only the first status line, and ask the policy layer for its decision before you look for a fault in the network. A deny with a body is an answer. A timeout is a fault. How this connects Where this is taught The policy page explains the scopes and check network , the proxy page reads the 403 and the log, and the failure modes lesson names the mode where an agent reports a cause it did not check. Recap What to keep from this case A quick refusal and a timeout are different failures. Read the tool's own message, not the agent's summary. Default-deny is policy; allow hosts deliberately. Scope allow rules to the sandbox that needs them. a2122: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems CUDA Graphs Turned Off for Faster Startup Lesson 21.22 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-breadth, design-review. Roles : inference engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first Pods take six minutes to become ready, and an engineer proposes disabling CUDA graph capture to save startup time; a reviewer fears decode will slow down. Both guessed sizes without measuring. Capture took about 40 seconds of a 373-second start, because loading the weights took 322 seconds. The case trains measuring each phase's share before arguing about it. A team runs Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on GB10 nodes behind an autoscaler. New pods take more than six minutes to become ready, so the autoscaler starts extra pods during every ramp and the bill grows. An engineer reads the startup log, sees that it captures CUDA graphs twice, and proposes to disable both graph backends: "capture is pure startup cost, and the prefill capture alone takes half a minute". A reviewer blocks the change: "graphs are what make decode fast, you will double the time per token". Both have read the same log and neither has measured. The pod has been restarted with each setting, and the kit output for both servers is on the shared drive. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The server command with both graph backends disabled Copy The end of startup on the default server, with the timings line Copy The startup phases of the server without graphs Copy Median TPOT and output with and without graphs, three seeds, 1 to 64 users Copy One kit run at one user with graphs on Copy The same kit run at one user with graphs off Copy The position of the manual on graphs, memory and startup Copy Questions to answer first From the startup timings line, where do the six minutes go, and how much of that is graph capture? What does a CUDA graph remove from a decode step, and on which model and GPU is that removal worth the most? Read the two kit runs at one user. What did graphs change in the typical token gap, and what in the worst one? The three-seed table shows a GB10 result that differs from the L4 result in the manual. Why would two cards disagree about the same feature? Does disabling graphs fix the autoscaler? What does? When would the reviewer be right? Name the model shape and the load. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Disabling graphs removed about 40 s of capture, and the start still took 346 s. ✗ Capture is the main cost of a slow start. The weight load dominated: 322 s of the start. ✓ On this model and card, decode time per token changed by 3 percent or less without graphs. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the timings line of the default server. It reads load_weight=323.61 , kv_cache_allocation=2.09 , scheduler_e2e=369.03 , cuda_graph={prefill=35.06, decode=4.61, ...} and tokenizer_e2e=373.52 . The weight load is 323.61 s of a 373.52 s start. The prefill capture took 35.06 s and the decode capture 4.61 s. The captures also cost memory: the section gives 2.14 GB for prefill and 1.73 GB for decode. Read the startup without graphs. The server logged that the prefill graph was disabled because the config resolved the backend to disabled , allocated a pool of 258017 tokens against 227243 with graphs, and finished with scheduler_e2e=341.39 and tokenizer_e2e=346.34 , with every graph field at 0.00. Its weight load was 322.24 s. So the change saved the capture time and bought a larger pool, and the start still took 346.34 s, because 322.24 s of weight load sit inside it. Know what a graph saves. A decode step is hundreds of small kernel launches, one token per request each. A graph records them once and replays them with one CPU call. The saving is launch time, a fixed cost per step that matters when the step itself is short: a small dense model on a fast GPU at batch 1 is the case the mechanism was built for. Read the three-seed table. On this mixture-of-experts model on the GB10, the median TPOT was 32.52 ms with graphs against 33.09 without at one user, 102.21 against 104.77 at 8 users, and 254.06 against 253.77 at 64. Output was 29.14 against 28.72, 74.11 against 73.46, and 235.38 against 235.79. The manual's reading: a step of this model takes about 32 ms at batch 1, memory bandwidth sets that time, and the launch time a graph removes is small next to it. Read the kit's single runs. At one user with graphs: a median TPOT of 30.84 ms, a median ITL of 30.79 and a P99 ITL of 32.21. Without graphs: 31.29, 31.40 and 41.72. The medians agree with the three-seed table. The P99 ITL moved more, from 32.21 to 41.72 ms, but these are single runs with no clock record, so the tail is a lead to measure, not a result. At 8 users the kit read 97.30 against 100.03 ms. Do not use the first-token column of these runs for the comparison, because the kit never flushed the cache between runs. Read the position. Keep graphs on and size them to your traffic. Do not turn them off to fix memory; lower --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode or --mem-fraction-static instead. On the GB10 graphs changed decode by 3 percent or less, and on the L4 with a dense 8B model they saved about 1 percent of each step. The old flag --disable-cuda-graph still works at v0.5.22 and is deprecated in favor of the two per-phase flags in the command. What actually happened Neither engineer was right about the size. Disabling the graphs saved the capture, 35.06 s for prefill and 4.61 s for decode, and the start still took 346.34 s instead of 373.52, because 322.24 s of weight load dominate the start. On the decode side the reviewer's fear did not materialize on this model and card: the median time per token changed by 3 percent or less from 1 to 64 users, and the output stayed within the seed spread. So the change does not solve the ramp, and the weight load is the problem to work on. Keep the weights on a local drive, keep the server running between ramps, mount the kernel caches and the model cache on volumes that survive the pod, and set the readiness probe and the scale-up policy from the measured 373.52 s, as the operating page describes. Keep the graphs on, because a server without decode graphs pays launch time on every token for every user, and that cost shows on smaller dense models where the step is short. If the team wants the memory back, the lever is --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode , not the capture itself. Before any change of this kind, measure the pair with a clock record and three seeds, as the table did, and read the tail as well as the median. Wrong turns "Capture is pure startup cost, so remove it." It is 35.06 plus 4.61 s of a start that spends 323.61 s loading weights. Removing it moved the start from 373.52 to 346.34 s and left the ramp problem in place. "Without graphs the time per token doubles." On this mixture-of-experts model on the GB10, the median TPOT moved from 32.52 to 33.09 ms at one user and from 254.06 to 253.77 at 64. The step is bound by memory bandwidth, not by launches. "The GB10 result settles it for every model." On the L4 with a dense 8B model the graphs saved about 1 percent of each step, and on a small model on a fast GPU the launch share is larger still. The saving is a property of the step length. "Turn graphs off to get the KV pool back." The pool grew from 227243 to 258017 tokens, but the manual says to lower the graph batch size or the memory fraction instead, so that decode keeps its graphs. "Read the kit's first-token column to settle the tail." The kit never flushed the cache between runs, so the first token is not comparable. The P99 ITL gap at one user, 32.21 against 41.72 ms, needs a run with seeds and a clock record first. The lesson to carry Read where the time goes before you remove a phase. A startup, like a decode step, is a sum of parts of very different sizes, and the part that is easy to remove is rarely the part that dominates. Measure the cost and the gain of a feature on your own model and GPU, at your load, with seeds and a clock record, because a saving that is real on one step length is noise on another. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual measures the pair on the GB10 and on the L4 in the CUDA graphs page and breaks a cold start into its phases in the operating page . Recap What to keep from this case Measure each phase before arguing about one. Optimizing a small phase cannot fix a large total. Measure the cost of a change on both startup and serving. Address the dominant phase in the design. a2123: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Five Identical Tool Calls and a Run That Ended Itself Lesson 21.23 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : docker-agent v1.149.0 and sbx v0.47.0 Model : ai/qwen3:4b through the local model runner, at temperature 0 Hardware : one Mac, no GPU The situation In plain words first A nightly agent job calls the same tool five times and stops. In a run nobody watches, a tool that needs permission asks, nobody answers, the ask becomes a rejection, and the model simply tries again. The repeat limit did its job by ending the loop. The case trains reading the loop as a permission problem, not raising the limit. A coordinator agent runs in a nightly job with --exec , and nobody watches a terminal. Its agent file gives it one sub-agent, a writer, and the background_agents toolset, so that it can start the writer in the background, wait, and repeat the writer's sentence. The job has worked for weeks when the coordinator used transfer_task . A teammate changed the user message to ask for a background agent, and the next run stopped with exit 1 and the line Agent terminated: detected 5 consecutive identical calls to run_background_agent . The teammate reads the line as a runtime bug: the model was working, and the runtime killed it. The proposed fix is to raise the limit on repeated calls and to swap the model. You review the run before either change ships. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The coordinator agent of the team file Copy The same coordinator one run earlier, with transfer_task Copy The user message, the first background-agent call, and what came back Copy The next five calls and their five answers Copy One round in the event stream, from the tool call to the next message Copy The last line of the run Copy What each safety mode does with a call that no pattern matched Copy Questions to answer first Before you open the event stream, list what the model could have received after its first call, and what a well-behaved agent does with each answer. The runtime asked for a confirmation six times, and nobody answered. Why did the asks happen, and what turned each ask into a rejection? Compare the arguments of the six calls. What changed after the first round, and what does that tell you about how the model read the answer? Name the gate that ended the run, its default, and why the same agent file worked one run earlier. Write the change to the agent file or the command that lets a headless coordinator start a background agent, and say what you would leave as it is. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ In a headless run, every permission prompt becomes a rejection. ✗ Raising the repeat limit fixes the job. The model would repeat the rejected call more times; the missing permission remains. ✓ An explicit allow pattern for the background-agent tool lets the job run unattended. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the agent file. The root agent has max_iterations: 6 , sub_agents: [writer] , handoffs: [reviewer] , and one toolset of type background_agents . The file has no permissions block, and the command chose no safety mode. So any call that is not approved by default has to ask someone. Read the first round. The runtime raised tool_call_confirmation for run_background_agent , with safety_label unknown in the metadata. Under --exec there is no terminal to answer, so the runtime turned the question into a refusal. The tool response went back to the model as plain text: The user rejected the tool call. Read the five rounds after it. The model sent the same call again, five times, with the same agent and the same task. It dropped expected_output after the first round and changed nothing else. A rejection is a final answer about that call. The model treated it as a transient error and retried. Read one round in the event stream. The tool call carries safety_label: unknown . The two hook events are tool_input_transform and tool_response_transform , the built-in transforms, and both report allowed: true . No pre_tool_use hook and no allow pattern decided anything. The result has isError: true , then message_added , and the next model turn starts from the same state. Read the last line. The runtime stopped the run after five identical calls in a row. The manual names the limit, max_consecutive_tool_calls , and a value of 0 means the default of 5. The runtime caught a loop that the model did not. One run earlier the same coordinator called transfer_task , which is the one tool that is always approved without a prompt, so that run raised no confirmation. Read the safety-mode table. A run that chose no mode keeps the old default: read-only tools run, and every other tool asks. The background-agent tool is not read-only and its label is unknown . Under restricted an unknown label is denied, and under strict or balanced it asks again. Only an allow pattern or autonomous lets the call through. The manual adds that inside a running task, a call that would ask is denied automatically, so a headless coordinator needs an allow rule for run_background_agent and for the tools its sub-agents call. What actually happened The cause is a headless run with a tool whose label is unknown and no allow pattern. Every call asked, every ask became a rejection, and the model repeated the call. The repeat limit worked as designed: it turned an endless loop into one exit code. The fix is a permission, not a higher limit. Add an allow pattern for run_background_agent to the agent file, and allow patterns for the tools the writer will call, then rerun with --exec . The manual did not run the repaired configuration, so the check is yours: the first run_background_agent call must return a task id in the stream instead of a rejection, and the run must end with the writer's sentence and exit 0. Keep the limit at its default. Keep the safety mode out of autonomous . The proof that the permission was the cause is already in the stream: every round shows a confirmation with no one to answer it, a result with isError: true , and no rule or hook in the decision. The run with transfer_task on the same file shows the other side: a tool that needs no approval ran once and returned. Wrong turns "Raise the limit on consecutive calls so the run can finish." Every call hit the same rejection. More rounds give more rejections, and the limit is the only thing that ended the run. "Run the job with --yolo ." That is --safety autonomous : every tool is allowed, including every tool of the sub-agents. One allow pattern for one tool is the smaller change. "The model is at fault, swap it." The model received an error string and nothing else. Another model can retry the same way, and the runtime holds the gate for that reason. Check the permission before the model. "Add a pre_tool_use hook that answers allow." From a preempting hook, an allow verdict is advice. The hook can deny or ask, and it cannot grant. The lesson to carry A tool result that returns to the model as text is an input the model may ignore. When a run has nobody to answer a question, give the agent explicit allow patterns for the tools it must call and nothing more, and keep the runtime limits that stop a repeated step. Read a termination line as a gate that worked, then find the reason the model needed it. How this connects Where this is taught The sub-agents section records this run, the permissions section gives the decision order, and the failure modes lesson names a repeated step as a failure to gate. Recap What to keep from this case Headless runs need explicit permissions for every tool they use. A repeated identical call often means a rejected one. Loop limits are a safety net, not a fix. Change one thing (the message) and check what it affects. a2124: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Four Failed Starts after a pip Install: JIT Kernel Builds Lesson 21.24 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, screen. Roles : inference engineer, forward deployed AI engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 from pip, and vLLM 0.31.0 from a uv install Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : a node with two L4 GPUs, an NVIDIA driver and no CUDA toolkit The situation In plain words first After a clean pip install, the server fails to start four times with four different errors, and the team plans to reimage the node because "the driver must be broken". Every error names a compiler, a header or a linker: parts of a kernel build that runs on first start and needs a full CUDA toolkit, which the host does not have. The case trains reading what the errors have in common. A platform team gets a new node with two L4 cards. The host runs Ubuntu 24.04 with a driver, and nothing else from CUDA is on it. They install SGLang with pip, and the install prints no error. The first sglang serve dies with a C compiler message about a missing header. They repair it and start again. A new error. They repair that one too. After an afternoon, they have four failed starts and four different errors, each from a different component. The other team on the same node tries vLLM through a uv install. Their server dies with Engine core initialization failed right after a kernel build. Both teams now believe the driver on the node is faulty, and they file a ticket to reimage it. You are asked to review the logs before the node goes down. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The first two starts: a missing Python header, then no CUDA compiler Copy The third start: the compiler and the headers do not match Copy The fourth start: the linker cannot find the CUDA runtime library Copy The other engine on the same host: the sampler choice and the JIT build Copy The other engine: the engine core fails, and the three packages behind it Copy The one fact behind the four failures, and the repair for each Copy The troubleshooting entry for the sampler build on the other engine Copy Questions to answer first Four errors name four components. What is the one fact that all four share? Why does a serving engine need the Python headers at all, and which part of the stack asked for them? The third failure appeared only after the second one was repaired. What did that repair cause? The second engine failed on the same host with the same preprocessor check. Is it the same cause, and what is the one-variable workaround for a greedy benchmark? What do you tell the team about the reimage ticket, and what is the fix for production? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Four different errors can share one cause. ✗ A missing header at startup points to a broken GPU driver. It points to a build toolchain missing from the host. ✓ The pinned container image ships the toolkit the first-start build needs. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the first error of each start, not the traceback. Attempt one stops in triton/backends/nvidia/driver.c on Python.h: No such file or directory . Triton compiles a small C helper against the Python headers when the server starts, and the system Python has none. The manual changed to a Python build that ships its headers, from uv . Attempt two stops with Could not find nvcc and default cuda_home='/usr/local/cuda' doesn't exist . The pip wheels carry an nvcc at version 13.4 under nvidia/cu13 in site-packages, but nothing points at it, so the manual set CUDA_HOME to that directory. See how one repair exposed the next failure. With a compiler in reach, FlashInfer built its attention kernels with that nvcc against its own bundled headers, and the versions did not match. The Ninja build stops on one preprocessor line: CUDA compiler and CUDA toolkit headers are incompatible . The manual installed flashinfer-jit-cache , which holds kernels compiled in advance for SM 8.9, so nothing has to compile them on the host. Read the fourth error as a linker problem. The JIT kernels of SGLang link with -lcudart from $CUDA_HOME/lib64 . The wheel has only lib/libcudart.so.13 , so ld finds no libcudart.so . The manual made a CUDA_HOME with a lib64 directory that holds the library. The fifth start served requests. Check the second engine against the third failure. vLLM chose FlashInfer for top-p and top-k sampling and started to build the sampling JIT module. The build stopped on the same header check, and the engine core never came up. The package list under the error gives the cause in three lines: the kernel library flashinfer_python-0.7.0.post1 , the headers nvidia_cuda_cccl-13.3.4.3.1 and the compiler nvidia_cuda_nvcc-13.4.92 come from three packages with three versions. The vLLM manual gives two fixes: a toolkit that matches the PyTorch build, or VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 , which skips the sampler build and is enough for a greedy benchmark. Name the one fact. SGLang, Triton and FlashInfer compile kernels on the target machine at startup, and a compiler needs a complete toolchain. The driver was never part of any error. The manual's GB10 never hit this, because its DGX operating system has a full toolkit under /usr/local/cuda . What actually happened Cancel the reimage. Nothing in the logs names the driver. Every error names a compiler, a header set or a linker, and all of them belong to the kernel build that runs on the first start. For production, run SGLang from the pinned image, or on a host with a full CUDA toolkit. The pip path works on a host with only a driver after the four repairs above, and the manual warns that each SGLang upgrade can need them again. For vLLM, use the image or a toolkit that matches the PyTorch build; set VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 only when you need a quick greedy benchmark on a host without one. The proof of the fix is the fifth start, which served requests, and the position in the manual that came out of it: run outside the image only on a host with a full toolkit. Wrong turns "The driver is broken, reimage the node." No error names the driver. The four messages come from a C compiler, the CUDA compiler lookup, a header check and the linker. "pip install finished without errors, so the install is complete." The install does not compile kernels. The first start does, and that is where the toolchain is checked. "Install the distribution's CUDA toolkit and keep the wheels." The toolkit must match the CUDA build of PyTorch. A host toolkit at nvcc 13.4 gave the header mismatch on this node. "Fix one error and declare the node ready." Each repair revealed the next failure. Run a full start and one request before you close the ticket. The lesson to carry An engine that compiles kernels at startup has a second install step, and it runs on the first start, on the machine you serve from. When that step fails, read the first error line and ask which tool failed: the compiler, the headers it reads, or the linker. Fix the toolchain or use the image that carries it. A driver bug announces itself in the driver's own words, not in a build log. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual records the four starts and their repairs in the pip install part of its operating page , and the vLLM manual gives the matching entries for the missing compiler and the sampler build . Recap What to keep from this case Look for what successive errors have in common. A pip install without errors can still lack build tools. Prefer the pinned image in production. Do not reimage before the evidence points at the host. a2125: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems FP8 Quantization Cleared the Queue at 64 Users Lesson 21.25 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.8 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B in BF16, against Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 with an FP8 KV cache Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory The situation In plain words first At 64 users the first token takes 18 seconds and the plan is to buy a second GPU. One scheduler line explains it: 38 requests running, the cache 99 percent full, 26 waiting. The wait was a full cache, not a slow GPU. Switching to FP8 weights and cache made it about six times larger on the same card, and the queue disappeared. The case trains reading the scheduler before buying hardware. A team serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B in BF16 on one L4 for an internal assistant. At 64 concurrent users the median first token is about eighteen seconds and the GPU reports full utilization. The on-call engineer reads one decode line from the scheduler log: 38 running requests, a token usage of 0.99 and 26 requests waiting. The team's first plan is a second L4 and a load balancer in front of the pair. A colleague proposes a checkpoint of this model in FP8, with an FP8 KV cache on the same card. The team worries about accuracy, and about a change of two things at once. You have the startup logs of both servers from the same sweep, one decode line from each at 64 users, the accuracy run and the manual's table. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. One decode line from each server at 64 users Copy The BF16 server at startup: weights and pool Copy The FP8 server at startup: weights and pool Copy The FP8 start: the checkpoint detection and the warning about scales Copy Throughput and first token from 1 to 64 users, both servers Copy What the scheduler log says about 64 users, and the goodput result Copy GSM8K accuracy on 500 questions for the four SGLang configs Copy Questions to answer first Read the two decode lines. Why does the BF16 server run 38 requests and not 64, and what does the usage column tell you? From the two startup listings, which two numbers changed, and which of them grew the pool? The FP8 log prints a warning about scaling factors. What does it mean, and what must you check before you trust it? The table shows FP8 faster at one user too. Why does the pool not explain that row? Two things changed at once. What can you claim from this sweep, and what would you still measure before the rollout? Which goodput target did the manual use, and what did each server deliver at 64 users? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Requests waiting with a full cache means the cache size limits concurrency. ✗ Full GPU utilization proves the GPU needs more compute. Here the waiting time came from the cache running out of room. ✓ FP8 must still be checked for quality on the team's own prompts. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the pool in the decode line. The BF16 line holds 23810 tokens at usage 0.99, so the pool is full. Each request in the sweep carries 512 input tokens and 128 output tokens, and the manual counts that the BF16 pool holds about 37 such requests. The server ran 38 and parked the other 26 in the queue, and each parked request added its wait to its own first token. The FP8 line runs all 64 requests at 40635 tokens and usage 0.29 with an empty queue. The GPU was busy on both servers, so utilization never showed the difference. The pool did. Read what changed at startup. Two numbers moved. The weights took 15.28 GB in BF16 and 8.81 GB in FP8, and the freed memory went to the pool. The cache data type went from bfloat16 to float8_e4m3fn, which halves the bytes per token. Together the pool went from 24094 tokens to 142369, which the manual gives as 5.91 times as many. The data type alone would double the pool, and the smaller weights give the rest. Both servers used one memory fraction, 0.85, so the comparison is fair on memory. Read the warning. The FP8 start detects the checkpoint, then prints that no scaling factors were provided and that every scale defaults to 1.0. The checkpoint carries weight scales and no KV scales, so every key and value is stored with a scale of 1.0. The accuracy file says the same in its first line. Before you trust that, search the weight index for tensor names that end in k_scale or v_scale , and read the load log for scales that the loader skipped. The scenario on the other engine shows what happens when a loader drops scales that exist. Read the table at one user. FP8 gave 24.53 output tokens per second against 13.42, and a first token of 140.72 ms against 189.16 ms. At one user the pool does not matter, so this row is the weights. Decode on an L4 reads every weight for every token, and FP8 weights are half the bytes; the manual gives 39.66 ms per token against 60.16 ms. At 32 users the BF16 first token was already 2,969.61 ms against 199.09 ms, and at 64 users it was 18,348.57 ms against 296.42 ms. The BF16 throughput fell from 270.11 to 250.85 tokens per second between 32 and 64 users, because more requests waited. Read the goodput. The manual's target was a first token under 1 s and a time per token under 100 ms. BF16 served 0 requests per second within target at 32 and at 64 users. FP8 served 2.87 requests per second within target at 64. That is the number a user feels, and it is the number to put in the proposal. Read the accuracy check. On the first 500 GSM8K questions, 8-shot and greedy, the four SGLang configs scored 458, 456, 458 and 460 correct, and every interval overlaps every other. The run did not show a difference. It also cannot rule out a loss of a few points at this sample size, and it covers one model and one benchmark. What actually happened The queue was the pool. The BF16 pool of 24094 tokens held about 37 requests of this shape, so 26 of 64 users waited, and the wait went into their first token. FP8 weights and an FP8 KV cache made the pool 5.91 times larger on the same card. At 64 users the queue was empty, the median first token was 296.42 ms, and the server delivered 2.87 requests per second within the goodput target where BF16 delivered none. The team ships the FP8 pair with three conditions written next to the result. The sweep changed the weights and the cache together, so the gain is claimed for the pair, not for either alone. The KV scale was 1.0 on this checkpoint, and the manual's check for scales in the index and in the load log is recorded with the deployment. The accuracy check on 500 questions bounded the loss at a few points on one benchmark, so the team repeats it on their own prompts before the switch. The second L4 waits until the FP8 pool fills. Wrong turns "Buy a second L4 and balance across both." The queue came from a pool of 24094 tokens that held about 37 requests. A second card doubles the pool at twice the cost, and the FP8 pool was 5.91 times larger on one card. "Change one thing: keep BF16 weights and switch only the KV cache to FP8." A fair experiment, and this sweep did not run it. The manual's evidence for an FP8 cache alone is a field report, and that cache needs a scale file. "The accuracy matched, so FP8 is safe for every model." The check covered one model, one benchmark and 500 questions. It bounds the loss at a few points, and a different model can lose more. "FP8 is faster per token, so switch for speed." The manual's position is to choose the KV cache data type from memory, not from speed. Here the queue was the symptom and the pool was the cause; the speed gain at one user is a second effect. The lesson to carry When requests queue while the GPU is busy, read the pool before you read the kernels. A full pool is a capacity problem, and the cheapest capacity on one card is bytes per token: smaller weights free memory for the cache, and a smaller cache data type doubles what fits. Pay for it with an accuracy check on your own task, and write down which scale the cache used. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual runs this pair on the L4 in the quantization page and sizes the pool in the KV bytes page , the vLLM manual measures FP8 weights at a fixed pool in the FP8 weights page , and the inference metrics lesson defines the goodput that settles the decision. Recap What to keep from this case Read running, waiting and cache usage before buying hardware. Waiting time goes into time-to-first-token. Smaller number formats enlarge the cache on the same card. Check output quality after changing formats.
