a2126: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems One Error, Two HTTP Status Codes Lesson 21.26 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : A2A 1.0.1 with the manual's capture kit (the test-runner, code-reviewer and deployer agents) Model : no model; the agents are deterministic fixtures Hardware : one machine, localhost, no network The situation In plain words first A client built for a REST service treats HTTP 2xx as success and 404 as "not visible yet, retry". Talking to an agent over JSON-RPC, it received a 200 whose body was an error ("task not found") and logged it as success. Over the REST binding the same error retried forever. The case trains decoding the protocol, not only the transport, and classifying errors by their reason. A planner delegates test runs to a remote test-runner agent. Its transport layer was written for a plain REST service. A 2xx reply is a success. A 404 means the record is not visible yet, so the client waits and asks again. A 5xx gets a retry with backoff. The planner first talked to the agent over its JSON-RPC interface. Last night it looked up a task id that the agent had purged, logged the lookup as a success, and then crashed on an empty result. A teammate moved the planner to the agent's HTTP+JSON interface this morning, "so that we get real status codes". The same lookup now comes back as a 404, and the planner has asked again every two seconds for an hour. You are asked to make the client stop at the right time in both bindings, without a special case for each error. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. A GetTask for an unknown id over JSON-RPC, status and code Copy The detail inside data of the same JSON-RPC error Copy The same lookup over HTTP+JSON, status and body head Copy The detail inside the HTTP+JSON error Copy Every A2A error with its code in each binding Copy Which errors a client may retry Copy Questions to answer first In the JSON-RPC reply, where is the fact that the lookup failed, and what does the HTTP status tell you? Which field is identical in both replies, and which fields differ? How many of the nine A2A errors share one HTTP status, and what does that do to a policy that keys on the status alone? Which errors may a client retry, and what should it do with a task that is not found? The planner also retries a SendMessage after a timeout. What must it keep the same, and why? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A JSON-RPC error can arrive inside an HTTP 200. ✗ A 404 always means "try again soon". For a purged task it means stop; the error reason says which. ✓ One error reader for both bindings keeps behaviour consistent. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the JSON-RPC reply. The status line says 200 OK , and the body has no result . In its place sits an error member with the code -32001 and the message Task not found . In this binding every reply is a 200, so the status carries no information. The client must open the body and test for error before it reads result . Read the detail in data . It is a list with one object. Its reason is TASK_NOT_FOUND , its domain is a2a-protocol.org , and its metadata repeats the task id. The reason is the name of the error without its suffix. This is the field a client can decide on. Read the HTTP+JSON reply. The status line says 404 Not Found . The body is a Status object with code 404, status NOT_FOUND , the same message, and details where JSON-RPC had data . Inside the details sits the same detail object with the same reason. The envelope changed, and the error did not. Read the table. Seven of the nine A2A errors map to HTTP 400, and InvalidParamsError maps to 400 as well. The three JSON-RPC parse and request errors have no HTTP status at all. A rule keyed to the status cannot tell a task that cannot be canceled from a request with a bad field. Only TaskNotFoundError maps to 404, so a REST policy that waits on 404 waits on the one error that never clears. Apply the retry rules. -32603 , HTTP 500 or 503, or a dropped connection: retry with backoff and honor Retry-After . HTTP 401: get a fresh credential. -32600 , -32602 , -32005 and -32009 : fix the request. -32001 : stop, because the id is wrong, purged, or hidden from this caller. -32002 , or -32004 on a terminal task: start a new task. -32003 or -32007 : read the card again. A server must not reveal a task that the caller may not see, so not found can also mean "not yours". Check the other retry. A SendMessage that timed out may have created a task. Duplicate detection by messageId is optional, so a resend with a fresh id can start a second task. The planner resends the same bytes with the same messageId , and the server gets its one chance to recognize the duplicate. What actually happened The client decoded the transport and never the protocol. The fix is one error reader for both bindings. Read the HTTP status, then the error member or the Status body, then the reason of the first detail. Classify by reason into retry, re-authenticate, fix the request, or stop. On TASK_NOT_FOUND the planner stops after one reply, in either binding, which is what the capture shows: one request and one reply for the unknown id over JSON-RPC, and one request and one reply over HTTP+JSON. A retried send keeps its messageId . The hour of repeated lookups does not come back, because the decision no longer depends on a status code that one binding does not even use. Wrong turns "Move every client to HTTP+JSON, then the status codes are real." Seven of the nine A2A errors arrive as 400 there, next to invalid parameters. The status still does not name the error. "Match on the message text." The message is for a person. The reference implementation answers the same cases with other words and other field names, so a text match breaks on the next server. "Treat 404 as eventual consistency and keep polling." The specification tells a server to answer not found for a purged id and for a task the caller may not see. No later call changes that answer. "Resend with a fresh messageId to be safe." Duplicate detection is optional, and a fresh id removes the only hint the server has. The suite can run twice. The lesson to carry A protocol carried over HTTP has two layers of status. The transport status says whether the bytes arrived. The protocol's own error says what happened to the request, and in some bindings it hides behind a 200. Decide on the protocol's discriminator, keep the set of retryable errors small and explicit, and give every retry an idempotency key that the server can see. How this connects Where this is taught The errors page of A2A 101 reads these two replies and gives the retry rules, the error table maps every error into the three bindings, and the failure modes lesson names the cascade that follows a client that cannot tell failure from success. Recap What to keep from this case Decode the protocol, not just the HTTP status. Classify errors by reason: retry, re-authenticate, fix, or stop. Use one error reader across bindings. Stop after one reply for a permanent "not found". a2127: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Six Steps into RL Training: Is It Learning? Lesson 21.27 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first Six steps into a reinforcement-learning run, the reward dipped three times and a teammate wants to stop and halve the learning rate. Rewards on small batches are noisy; six points are not a trend. The manual lists what to read in the first ten steps and the healthy ranges for each. Read that way, the run is fine. The case trains judging early training by stated ranges, not by the last three numbers. A GRPO run on GSM8K is six steps old. A teammate posts the reward of each step as the log printed it: 0.62890625, 0.59375, 0.7578125, 0.69140625, 0.58984375, 0.5859375. The last three fell. He says the model is getting worse, wants to stop the run, and wants to halve the learning rate before the next start. A second teammate opens the step 0 line and finds that the loss and the advantages are so close to zero that the log prints them in scientific notation. She concludes that no training happens at all and that the run is a waste of a GPU. You pull the log again a little later, when ten steps have finished, together with the three lines that the first step wrote. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The reward of the first ten steps Copy The log probability gap of the first ten steps Copy The perf line of the first rollout Copy The rollout 0 line of the trainer Copy The step 0 line of the trainer Copy The healthy ranges of five numbers over the first ten steps of three seeds Copy The signs of a broken run Copy Questions to answer first Three falling steps in a row. How large is a normal move between two steps on this setup, and over how many steps do you read the reward? The gap between the engine and the trainer: what is its range over the ten steps, and what would a different shape of that series mean? Why are the centered rewards and the advantages of the first rollout near zero, and what number on the same line is the real signal? The step 0 loss is near zero, the clip fraction is 0 and the ppo_kl is 0. Which of those three are expected at step 0, and which number proves that a gradient exists? How many of the 32 groups gave no learning signal in the first rollout, and how do you read that count? Write the rule that decides, at any step, whether this run stops. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Step-to-step reward on a small batch is noisy. ✗ A loss and advantages near zero at step 0 mean the run is dead. Centering makes them near zero by design. ✓ Comparing with the healthy runs' ranges is the right test. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read all ten rewards, not six. The ten values run from 0.5859375 to 0.7578125, and the four steps after the posted six are 0.6875, 0.67578125, 0.74609375 and 0.6484375. The manual measured steps 0 to 9 of three seeds of this recipe: rewards from 0.53 to 0.74, with a per-seed mean of 0.62 to 0.65, and moves of up to 0.14 from one step to the next. The fall after step 2 is a move of that size, and the three steps that fell are followed by four that did not. The manual's rule is to read the mean over five or more steps, never one step. Read the gap. The ten values of train/train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff run from 0.014312651939690113 to 0.01628461480140686, inside the manual's range of 0.0141 to 0.0164 for steps 0 to 9. The series is flat. A gap that grows step after step would mean that the two sides hold different weights, which is the one shape that stops a run at once. Read the first perf line. The answers had a mean length of 739.92578125 tokens and a median of 759.5, with the longest at the limit of 1024 and the shortest at 259. The field rollout/truncated_ratio is 0.3203125, so about a third of the answers hit the cap, inside the range of 0.19 to 0.43. The fields rollout/zero_std/count_1 and rollout/zero_std/count_0 are 7 and 3: ten of the 32 groups had every answer right or every answer wrong. Those groups teach nothing. The rest do. Read the rollout 0 line. rollout/rewards is about minus one point six times ten to the minus nine and rollout/advantages is about four point seven times ten to the minus ten. GRPO subtracts the mean reward of each group from each answer, so the mean of the centered rewards is zero by construction, and the advantages are centered the same way. The signal on that line is rollout/raw_reward , 0.62890625, the share of correct answers before centering. Read the step 0 line. train/loss is near zero for the same reason, because the advantages sum to zero across the batch. train/pg_clipfrac is 0.0 and train/ppo_kl is 0.0, and both must be 0 at step 0, because nothing can be clipped and the old and new probabilities are the same before the first update. train/grad_norm is 0.5216571092605591, inside the range of 0.35 to 4.95 over the whole run. That is the gradient. The gap on this line, 0.015336457639932632, sits inside the step-0 range of 0.0148 to 0.0157 that the manual recorded over 17 runs of this model. Check the four signs of a broken run. Step lines appear, so both processes started. No run of 503 Service Unavailable lines goes on for minutes. The gap does not grow. The reward is not flat, and most of the 32 groups score with a spread. None of the four signs is present. What actually happened The run is healthy on every number that the manual asks you to read, and it stays on. The reward over ten steps sits in the range of the three healthy seeds, the gap is flat and in range, the cut share is in range, the gradient norm is in range, and the two step-0 values that must be zero are zero. The near-zero loss and advantages are what centering does, not a sign of a dead run. The rule for stopping is the table of signs, not the last three rewards: stop when no step line appears within ten minutes, when the error lines do not stop for minutes, when the gap grows step after step, or when the reward stays flat while most groups score the same. For the trend, read means over five or more steps, and expect what the three seeds of the longer run showed: the reward rose, the answers got shorter, from about 720 to about 460 tokens, and the gap stayed flat. Wrong turns "Three falling steps, halve the learning rate." A move of up to 0.14 between two steps is normal on this setup, and the gradient norm sits in its range. A learning rate change now answers noise with a new variable, and the next run cannot be compared with this one. "The loss is zero, so nothing trains." The advantages are centered in each group and sum to zero, which puts the loss near zero by construction. The gradient norm of 0.5216571092605591 is the proof that an update happened. "A third of the answers are cut, raise the length limit." The cut share of 0.3203125 is inside 0.19 to 0.43, and it falls on its own as the model learns shorter answers. A higher limit makes every rollout slower. "Ten groups out of 32 give no signal, so the data is wrong for this model." Those groups cost rollout time and teach nothing, and the rest still teach. The sign to act on is a flat reward with most groups the same, and the reward here is not flat. The lesson to carry One number read at one step tells you almost nothing, and the number that everyone reads first, the reward, is the slowest to show a fault. Build a short list of signals with a healthy range for each, from your own seeds, and read them together before you touch a run. Know which values are zero by construction, so that a zero does not look like a dead run, and decide a stop from a sign of breakage, never from a dip. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual gives the five numbers and their ranges in the first ten steps page , the step-0 zeros of the clip fraction and the KL in the first step page , the eight signals of a run in the read the run page , and the noise between seeds in the repeat page . Recap What to keep from this case Six noisy points are not a trend. Read every signal the manual lists, against healthy ranges. Near-zero values can be correct by construction. Do not change the learning rate on a hunch. Mark complete and continue Mark as not done Previous 21.26 · One Error, Two HTTP Status Codes Next 21.28 · The Draft Model That Declared 2,048 Positions
a2128: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems The Draft Model That Declared 2,048 Positions Lesson 21.28 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 with the lmsys/SGLang-EAGLE3-Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-SpecForge-Nex draft, and Qwen/Qwen3-8B with the Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3 draft Hardware : one GB10 with unified memory, and one L4 as the second machine The situation In plain words first Adding speculative decoding fails at start: the draft model declares 2,048 positions and the main model 262,144, and a safety check refuses the mismatch. The team almost files a bug against the draft model. The recipe they copied sets an environment variable for exactly this pair, and with it the server starts. The case trains reading a refusal as a deliberate check and finding the documented override. A team adds EAGLE-3 speculation to its mixture-of-experts server on a GB10. They take the draft model and the shape from the cookbook: three steps, a top-k of one, four draft tokens. The start fails inside the draft worker with a ValueError about two context lengths, and the scheduler child exits. Earlier the same day a colleague turned on the same feature for the dense 8B model on an L4, with its own trained draft, and the server came up without any change. The team concludes that the draft published for the 30B model is defective and prepares an issue for its authors, with a request for a new draft. You are asked to look at the two logs before the issue goes out. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The end of the traceback of the refused start Copy The 8B target and its draft on an L4, with no override Copy The settings line of the L4 start Copy The command of the start that worked Copy The same check with the override set Copy The two pools of the target and the draft Copy What the override does and does not do Copy Questions to answer first Which component raised the error, the target or the draft, and which two numbers does the check compare? The L4 pair started with no change. What differs between the two draft configs? The error message names an environment variable. What does setting it change, and what does it leave as it was? Read the pool lines of the start that worked. What did the draft cost in memory, and which request limit did speculation set? The benchmark prompts had 512 tokens. Which incident in the manual shows what a draft with 2,048 positions does on long inputs, and how would you test that before production? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A check that refuses mismatched context lengths is a safeguard, not a crash. ✗ The draft model is defective because its config says 2,048. It was trained that way; the cookbook's command allows the pairing. ✓ The same feature working on another model does not mean the settings carry over. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the traceback from the bottom up to the first frame you recognise. The frames run from the scheduler into maybe_init_draft_worker , then into the EAGLE draft worker, then into a model config, and the error is raised in _derive_context_length . So the check belongs to the draft's model config. It compares the target's context length, 262144, with the length it derived for the draft, 2048, and refuses because the target is larger. The last sentence of the message names the way out: set SGLANG_ALLOW_OVERWRITE_LONGER_CONTEXT_LEN=1 . Compare with the L4 pair. On the L4 the target loaded with 6.41 GB free, the draft of type LlamaForCausalLMEagle3 loaded 1.90 GB more, the pool came out at 8,827 tokens, and the settings line reads context_len=40960 . That draft declares 40,960 positions, the same as its target, so the check had nothing to refuse. The variable belongs to one draft config, not to EAGLE-3. The manual's rule is to compare max_position_embeddings in both configs before you set it. Read the start that worked. The cookbook command for this pair begins with the variable. With it set, the same warning about 262144 against 2048 still prints, and the next line says what changed: the draft's max_position_embeddings is overridden to 262144. The manual is exact about the meaning. The variable only removes the check. It does not teach the draft to read long prompts. Read what the draft cost. The target pool holds 216,775 tokens at 9.92 GB each for K and V. The draft has a pool with the same token count at 0.21 GB each, after loading 1.58 GB of weights in 1.30 s. The start also reset max_running_requests to 48, the cap that every speculation handler sets when you do not set it yourself. On the L4 the same draft design cut the pool from 24,094 tokens to 8,827, so on a small card the draft takes the memory that the batch needs. Find the incident that the override hides. Issue #6783 in the manual's incident list ran a 70B model with EAGLE-3 and a draft config of 2,048 positions and no rope scaling. Acceptance was 3.2 tokens at 1k input, 1.6 at 3k and 1.2 at 10k, and at 10k the server produced 63.9 tokens per second against 102.7 without speculation. Adding rope scaling and 131,072 positions to the draft config fixed it. The manual's GB10 run used 512-token prompts and says that it tells you nothing about long contexts. The test is to read accept len on the decode log lines, or sglang:spec_accept_length from the metrics, on your own longest prompts, and to compare the time per token with speculation off at the same prompts. What actually happened The draft is not defective. Its config declares 2,048 positions, and the context length check refuses that against a 262,144-token target. The cookbook's command sets the variable for this pair, and with it the server started with a target pool of 216,775 tokens, a draft of 1.58 GB, and a cap of 48 running requests. The issue to the draft's authors was not sent. The team then treated the variable as a removed check rather than a fix. They measured the acceptance length on their longest prompts with the decode log and the endpoint for metrics, and set --max-running-requests themselves from the concurrency where speculation still won in their sweep. If acceptance falls on long prompts the way it did in issue #6783, the next step is a draft config with rope scaling and enough positions, or no speculation for that traffic, not a larger override. Wrong turns "The draft model is broken, ask for a new one." The draft loaded and served once the check was removed. A config that declares 2,048 positions is a limit of that draft, not a defect in its weights. "Set the variable everywhere EAGLE-3 runs." The L4 draft needed no variable, because its positions matched its target. Set it only for the draft config that needs it, after you compared the two configs. "The override fixed it, so long prompts are fine." The override removes a check. In issue #6783 a draft with 2,048 positions fell to 1.2 accepted tokens at 10k input and made the server slower than no speculation. "Lower the target's context length to 2048 so the check passes." That caps every request at the draft's limit and gives up the long contexts the 30B model was chosen for. Fix the draft config or test the limit instead. The lesson to carry A refusal at startup is a contract check between two components, and the fastest way out is to turn the check off. Before you do, read what each side declared and what the check protects. An override that removes a check leaves the mismatch in place, so the measurement that the check stood in for, here the acceptance length on long prompts, becomes your job. Compare the two configs, remove the check only for the pair that needs it, and measure what it guarded. How this connects Where this is taught The speculative decoding page of SGLang 101 records both starts in what we measured on a GB10 , gives the cap in the limit nobody asked for , and lists the long-prompt failure under incidents . Recap What to keep from this case Read refusals as checks with reasons. Follow the documented recipe for the specific pair. Settings that work on one model may not transfer. Verify the cache and limits after enabling speculation. Mark complete and continue Mark as not done Previous 21.27 · Six Steps into RL Training: Is It Learning? a2129: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems The API Key in the Log Was a Placeholder Lesson 21.29 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : sbx v0.47.0 Model : none; shell commands inside the sandbox Hardware : one Mac with the microVM runtime The situation In plain words first An agent printed its environment into a shared log, including something that looks like a key, and a reviewer files a ticket to rotate it. The value is a placeholder: the real secret never enters the sandbox; a proxy swaps it into requests to two approved hosts only. The case trains checking where a secret actually exists before treating a value as leaked. A security reviewer reads the transcript of a sandboxed agent session. The agent was asked to debug a failing request, so it ran env and printed its environment into the log that the team shares. One line reads M101_RECV_KEY=sbx-cs-<rand> , where the capture masks the random part. The reviewer files a ticket: the agent holds a credential in plain text, the value sits in a shared log, rotate it now. The platform engineer disagrees and says the value is not a secret. Nobody can show why. You get the printed lines, the record of the secret in the store, four requests sent from inside the same sandbox, and the log kept by the host receiver that those requests reached. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The two custom lines of the environment inside m101-secret Copy A custom secret with a chosen placeholder prefix Copy The record of M101_RECV_KEY in sbx secret ls Copy Four requests from the sandbox that carry the placeholder Copy The three requests as the receiver on the host saw them Copy Questions to answer first Is the printed value the credential? What in the store record settles it? The first three requests returned 204. What did the receiver get in each header, and what does that say about where the swap happens? The fourth request got no reply and the code 000. Why, and what does that tell you about a placeholder sent to a host it is not bound to? Which row of the manual's claims ledger does this evidence confirm, and which claim about the proxy stays unchecked? What should the ticket become? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A secret proxy keeps the real credential outside the sandbox. ✗ Any key-shaped value in a log is a leaked credential. Here it was a placeholder; the real value exists only in requests the proxy rewrites. ✓ Requests to unapproved hosts carry the placeholder or are blocked. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the two printed lines. M101_RECV_KEY holds sbx-cs-<rand> , and the other custom line holds the word proxy-managed . The manual names three sentinel formats in this release: proxy-managed for the provider keys, a token-shaped value for the git host, and sbx-cs-<rand> for custom secrets. The printed value has the custom shape. Read how a placeholder is made and stored. set-custom saves a placeholder for a target host and an env name, and with --placeholder 'sk-{rand}' the saved value is sk-<rand> . The secret ls record for M101_RECV_KEY has two fields that matter: placeholder is sbx-cs-<rand> , and secret is masked as m101-d**************0000 . The environment inside the sandbox holds the first field. The second never left the store. Follow the placeholder to a bound host. From inside, three requests to host.docker.internal:18080 returned 204: one with the variable inside Bearer , one with the placeholder typed as a literal, and one with the bare value and no scheme. The receiver logged Bearer m101-dummy-receiver-0000 for the first two, the same value in X-Demo , and the bare value as the whole Authorization header for the third. The real value appears only on the host side, wherever the placeholder stood. So the swap is a substring replacement in the forward proxy, and it happens for a host that the secret is bound to. Follow it to another name. The fourth request went to gateway.docker.internal:18080 . That name is in NO_PROXY , so curl skipped the forward proxy and opened a direct connection. The transparent proxy blocked it: an empty reply, the code 000 and exit 52. Nothing was swapped. A placeholder sent anywhere else stays a placeholder. Place the result in the ledger. The manual's claims table marks "credential values never enter the VM" as confirmed by these two files, and the header swap for a bound host as confirmed on both sides. It marks TLS interception as not checked, because no certificate chain was read, and the question of data leaving through an allowed host as disputed, with no capture. Say exactly that much. What actually happened The value in the log is the placeholder of a custom secret, not the credential. The credential stays in the host store. The forward proxy puts it into requests to the two bound hosts only, and the receiver log shows that this is where the real value first exists. A request to any other name carries the placeholder or is blocked. The ticket closes as no leak, with two notes: the placeholder tells a reader that a bound secret exists for those hosts, and the sandbox could reach localhost:18080 only because a policy rule allowed it, so the receiver was a host the operator chose. Two checks go into the runbook. For a suspected leak from a sandbox, compare the printed value with the placeholder field of sbx secret ls --json before anything is rotated. For a new custom secret, bind it to exact hosts and send one request to a receiver you control, so the swap is proven once, as the capture did. Wrong turns "Rotate the key and purge the log." Nothing in the log is the key. A rotation costs a change on the host and on the receiver and fixes nothing, and the next transcript shows the same placeholder. "The agent read the host keychain." The guest has no path to the store. The swap happens in the proxy on the host, after the request leaves the VM. "Pass the real key with -e so the agent can call the API itself." A plain variable is not a secret, and the sentinel exists so that the value never enters the VM. The store and the binding are the supported path. "The proxy touches only the Authorization header, so a value in another header is safe." The receiver shows the value in X-Demo too. A custom secret is replaced wherever the placeholder appears in a request to a bound host, so bind it to exact hosts. The lesson to carry A secret shown by a process inside a boundary is a secret only if the same bytes work outside the boundary. Before you call a leak, find where the value is stored, compare the printed bytes with the stored placeholder, and send the printed bytes to a receiver you control from an intended and from an unintended destination. Then write down what the test proved and what it did not, with the file names. How this connects Where this is taught The manual's secret page records the placeholder, the swap and the receiver, the proxy page explains the two proxy paths, and the claims ledger says which claim these files confirm. Recap What to keep from this case Find where the real secret lives before declaring a leak. Placeholders let agents work without holding credentials. Still avoid printing environments into shared logs. Check the receiving side to see where the real value appears. a2130: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems RadixAttention Prefix Cache Turned Off for Predictability Lesson 21.30 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.6 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, screen, ml-breadth. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22, with vLLM 0.31.0 as the second engine Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on the GB10, and Qwen/Qwen3-8B on the L4 Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory, and one L4 with 24 GB of memory The situation In plain words first After a benchmark misled a team, a new policy turned off prefix caching everywhere "for predictability". A customer who sends the same 2,000-token system prompt with every question saw first-token time triple. The cache was never what made the benchmark wrong; the benchmark's method was. The case trains fixing the cause of a misleading measurement instead of removing a useful feature. After a benchmark incident in which a warm prefix cache made a loaded server look faster, a platform team writes a new policy: production and benchmarks must agree, so every SGLang server starts with --disable-radix-cache , and the vLLM replicas start with --no-enable-prefix-caching . The rollout goes out on a Friday. On Monday a customer whose assistant sends a system prompt of about two thousand tokens with every question reports that the first token now takes several seconds instead of under one, and that the service answers fewer questions per minute at the same user count. The platform team replies that nothing changed in the model or the hardware, and that the new numbers are the "true" ones. You are asked to settle it. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The shared-prefix benchmark: four groups of 16 prompts with one system prompt each Copy The shared-prefix run on the GB10 with the radix cache on Copy The same run on the GB10 with --disable-radix-cache Copy Two prefill lines on the L4 with the cache, 2,048 shared tokens Copy Two prefill lines on the L4 without the cache, 4,096 shared tokens Copy The same test on the other engine, cache on and off by shared length Copy The SGLang table on the L4 by shared length, with the clock caveat Copy Questions to answer first What does a prefix cache change about the work a server does, and what does it leave the same? From the two GB10 runs, how much did the first token and the throughput move, and which line proves that the same work was requested? Read the four L4 prefill lines. What do #new-token , #cached-token and #pending-token say about each configuration? Both engines were measured. Does the effect belong to one engine, and how does its size depend on the shared length? The policy wanted predictable numbers. Which fix gives that without the cost? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A warm cache can make a badly designed benchmark look faster. ✗ Disabling the cache in production makes benchmarks honest. The benchmark needed flushing and varied seeds; production needed the cache. ✓ On the GB10 the shared-prefix median first token rose from 691 ms to 2,542 ms without the cache. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Know what the cache saves. The tree indexes the KV entries of every prompt the server has seen. A new request reuses the longest matching prefix and prefills only the tokens after it. The decode work stays the same, so a cache hit removes prefill time and nothing else. A system prompt that every request repeats is the best case: the whole shared part comes from the tree. Read the workload. The kit runs the engine's own shared-prefix benchmark: four groups of 16 prompts, one system prompt of 2,048 tokens per group, a 128-token question on each prompt, and a cap of eight requests at once. The second server starts with the cache disabled. Compare the two GB10 runs. Both report 146646 input tokens over 64 requests, so the client asked for the same work. With the cache the run took 28.97 s and gave 141.38 output tokens per second with a median TTFT of 690.96 ms. Without it the run took 50.26 s, the output fell to 81.49, and the median TTFT rose to 2542.06 ms, with a P99 of 3304.86 ms against 2051.54. The input tokens per second tell the same story: 5061.63 with the tree and 2917.46 without. The customer's two complaints, a slower first token and fewer answers per minute, are both in this pair. Read the L4 prefill lines. With the cache and a 2,048-token shared prompt, one batch prefilled 405 new tokens and took 12952 from the cache, and the next prefilled 546 new with 17269 cached. Without the cache and a 4,096-token shared prompt, each batch prefilled 4096 new tokens with 0 cached, and 5527 tokens were still pending for the next chunk. Every request paid for its whole prompt, in chunks of the prefill size, while the others waited. Check the other engine. On the L4 with vLLM, the cache kept the median first token near 400 ms at every shared length: 408, 488, 396, 410 and 375 ms. Without it the first token grew with the shared part: 392, 753, 1,213, 2,550 and 13,353 ms, and the output fell from 113.6 to 19.6 tokens per second. The manual asks to read the last two rows with care, because the GPU throttled there, and names the 1,024-token row as the clean comparison: about three times the first token and 50 percent more output with the cache. The effect is the same on both engines, and it grows with the shared length. Bound the factor. The SGLang table on the L4 reads 479 ms against 14,706 ms at 4,096 shared tokens, 30.7 times, and 4.3 times the throughput. The run without the cache ran at 930 MHz against 1,440 with it, with a thermal flag in 62 percent of its samples, so the manual treats both factors as upper bounds and notes that a 35 percent clock gap cannot explain a factor of 30. Read the GB10 pair, which had no such gap, for the size you can trust. What actually happened The policy caused the incident. The cache was never what made the benchmark lie; the method was, because the kit reused one seed on one server and never flushed between runs. Removing the cache from production removed the work-saving that the customer's traffic depends on. On the GB10, the shared-prefix run saw its median TTFT go from 690.96 ms to 2542.06 ms, and its output went from 141.38 to 81.49 tokens per second, for the same 146646 input tokens. The fix is to turn the cache back on, on both engines, and to make the benchmarks predictable by protocol: flush the cache before each run that you compare, use a new seed per run, and record the cached tokens next to the result. Prove the production fix with #cached-token in the prefill lines, which should carry most of each shared prompt, and with the median TTFT of the customer's traffic back near the cached level. Keep the manual's one exception: turn the cache off only to test whether a wrong answer comes from reused KV, and try --kv-canary log first. Wrong turns "The cache made the benchmark lie, so it has no place in production." The benchmark lied because it reused its prompts without a flush. The cache in production serves prompts that really repeat, and the customer's system prompt is exactly that. "Only the first token is affected, throughput is unchanged." On the GB10 the output fell from 141.38 to 81.49 tokens per second and the run took 50.26 s instead of 28.97. Prefill that is computed again occupies steps that decode would have used. "The effect is an SGLang detail." The other engine moved from 396 to 1,213 ms at 1,024 shared tokens and from 375 to 13,353 ms at 4,096, on the same card. "Shorten the customer's system prompt instead." The prompt is the customer's product. A server feature that removes the repeated work is the cheaper fix, and the manual measured no cost from the cache when nothing is shared. "Keep it off, because a wrong answer might come from reused KV." That is the one reason the manual accepts, and even then it asks you to try --kv-canary log first and to turn the cache off only for the test. The lesson to carry A measurement artifact is fixed in the measurement, not in the system. When a cache or any other state carries over between benchmark runs, reset the state between runs and record it; do not remove the mechanism from production, where the same state is the point. Before you change a default that saves work, measure the traffic that repeats and count what the default saves there. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual measures the pair in the RadixCache page , the vLLM manual measures the other engine in the prefix cache page with the full table in the lab notes , and the RadixAttention lesson teaches the tree and where it wins and loses. Recap What to keep from this case Fix the measurement method, not the system being measured. Prefix caching is essential for repeated system prompts. Benchmarks should flush caches and vary seeds. Check who depends on a feature before removing it. a2131: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Two Refusals, Two Wordings, One Agent Permissions File Lesson 21.31 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-breadth. Roles : agentic AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : docker-agent v1.149.0 and sbx v0.47.0 Model : ai/qwen3:4b through the local model runner, at temperature 0 Hardware : one Mac, no GPU The situation In plain words first Two engineers report the same agent "refusing" commands, with different wording. One refusal is a deny rule that blocks rm in every mode, which is working as intended. The other comes from a person declining a prompt. The case trains reading the exact wording of a refusal to tell which layer produced it: a policy, a mode, a hook or a human. Two tickets arrive on the same morning about one agent file. The file gives an agent a shell toolset, an allow pattern for echo , a deny pattern for rm , and a logging hook on every shell call. Both engineers sent the same three messages: run echo m101-ok , run pwd , run rm -rf work/m101-nothing . The first engineer runs the agent in a pipeline with --exec --safety restricted . The ticket says that the agent refuses rm with the text Tool 'shell' is denied by permissions configuration and asks for the deny pattern to be removed, because the pipeline needs a cleanup step. The second engineer runs it on a laptop with --exec --safety strict . The ticket says that the agent refuses pwd with the text The user rejected the tool call , that no prompt ever appeared, and that the hook must be broken, because it answers allow on every call. You hold both tickets and the capture of both runs. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The toolset, the hook and the two patterns of the guarded agent Copy The three commands under --safety restricted Copy The second and third commands under --safety strict Copy The three records the hook wrote, one per call Copy The hook script Copy The shell tool called directly, with no model in the loop Copy The order the runtime applies to every tool call Copy Questions to answer first The two refusals have two wordings. Before you open the agent file, say what each wording tells you about where the decision was made. No pattern names pwd . Why did it run in one mode and not in the other? The hook answered allow on all three calls. Why did that change nothing, and what could the hook have changed? What does the direct tool run prove, and what does it not prove? Which ticket reports a bug, which reports the design at work, and what do you change for each? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A deny pattern overrides every allow, ask and mode. ✗ Both refusals have the same cause because the same commands were sent. One came from policy, the other from a user's answer to a prompt. ✓ A pipeline that must delete files should do it outside the agent or with a narrower rule. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the agent file. One toolset of type shell . A pre_tool_use hook with matcher: shell and preempt_yolo: true , which runs a script. Under permissions , allow holds shell:cmd=echo* and deny holds shell:cmd=rm* . Nothing names pwd . Read the restricted run. echo ran and printed m101-ok . pwd ran and printed the working directory. The rm call never reached a tool: the response says that the configuration denies the tool. That is the deny pattern, which matches rm* . Read the strict run. echo ran again. For pwd , the runtime raised tool_call_confirmation with metadata blast_radius: safe , category: fs-read , and safety_label: safe . Under strict , every label asks. With --exec there was no terminal, so the ask became a rejection, and the model got a message that said the user rejected the call. The rm call got the same denial as in the other mode. The two wordings mark two decision points: a denial names the policy, and a rejection names the person who was asked. Read the hook records and the script. The hook wrote three records in the restricted run, one per call, including the rm call. The records carry safety_policy: restricted and the full tool_input . The script appends the record and prints permission_decision: allow . The order of decisions puts preempting hooks first, and from there an allow is advice only: a deny or an ask from the hook would have ended the call, an allow does not grant it. The deny pattern then blocked rm at the second step. Read the direct tool run. debug tool called the shell tool of the same agent file with echo m101-direct and printed m101-direct with exit 0. The tool works. The refusals are decisions, not tool failures. The direct run does not say what the model would call, so it closes only the question about the toolset. Map each command to the order. echo : step three, an allow pattern. rm : step two, a deny pattern, in both modes. pwd : no pattern, so step five, the safety mode on the label safe : restricted allows a safe label, and strict asks. What actually happened The first ticket describes the policy doing its job. A deny pattern blocks the call in every mode, and the manual's order places it above every allow, every ask, and every mode. Keep the pattern. A pipeline that must delete files does that outside the agent, or with a narrower deny that still excludes rm -rf . Removing the one rule that no mode and no hook can override leaves an unattended agent with no gate. The second ticket reports a mode that does not fit an unattended run. strict asks on every unmatched call, and --exec without a terminal turns every ask into a rejection. The fix is --safety restricted for the laptop run, which lets a safe label run and refuses destructive and unknown , or an allow pattern for pwd . The hook is not broken: a preempting hook grants nothing, and its log of three records shows that it saw every call. The proof is the restricted run: pwd printed the working directory, rm stayed refused, and the hook recorded all three. One line from the manual belongs in both ticket replies: the client enforces permissions, they stop accidents, and they are not a security boundary. For an agent you do not trust, run it in a sandbox. Wrong turns "The hook is broken, because it returned allow and the call was still refused." From a preempting hook an allow verdict is advice. Its deny or ask would have ended the call. Nothing is broken. "Remove the deny pattern so the cleanup step runs in the pipeline." The deny is the one rule that no mode and no hook can override. An unattended agent with rm allowed has no gate left. "Run with --yolo so nothing asks." That is autonomous : every unmatched call runs, destructive and unknown included. The pwd case needs restricted or one allow pattern. "The shell toolset is misconfigured on the laptop." The direct run printed m101-direct with exit 0 against the same agent file. The tool works, and the decision layer refused. The lesson to carry Read the wording of a refusal first. A denial names the policy, a rejection names the user, and a prompt in a headless run becomes a rejection. Then map each call to the decision order: preempting hooks, deny, allow, ask, mode. Choose the mode by who is watching the terminal, and remember that none of this is a security boundary. How this connects Where this is taught The permissions section runs these three commands in both modes and gives the decision order. Recap What to keep from this case Read the exact wording of a refusal. Know the order: deny rules beat everything. Keep the rule that no mode can override. Different layers refuse in different words. a2132: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Engine or Input: Which Side Failed? Lesson 21.32 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 2 (Working). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, screen. Roles : agentic AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : rea 6.7.0 at 27dc42d with the Ghidra provider Model : no model; the fixtures are the ledger binaries built at -O1 and -O2 Hardware : one aarch64 Mac The situation In plain words first An overnight analysis wrapper restarted its engine eleven times, paying for a fresh import each time, and every retry failed the same way. Neither failure was the engine's fault: one was a tool provider that cannot run on that host, the other a wrong argument. The case trains classifying a failure before reacting, and using the category and retry hints the tool already returns. A team wraps rea in an agent pipeline that analyses binaries overnight. The wrapper has one rule for failures: on any failed call, close the target, stop the Java process, open the target again, and retry. The night log shows the engine restarted eleven times, each restart followed by the same failure, and the import of the target paid for again each time. Two failures appear in the log, and the wrapper treated them the same way. The first came from the command line on the Mac that runs the pipeline: a layout inspection of an object file exited 1. The second came from the MCP session: analyze_function returned an error for a procedure name that the agent had typed. You have the command record, the two error envelopes, the session index and the server log. Say what each failure was, and write the retry rule that the wrapper should have had. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The CLI call that exited 1 Copy The whole envelope of that call Copy Three consecutive calls of the MCP session Copy The decoded error of the MCP call Copy The end of the diagnostics object Copy The server log around the failed call Copy Questions to answer first Both envelopes have the same five fields. Which two fields decide what to do next, before you read the message? The first failure says that a profile supports Linux x64 only. What was wrong, the host, the file, or the engine, and what is the right next call? The second failure is retryable: true . What would a retry with the same arguments return, and what has to change? How does the diagnostics object tell you that the Ghidra process was healthy when the call failed? Name the codes for which a restart of the engine is the correct response. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A failure caused by the input repeats no matter how often the engine restarts. ✗ Restarting the engine is a safe universal recovery. It cost an import each time and could not fix either cause. ✓ A wrong argument becomes retryable once the argument is changed. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read code, category and retryable first. Every rea error carries code , category , message , retryable and remediation . The code is the discriminator, one of twenty. The category is one of ten and names the kind of problem. The flag says whether the same call can succeed later. The message is for a person. A wrapper branches on the first two fields and the flag, never on the message text. Read the CLI failure. The command record shows inspect-binary-layout on the object file, exit 1 after 0.6 s. The envelope has code capability_unavailable , category unsupported_provider , and retryable: false . The details name the provider pwntools-elf and the operation. That provider runs on one platform, Linux x64, and the pipeline runs on a Mac. The engine never ran. The right next call is another provider or another host, and the manual uses inspect-macho as the layout tool on this machine. No restart can change a provider that does not run here. Read the MCP failure. The session index shows the call before and the call after both completed on the same open target, and the failed call took 4 ms. The decoded error has code invalid_request , category invalid_input , and retryable: true . The one issue in the details says that the procedure name is unknown. The flag means that a corrected call can succeed on the same connection. A retry with the same name returns the same error, so the argument has to change, and list_procedures gives the names that exist. Read the diagnostics. failure_output holds the stdout and stderr that Ghidra wrote during the failed request: both empty, with complete: true . The remote code is not_found . An empty, complete output with a remote code says that the engine answered the question and the answer was no. The server log agrees: two lines at level 40, one for the bridge layer and one for the server layer, with a duration of 2.73 ms, and the next line is close_binary with status ok . The engine was healthy before, during and after. Place the restart. A restart answers a different family of codes: provider_unavailable , provider_timeout , and an execution_failure whose diagnostics show incomplete output. The manual names provider_timeout as the code of a first Ghidra-backed call that passes the startup deadline of 330,000 ms, and target_unavailable as the code of every provider tool before open_binary . Neither appeared in these two failures. What actually happened Neither failure was the engine's. The first was a provider that does not run on the host, not retryable, fixed by a different tool. The second was a wrong argument, retryable after the argument changes, and the Ghidra process stayed up and served the next call in the same session. The eleven restarts bought nothing and cost an import each. The wrapper now reads category and retryable before anything else. unsupported_provider and unsupported_target route to a different provider or host and stop. invalid_input corrects the argument from a listing and retries once. unavailable , timeout and an execution_failure with incomplete output restart the engine, with a bound on the count. Everything else is reported to a person with the message and the remediation. After the change, the next night ran with no restart, and the two failures became one line each in the report. Wrong turns "Exit 1 means the engine crashed; restart it." The envelope says unsupported_provider , not retryable. The provider never started, and a restart starts nothing new. "retryable is true, so retry the same call." The flag says that the call can succeed later, after the input changes. The same unknown name gets the same answer. "Match the message text to decide the branch." Messages are written for people and can change between releases. The code, the category and the flag are the contract. "Any level 40 line in the server log means the bridge is unhealthy." Both lines record one failed request that completed in 2.73 ms, and the next line records a successful call on the same connection. The lesson to carry An error envelope is a typed answer, and a retry policy that ignores its type turns every failure into the most expensive one. Read the discriminator and the retryable flag, keep a table from category to action, and look at the diagnostics for proof that the engine was alive before you restart it. The cheapest fix for most failures is a changed input, and the most expensive is a cold start, so the policy must tell them apart. How this connects Where this is taught The errors reference of Reverse Engineering 101 lists the five fields and the twenty codes, the dossier page reads the unknown-name error and its log lines, the MCP server page gives the startup deadline and the recovery that a timeout deserves, and the failure modes lesson names cascading errors as the mode where one wrong response triggers more calls. Recap What to keep from this case Classify failures: engine, input or environment. Read the error's category and retry hint. Restart only for engine faults. Keep sessions alive when the engine is healthy. a2133: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Disaggregated Benchmark That Counted Failures as Wins Lesson 21.33 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.22 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 with the mooncake_tcp transfer backend Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : two L4s in one node, the second shared with another team The situation In plain words first A benchmark of a split prefill/decode deployment reports 240 of 240 requests successful at 8 per second. In fact the cache transfer between the two GPUs failed and the router counted empty responses as successes. The case trains distrusting a benchmark that looks perfect: check that successes contain output, and refuse runs whose numbers are physically impossible. A team wants to stop long prompts from pausing other users' streams, so they split Qwen/Qwen3-8B into a prefill server on the first L4 and a decode server on the second L4, behind the router. The two cards have no RDMA, so the KV cache moves over TCP. The second card also runs another team's pods. They run the fixed-rate sweep through the router. At a fixed rate of 8 per second, the summary prints 240 successful requests of 240 and output throughput of 751.85 tokens per second, higher than the 728.61 of their best single server at the same rate. The slide is ready. A reviewer reads the summary once more and stops at one line: the mean time to first token is 0.00 ms. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The transfer backend and the two KV pools at startup Copy The decode server waits, the transfer queue fills, the session dies Copy The count of failed transfers and the benchmark summary at 8 requests per second Copy The summary lines of the sweep with prefill on the full card and decode on the shared card Copy The same sweep with the roles swapped Copy Questions to answer first Read the two pool lines. What asymmetry do they describe, and what does it do to a request that prefills on one card and decodes on the other? The decode line shows 2 running requests and 19 pre-allocated. What is the decode server waiting for, and what piles up on the prefill side while it waits? After the session failed, every later request still counted as a success. How can a router return a 200 with no text, and which two summary numbers expose it? The swapped split worked up to 8 users and lost text from 16. What does that say about where the small pool hurts? Write the rule that your benchmark kit applies before it prints a throughput number. When is a prefill-decode split worth its new failure modes, and what measurement must exist before you keep one? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ An empty response counted as a success makes a benchmark lie. ✗ 100 percent success at a high rate proves the split design works. Here no request produced tokens; there is no valid result for the split under load. ✓ A benchmark kit should reject runs where every request has no first token. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Start with the pools. The prefill server allocated a KV cache of 24,094 tokens, and the decode server, on the shared card, allocated 2,925 tokens. A request prefills on the large pool and must then find room on the small one. The decode pool holds about four requests of our size at once, so almost every request that the prefill side finishes has to wait for decode memory. The second listing shows the wait. The decode server ran 2 requests, with 19 more pre-allocated and waiting for memory. Prefill kept producing KV caches for them, and the TCP transfer lane to decode filled: the log counts 4,096 queue-full rejections. About three minutes into the sweep the transfer session failed. Every transfer after that failed too, from both sides: prefill could not send its KV chunk, and decode could not get the cache from a prefill instance that it thought was dead. The session never came back. The third listing is the dangerous part. The prefill log holds 2,902 transfer failures, and the benchmark still counts every one of its 240 requests as a success at that rate, with 30,720 generated tokens. Two numbers give it away. The retokenized token count is 0, so no text came back for the client to count. The mean TTFT is 0.00 ms, because no first token ever arrived. The router returned 200 for a request whose decode never ran, and the client counted the requested output length as generated. That is how a throughput of 751.85 came from a server that wrote nothing. The sweep summary lines show that the split failed early at every load. At 2 users only 512 of 2,048 generated tokens came back as text, and at 4 users none did, while the printed throughput jumped to 2,516.97. The fixed-rate sweep lost most of its text from 0.5 requests per second. The swapped split, with decode on the full card and prefill on the shared one, worked from 1 to 8 users with every token retokenized. At 16 users 2,048 of 8,192 tokens came back as text, and at 32 users none did, while the printed throughput still read 333.41. So the small pool breaks the split on whichever side it sits, only later when it sits on the prefill side. What actually happened There is no measured result for the split under load on this pair of cards, and the team must not claim one. The transfer session between the two servers failed under the asymmetric pools and did not recover, and the router then counted empty responses as successes. Three fixes follow. First, the benchmark kit refuses any run in which every request has a time to first token of 0, and reports Total generated tokens (retokenized) next to the generated count on every summary. Second, a split needs two pools of a size that matches the traffic, which the shared card could not give, and the metrics sglang:num_transfer_failed_reqs_total and sglang:num_bootstrap_failed_reqs_total must stay flat during the run. Third, the team goes back to one server, measures the inter-token latency when long prompts arrive, and splits only if that measurement shows prefill interference that data-parallel copies behind the gateway cannot remove. Wrong turns "The split gave 751.85 tokens per second, more than the single server." The retokenized token count was 0. The throughput counted tokens that the client asked for, not tokens that arrived. "240 successful requests of 240 means the router and both servers are healthy." The router returned 200 for requests whose transfer had failed. Only the retokenized count and the first-token time show that the text was empty. "Raise the transfer queue size so the lane does not reject." The lane filled because decode could hold two requests in a 2,925-token pool. A larger queue delays the same failure. "Give decode the full card, then the split works." The swapped split lost text from 16 users and everything at 32. The small pool breaks the split on either side, only at a different load. "Add a fifth check later, the slide is due." A throughput number from a run with no text is not late, it is wrong. The acceptance rule belongs in the kit before the first slide. The lesson to carry A pipeline of two services can report success at the boundary while the work never happened, because the component that answers the client is not the component that failed. Every benchmark summary needs a check that the output exists, not only that the request returned, and every split architecture needs a single-server baseline and a transfer-failure counter before its number means anything. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual records both splits in the disaggregation page , gives the benchmark client in the benchmark page and the router in the gateway page , the vLLM manual covers the same split in its prefill and decode page , and the load testing lesson explains why a client can lie. Recap What to keep from this case Check that successes contain real output. Treat perfect results as a reason to look closer. Do not claim a result the run did not measure. Fix the tooling so it refuses impossible runs. Mark complete and continue Mark as not done Previous 21.32 · Engine or Input: Which Side Failed? Next 21.34 · FP8 KV Cache Scales Silently at 1.0
a2134: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems FP8 KV Cache Scales Silently at 1.0 Lesson 21.34 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory The situation In plain words first Switching the KV cache to FP8 started fine after a backend flag, ran slightly faster and passed an accuracy check. The question nobody asked: where did the scaling factors for FP8 come from? For this model they defaulted to 1.0, which happened to be harmless; for the production model it may not be. The case trains asking what a precision change silently assumes, and checking it before rollout. A team serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4. Requests queue because the KV pool is full, so they add --kv-cache-dtype fp8 to store each cached value in one byte instead of two. The first start fails with a compiler error from a kernel library. A colleague adds a backend flag, the server starts, and a quick benchmark shows the time per token a little lower than before. Before the rollout, the team runs GSM8K on its first 500 questions in BF16 and in FP8 and sees the same accuracy within the error bars. They ship. In the review, a staff engineer asks one question: "Which scale did the cache use?" Nobody knows. The production model is not this one, it is a newer family whose checkpoint ships calibrated scales. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The first start with an FP8 KV cache on the L4 Copy The FP8 KV cache with the Triton backend against the BF16 default, pool held fixed Copy GSM8K accuracy of the four configs on both engines Copy Three rows of the incident index at 0.31.0 Copy The manual's check for scales in the checkpoint and in the startup log Copy Questions to answer first The server picked a different attention backend when the KV data type changed. Why does the data type decide the backend, and why did that backend fail on this host? Two things changed between the BF16 and FP8 runs in the speed table. What can you claim from it, at which user count, and what can you not claim? What is a KV scale, what does a scale of 1.0 do to an FP8 value, and for which checkpoints is 1.0 the only option? Every interval in the accuracy table overlaps. What does that prove, and what can 500 questions not rule out? The production checkpoint carries calibrated scales. Give the three checks, in order, that prove the running server uses them. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ FP8 caches need scaling factors; without them the default may be 1.0. ✗ Passing an accuracy check on one model proves the setting is safe for another. The production model needed its own proof: scale tensors present and no 1.0 warning. ✓ A startup warning about a default scale is evidence worth reading. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Start with the failed start. The second line shows the backend choice: FLASHINFER out of the two candidates FLASHINFER and TRITON_ATTN . FlashAttention is missing from that list. On an L4, vLLM tries FlashAttention first, but at 0.31.0 FlashAttention reads an FP8 KV cache only on Hopper and Blackwell data center GPUs, and the L4 is an Ada GPU with SM 8.9. So vLLM moved to the next backend in its list. FlashInfer builds its kernels on the first start, and the fourth line shows that build failing because the CUDA compiler and the CUDA headers came from different releases. The fix is --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN , which reads an FP8 KV cache without that build, plus VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 because the sampler fails to build in the same way. The speed table holds the pool at 24,096 tokens in both runs, so it does not show the larger pool at all. It shows the change in speed. At one user, FP8 was 2.3 percent faster per token, 101.8 against 104.1 ms, at the same clock of 210 MHz, and the seed ranges did not overlap. At 32 users the seed ranges overlapped and the FP8 run had the higher clock, 480 against 450 MHz, so no claim holds there. Two things changed together, the KV data type and the backend, so even the gain at one user cannot be attributed to the data type alone. The accuracy table starts with the sentence that answers the staff engineer. Neither checkpoint carries KV scales, so the FP8 KV runs used a scale of 1.0. An FP8 value has few bits, and a scale maps the range of the real keys and values onto that range. With no calibrated scale the server stores the values as they are. For this model the result was 454 of 500 correct against 459 in BF16, 90.8 percent against 91.8, with intervals of 87.9 to 93.0 and 89.1 to 93.9. Every interval overlaps every other one. That means the run did not show a difference. It does not mean there is none. With 500 questions the test cannot rule out a loss of a few points, and it covers one model and one benchmark. The incident index adds the part that makes the question dangerous. Issue 54623 reports that the Qwen3.5 model family never loads its checkpoint KV scales, so an FP8 KV cache runs at scale 1.0 even when the checkpoint has calibrated scales. Issue 60333 reports the same for one MTP draft loader. Both are open at 0.31.0. So a checkpoint with scales does not prove that the server uses them. The last listing gives the check. Search the weight index for tensor names that end in k_scale or v_scale . No output means the checkpoint has no scales. Then read the startup log for the warning Using KV cache scaling factor 1.0 . If the checkpoint has scales and the warning is still there, the loader dropped them. Last, run your own prompts with and without FP8 and compare the answers. What actually happened The incident is a missing question, not a crash. For Qwen/Qwen3-8B a scale of 1.0 was the only option, and the accuracy check on 500 questions could not tell the two configs apart. For the production model the team had to prove three things before the rollout: that the checkpoint holds k_scale and v_scale tensors, that the startup log does not print the scale 1.0 warning, and that a sample of their own prompts gives the same answers with and without FP8. They also had to read the backend line after every change to the KV data type. On this L4 the change moved the server from FlashAttention to Triton, and the speed table measured that move as much as the data type. Write the backend, the scale and the accuracy interval next to the result, and keep the accuracy test on your own task, because a model with a different attention layout can lose more. Wrong turns "The accuracy matched, so FP8 is safe for every model." The check covered one model with no scales, one benchmark and 500 questions. It could not rule out a loss of a few points, and a different model can lose more. "The checkpoint has scales, so the server uses them." At 0.31.0 two open issues report loaders that drop the scales and run at 1.0. Only the startup log proves what the server used. "FP8 made each token 2.3 percent faster, so the data type paid off." The backend changed in the same run, and the gain held only at one user. The table cannot say which change gave it. "Fix the compiler error so FlashInfer builds." That is a host repair, not a serving decision. The Triton backend reads the FP8 cache without the build, and the backend line in the log says which one runs. The lesson to carry A quantized store needs a scale, and a default scale of 1.0 is a silent choice that the server makes for you. Whenever you change a data type, read the three lines that follow from it: which kernel now runs, which scale it uses and what the quality check can and cannot detect at its sample size. A test that shows no difference bounds the loss, it does not remove it. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual turns on the FP8 KV cache and checks the scales in the FP8 KV cache page , explains the backend choice in the attention backend page and lists the open loader issues in the incident index , and the SGLang manual runs the same accuracy check in its quantization page . Recap What to keep from this case Ask what a precision change assumes. Check that calibration scales exist in the checkpoint. Read startup warnings, not just whether it started. Validate accuracy on the model you will ship.
