a2135: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Ray Stopping the Trainer on Unified Memory Lesson 21.35 20 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 20 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-4B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first A training run on a machine with unified memory (CPU and GPU share it) is stopped by Ray, not by a CUDA error, after the first rollout. Ray's memory monitor counts the whole node, and on unified memory that includes the GPU's allocations, so 95 percent really means the machine is nearly full. The case trains understanding what a watcher measures before deciding whether its alarm is real. A team trains with GRPO on one GB10. Their runs with a 0.6B model work, so they move to Qwen/Qwen3-4B for better rewards. The run starts, loads the trainer, loads the engine, and finishes its first rollout. Then it stops in the training phase of that same step, about 15 minutes after the start. The log has no CUDA out-of-memory error. The on-call engineer finds a Ray message that names the node, not a GPU, and lists three processes. The plan on the ticket has two steps: raise the Ray memory threshold, and give the engine a smaller memory fraction so the trainer gets more room. A second run with the fraction at 0.2 dies the same way. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. Three timestamps from the log of the failed run Copy The Ray message that stopped the trainer Copy The same run with the engine memory share lowered from 0.4 to 0.2 Copy The trainer state estimate by model size, and what happened on the GB10 Copy What a very small engine share did to the pool and the rollout time Copy Questions to answer first The log has no CUDA out-of-memory error. Read the kill line: which component stopped the trainer, what did it measure, and on what? The three listed processes hold far less than the node total. Where is the rest, and why can a process list not show it? The second run lowered the engine's share from 0.4 to 0.2 and died at a higher node total. What does that tell you about where the memory went? Raising the Ray threshold is a common fix on a machine with a separate GPU. Why is it the wrong fix here? Estimate the trainer state of a 4B model with mixed precision and an Adam optimizer, and pick the largest model that fits this machine. What does a very small engine share cost, and which line in the engine log tells you before the run starts? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ On unified memory, node memory includes GPU allocations. ✗ No CUDA out-of-memory error means GPU memory was fine. The pressure showed up in the node total Ray watches. ✓ The fix is a smaller model or setting, not silencing the watcher. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers The timeline gives the shape. The launcher started at 05:58, the trainer logged rollout 0 about six minutes later, and the fault-tolerance line reported phase=fail for the train function after 629.7 s. So the engine generated a full step of answers, and the trainer died while it trained on them. That is the phase that holds the most memory. The second listing is a Ray memory kill, not a CUDA error. Ray's memory monitor measured the whole node and read 115.86 GB of 121.69 GB in use, which the message itself gives as 0.952127. The table under it gives 36.77 GB for the trainer, 2.73 GB for the engine scheduler and 1.33 GB for the rollout executor. The rest of the memory in use is not in the process list. On a GB10 the CPU and the GPU use one pool of memory, so the GPU allocations, the model weights, the optimizer state and the KV cache, count in the number that Ray watches. A process list shows the host side of each process and cannot show that part. The third listing is the second run. With the engine share at 0.2 the node reached 119.18 GB before the kill, higher than before, and the trainer process held 36.75 GB, almost the same as the 36.77 GB of the first run. A smaller engine share made no room, because the trainer side is what does not fit. The estimate table says why. Full fine-tuning with Adam and mixed precision keeps about 16 bytes for each parameter. That gives about 10 GB for the 0.6B model, about 27 GB for 1.7B and about 64 GB for 4B. The 4B estimate alone is half the machine, and activations, the engine and the process overhead come on top. On this GB10 the 1.7B model fit for 4 steps with answers cut at 256 tokens, and the 4B model was stopped by Ray in the first step, twice. The last listing shows the cost of the other direction. With the engine share at 0.02 the pool held 3,082 tokens against 211,813 at 0.25, and the rollout of one step took about six times longer. A tiny engine share starves the rollout and buys nothing for a trainer that still does not fit. What actually happened The kill was real memory pressure, not a false alarm. On unified memory the number that Ray reads includes the GPU allocations, so a kill at 95.2 percent means the machine is close to full for every process on it. Change the run, not the watcher. Use a smaller model: on this machine the recipe fits 1.7B at most, and the team should test it at their real answer length for 4 steps while they read node memory with free -g . If they must train the 4B model, they need more GPUs or a recipe that keeps less optimizer state, such as LoRA on the Megatron trainer, which we did not test. Leave RAY_memory_usage_threshold at its default. Keep the engine share at the launcher default or near 0.25, because 0.2 did not prevent the kill and a very small share made the rollout several times slower. Wrong turns "Raise the Ray threshold." The threshold lets the node get closer to full. If it does run out, the operating system stops any process on the machine, and that stop leaves no Ray message to read. "Lower the engine fraction to make room for the trainer." The second run did that and died at 119.18 GB with the trainer at 36.75 GB. The engine was not the part that did not fit. "It is a CUDA out of memory, so lower the engine batch." The log has no CUDA error, and the engine scheduler held 2.73 GB. The kill came from node memory. "Set the Ray refresh to zero so the monitor stops killing." The log names that variable, and it only removes the warning. The operating system then stops whichever process it chooses, with no message. The lesson to carry On a machine where the CPU and the GPU share one memory, every tool that reads host memory also reads the GPU allocations, and every tool that reads GPU memory reads a number without a hard limit. Read a memory kill from such a tool as a true shortage, estimate the largest consumer from first principles before you start, and make the run smaller rather than the monitor quieter. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual reads the kill in the Ray page , explains the one pool in the unified memory page and sizes the model in the model size page , and the vLLM manual shows the same memory rule for serving in its DGX Spark page . Recap What to keep from this case Know what each monitor measures. On unified memory, CPU and GPU share one budget. Change the run, not the watcher. Test at the real answer length before scaling up. a2136: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems An Agent Card That Said Production: A2A Signature Checks Lesson 21.36 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 18.15 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : A2A 1.0.1 with the manual's capture kit (the test-runner, code-reviewer and deployer agents) Model : no model; the agents are deterministic fixtures Hardware : one machine, localhost, no network The situation In plain words first A planner trusted an agent card it fetched through someone else's caching proxy, and delegated a production deploy because the card said the agent could do that. The copy had been changed in transit. Cards are signed so that this can be detected, but the planner never verified the signature. The case trains verifying signed documents before reading any field that drives decisions. A planner builds its plan from the agent cards it fetches at startup. The cards pass through a caching proxy that another team runs, and the planner reads each card as a trusted description of what the agent will do. One morning the planner delegated the release step as Deploy build 2026.10.06-1 to production , because the copy of the deployer card it held described an agent that ships tagged builds to production. The deployer refused. The release stalled, and the on-call engineer found that the copy on the proxy differed from the card the agent serves in one word. The deployer card carries a signature. Nobody on the planner team had looked at it. The card loader parsed the JSON, dropped the fields it did not know, and planned. You have the published card, the agent's own answer to an authenticated card request, the refusal, and the kit's record of canonicalizing, signing and verifying the card, with a check on a copy whose description names production. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The skills and the signature of the published deployer card Copy What the deployer itself says to an authenticated caller Copy The canonical payload and the decoded protected header Copy The three rules a verifier follows to rebuild the signed bytes Copy The published signature entry and two verification results Copy When a client verifies, and with which algorithms Copy What the deployer answers to a production deploy Copy Questions to answer first What does the published card say the deployer does, and what did the agent say when asked with a token? What does the signature cover, and what does it leave out? One check returned True and the other False. What changed between the two, and why does one word matter? Why does the kit sign with HS256, and why is that not acceptable for a real deployment? Where in the planner's startup does verification belong, and what happens when it fails? The deployer refused the production deploy. Why is that refusal not the defense? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A signature is useful only if the reader verifies it. ✗ A card fetched over HTTPS cannot have been modified. It passed through a proxy that could serve any bytes. ✓ Keys must come from a trusted store, with an allowed list of algorithms. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the published card. The skill is Deploy a build , and its description says one tagged build to staging with operator approval. Its tags are deploy and staging , and its example is a staging deploy. Below the skills sits a signatures list with one entry: a protected header and a signature . The extended card, returned only to a caller with a bearer token, describes the same agent: it deploys to staging after an operator approves. The proxy copy alone named production. Read the canonical payload. It is the card without its signatures, with keys sorted and no spaces, as RFC 8785 defines. The description inside it says staging. The decoded header gives alg HS256, typ JOSE and kid deployer-key-1. The signing input joins the base64url header and the base64url payload with a period. Read the three rules. A verifier rebuilds those bytes from the card it received. A REQUIRED field is always present, even at its default. The JSON Canonicalization Scheme fixes the order and the form of every value. The signatures field stays out, because a signature cannot cover itself. So the signature binds every other field, the description among them. Read the two checks. On the published card the check returns True. On the altered copy, where the word staging became production, the canonical bytes differ, and the check returns False. One changed word changes the signed bytes, and the signature no longer matches. This is the test that the planner never ran. Read the algorithm line. The kit signs with HS256 because its standard library has no ECDSA. HS256 is an HMAC, so a verifier holds the signing key and could sign a card itself. Real cards use ES256 or RS256, with the public key published in a JWKS and fetched by kid and jku or taken from a trusted store. Verification has six MUST steps, and a client verifies at least one signature before it trusts a card, never with an expired or revoked key, and with an explicit list of allowed algorithms. Read the refusal. The deployer answered TASK_STATE_REJECTED and said that production deploys are outside its policy. That policy sits in the agent, and it caught this case. The card also names the interface URL the planner sends to. A copy that can change one word can change that field, and then the request goes to a server the attacker runs, where no policy refuses anything. What actually happened The planner trusted an unverified copy of a signed document. The loader now verifies at least one signature before it reads any field for planning. It rebuilds the canonical bytes under the three rules, takes the key for the kid from a trusted store, and allows only the algorithms the team lists. A card that fails the check is rejected and raises an alert, and the planner does not fall back to its content. For an authenticated session, the planner also replaces the cached public card with the extended card that the agent itself returns. The kit's record is the proof of the mechanism: True on the published bytes, False on the same card with one word changed, and the agent's own description agrees with the published one. Wrong turns "Pin the proxy cache and move on." The card is still unverified. The next edit passes the same way. "Compare the description with the version we saw last week." The version field is inside the signed payload, and an edited copy keeps it. Only the signature binds the fields together. "Verify with whatever algorithm the header names." A header is part of the input. Give the verifier an explicit list, so that a changed alg cannot pick a weaker check. "The deployer refused, so the system is safe." The refusal came from the honest agent at the published URL. A changed card can also change the URL, and the honest agent never sees the request. "Fetch the extended card instead, it needs a token." The extended card is a fuller card for an authenticated caller, and it comes back without signatures. It helps once the planner trusts the agent it talks to, and the public card's signature is what earns that trust. The lesson to carry Anything an agent reads from the network is input, not truth, and the metadata that describes other agents is the input with the most leverage. Verify the integrity of such a document before you plan on it, with a key that did not travel with the document, and treat a policy check at the far end as a second layer, never the first. How this connects Where this is taught The extended cards and signatures page of A2A 101 walks through this signing and both checks, the security schemes page covers the credential and the authorization scope, and the indirect prompt injection lesson explains why content an agent reads without a user in the loop is the attack surface that filters on user input never see. Recap What to keep from this case Verify signatures before reading fields that drive plans. Rebuild canonical bytes exactly as the specification says. Take keys from a trusted store; restrict algorithms. Reject and alert on documents that fail. a2137: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Dead Engine or Busy Engine: a Rollout Hang and an Overeager Watchdog Lesson 21.37 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.23 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer, agentic AI engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first A training run sat idle for an hour while its log grew to 147 MB: the inference engine had died at startup, and the trainer kept sending requests, reading each 503 as "busy". The team's new watchdog then killed healthy runs too. The case trains two things: reading the first error above the noise, and tuning a watchdog against what healthy runs actually do. A team runs GRPO on one GB10 and leaves a run alone for an hour. When they come back, the GPU is idle, the container is still running, and the log has grown to 147 MB. No failure appeared in the output of the run. The rollout engine had been started with an attention setting that this GPU cannot run, and it stopped during startup. The trainer did not stop: it went on sending requests to the dead engine. The team writes a watchdog. Every 30 seconds it counts the 503 Service Unavailable lines of the last 60 seconds and, when it finds more than 100 such lines in six checks in a row, it stops the container. The next day the watchdog stops a healthy run that generated 16 answers per prompt, in the middle of its steps. The team now distrusts both the run and the watchdog. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The engine failure and the first and last error from the trainer side Copy How many error lines the run wrote Copy The quietest and the busiest minutes of the dead run Copy The first fifteen minutes of errors in a run that finished every step Copy The watchdog against two containers that print the error on purpose Copy The watchdog rule replayed on the real error times of the healthy run Copy Questions to answer first The trainer never failed. Which component returned the 503, and why did the trainer treat it as something to retry? A count of errors alone cannot separate the dead run from the healthy one. Which property can, and how do you write it as a rule? Replay the six-check rule on the healthy run. Why did it fire, and in how many of the 30 start offsets? Pick the number of checks. What does each extra check cost when the engine really is dead? The script exits with 0, 1 or 2. What should a queue of runs do with each code? On a cluster of many GPUs you would not run this script. What replaces it, and what did the fault tolerance of the version we ran not cover? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A 503 from a dead engine looks the same to the client as a busy one. ✗ A watchdog that kills after a few failed checks is safe. Healthy runs reached 6 failed checks; the threshold needed to be above that. ✓ The assertion message named the attention backend to change. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the first listing from the top. The engine enabled deterministic inference for the on-policy target, then an assertion stopped it: the FlashAttention v3 backend needs an SM between 80 and 90, and the GB10 is outside that range. The parent received a SIGQUIT from the child. From that moment the trainer's rollout executor logged 503 Service Unavailable from the router at 172.17.0.3:20035 . The router is the small service that forwards each rollout request to an engine, and 503 is what it returns when no engine can take the request. The client retries a 503, because a busy engine returns it too. The last two lines are 63 minutes apart, from 21:03 to 22:06, and the second listing counts 200,533 such lines in that log. The third and fourth listings compare the two runs minute by minute. The dead run never went quiet. Its two partial minutes held 1,838 and 2,281 errors, and every full minute held at least 2,669, up to 3,719. The healthy 16-answer run logged 22,357 errors in total, but in bursts: 286 and 271 in the first two minutes, nothing for ten minutes, then 686 and 882, then 18. One minute reached 2,209. The client retried each request and the run finished all its steps. A count alone cannot tell these two runs apart. The time can. A dead engine produces errors in every window, a busy engine produces them in bursts with gaps. The watchdog turns that into a rule: every 30 s, count the errors of the last 60 s, and stop only once the count has stayed above 100 for a set number of checks in a row. The fifth listing tests it on two containers with no GPU. A container that prints ten error lines a second was stopped after 183 s with six checks, and the script exited with 1. A container that prints for 60 s and then stays quiet for two minutes, three times over, ran to its end after 541 s, and the script exited with 0. The last listing shows why six checks was still wrong. Replayed on the real error times of the healthy run, for each of the 30 possible start offsets of the checks, six checks stopped the run in 17 of 30 cases. Two bursts came 45 s apart, so the 60 s window held errors for six consecutive checks. No offset reached more than six checks in a row. With eight checks the rule stopped the healthy run in 0 of 30 cases, and with ten checks also 0 of 30. The cost is time on a dead engine: 153 to 182 s at six checks, 273 to 302 s at ten. What actually happened The engine died because of a backend assertion, and the run did not notice because a 503 looks like a busy engine to the client. The fix for the run is to read the engine lines above the first error and change the attention backend, as the assertion message says. The fix for the watchdog is the number of checks. Set it to 10, because a healthy run did not reach more than 6 checks in a row and 8 or 10 stopped it in 0 of 30 replays, while a dead engine is still stopped in about five minutes. Keep the limit at 100 errors per 60 s window and the check every 30 s. Test the script on the two fake containers before you trust it, and keep the replay against a real healthy log, because the fake burst container has quiet gaps of two minutes, longer than the real gaps of 45 s. Give the exit codes meaning. Exit 1 means the watchdog stopped the run, so a queue skips to the next run and keeps the log. Exit 0 means the run ended on its own. Exit 2 means the watchdog lost its view of the containers, so the run has no guard and a person must look. Wrong turns "Alert when the count of 503 lines in a minute is high." A healthy run logged 2,209 in one minute and finished every step. The count fires on bursts, the time between bursts is the signal. "Six checks in a row is enough, the test passed." The test container paused for two minutes between bursts. The real run had bursts 45 s apart, and the replay on its real times fired in 17 of 30 cases. "Raise the limit until the healthy run passes." The largest healthy minute held 2,209 errors and the quietest full minute of the dead run 2,669. A limit between them fits this pair of runs only, and a slower dead engine or a busier healthy run breaks it. The time rule does not depend on the rate. "Turn on fault tolerance instead of a script." On one GPU a dead engine means a dead run. In the version we ran, rollout fault tolerance did not work with a dedicated eval fleet or with the fully async colocated layout, and without it the trainer keeps sending requests to a dead engine and never fails. "Let the watchdog restart the engine." The script only stops the run. The cause is in the engine lines above the first error, and a restart with the same setting fails the same way. The lesson to carry A component that retries forever turns a dead dependency into a silent hang, and the only honest signal is time, not count. Build the alarm from the duration of the error condition, replay the rule on the logs of real healthy runs before you trust it, and give the alarm an exit code that a queue can act on. Then read the first error, not the last, because the cause sits above the noise. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual builds and tests the watchdog in the watchdog page , covers checkpoints and fault tolerance in the failures page , lists the engine causes in the troubleshooting page and explains the 503 in the router page , and the SRE for AI lesson frames the alarm design. Recap What to keep from this case Find the first error, above the flood that follows. Distinguish dead from busy explicitly. Tune watchdogs on healthy runs. Fix the cause the assertion names. a2138: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Dropped Stream That Ran the Test Suite Twice Lesson 21.38 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : A2A 1.0.1 with the manual's capture kit (the test-runner, code-reviewer and deployer agents) Model : no model; the agents are deterministic fixtures Hardware : one machine, localhost, no network The situation In plain words first When a load balancer closed a long-lived stream, the planner resent the request, and the whole test suite ran a second time, doubling the bill and hiding a flaky test. A streaming request is a command plus a view of its progress; resending repeats the command. The case trains reconnecting to the existing task instead of repeating the work. A planner watches a long test suite through a stream from the test-runner agent. A load balancer sits between them and closes connections that stay open for long. The planner's stream handler came from a REST client, and it has one rule for a connection that drops before the final frame: send the request again. Yesterday the suite of payments-api ran twice for every drop. The CI bill doubled, and a flaky test that passed in the first run failed in the second and blocked a release. A teammate patched the handler to call SubscribeToTask after a drop and to retry that call on any error. The next time the task had already finished when the handler reconnected, the call returned an error, and the handler logged "this server does not support subscriptions" and turned streaming off for the agent. You have the capture of the same sequence: a stream that the client closes after four frames, the call that picks it up, and a third call after the end. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The first stream, four frames, then the client closes the connection Copy The request that picks the stream back up Copy The second stream, six frames to the end Copy The artifact inside the first frame of the second stream Copy A third SubscribeToTask after the task completed, status and code Copy The detail inside that error Copy What a repeated messageId does on every implementation Copy Questions to answer first After the first stream closes at frame four, what has happened to the task, and what happens to the events the agent emits next? What differs between the two requests, and why does one of them create work while the other does not? What does the first frame of the second stream hold, and how does a client merge it with what it already has? The third call returns an error. What does it mean, and what is the next call? Does a repeated messageId protect the planner here? Why or why not? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A dropped connection ends the view, not the task. ✗ Resending the request is a safe way to resume a stream. It starts the work again. ✓ Subscribing to the task by id resumes watching the same run. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the first stream. Four frames arrive: a task in TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED , a statusUpdate to TASK_STATE_WORKING , an artifactUpdate that opens test-log.txt with the first test file, and an artifactUpdate that appends the second file. Then the kit's note says that the client closed the connection. No frame carried a terminal state, so the task is alive. The lifecycle of a task does not depend on any one stream. The agent goes on and appends two more files to its stored artifact, and those events have no open connection to travel on. Read the second request. The method is SubscribeToTask , and the params hold only the task id. There is no message and no messageId . This call opens a view on work that exists and creates nothing. The planner's old handler sent a new SendStreamingMessage instead, and a message without a taskId starts a new task every time. Read the second stream. Frame 1 is a complete task object, still in TASK_STATE_WORKING . Its test-log artifact already holds four parts, test_suite_01 to test_suite_04 , which includes the two files the first stream never carried. Frames 2 to 5 append test_suite_05 to test_suite_08 , and the last one sets lastChunk . Frame 6 is a statusUpdate to TASK_STATE_COMPLETED with 96 passed . Nothing is replayed, and the protocol has no cursor. The client replaces its partial log with the snapshot's artifact and then appends the frames that follow. Read the third call. The reply has Content-Type: application/json , not an event stream. It is an error with code -32004 and the reason UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION , and the metadata names the state TASK_STATE_COMPLETED . This is the terminal-task case of that code, not a missing feature. The client stops reconnecting and reads the final task with GetTask . Check the id rule. A retry of a send whose reply never came may reuse the same messageId . No implementation rejects a repeated id, and without a taskId each copy creates another task. So the id protects the planner only against a send that may not have arrived. Here the task exists, the client holds its id, and the right call is a subscribe, not a send. What actually happened The reconnect rule caused the double run. A SendStreamingMessage is a command plus a view, and resending the command repeats the work. The fix has four parts. A closed connection ends the reading and nothing else. If the last frame was not a terminal state, the handler calls SubscribeToTask with the task id. It rebuilds its copy from the task snapshot in the first frame and appends what follows. On -32004 it stops reconnecting and calls GetTask . The capture is the proof: one task id runs through both streams, the resumed stream delivers the four missing files and the final 96 passed , and the agent ran the suite once. Wrong turns "On a drop, send the request again." The request carries a message, and a message without a task id starts a new task. The suite runs again. "Resend with the same messageId, and the server will drop the duplicate." Duplicate detection is optional, no implementation rejects a repeated id, and each copy without a task id makes a new task. "The connection closed, so the task is finished." Only a terminal state in a frame ends a task. The kit also closes at an input request, and servers differ on when they close. Call GetTask after any close. "-32004 means this server has no SubscribeToTask." The metadata names the completed state. The result is one GetTask away. "Append the new frames to the old partial log." Two files were written while no connection was open. The snapshot holds them, so replace the copy first and append after. The lesson to carry Keep the work and the view of the work apart. A command that creates work must go out once, and a reconnect must open a view by the id of the work, never repeat the command. Resume from a snapshot that the server owns, and let a terminal state in the data, not the end of a connection, tell you that the work is done. How this connects Where this is taught The streaming page of A2A 101 follows this drop and the subscribe that recovers it, the message page explains what each implementation does with a repeated messageId , and the failure modes lesson lists the repeated step among the ways an agent loop goes wrong. Recap What to keep from this case Separate commands from views of their progress. On a dropped stream, reattach to the task by id. Rebuild local state from the first snapshot. Count side effects, not just messages. a2139: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Comparing the Wrong Sessions: a Flaky Agent Regression Check Lesson 21.39 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : AI evaluation reliability engineer, agentic AI engineer. Version : docker-agent v1.149.0 and sbx v0.47.0 Model : a recorded cassette of ai/qwen3:4b, replayed with no model Hardware : one Mac, no GPU The situation In plain words first A check comparing an agent's newest session with the previous one gave three different results in a week, while the agent never changed. It compared the wrong things: a relative reference into a store shared with other agents, and a command form the parser rejected. The case trains asking what exactly a comparison compares before trusting its verdict. A team keeps a small agent that lists the files of a repository and counts lines. Every change to its agent file goes through a check: run the agent, then compare the newest session with the one before it with sessions diff , and fail the job when the two differ. In one week the check gave three different results. Once it printed Error: unknown shorthand flag: '1' in -1 . Once it passed. Once it failed with sessions diverged and a first divergence at turn 0, where one side called list_directory and the other side called shell . The team reads the three results as proof that the agent is nondeterministic, and a pull request proposes to delete the check. You have the command lines, the outputs of the three comparisons, and the session store of the machine that ran them. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. Two runs of the files agent from the same cassette Copy The transcript that the cassette replays Copy The first attempt, in the form the help text gives Copy The two replays compared Copy The newest session against the third newest, with the CI flag Copy The first turn of the restricted run of the guarded agent Copy The sessions table and the five newest titles Copy Questions to answer first Which of the three results says anything about the agent, and which say something about the command? Two runs from the same recording agreed with each other. What does a cassette fix, and what does it leave free? The divergence names list_directory against shell at turn 0. What are the two sessions, and how do you know? What does the comparison compare, and why does it stop at the first difference? Rewrite the check so that a divergence can only come from a change to the agent. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A relative reference like "the previous session" depends on what else wrote to the store. ✗ A flaky check means the agent is non-deterministic. Here the operands were wrong; two replays of one recording matched on every turn. ✓ Pinning the model and comparing replays of one cassette gives an honest check. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the two runs. Same flags, same working directory, same cassette, same two messages, and the same final answer both times. A cassette holds the recorded model replies, and --fake replays them with no model. The model is out of the loop, so the only free parts are the operands and the measure. Count the turns. The transcript the cassette replays has five model replies: a list_directory call, an answer, a shell call that the user rejected, a read_file call, and an answer. Those five replies are the five turns the comparison reports. Read the failed command. The help text gives the form with bare negative references, and the parser reads the first one as a flag. The error names the flag parser and nothing else. Put -- before the references, as the second command does. This result says nothing about the agent. Read the pass. The two replays compared identical over all five turns, and the JSON form counts turns_a 5, turns_b 5, turns_matched 5. This is the result the check exists for. Read the failure. The comparison is between the newest session, with 5 turns, and the third newest, with 6 turns. The newest called list_directory first. The third newest called shell with echo m101-ok first. That first call matches the restricted run of a different agent file, the guarded agent, which answers a different user message. The reference -3 did not point at a run of the files agent at all. Read the session store. Relative references count every session in one session.db by creation time, and the table holds runs of every agent file plus the sub-sessions of the team runs. The five newest rows are all titled Running agent , so a title cannot tell runs apart. Whatever ran last on this machine is -1 . Read what the comparison measures. It compares the sequence of tool calls and ignores the prose of the assistant. After the first difference every later turn is downstream, so it reports one divergence and stops. What actually happened The agent did not change. The flaky result came from the operands: a relative reference into a shared session store that held runs of other agents, and a command form from the help text that the parser rejects. The one honest comparison, two replays of one cassette, matched on all five turns. The repaired check fixes three things. It fixes the model, by recording one cassette with --record=PATH and --models-gateway and replaying both sides with --fake , one tool call per message, because a turn with two parallel calls answers 500 on replay. It fixes the operands, by giving the check its own data directory with --data-dir , so that its session.db holds only its own runs, and by writing -- before the references. It fixes the measure, by running sessions diff --fail-on-divergence and reading only the first divergence. The proof is the pass that already exists: with one cassette on both sides, the report counted 5 matched turns of 5, and the exit code was 0. Wrong turns "The agent is nondeterministic, so delete the check." Two replays from one cassette matched on all five turns. The comparison that failed compared two different agents. "Quote the reference as '-1' to fix the flag error." The parser still sees a leading hyphen. -- ends flag parsing. "Compare the assistant text instead of the tool calls." Prose varies between live runs, and the comparison ignores it on purpose. The tool calls are the behaviour. "Read the turns after turn 0 to find more bugs." Everything after the first divergence is downstream of it and is not compared. The lesson to carry A regression check on an agent needs three fixed things: the model replies, the operands, and the measure. A cassette fixes the first. A private session store and explicit references fix the second. A comparison of tool calls that stops at the first difference fixes the third. When a check flips between pass and fail, find out what it compared before you blame what it measured. How this connects Where this is taught The sessions section shows the help form, the working form and this divergence. Recap What to keep from this case Know exactly which two things a check compares. Avoid relative references into shared stores. Replay recordings to remove model randomness. Test the command form you rely on. a2140: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Read-Only SQLite Database on a Read-Write Mount Lesson 21.40 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : agentic AI engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : sbx v0.47.0 and docker-agent v1.149.0 on the host, with the main build of docker-agent inside the template Model : none; the run stopped before its first model call Hardware : one Mac with the microVM runtime The situation In plain words first A sandboxed agent exits before answering: its session database is read-only, although the mount is listed as read-write. SQLite cannot write through that particular shared-folder filesystem on this host, and the launcher insists on keeping the database there. The sandbox itself works. The case trains testing what a filesystem actually supports rather than trusting how it is listed. A team runs its coding agent with --sandbox , so that its shell and filesystem tools act inside a microVM while the model stays on the host. The first sandboxed run on a developer's Mac prints a launch summary, pulls the template image, creates the sandbox, and exits with code 1 before the agent answers. The error names the session store: its migration could not create a table, because the database was read-only. The sandbox is still listed as running. The team splits three ways in the channel. One engineer says the template image is broken and wants to pin an older tag. One says the workspace must have been mounted read-only by mistake. One says SQLite is missing from the guest. Before the second attempt, the developer gives you the launch output, a second run with the state directories at their defaults, and a shell inside the running VM. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The sandboxed run, its state flags and the launch summary Copy The last five lines of the sandboxed run Copy The same run with the state directories at their defaults Copy A plain SQLite write inside the VM, then the mounts of the workspace Copy The auto-kit that docker-agent staged under the workspace Copy The version of the agent binary inside the VM Copy The same agent file started by hand inside the VM Copy Questions to answer first Where did the data directory sit, and which mount held it? Three mounts are read-only in the summary. Does any of them explain the error? What does the SQLite probe add that the error message does not? Why did the second run fail before it created anything? The last listing is a run that completed. What does it prove, and what does it not prove? How would you run this agent in a sandbox on this host today, and what would you file? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A mount listed as rw can still refuse some operations, such as database locking. ✗ The sandbox is broken. A run started by hand inside it worked; the session store's location was the problem. ✓ The fix is a supported location for the store, not a rebuilt sandbox. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the state flags first. The note after the command says that the config, data and cache directories sit under .m101/ in the workspace. The error comes from the session store, which lives in the data directory, so the database file is on the workspace mount. Read the four workspace lines. The workspace is (rw) . The agent file directory, the staged kit under .m101/cache/sandbox-kits/<hash> and .m101/cfg are (ro) . The data directory is none of those three paths, so the mount modes do not explain the failure. Rule out the mount flags with the probe. Inside the VM, a plain Python sqlite3 write under .m101/probe/ fails with the same attempt to write a readonly database message. The mount table on the lines below lists the workspace as a virtiofs mount with rw . The kernel reports the mount as writable, and SQLite still cannot write a database through it. The fault sits between SQLite and this mount, not in the sandbox settings and not in a missing package: the probe imported sqlite3 and connected without error. Read why the defaults are no escape. The run with the default state directories was refused before it made a sandbox: --data-dir must be inside the writable workspace. So the launcher forces the database onto the one mount where, on this host, SQLite cannot write it. Separate the kit from the store. The staged auto-kit holds a manifest.json with agent_ref and built_at , plus prompt_files and skills . Nothing in it configures a database. The template runs docker-agent version main , not the release the host runs, so the image tag is a second finding to record. The probe fails for any program, though, so a different agent build would not change the result. Prove the model path with the run by hand. Started inside the VM with its three state directories under /tmp/m101 , the guest's own filesystem and not a mount, the same agent file answered with exit 0: the README has 1 line. The provider at host.docker.internal:12434 was reached through the proxy. So the model path, the allowlist and the agent file are sound. Only the location of the session store fails. What actually happened The session store could not write because SQLite cannot write a database through the virtiofs workspace mount on this host, although mount lists it as rw . The launcher requires the data directory inside that workspace, so a --sandbox launch has no supported place for the store on this machine. The sandbox itself worked: a run started by hand inside the VM, with its state under /tmp/m101 , completed with the correct answer, and the same agent file reached the model through the proxy. What to do: On every new host, before the launcher is used with --sandbox , test a SQLite write inside the workspace from a shell in the VM, as the manual's checklist says. Until the data directory rule changes, start the agent inside the VM by hand with sbx exec , with --data-dir on the guest filesystem, and keep the host launcher for machines where the probe passes. Remove the sandbox with sbx rm when you are done, because the launcher leaves it running after the error. File two open items: the template runs the main build and not the pinned release, and the run printed no safety mode, so the mode a sandboxed run uses stays unknown, which is conflict C62 in the manual. Wrong turns "The workspace was mounted read-only." The summary lists it as rw, and the mount table inside the VM agrees. The three read-only mounts are the agent file directory, the staged kit and the config directory, and the database is under none of them. "Pin an older template tag." The probe fails for a plain Python script with no agent involved, so the agent build is not the cause. The main build is worth a ticket, not a fix. "Move the data directory to the host default." The launcher refuses a data directory outside the writable workspace, before it creates anything. "SQLite is missing from the guest." The probe imported the module and opened the database. It failed on the first write. The lesson to carry When a program reports a permission error on a path that the system lists as writable, repeat the operation with the smallest program that performs it, on the same path, outside the product. A failure there moves the fault from the product's settings to the layer under it, and a pass narrows it to the product. Then check whether the product gives you a way around that layer, and if it does not, write down the exact rule that blocks you. How this connects Where this is taught The manual's end to end run records this failure and the probe, the run page explains the state flags, and the conflicts register keeps conflict C62 open. Recap What to keep from this case Test filesystem features directly; listings are not guarantees. Databases need locking support from their filesystem. Separate the component that failed from the one that hosts it. Report a launcher constraint as such. a2141: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Alert Fatigue: a Driver Log Line That Paged Nine Times Lesson 21.41 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.23 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Hardware : one GB10 with 121.7 GiB of unified memory, shared with other users The situation In plain words first A new alert paged on-call nine times in an afternoon for a GPU driver line, and every server was healthy each time. The line is printed whenever a server allocates memory at start, so the rule paged on normal starts. The case trains designing alerts on symptoms users would feel (a server that does not become ready, a probe that fails) and keeping mechanism lines as diagnostics. A platform team runs SGLang on desktop machines with unified memory, which several teams share. After a memory incident elsewhere, they add an alert rule to the kernel log: page on-call whenever the GPU driver logs NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY . On the first afternoon the rule pages nine times between 13:52 and 16:46. Each page is a burst of 3 to 13 identical lines inside one minute, then silence. On-call finds no user complaint, no failed request and every server healthy. The team proposes to keep the rule and raise its threshold so that only a long burst pages. You review the alert design before the next on-call week, with the burst table, the server log of one start on that machine and the manual. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The kernel log bursts that the alert rule matched, by minute Copy A server start on the same machine: the probe before and after the ready line Copy The weights and the pool of one start on unified memory Copy What the manual says about the driver line and what it could not match Copy The row of the incident index for this line Copy Questions to answer first Read the burst table. What pattern do the timestamps and the counts show, and what does a server do at those moments? The server log shows a 503 and then a 200 on the health route. Which signal did on-call need, and did the rule carry it? The manual could not match each burst to one start. Why not, and what does that say about the evidence you keep? Design the alert: which signal pages a person, which signal is a diagnostic, and where does the driver line go? Which runbook turns this page into a five-minute check instead of an investigation? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A log line that appears during normal work makes a noisy pager. ✗ Raising the threshold fixes the alert. It silences it without making it a signal. ✓ Health transitions are what on-call can act on. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the shape of the bursts. Nine minutes carry lines, over about three hours of 2026-10-16, and every burst sits inside a single minute. The manual dates them: that was the day of the first test and sweep starts on that machine. A server start on unified memory is a burst of allocation. In the startup listing the weights settle at 57.75 GB, and three seconds later the pool takes 10.40 GB for keys and 10.40 GB for values. The manual's position is that every other program on the machine sees that memory go. The driver line is something the machine prints around a start, and the rule paged on starts. Read the signal that matters. In the server log the first health probe returns 503 at 14:19:12, because the server is still starting. Two seconds later the ready line prints, and the probe at 14:19:15 returns 200. That transition answers the on-call question: did the server come up and serve? The driver line answers nothing about that. It fires on an allocation whether the start succeeds or fails, so it carries no health information at all. Read what could not be matched. The manual says the server logs of that day were not kept, so no burst can be matched to one start, and that every server in the later captures became healthy and finished its benchmarks. The incident index records the same status and the same rule: alert on health, not on this line. The evidence lesson sits inside that sentence. A kernel line without the server log of the same minute is a clue with no suspect. Keep both logs, with timestamps, or you cannot say which process caused which line. Design the alert. Page on a server that does not reach its ready line inside its start budget, and on a server that stops answering its readiness probe after it was ready. Page on a queue that grows for longer than the users accept. Turn the driver line into a counter on the dashboard, attached to a page as context and never a page on its own. On a shared machine of this kind the manual adds two more measures: run the server in a container with a memory limit, and log the free memory of the machine once a second during startup, so that the next burst comes with the number that explains it. Write the runbook. The SRE lesson gives the shape: symptom, hypothesis, verify, act. Symptom: a burst of the driver line. Hypothesis: a server allocated its pool in that minute. Verify: find a start in the server log within the same minute, and read the health transition after its ready line. Act: nothing if the server became healthy; if a start failed, the startup page of the manual takes over. With the logs kept, this is a five-minute check. What actually happened The rule measured allocations, not failures. It paged on every start of a healthy server, nine times in one afternoon, and gave on-call nothing to act on. The rule is retired as a pager and kept as a diagnostic counter. The pages that replace it are the health transitions: a start that does not reach its ready line in its budget, and a ready server whose probe fails. On the days with server logs, every start on that machine reached its ready line, so the health rule pages zero times where the driver rule paged on every start. Two changes to the evidence come with it. The kernel log and the server log of each machine are kept together, so that a future burst can be matched to a process. During startup the machine's free memory is logged once a second, which puts the allocation that the driver line reports next to the pool size the server prints. The threshold proposal is dropped, because a higher threshold silences a rule that was never a signal. Wrong turns "Raise the threshold so that only a long burst pages." The bursts were 3 to 13 lines. A threshold above them silences the rule on a day like this one, and on a worse day it still says nothing about whether a server serves. "Lower the memory fraction until the driver stops complaining." Nobody matched a burst to a start, so nobody knows that a smaller pool removes the line, and a smaller pool costs users at every load. Set the fraction on purpose for the shared machine, for its own reason. "Keep the page, a driver error is always serious." Every server in the later captures became healthy. A page with no action teaches on-call to ignore pages. "Drop the line from the log pipeline." Keep it as a diagnostic next to the health signal. It dates an allocation, and with the server logs kept it names the process. The lesson to carry Alert on the symptom a user would feel, and keep the mechanism lines as diagnostics. A line that fires on normal work pages you on every success. Before a rule pages a person, replay it against a known-good day, and keep the logs that let you match each firing to a cause. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual records the bursts and sets the rule in the shared-pool part of the memory page , lists the status in the incident index , names the health endpoints in the operating page , and the SRE for AI lesson gives the runbook shape. Recap What to keep from this case Alert on symptoms users feel. Keep mechanism lines as diagnostic counters. Replay a rule against a known-good day first. Keep logs that let you match each firing to a cause. a2142: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems An Empty Callee List an Agent Read as None Lesson 21.42 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : rea 6.7.0 at 27dc42d with the Ghidra provider Model : no model; the fixtures are the ledger binaries built at -O1 and -O2 Hardware : one aarch64 Mac The situation In plain words first A security review said a function "calls nothing", citing an empty list of callees returned by a tool. The sentence happened to be true, but an empty list is not proof: it can mean "none found" or "could not resolve". The case trains telling "known empty" from "unknown", and citing the evidence that actually supports a claim (here, the assembly with no call instruction). A coding agent investigates the arm64 executable ledger-arm64-O1 through the rea MCP server, with the Ghidra provider behind it. Its task is a security review of the division in _percent_change . The agent calls analyze_function once and writes in its report: "The function is a leaf. It calls nothing, so the division cannot reach a callback or a handler." A reviewer asks where that sentence comes from. The agent points at one line of the dossier, the callees array, which is empty. The reviewer does not accept the line as proof and asks you to say what the dossier does and does not establish. You have the dossier, the row of the same record in the bundle summary, and the manual pages that describe both. The report is due in an hour, and the sentence about the leaf is the one that the rest of the review rests on. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The callees array of the dossier Copy The unresolved_calls array of the same dossier Copy The relationship_coverage block of the record Copy The ten limitations of the record Copy The value_flow counts of the same record in the bundle summary Copy The head of the bundle summary Copy The assembly facet of the same dossier Copy Questions to answer first The callees array is empty. Name two different states of the world that produce that same line. Which field of the record says how complete the callees set is, and what does its value cover? The limitations list is long. Which one qualifies the callees array, and how does it change the sentence in the report? The bundle summary reports counts for the value flow. Why does rea stand behind a zero there and not behind an empty array in the dossier? What evidence in the same record settles whether the function makes a call? Write the sentence that the report should carry instead. If no facet settled the question, what would you record, and what would close it? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ An empty list can mean the tool looked and found nothing, or could not look. ✗ The original sentence was wrong. The claim was right; the evidence cited under it was not enough. ✓ Coverage fields in the response say how complete the list is. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Separate the array from the claim. An empty callees array says that the provider returned no resolved call reference. It does not say that no call exists. The two states that give the same line are a function with no calls and a function whose calls Ghidra could not resolve to a target. The agent picked one state without looking further. Read the second empty list. unresolved_calls is also empty. That removes one case: Ghidra saw no call site with an unknown destination. It does not remove computed or indirect flows that never became a reference at all. Read the coverage block. relationship_coverage.status is complete , and its diagnostic says that only resolved Ghidra call references are returned, and that unresolved computed or indirect calls remain unknown. Complete means that rea returned the whole resolved set without a read limit. It is a statement about the provider's read, not about the program at run time. Find the limitation that applies. The seventh of the ten strings says that resolved reference metadata identifies the edges that Ghidra found, and that unresolved targetless flows remain unknown. The record itself tells you how to read its empty arrays. The manual's rule is the same: missing coverage means unknown, not absent. Compare with a count that carries a statement. The bundle summary shows the value_flow object of the same record: truncated is false, and the omitted operations, inputs and edges are all 0. Those zeros come with a flag that says nothing was cut. The callees array carries no such flag. A zero with a truncation statement is a count. An empty list without one is an observation that nothing was seen. Read the unknown counters. The summary head says unknown_revisions is 0. That number means that no unknown had been recorded when the bundle was exported. It does not mean that the investigation has no open questions. Use the observed facet. The assembly facet holds six instructions: a compare and branch on zero, a subtract, a move of the constant, a multiply, a signed divide, and a return. None of them transfers control to another function. The assembly is the Listing text that Ghidra observed, and it is the evidence that the leaf claim needs. The callees array was the wrong line to cite for a true sentence. What actually happened The claim in the report was right, and the evidence under it was wrong. The corrected sentence reads: "The assembly of _percent_change has six instructions and no call instruction; the dossier reports no resolved callee with complete coverage over resolved references, and the record states that unresolved targetless flows remain unknown." The report cites the assembly facet, the coverage block and the limitation, and it quotes the callees array as a secondary observation only. The team also changes how the agent writes. A rule in its instructions now says that an empty list is reported as "none observed" with the coverage status beside it, never as "none". When no observed facet settles a question, the agent calls record_unknown with the question, the authority that would close it, and a recommended probe. For a call question that would be shipped-artifact authority and observed confidence, from the assembly or a process capture, as the unknowns that compare_functions opens already ask for. Wrong turns "The callees array is empty and the coverage is complete, so the function provably calls nothing." Complete covers the resolved references that Ghidra returned. The record's own limitation says that unresolved targetless flows stay unknown. "Record a residual unknown and ship the report with the question open." The same record holds an observed facet that answers the question. Read every facet before you open an unknown. "The bundle summary says zero unknowns, so nothing is open." That counter reports the unknowns that were recorded. It cannot count the questions that nobody wrote down. "Trust the pseudocode; it shows no function call either." The pseudocode is a decompiler reading with low-confidence types, as the same manual shows for this function. Cite the instructions, not the reading of them. The lesson to carry A list in a tool result is a claim about what the tool saw, not about what exists. Before you turn an empty list into "none", find the field that states the coverage of that list and the limitation that qualifies it, and prefer a count that comes with a truncation flag over an array that comes with nothing. When one facet is an interpretation, look for the facet that is an observation of the same thing, and cite that one. When no observation settles the question, write the question down with the evidence that would close it. How this connects Where this is taught The coverage page of Reverse Engineering 101 reads these same lines, the dossier page lists the sixteen facets and shows the six instructions, the failure modes lesson names a claim that outruns its evidence as an agent hallucination, and lesson 35 builds the unknowns ledger in Python. Recap What to keep from this case Separate known-empty from unknown. Read the coverage and completeness fields. Cite evidence that supports the claim directly. State what remains unknown. a2143: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems An RL Rollout Speedup That Was Only Noise Lesson 21.43 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : design-review, ml-depth, behavioral. Roles : AI evaluation reliability engineer, inference engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory, with a heat guard that pauses the run at 84 C The situation In plain words first A teammate reported a 12 percent faster rollout from one change and a reward gain from another, each on a single pair of runs. On this machine, heat pauses and step-to-step noise are larger than the claimed effect. The case trains experiment hygiene: paired runs on the same day, clean steps only, several seeds, and an honest statement of what the data supports. A teammate posts a result in the team channel: keeping the rollout engine loaded between phases makes the rollout 12 percent faster. The post shows two runs on the GB10, a baseline with a median rollout of 59.1 s and the new setting at 52.0 s, and proposes to make the new setting the default. The same post reports a reward gain of 0.01 from a second change, on one seed, with a loss curve that "looks better". A reviewer asks for the run manifest. The two runs were four days apart. The memory fraction for the engine was not the same in the second run either. The medians cover different steps, because the heat guard put the container on hold whenever the GPU reached 84 C, 1,005 times that week. A third teammate, who wants the trainer and engine log probabilities to agree more closely, has switched the engine to FP16 and left the trainer in BF16. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The rollout time per step of every run, over all steps and over clean steps Copy The same-day pair that changed only the engine offload Copy Three seeds of the same 48-step run Copy The engine settings of five runs, read from their logs Copy The image digest, the commit and the engine version that every run used Copy The log probability gap between the engine and a trainer forward pass, by dtype Copy Questions to answer first Two runs, two medians, 12 percent. List everything that differed between the runs before you believe the number. The same-day pair shows 60.7 s against 56.7 s over different clean steps. Why is even that not enough, and what comparison is? Three seeds of the baseline ended at 0.758, 0.736 and 0.766. What does a gain of 0.01 on one seed mean, and what would make it reportable? The heat guard paused the container 1,005 times. How does a pause enter a median, and which steps may you time? Predict from the dtype table what FP16 on the engine alone does to the gap. Write the manifest that every run records before it starts, and the rule for reporting a change. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Noise between steps on this machine is larger than the claimed gain. ✗ A loss curve that looks better is evidence of a reward gain. One seed and a visual impression are not a result. ✓ Comparing only steps clean in both runs removes heat-pause effects. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Start with the timing table. Every row has two medians, one over all steps and one over the steps whose rollout overlapped no heat pause. For the baseline, e6a-base , they are 83.9 s and 59.1 s, from 6 clean steps of 12. For the two runs of the offload pair at a fraction of 0.25 they are 102.0 against 60.7 s and 102.2 against 56.7 s, from 4 and 3 clean steps. The 48-step run from before the heat guard existed, plain-48 , has 47.5 s in both columns, because no pause could touch it. A 16-answer run has no clean step at all. So a median over all steps is a median over pauses, and the pause count differs between any two runs. The same-day pair is the honest version of the claim. Only --no-offload-rollout differed, the fraction was 0.25 in both runs, and the clean medians were 60.7 s against 56.7 s. Even that is not a fair pair, because the two medians come from different steps. The rollout time follows the answer length, and answers get shorter as the model learns, from about 800 tokens in early steps to about 690 later. On the three steps that were clean in both runs the engine kept loaded saved 69.4 against 68.0 s, 58.5 against 56.7 s and 55.8 against 55.2 s. That is 0.6 to 1.8 s of a rollout of about a minute, 1 to 3 percent, on one seed. The original 12 percent came from a pair that changed the fraction as well and compared different steps. The three seeds give the noise floor. Seeds 1234, 2 and 3 of the same 48-step recipe reached final rewards of 0.758, 0.736 and 0.766 over the last 8 steps, with answer lengths of 447, 480 and 456 tokens. All three learned, and the final reward still spread by 0.03 with nothing changed. One seed cannot see a gain of 0.01 inside that spread. A change of 0.05 on two seeds is worth a third run. The engine settings table is what a manifest looks like after the fact. It was read from the server arguments line of each run log, and it shows which runs differ in one column only: the deterministic runs differ from the base in the flag, the sampler and sometimes the backend, and the top-p run differs in the two sampler flags alone. The identity listing is the other half, taken before the runs: the image digest, the commit inside the image and the version of the engine build. Without those three lines, a run from last week cannot be compared with one from today, because the latest tag moves. The dtype table answers the third teammate before the run. With BF16 on both sides the median gap per token was 0.0073. With FP16 on the engine only it was 0.0085, and with FP16 on the trainer only 0.0079. Neither helped. With FP16 on both sides the median fell to 0.00094, about 7.8 times lower. The BF16 engine stayed near 0.0076 even against an FP32 trainer, so the rounding of the engine set that floor. A dtype change pays only when both sides make it. What actually happened The 12 percent is withdrawn. The defensible statement is that keeping the engine loaded saved 0.6 to 1.8 s of a rollout of about a minute on the steps that were clean in both runs of a same-day pair, on one seed, which is inside the step-to-step noise of this machine under heat pauses. The default offload stays. The reward gain of 0.01 is not reportable until it appears on two seeds and falls outside the 0.736 to 0.766 spread of the baseline seeds. Before it starts, every run now records the image digest, the commit, the engine version, the full command, the seeds and the names of its log files. During the run the trainer, the engine and the heat guard each write their own log, and at the end the run writes one exit code line. A change gets one run against a baseline from the same day with one setting different, two seeds, and a comparison on the same step numbers, from clean steps only. The dtype of the engine and the trainer move together or not at all, and deterministic inference is kept for repeating an experiment, because it made the engine repeat its step 0 exactly and left the gap at 0.01518 against 0.01526 while it cost 40 to 45 percent more rollout time. Wrong turns "Both runs had pauses, so the medians over all steps are fair." The pauses are not equal. The two runs of the pair had 4 and 3 clean steps, and their all-step medians of 102.0 and 102.2 s sit forty seconds above their clean medians. "The run from before the heat guard is the clean baseline." Its 47.5 s covers 48 steps, with the late short answers inside. On the same 6 step numbers as the later run it took 60.9 s. Compare step numbers, not whole runs. "A gain of 0.01 is small but the curve looks better." Three seeds of the same recipe spread by 0.03 at the end. One seed cannot see 0.01. "Switch the engine to FP16 to lower the gap." On one side only the gap was 0.0085 and 0.0079, no better than 0.0073 with BF16 on both. Both sides or neither. "Turn on deterministic inference so runs are comparable." It makes the engine repeat itself and costs 40 to 45 percent of the rollout time. The gap stayed between 0.01515 and 0.01526, and the trainer still drifted from step 1. The lesson to carry A measured difference is a claim about everything that differed between two runs, so write down what differed before you write down the number. Hold the machine, the code and the data identity fixed, change one thing, pay for a second seed, and compare like with like down to the step. A result that survives that is small, and it is yours. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual gives the manifest in the comparable runs page , the seeds and the clean steps in the repeat page , the same-day pair in the offload page , the deterministic runs in the repeatable engine page and the clean-step rule in the lab notes . Recap What to keep from this case Compare paired runs from the same day. Exclude steps disturbed by the machine. Use several seeds before reporting a gain. Report the size the data supports, or nothing.
