a2144: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems LRU Thrashing in a Small KV Cache Pool, Then a Crash Lesson 21.44 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.6 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, agentic AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : the shared second L4 of a two-GPU node, with no clock lock The situation In plain words first A small cache pool, sized to share a GPU, could not hold the sessions that came back for more turns, so from turn 4 the cache kept evicting what it would need next (thrashing), and first tokens slowed to 716 ms. Under that heavy eviction a crash path appeared too. The case trains separating two stacked problems and fixing the capacity one first. A coding assistant keeps a session for each user and resends the whole history on every turn. The team serves a small model with SGLang on a GPU that another team also uses, so they set --max-total-tokens 8192 to leave the neighbour room. In a load test with 24 sessions of 6 turns at 8 users at once, the first turns are fast. From the fourth turn the first token takes up to 716 ms, and the metrics endpoint shows the cache hit rate falling toward zero. Then two kinds of failure appear. In some runs the server stops with CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered . In other runs the log stops with no error while the GPU stays at 100 percent and every client waits. The team suspects the eviction policy and asks whether to switch from lru to lfu . The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The engine, the model and the multi-turn trace Copy The hit rate over the whole trace and per turn, by pool size and policy Copy The median time to first token at turns 5 and 6 Copy The server command, the trace, and the tally of aborts and hangs by variant Copy The abort, the hang, and what hid the fault Copy Questions to answer first What does eviction remove, what does it never remove, and how does lru pick the victim? Read the per-turn hit rates of the first row. Describe the pattern in words and name the mechanism behind it. At the same pool size, lfu and slru kept the late turns alive. What does that tell you about the working set, and what else fixes it? Both failures stop in one call of the scheduler. Which two changes made the fault disappear, and what does each one cost? Order the fixes: a larger pool, a different policy, graphs off, launch blocking. Which do you ship, which do you test, and which never goes to production? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Thrashing happens when the working set is larger than the pool. ✗ Changing the eviction policy is the main fix. Growing the pool to 16,384 tokens fixed the hit rate even with the default policy. ✓ The crash was a second problem that heavy eviction exposed. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Eviction removes cached tokens that no running request holds, from the leaves of the radix tree. It never removes the KV of a running request. With the default policy the leaf with the oldest last access goes first. That rule assumes that the next request looks like the recent ones. The trace in the first listing breaks that assumption. Twenty-four sessions take turns at a concurrency of 8, and every turn resends a history that grows. The second listing shows what the pool did with it. With 8,192 tokens and lru , the hit rate per turn was 0.11, 0.31 and 0.58 for the first three turns, then 0.39, 0.016 and 0.013. By turn 5 the cycle of 24 growing histories was larger than the pool. The policy evicted each session's prefix just before that session came back, so almost every late turn paid a full prefill. Over the whole trace the hit rate was 0.19 in both clean runs. The same pool with lfu reached 0.375 over the trace and kept 0.34 and 0.25 at turns 5 and 6. With slru it was 0.367, with 0.31 and 0.26. So the frequency policies helped exactly where the pool was too small for the sessions that return. The rows below show the real fix. At 16,384 tokens, lru reached 0.685 and the hit rate rose to 0.83 at turn 6. The default pool gave 0.687. Every policy we ran at the larger pools landed near 0.69. The third listing turns this into time. At turns 5 and 6 the median first token was 699 and 449 ms in one lru run and 716 and 355 ms in the other, 143 to 214 ms with lfu or slru , and 56 to 160 ms with the larger pools. The card had no clock lock, so compare these numbers only with each other. The fourth listing is the failure tally. With the defaults, CUDA graphs and the overlap scheduler on, 6 runs gave 1 abort, 3 hangs and 2 clean runs. With CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 , 3 of 3 were clean. With --disable-cuda-graph , 4 of 4 were clean. When hierarchical caching was on, 1 of 3 still aborted. The fifth listing shows that the abort and every hang stopped in the same place, the synchronize call that waits for the copy of a decode result, under the overlap event loop. The fault did not appear with launches serialized or with graphs off, so no traceback names the kernel. Nothing was filed upstream. What actually happened Two problems sat on top of each other. The pool was smaller than the working set of the sessions that return, so lru thrashed from turn 4 on. Under that heavy eviction, the default path with CUDA graphs and the overlap scheduler hit the memory fault or hung in 4 of 6 runs. Grow the pool first. At 16,384 tokens the same trace reached a hit rate of 0.685 with the default policy, and the late turns kept 56 to 160 ms to the first token. If a cap such as --max-total-tokens sets the pool, raise the cap. If memory sets it, on a shared card that means a larger --mem-fraction-static or an FP8 KV cache, not a new policy. Then read max_total_num_tokens in the startup log to confirm the new size. Then measure the policy again. On this trace a different policy paid only at the pool size that was too small. For the crash, ship --disable-cuda-graph as the workaround while the pool is small. On our L4 with an 8B model, graphs saved about 1 percent of each decode step, so measure the cost on your model. A larger pool stopped the thrash, but we did not count crashes at the larger pools, so treat it as untested for the fault. Keep CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 for debugging only. Wrong turns "Switch to lfu and ship it." A frequency policy keeps yesterday's popular prompt in memory and makes today's prompt pay for it. It helped here only because the pool was too small, and the larger pool made every policy equal. "Set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 in production." It hid the fault in 5 of 5 runs, and it makes every kernel launch wait for the one before it. Use it to debug, never to serve. "Turn on hierarchical caching to stop the crash." With the host tier on, 1 of 3 runs still aborted. The host tier keeps evicted prefixes, it does not change the path that faulted. "Raise the running-request cap so the sessions do not wait." More running requests hold more of the pool, so eviction gets heavier, and the hit rate falls further. The lesson to carry When a hit rate falls on later turns while early turns are fine, the working set has outgrown the cache. Size the cache before you tune its policy, because a policy only chooses which part of a too-small set to lose. And when a fault appears only under one load shape, change the execution path one switch at a time, and keep the switch that serializes work for the debugger, not for the users. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual measures the trace and the policies in the eviction and HiCache page , records the crash in the operating page , sizes the pool in the memory fraction page and weighs the graphs in the CUDA graphs page , and the RadixAttention lesson builds the tree that the policies walk. Recap What to keep from this case Size the pool to the returning working set. Watch the hit rate by turn. Separate stacked failures; fix capacity first. Reproduce a crash path after the capacity fix. a2145: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems More Load, Faster TTFT: a Benchmark Cache Artefact Lesson 21.45 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.22 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Hardware : one GB10 (DGX Spark) The situation In plain words first A load sweep reported a faster first token at four times the load. Each run reused one seed on one server without flushing its prefix cache, so later runs found earlier prompts already cached. With fresh seeds the first token got slower with load, as queues predict. The case trains suspecting results that contradict how a system must behave. A benchmark kit starts one SGLang server with Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and runs a load sweep against it. Each run sends random prompts of 512 tokens and asks for 128 tokens back. The kit runs each concurrency cap once, one after the other, on the same server. The report says that a cap of 8 gave a median first token of 677.61 ms, and a cap of 32 gave 390.38 ms. Four times the load gave a faster first token. A teammate wants to publish the result as "the scheduler gets more efficient under load". You review the run before it goes out. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The server command Copy The first-token block at a cap of 8 Copy The first-token block at a cap of 32 Copy The client arguments Copy Two prefill lines from the run at a cap of 32 Copy The same caps with three seeds Copy One load four times in a row Copy Questions to answer first Which explanations fit a median first token that falls when the load rises? Name at least two before you read the logs. The mean and the P99 at a cap of 32 are much higher than the median. What does that shape tell you? What in the client arguments makes two runs send the same prompts? What do the prefill lines prove, and what do they not prove? How do you run the sweep again so that the result is trustworthy? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Reusing a seed on a warm server lets the prefix cache serve repeated prompts. ✗ The server got faster under more load. Clean runs gave 209.98 ms at 8 and 416.37 ms at 32. ✓ The fix is a benchmark protocol: new seeds, flush or restart between runs. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Doubt one sample. No queue model makes the first token faster under more load. Each cap ran once, so the first suspect is the method, not the scheduler. Write down the candidate causes: a warm cache, a different GPU clock, a different pool, or noise in one run. Read the whole distribution. At a cap of 32 the median was 390.38 ms, but the mean was 1166.51 ms and P99 was 2910.22 ms. A median far below the mean says the requests split into a fast group and a slow group. Something made part of the requests cheap. Read the client arguments. The run used the random dataset with seed=7 and flush_cache=False . The same seed sends the same first prompts in every run. Nothing cleared the cache between runs on the same server. Read the server log. Two prefill batches admitted 14 and 15 requests that needed one new token each, with 6879 and 7634 cached tokens. Those prompts were already in the cache from the run before. A cached prompt skips its prefill, so its first token comes fast. Count, then test. The manual counted the prefill lines of each run. At a cap of 32, 64 of the 128 prompts were in the cache before the run started. At a cap of 8, 16 of the 64 were. Half of the requests had the advantage at 32, and a quarter at 8. Then change the variable that the reading blames: run each cap with three seeds, and the 677.61 ms result does not come back. What actually happened The prefix cache made the result. The kit reused one seed and one server and never flushed the cache, so each run found the prompts of the run before it. The sweep with seeds 1, 2 and 3 gave a median of 209.98 ms at a cap of 8 and 416.37 ms at a cap of 32. With clean runs, the first token gets slower as the cap grows, as the queue predicts. The fix is a protocol, not a server flag: Start each run with an empty cache. Pass --flush-cache to the benchmark client, call POST /flush_cache , or restart the server. Check that the flush ran. The server flushes only when no request runs or waits. Use a new seed for each run, so that the client sends new prompts. Record sglang:cached_tokens_total before and after each run, and write the cached tokens next to the result. A separate test on an L4 measured the size of the effect. A repeat without a flush read a median first token about 4.8 times lower than the fresh run. After a flush, it went back near the fresh run. Wrong turns "The scheduler batches better at a high cap." A queue can only add wait time. The median fell because the cache removed prefill work. "Turn the prefix cache off for the benchmark." Production runs with the cache on. Reset it between runs and record the hits, so that the test measures the real server. "Run more requests at each cap with the same seed." More requests with the same seed repeat the same prompts and keep the cache warm. "Blame the GPU clock." A clock change can move a result, but the prefill lines show cached tokens, which a clock change cannot make. The lesson to carry A benchmark that repeats its inputs measures its own cache. Before you trust a result that runs against the expected direction, read the full distribution, check which state carries over between runs, and change the one variable that your explanation blames. Run three seeds per point and report the range. The time per token is less exposed to this error than the first token, because a cache hit removes prefill work and leaves the decode work the same. How this connects Where this is taught The benchmark section of SGLang 101 finds this result and its cause, and the load testing lesson explains why identical prompts in a loop test only one point. Recap What to keep from this case Distrust results that defy queueing. Use different seeds and a cold cache per run. Write the protocol into the kit. Rerun before you publish. a2146: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Speculative Decoding Tuned on Random Prompts Lesson 21.46 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B with an EAGLE3 draft of 3 tokens, and NGRAM with its defaults Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory, SM clock locked at 900 MHz The situation In plain words first A team picked one speculative decoding setting for three products after benchmarking random prompts. The gain from speculation depends on how predictable the text is, so random prompts said little about math answers or code. Measured per product, the right choice differed. The case trains benchmarking with each product's own traffic. An inference team serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B on L4 cards to three internal products: a support chat, a math tutor and a code assistant. To pick one decode setting for all three, they benchmark the engine on the random dataset of the benchmark client at 8 users. EAGLE3 roughly halves the time between tokens, and the n-gram method changes nothing. They turn EAGLE3 on for every product and close the n-gram ticket as "no gain". Two weeks later the support chat reports that at busy hours the first token comes seconds later than before the change, with no more answers per minute. The math tutor reports the opposite: the service got much faster under load. The code assistant team, which never got n-gram, reads a paper that says n-gram pays on code and asks why it was rejected. You are asked whether one setting can serve all three. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The machine, the model, the two drafts and the four datasets Copy Median time per output token at 8 users, by dataset and method Copy Mean acceptance length at 8 users, by dataset Copy Output tokens per second at 32 users, by dataset and method Copy The first token with EAGLE3 and the worst gap with NGRAM at 32 users Copy What the random dataset is, and what other studies found on real prompts Copy The four numbers to compare on your own traffic Copy Questions to answer first Before the tables, say why one benchmark dataset cannot decide a speculation setting for three different products. From the acceptance table, which dataset gives the draft the fewest accepted tokens, and what in that traffic explains it? At 32 users, where does EAGLE3 lose output, and what does it cost there besides output? The n-gram method had no gain on the random set. On which traffic did it pay, and what did it do to the tail? What is the random dataset made of, and why did it hide both the loss and the gain? Give one setting per product, and the measurement on production traffic that confirms each. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Speculation pays off when the next tokens are predictable. ✗ N-gram speculation has no gain because it did nothing on random prompts. Random prompts have no repeated text for n-grams to reuse. ✓ Each product needs its own measurement and setting. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Check the method before the result. The test ran on one L4 with the clock locked at 900 MHz, the cache flushed before each run, two seeds, and 128 output tokens with ignore-eos. Only runs at a median clock of 900 MHz count. Four datasets: the random set, ShareGPT, GSM8K and code. So a difference between rows is the dataset and nothing else. Read the time per token at 8 users. EAGLE3 cut the median TPOT on every dataset: 67.6 to 68.2 ms fell to 33.8 to 39.4 on random, 66.4 to 68.6 fell to 39.5 to 43.1 on ShareGPT, 65.5 fell to 33.3 to 34.3 on GSM8K, and 65.9 to 66.4 fell to 36.8 on code. At this load the gain holds for everyone. N-gram is another story. On random and ShareGPT it was a little slower than the default, 68.2 to 71.4 and 69.5 to 72.4 ms. On GSM8K it gave 54.6 to 55.0 and on code 58.2 to 58.8. The random-set result for n-gram was the one result that did not transfer. Read the acceptance. EAGLE3 committed 2.69 to 2.78 tokens per step on GSM8K and 2.35 to 2.43 on ShareGPT. N-gram committed 1.44 to 1.46 on GSM8K and only 1.22 to 1.25 on ShareGPT. Chat answers repeat little of the prompt, so a method that copies from the prompt finds almost nothing there, and a learned draft guesses worse too. Math and code repeat structure, so both methods guess better. The acceptance column predicts every later column. Read the output at 32 users. On random, EAGLE3 gave 239 to 242 tokens per second against 250 to 254 for the default. On ShareGPT, 277 to 283 against 281 to 288. On both chat-like sets it lost output under load. On GSM8K it gave 648 to 660 against 397, and on code 566 to 581 against 365 to 366. The manual calls that 1.6 times the output on GSM8K and code, and no more output on the other two. At a full batch every rejected draft token is compute taken from another user, so the gain survives only where the acceptance is high. Read the first token and the tail. At 32 users EAGLE3 moved the median first token on random from 3.2 to 3.5 s up to 8.6 to 8.7 s, and on ShareGPT from 2.7 to 3.0 s up to 5.7 to 7.0 s. The manual's reading is that the draft took pool space that the queue needed, so requests waited longer for a slot. That is the support chat's complaint. N-gram at 32 users raised the P99 ITL to 244 to 779 ms against 83 to 106 ms for the default: a smoother median hid a rougher stream. The one-user default runs throttled below 300 MHz and were left out, which is the right call. Ask what random is. The random dataset takes the first turn of ShareGPT conversations and cuts or repeats it to 512 tokens. It is real text, but it is not any product's traffic, and the repetition inside a cut-and-repeated prompt is not the repetition of a math answer. The studies the manual cites agree: synthetic prompts overstated speculative throughput by 23 percent on average, the best draft length fell to 1 as the batch grew, and on long answers the acceptance fell from about 3.7 to about 1.5. Use the manual's check. Run a sample of your own traffic with and without speculation, with real output lengths and --disable-ignore-eos . Compare the acceptance length from sglang:spec_accept_length , the output and the median time per token, the P99 ITL and the P99 TTFT, and the acceptance of your longest answers alone, which each /generate response gives in meta_info . What actually happened One setting cannot serve the three products, because the gain of speculation is a property of the traffic, not of the engine. For the math tutor, EAGLE3 stays on: 648 to 660 tokens per second against 397 at 32 users, and 33.3 to 34.3 ms per token against 65.5 at 8 users. For the code assistant, EAGLE3 is the first choice, 566 to 581 against 365 to 366 at 32 users, and n-gram is a cheaper second that pays on code at 8 users, 58.2 to 58.8 against 65.9 to 66.4, if its P99 ITL stays inside the product's target. For the support chat, EAGLE3 comes off at busy hours: on ShareGPT at 32 users it gave no more output and moved the median first token from 2.7 to 3.0 s up to 5.7 to 7.0 s. If the chat wants the 8-user gain, it needs a user cap per replica low enough that the pool is never the limit. Each product confirms its setting on its own traffic: the acceptance from the counter, the median and the P99 ITL, the P99 TTFT, and the acceptance of the longest answers, with the clock recorded. The random set is retired as a decision tool and kept as a smoke test. Wrong turns "EAGLE3 halved the time per token, so it helps everyone." At 8 users it did, on every dataset. At 32 users on ShareGPT it gave 277 to 283 tokens per second against 281 to 288 and a first token of 5.7 to 7.0 s against 2.7 to 3.0 s. The gain is a function of load and acceptance. "N-gram showed no gain, close the ticket." It showed no gain on a dataset that copies nothing. On code it cut the time per token from 65.9 to 66.4 ms down to 58.2 to 58.8 at 8 users, and on GSM8K down to 54.6 to 55.0. "The random set is real text, so it is representative." It is the first turn of ShareGPT conversations, cut or repeated to 512 tokens. It behaved like ShareGPT for the draft and like nothing in particular for n-gram. "Fix the chat's first token with a deeper draft." The first token grew because the draft took pool space the queue needed. A deeper draft takes more pool space, not less. "Compare medians, the tail takes care of itself." N-gram raised the P99 ITL at 32 users to 244 to 779 ms against 83 to 106 ms while its median looked fine on two datasets. The lesson to carry A decode optimization that depends on guessing right has a value that depends on what it guesses about, so its benchmark must use the traffic it will serve, at the load it will serve, and report the tail and the first token next to the median. One synthetic dataset gives one point in that space, and a decision for several products needs one measurement per product. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual runs the four datasets in the speculative decoding page , and the vLLM manual gives the limits of a random-prompt gain in the EAGLE3 page and the copy-heavy case in the n-gram page . Recap What to keep from this case Benchmark with the real traffic of each product. Speculation gain is a property of the text. Pick settings per product when they differ. Reopen tickets closed on unrepresentative data. a2147: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Speculation Depth vs Batch Size Lesson 21.47 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 and SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B with the Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3 draft Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory, SM clock locked at 900 MHz, and a GB10 as the second machine The situation In plain words first A deeper speculative draft nearly halved time per token for one user, but at 32 users the server produced no more total output. Each draft guess costs work and memory, and under load that cost competes with real requests. The case trains measuring a setting at the load you serve and noticing what else it changes, such as the size of the cache pool. A team serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 and wants shorter answers for its users. They turn on EAGLE3 with a trained draft and set the draft depth to 5, because a deeper draft guesses more tokens in each step. At one user the time per token almost halves, and the demo is a success. The load test at 32 users tells another story. Each token still arrives faster, but the server writes no more total tokens each second than it did without speculation, while the first token now takes several seconds. The team concludes that speculation does not scale and schedules its removal. A second team, which serves a model of a second family on a GB10 with the same method, reports that their gain holds at 64 users and asks what the first team did wrong. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. EAGLE3 at three draft depths against no speculation, with the clock locked Copy The same draft on the other engine, time per token against output on the L4 Copy The startup lines of the server with the draft loaded on the L4 Copy The one warning that sets the request limit Copy EAGLE3 with its own draft on a mixture-of-experts model on the GB10 Copy The acceptance length on answers of about 2,000 tokens, both engines Copy Questions to answer first Why does a deeper draft pay at one user and cost at 32? Name what a wrong guess spends in each case. From the depth sweep, which depth wins at 32 users and which at one user, and how do you know that the gain is real and not noise? On the L4 each token got faster at every load, and the output stopped growing from 32 users. Which two startup lines explain that, and what does each one cost? On the GB10, an MoE model with its own EAGLE3 draft kept its gain at 64 users. The model, the draft and the card all changed. Which change do you think explains most of the result, and how would you test it? Acceptance stayed between 2.32 and 2.69 tokens per step on long answers. Why would you still measure it on the longest answers that your users get? Design the rollout: which depth, which limits you set by hand, which metrics you read, and which runs come before production. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A setting that helps one user can hurt total output at high load. ✗ Deeper drafts are always faster because they guess more tokens. Depth 3 gave 1.6 times the output at 32 users; depth 5 lost output. ✓ The draft model shrank the cache pool, which mattered under load. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers A draft model guesses the next tokens, and the target model checks all the guesses in one pass. At one user the GPU has spare compute in each step, so the extra guesses are almost free and each accepted guess is a token that the target did not have to compute alone. At 32 users each step is already full, and every wrong guess takes compute from a real token of another user. The depth sweep shows that trade with the clock locked at 900 MHz. At 32 users the run without speculation gave 208.8 tokens per second. Depth 1 gave 271.1, depth 3 gave 333.6 and depth 5 gave 289.5. Depth 3 is 1.6 times the baseline, and its seed range did not overlap with any other config. Depth 5 lost output against depth 3, so its extra guesses cost more than they gave. At one user depth 3 cut the time per token from 39.4 to 27.8 ms against depth 1, and depth 5 at 26.2 ms tied with it inside the seed spread. The one-user run without speculation fell to 210 MHz, below the lock, so it is left out of the comparison. One more cost hides in the median: the ITL at 32 users rose from 84 ms to 133 ms at depth 3, because each step now delivers several tokens at once and the stream arrives in larger, less frequent groups. The second listing is the other engine with the same draft on the same card. Each token came out 1.6 to 2.3 times faster at every load. At 32 users the output was 269.42 against 270.11 tokens per second without the draft, a ratio of 1.00, and at 64 users 245.34 against 250.85. The startup lines explain it. With the draft loaded, the KV pool held 9,951 tokens against 24,094 without it, about 15 of our 640-token requests, because the draft took its share of the card. And the server set max_running_requests=48 by itself. The fourth listing is the warning that does it: when nobody sets the limit, the engine resets it to 48 for speculative decoding, prints that once, and the line scrolls away. At 32 users the first token took 8,040 ms with the draft against 2,970 ms without, because the pool held about 15 requests and the rest waited. The GB10 run is the counterexample, with a caveat: that run used another model, another draft and another card, so it does not isolate the architecture. On a mixture-of-experts model the time per token fell by 1.56 times or more at every load, with a peak of 1.89 times at 32 and 1.84 at 64, and the acceptance length stayed between 2.71 and 2.74 tokens per step. A dense model reads all its weights in each step, so a larger batch already uses the spare compute that speculation needs. A mixture-of-experts model reads only the experts that the tokens of the step chose, and the verify pass scores four positions per request with the expert weights that it already read. Even there the cap bit: at 64 users the output was 276.32 against 235.38, but the median first token was 7,772 ms against 557 ms, because 48 requests ran and 16 waited. The last listing is the acceptance on long answers at 8 users: 2.68 and 2.32 tokens per step on two datasets for one engine, 2.69 and 2.35 for the other, with the first draft position accepted 0.77 and 0.67 of the time and each later position less. It did not fall from 128-token answers to answers of about 2,000 tokens. That is our measurement, on two datasets. A 2026 study of reasoning answers that ran toward 20,000 tokens found the acceptance length fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5, and another found that synthetic prompts overstate the gain of real prompts. So the number to trust is the one from your own longest answers. What actually happened For this model and draft on the L4, the right depth is 3. With the clock locked it gave 1.6 times the output at 32 users and tied depth 5 at one user, while depth 5 lost output under load. The first team measured depth 5 at one user and read that result as a property of speculation. Two settings decided the load test, and neither was the draft depth. The draft shrank the pool to 9,951 tokens, which holds about 15 of the 32 requests, and the engine capped the running requests at 48 without being asked, which binds at 64 users. Read the pool line and the cap warning after you load a draft, set --max-running-requests yourself, and count how many of your requests fit in the smaller pool. Then measure on your own traffic without --ignore-eos : the acceptance from the draft and accepted token counters, the median time per token and the output, and the P99 ITL and P99 TTFT, because a better median can hide a worse tail. Lock or record the clock for every pair. The second team was right for their machine and wrong to generalize: on a mixture-of-experts model the gain held as the batch grew, and on a dense 8B model it did not. Wrong turns "A deeper draft always gives more tokens per step." At 32 users depth 5 gave 289.5 tokens per second and depth 3 gave 333.6. Past the depth that the acceptance supports, each extra guess is compute taken from another user. "Speculation does not scale, remove it." The output tie on the dense model came from a pool of 9,951 tokens, not from the draft. At 32 users the cap of 48 did not bind; at 64 users it did. The mixture-of-experts model kept 1.84 times at 64 users. "Compare against the run without speculation at one user too." That run fell to 210 MHz while the others held 900. A clock gap that large hides the effect, so the row is left out. "The acceptance from the 128-token benchmark is the acceptance we will see." Our long answers held it, but a study of answers toward 20,000 tokens saw it fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5. Measure your own tail. "Raise the running request limit and the queue disappears." The pool holds about 15 requests of 640 tokens. A higher limit does not add memory, it adds waiting on a different line of the log. The lesson to carry A feature that spends idle capacity pays when the capacity is idle and costs when it is not, so its value is a function of the load, the model architecture and the memory it takes, not a property of the feature. Measure it across the load range you serve, read every startup line that a new component changes, and treat a default that a component sets for you as a setting you now own. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual sweeps the depth in the EAGLE3 page and explains the check in the speculative decoding page , and the SGLang manual measures the dense and the mixture-of-experts case and names the request limit in its speculative decoding page . Recap What to keep from this case Measure at the load you will serve. Count throughput as well as per-token time. Check what memory a feature takes. Lock clocks for fair comparisons. a2148: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Temperature 0 Still Gave Two Answers: Nondeterminism Lesson 21.48 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : AI evaluation reliability engineer, inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 and vLLM 0.31.0 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on the GB10, and Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B on the L4 Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory, and the shared second L4 of a two-GPU node The situation In plain words first Two evaluation runs at temperature 0 differed by a point. Temperature 0 picks the most likely token, but the numbers behind "most likely" change with the batch a request joins, with whether its prompt was cached, and with the number type. The case trains listing everything that has to be held fixed for an exact repeat. An evaluation team runs its benchmark twice against the team's serving endpoint, at temperature 0, with an identical prompt list in an identical order. The two scores differ by about a point. They take one question whose answer changed and send it alone, twice. The two texts are identical. Then they send it alone five times and inside a batch of 16 five times, against a GB10 server that runs a model with mixture-of-experts layers. The first of the five single requests gives one text. The next four give another text, which leaves the first after a few hundred characters. All five batched requests give the first text again. The ticket says that the weights or the tokenizer must be corrupt, because temperature 0 is deterministic by definition. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The summary of the probe on the default GB10 server Copy The same probe on the L4, default server against the deterministic flag Copy Three startup lines of the GB10 server with the deterministic flag Copy The summary of the probe with the deterministic flag on the GB10 Copy How many greedy outputs changed with the cache state and with the batch, both engines Copy How many greedy outputs changed between BF16 and FP16 Copy The speed cost of the batch-invariant mode on vLLM, clock locked Copy Questions to answer first Temperature 0 takes the token with the highest logit. What can change the logits of one prompt between two requests on a serving engine, when nothing in the request changes? In the GB10 probe the first of the five single requests differed from the next four, and the batched requests matched the first. Explain both facts with one mechanism. On the L4 the default server gave three texts: A, B, B, B, B, then C, B, B, B, B. What did the batch add? The deterministic flag made all ten requests match. List what it switched, and what each switch costs. The counts table separates three causes. Which one does a cache reset fix, which one needs batch-invariant kernels, and which one is neither a bug nor fixable by a flag? Write the protocol for an evaluation that must repeat exactly, and say what you give up for it. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Batching can change floating-point results, and so the chosen token. ✗ Different answers at temperature 0 mean the weights changed. Weights and tokenizer were fine; the cache, batch and dtype differed. ✓ Flushing the cache and fixing batch and dtype gives repeatable runs. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Floating-point addition is not associative. A matrix multiply, a softmax or a norm splits its sums into tiles, and many kernels pick the split from the batch size and from the path that the prompt takes. A difference in the last bit can change which token has the highest logit, and after one different token every later token is conditioned on a different text. So the request did not change, the arithmetic around it did. The first summary has three counts. Five requests alone gave two distinct texts, five requests in a batch gave one, and all five batched texts matched the first request alone. Our reading, from the manual: the first request computed its prompt from nothing, and the four later ones found the prompt in the radix cache and ran a different prefill path. The 238 characters that the two texts share are the tokens before the first bit flipped. The L4 probe adds the batch. On the default server the pattern was A, B, B, B, B, C, B, B, B, B: the first request alone differed from the four later ones, and one batched request landed on a third text. The batch changed the tile split once more. The third listing shows what the flag did at startup on the GB10. The sampling backend moved to the PyTorch sampler. With no attention backend given, the server fell back to FlashInfer and listed the six backends that the mode accepts. And the radix cache went off, because at this version the cache is not compatible with FlashInfer in deterministic mode. On the L4 the same flag fell back to fa3 , which keeps the radix cache on. The fourth summary is the result on the GB10: one distinct text alone, one in the batch, and all five batched matching alone. The price on the GB10 was 18 percent of the throughput at a concurrency of 8, from 78.92 to 64.83 tokens per second, with the median time per token up from 97.30 to 117.43 ms, and the workload paid again for every repeated prefix. The fifth listing separates the causes at one user. A repeat after a cache flush changed 0 of 32 outputs, and so did a repeat with the cache off, on both engines. The same prompts against a warm cache changed 21 of 32 outputs on one engine and 11 of 32 on the other. At 64 requests sent at once, two runs with the cache off still differed in 27 of 64 and 50 of 64 outputs, so the batch alone changed most outputs and the cache effect could not be separated at that load. The dtype listing is the third cause: BF16 against FP16 changed 51 of 64 and 48 of 64 outputs for the small model, and a repeat in the same dtype changed none. The last listing is the cost of the other engine's fix. With the clock locked, the batch-invariant mode made the time per token 2.4 times longer at one user on the small model and 1.4 times at 8 users on the 8B model, with 58 and 27 percent less output. The probe on that engine gave identical text alone and in a batch of 32 with the mode on, and different text with it off. What actually happened The weights and the tokenizer were fine. A repeat after a cache flush gave identical text for every prompt. Three causes changed the scores: the prefix cache, which ran a different prefill path for a warm prompt, the batch that each request landed in, and the dtype, which the team had not held fixed between the two endpoints. When an evaluation must repeat exactly, flush the cache or restart the server between the two runs, keep the dtype, the engine version and the hardware the same, and run one request at a time. That gives an exact repeat with no flag. Under load, turn on the deterministic mode or the batch-invariant mode and pay for it: 18 percent of the throughput on the GB10 at a concurrency of 8, and 1.4 to 2.4 times the time per token on the other engine. Set a sampling seed on every request that samples. Compare outputs token by token, not only scores, and run the engine's determinism test on your model, your backend and your parallel layout before you rely on it. Leave the mode off for production traffic, where the cache and the faster kernels are worth more than identical bits. Wrong turns "The weights or the tokenizer are corrupt." A repeat after a cache flush changed 0 of 32 outputs on both engines, so every text matched. Corrupt weights do not heal with a flush. "Set a seed and the problem goes away." Greedy decoding samples nothing, and the engine already fixes a seed. The order of the sums changed, and a seed does not touch it. "Turn the deterministic flag on in production." It cost 18 percent of the throughput at a concurrency of 8 and turned the radix cache off on the default backend. Pay that for evaluations and rollouts, not for users. "The scores are within a point, so the runs agree." Two runs can land on the same score with different outputs, and the next run can land elsewhere. Compare the tokens. "Temperature 0 is deterministic by definition." It picks the largest logit, and the logits changed with the cache state, the batch and the dtype. The GB10 gave two texts from one prompt with nothing in the request changed. The lesson to carry Determinism is a property of the whole execution, not of the sampling rule. Any change in the batch, the cache state, the data type, the kernel or the hardware can move a logit by one bit and the text by a paragraph. Decide which of those you hold fixed, measure what the fix costs, and write the cache setting and the cached tokens next to every evaluation result. How this connects Where this is taught The SGLang manual runs the probe and lists the switches in the deterministic inference page and gives the flush route in its benchmark page , and the vLLM manual counts the three causes and prices its own fix in the reproducibility page . Recap What to keep from this case Temperature 0 is not the same as determinism. Hold cache, batch and dtype fixed. Test one prompt alone and in a batch. Write down the settings of each evaluation. a2149: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems TP Refused, DP Starved: Two GPUs and a Shared Card Lesson 21.49 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : a node with two L4 GPUs, the second shared with another team's pods The situation In plain words first A team tried to use two GPUs for more capacity. Tensor parallel refused to start because the second card was partly used by another team; data parallel started but gave that copy a tiny cache, then sent it half the traffic. One card beat the pair at every load. The case trains reading what a failure says about the environment, not just trying the next layout. A team serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B from one L4 and wants more capacity. The node has a second L4, so the plan is to use both. The first attempt is --tp-size 2 . The server dies two seconds after NCCL comes up, with a RuntimeError that says the memory capacity is unbalanced and that some GPUs may be occupied by other processes. A quick look at the node shows two small pods from another team on the second card. The second attempt is --dp-size 2 , two copies of the model behind one controller. It starts, and the team runs its load sweep. At 64 users the pair delivers less output each second than the single card did, and each first token takes many seconds. An engineer from the other team suggests that the node itself is half broken and asks for a hardware ticket. You are asked to read the logs first. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. What the second GPU held minutes before the start Copy The tensor parallel start, two seconds after NCCL came up Copy The data parallel start: the weights and the pool of each rank Copy Four decode lines of the two ranks under a load of 64 requests Copy What the tensor parallel check does, and why it is right Copy How the default load balancing method filled the small copy Copy The same pair with requests routed by token count Copy Questions to answer first What does the tensor parallel check compare, and why did the data parallel start pass where it failed? The two copies loaded the same weights. Why is one pool an eighth of the other? Under load, which rank held the queue and which one sat near idle? Which default sent the work there? Would two copies with equal pools have doubled the capacity? What would you read before you claim it? Name two fixes that keep both cards and one that does not, and say which of them the manual measured. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ The balance check stopped tensor parallel because the second card was shared. ✗ Data parallel worked, so the shared card did not matter. Its copy got a pool of 2,925 tokens and still received half the requests. ✓ The right next step was asking for a dedicated card. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the check in the tensor parallel error. Before it loads weights, each rank measures its free memory, and the group keeps the smallest value. If that value is below 90 percent of the local free memory, the server stops. The error prints the three numbers: the free memory before loading, 18.28 GB, the local memory of the card, and 90 percent of that local memory, 19.53 GB, as the line. The second card had 3,506 MiB in use by two pods of 1,746 MiB each, and that put it under the line. No flag turns the check off at this version. The check is right to stop, because every rank of a tensor parallel group holds the same share of the weights and the same pool, so the smallest card would set the pool for both. Read why data parallel started. Each copy sizes its own pool, so there is no balance check. Both ranks loaded 15.28 GB of weights. Rank 0 then had 6.59 GB free and rank 1 had 3.17 GB, because the pods held the rest. The pools came out at 24,094 tokens against 2,925. Four requests of 640 tokens fill the small one. Read the four decode lines. Rank 1 ran 4 requests at a token usage of 0.82 to 0.87, wrote about 25 tokens per second, and had 59 requests in its queue. Rank 0 ran 1 to 3 requests at a usage of 0.02 to 0.07, wrote under 10 tokens per second, and had no queue. The controller's default method, auto , resolves to round_robin outside disaggregation, and round robin does not look at pools or queues. The benchmark keeps 64 requests open, so 63 of them sat on the small copy, 4 running and 59 waiting, and the client could not send the large copy more work until the small copy gave a slot back. Put a number on the loss. At 64 users the pair gave 41.7 tokens per second against 250.9 on one L4, and the median P99 time to the first token over three seeds was 391 seconds for the pair and 33.4 for one L4. The pair also ran at 765 and 675 MHz at the two highest loads, under the clock floor, while the single card ran at 1,320 and 1,080 MHz, so part of the loss is the clock. Up to 4 users the pair was already 16 to 41 percent slower, for a reason the manual did not isolate. Read the one fix that was measured. With --load-balance-method total_tokens , each request goes to the copy that holds the fewest tokens. The same uneven pair then gave 114.7 tokens per second at 64 users, against 41.7 with round robin and 250.9 on one card, and the median first token fell from 4,763 to 3,977 ms. The clock was 1,020 MHz in that run against 675 before, so part of that gain can be the card. The manual did not measure a pair with equal pools, and it did not measure two servers behind a gateway with weights. Its expectation is that data parallelism adds capacity only when every copy has about the same pool. What actually happened The node is not broken. The second card carries another tenant, and both layouts answered that fact in their own way: the balance check stopped the first layout before it loaded, and the second layout gave one copy a pool of 2,925 tokens and then fed it every second request. The team went back to one L4 for production traffic, because it beat the pair at every load, and asked for the pods to move. With two whole cards, they will start --dp-size 2 again and accept it only after the two #tokens lines of the DP0 and DP1 ranks read about the same. The pair of decode lines is the evidence for this reading: the rank with the small pool held 59 waiting requests while the rank with the large pool used 2 to 7 percent of its pool. Routing by token count raised the pair from 41.7 to 114.7 tokens per second at 64 users and still lost to the single card, so the pool, and not the router, is the limit to fix. Wrong turns "Tensor parallel is refused, so use data parallel, which starts." Starting is not serving. Read the #tokens line of every rank before the load test, because each copy sizes its own pool and nobody checks them against each other. "Lower the memory fraction so the tensor parallel check passes." The check compares free memory before the weights load, not the fraction. The smaller card would still set the pool for both ranks. "Round robin is fair, so the loss must be the hardware." Round robin does not read pools or queues. At 64 open requests, 63 sat on the copy with the small pool. "Fix the routing and the two copies will double throughput." Routed by tokens, the pair gave 114.7 tokens per second against 250.9 for one card. The small pool is still there, and part of the gain was a higher clock. The lesson to carry A parallel layout is a promise that every member carries an equal share. Tensor parallelism checks that promise before it loads and stops when a card is short. Data parallelism makes no check and gives each copy what its card has left, so a shared card becomes a small copy that a blind router fills first. Before you add a GPU, read what else lives on it, and after the start, read the pool line of every rank. Capacity that you did not verify per rank is a sum that does not add. How this connects Where this is taught The parallelism page of SGLang 101 records both starts and the routing fix in what happened on two L4s and data parallelism on the same pair lost , and the memory page explains why a pool is sized from the free memory of its own card in how SGLang decides the split . Recap What to keep from this case Read what a refusal says about the environment. Check per-replica capacity before routing evenly. Compare against the single-card baseline. Fix the shared resource, not the layout. a2150: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems The Latency Knee and a Concurrency Cap That Made It Worse Lesson 21.50 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.8 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 against SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory; the first sweep ran at the full clock, and the reruns locked the SM clock at 900 MHz The situation In plain words first A chat service stalled at 64 users while the throughput chart looked fine. It was past its knee, the load where latency starts rising sharply, and a cap on running requests only moved the waiting elsewhere. The case trains finding the knee with clean measurements and treating overload as a capacity problem. A chat service streams answers from Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 with vLLM. Its target is a first token within one second and 100 ms or less between tokens. At busy hours the service has 64 users at once, and the stream stalls: users see a token, then a gap of more than a second, then a burst. Throughput on the dashboard still looks fine, 241.39 tokens per second. An engineer reads that --max-num-seqs limits the requests that run at once, and lowers it from the default of 256 to 16 to make each stream smoother. The next morning the gaps are still there, and the median wait for the first token is now about a minute. A second engineer proposes to switch the engine, because a competing engine kept the gaps near 150 ms on the same card in a published table. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The chat sweep with the share of requests that met the target Copy The share that met the target and the P99 ITL, with and without a cache reset before each run Copy A cap of 16 sequences against the default at 32 users Copy Two engines with the same pool, from 1 to 64 users Copy The SGLang pool and one decode line at a cap of 64 Copy The vLLM pool and one stats line at a cap of 64 Copy Every admission cap that we tried at 64 users Copy Questions to answer first Which two numbers does a chat user feel, and why is throughput the wrong number to watch here? Read the first listing. At which user count does the service stop meeting the target, and what rises first, the first token or the gaps between tokens? What does a cap on running sequences change inside one scheduler step, and what does it leave unchanged? Both engines write the same tokens per second at 64 users. Explain from the two log lines why one gives the first token sooner and the other keeps the stream smooth. The last listing tries six caps. State the result in one sentence, then say what does fix the gaps on this card. Suppose you must keep vLLM. Which flag, which replica count, and which metric do you set, and how do you prove the fix? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Total throughput can look healthy while each user's stream stalls. ✗ Lowering the cap on running requests fixes overload. It turned a capacity problem into a queue and made things worse. ✓ The knee on this card was between 8 and 16 users. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers A chat user feels the time to the first token and the gap between tokens, the inter-token latency. Throughput is the bill, not the experience. One long pause in a stream feels worse than a slightly slower stream, so the number to watch is the P99 ITL, the worst gap in 100. The first listing is the sweep from the full-clock session. At 8 users, 75 percent of the requests met the target and the P99 ITL was 67 ms. At 16 users the share was 64 percent at 85 ms. At 32 users the output still rose to 275.1 tokens per second, but the P99 ITL grew to 613 ms and no request met the target. At 64 users the first token took 11.18 s and the P99 ITL was 1,233 ms. So the gaps break before the output stops growing. This sweep did not reset the prefix cache between user counts, so the low rows read the first token too fast. The second listing holds the rerun that reset the cache ahead of every run and the clock locked at 900 MHz. At 8 users, 50 percent met the target against 75 to 81 percent without the reset. At 16 users it was 25 percent against 64 to 66 percent, and the P99 ITL was 522 to 523 ms with the reset against 82 to 84 ms without. So the stream breaks between 8 and 16 users on this card. The third listing shows what the cap did. With --max-num-seqs 16 at 32 users, the median ITL fell from 80.5 to 69.8 ms and the P99 ITL from 613 to 595 ms. The first token moved from 1.8 s to 12.3 s, and output fell from 275.1 to 171.8 tokens per second, a loss of 38 percent. The cap run had the higher clock, so the clock does not explain the loss. A cap does not make room for more users. It only chooses who waits, and it moves the wait from the stream to the queue. The fourth listing compares two engines on the same pool of 24,096 tokens. Up to 32 users they tie on output. At 64 users SGLang gave 256.62 tokens per second and vLLM 241.39. The medians for the first token were 18,356 ms against 10,953 ms, and the P99 ITL was 114 ms against 1,363 ms. The two log lines say why. SGLang ran 37 requests and kept 27 in its queue with the pool 92 percent full. vLLM ran 40 requests and kept 11 waiting, filled 99.5 percent of its pool and prefilled new prompts at 460.3 tokens per second while the others decoded. Each new prefill shares the step with the running streams, so the streams stall. vLLM chose the first token, SGLang chose the stream. The last listing tries to buy the smooth stream back with caps. The clock did not hold at 900 MHz in every run, so read the clock column before the cap. Three rows ran at 900 MHz. The SGLang default gave a P99 ITL of 143 to 153 ms with a first token at 19.4 s. The vLLM default gave 1,359 ms at 11.8 s. --max-num-active-seqs 48 gave 1,329 to 1,373 ms at the same 11.8 s, so that cap changed nothing. --max-num-seqs 32 ran at 900 and 795 MHz, gave 1,163 to 1,399 ms and pushed the first token to 17.2 to 20.6 s. --max-num-active-seqs 16 ran at 795 and 683 MHz, so it is not a matched result, but it gave 1,133 to 1,139 ms with a first token at 44.8 to 48.8 s and the output down to 129 to 136. No cap brought the P99 ITL under 1.1 s, and the caps that changed anything moved the wait to the first token. What actually happened Two things were wrong. The service ran past its knee, and the cap treated a capacity problem as a scheduling problem. The knee on this card, measured with a cache reset, sits between 8 and 16 users. At 64 users the pool holds about 37 to 40 requests of 640 tokens, so the rest wait, and every new prefill that enters a step pauses the running streams. The fix is fewer users per replica. On this card, 8 users per replica met the target for half the requests and 16 users for a quarter, so the replica count comes from the target, not from the throughput peak. Remove the --max-num-seqs 16 setting, because at 32 users it cut output by 38 percent and pushed the first token from 1.8 s to 12.3 s at the median while the P99 ITL stayed near 600 ms. Keep the default admission and add replicas until the P99 ITL and the first token both meet the target at the busiest hour. The engine switch is a real option, not a fix. On the same pool at 64 users SGLang kept the P99 ITL at 114 ms and made users wait 18,356 ms for the first token. vLLM did the reverse. Pick the engine by which of the two numbers your users forgive, and measure the pair on your own card. Wrong turns "Lower the batch so each step is faster." A cap on sequences does not add room. It picks who waits, and the first token then waits in the queue. At 32 users the cap cost 38 percent of the output. "Throughput is fine, so the server is fine." At 32 users the output still rose while no request met the target. Throughput measures the bill, the P99 ITL measures the user. "Shorten the maximum model length to fit more users." The pool stays the same size, so the same number of 640-token requests fit. Only a larger pool or fewer users changes that. "The other engine is faster." Both engines wrote about the same tokens per second at every user count. They differed in which wait they chose at a full pool, not in speed. "Set a cap at 48 so the pool never fills." The cap at 48 active sequences left the P99 ITL at 1,329 to 1,373 ms, the same as the default. The gaps come from the prefills that share each step, not from the number of running sequences alone. The lesson to carry When a service runs past its knee, every admission knob trades one latency for another and none of them adds capacity. Measure the two user-facing numbers together with throughput, find the last user count that meets both, and size replicas from that count. When two systems tie on throughput, their difference is the choice they make at saturation, so read the tail of the first token and the tail of the stream side by side before you switch. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual measures the sweep and the caps in the chat tuning page and explains the shared step in the token budget page , the SGLang manual covers the queue in the admission page and the two engines side by side in the benchmark reading page , and the inference metrics lesson defines the numbers. Recap What to keep from this case Watch per-user latency, not only total throughput. Find the knee with clean runs. Add capacity past the knee. Caps manage queues; they do not add capacity. a2151: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems The Logprob Gap That Jumped with a New Engine: Top-p Renormalisation Lesson 21.51 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 and vLLM 0.31.0 as rollout engines, with Miles main 08752a12 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 Hardware : the shared second L4 of a two-GPU node, with no clock lock The situation In plain words first After moving rollouts to a new engine, the gap between the trainer's and the engine's log probabilities jumped. Nothing was broken: the engine returned probabilities after top-p renormalisation, while the trainer used the full vocabulary. The case trains checking that two systems mean the same quantity before comparing them. An RL team samples its rollouts at temperature 1 with top-p 0.9. The trainer scores each sampled token against the whole vocabulary and compares that score with the log probability that the engine returned. The gap between the two, train/train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff , has sat between 0.0148 and 0.0157 at step 0 in all healthy runs. The team moves the rollouts to a second engine. That engine has a flag for which log probability it returns, and the engineer picks the processed value, "because that is the distribution we sampled from". The step-0 gap of the new run lands about 0.053 above the old range. One teammate says the new engine's kernels are worse and wants to switch back. Another wants to switch the engine to its deterministic mode. A third says the gap is a constant and the trainer can subtract it. You have a probe that a colleague ran on the lab L4. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The probe: two engines, one model, one float32 reference Copy Returned logprob minus the reference, by engine and mode Copy What the shifted value is Copy How much mass top-p dropped on these tokens Copy The engine settings of five Miles runs Copy The gap with and without sampling replay, 12 steps, one seed Copy Questions to answer first Three of the four rows agree with the reference and one does not. Which number is the kernel gap, and which is something else? Derive the shifted value. In which direction does it move from the full-vocabulary value, and by how much for a token whose kept mass is 0.9? The teammate calls the gap a constant to subtract. Is it constant across tokens, and which direction does it push the importance ratio? Which value must the engine return for a trainer that scores the full vocabulary, and which setting pairs with a trainer that scores the kept set? Why did the Miles run with top-p 0.95 and top-k 64 end with a lower gap than the run without them? What does the deterministic mode change about this gap, and what does the temperature change about the value the first engine returns? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Top-p renormalisation raises the log probability of kept tokens. ✗ A jump in the gap means the engine's kernels are wrong. In raw mode the second engine matched the trainer. ✓ The engine's flag decides which log probability it returns. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the probe. Both engines ran the same model in BF16 on the same GPU. The client sent 16 prompts and sampled 48 tokens for each, at temperature 1 and top-p 0.9. The reference is a float32 forward pass over the same tokens with a full-vocabulary log_softmax . The GPU was shared and had no clock lock, which changes the speed and not these values. Read the four rows. The second engine in raw mode returned the reference value, with a median difference of 0.0000 and a median absolute difference of 0.005. The first engine returned the reference value too, with a median absolute difference of 0.0066, with its environment variable at 0 and at 1. The second engine in processed mode returned a value higher than the reference by a median of 0.0527. The 0.005 and the 0.0066 are the kernel gap. The 0.0527 is a definition. Check the formula. Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least 0.9, then scales the kept probabilities so that they add up to 1 again. The log probability of a kept token after that scaling is the score over the whole vocabulary minus the log of the kept mass. The probe subtracted that formula from the processed value and got a median residual of 8e-9. So the processed value is the log probability inside the renormalized nucleus, and the raw value is the full-vocabulary one. Read how often the cut bites. The kept mass was below 0.99 for 74 to 79 percent of the sampled tokens, and the median of minus the log of the kept mass was 0.055 to 0.067. That is the size of the shift, and it differs from token to token. Because the kept mass is never above 1, the shift is never negative. It pushes the trainer-to-engine ratio the same way on every token, so it is a bias and not noise. Read the Miles runs. The engine settings table shows a run that passed --rollout-top-p 0.95 and --rollout-top-k 64 , and a base run that passed neither. Miles turns on sampling replay when top-p is below 1 or top-k is above 0: the engine returns the set of tokens that each step could sample from, and the trainer then scores every token over that set only. The replay run had a median gap of 0.0135 against 0.0153 for the base run over 12 steps, with no overlap between their step ranges. Both sides meant the same log probability, so the sampler part of the gap went away and the kernel part stayed. Place the other two proposals. Deterministic inference makes the engine repeat itself and changes nothing about which value the sampler reports. The first engine computes its returned value as log_softmax(logits / temperature) unless its original-logprob variable is set, so at a temperature other than 1 that engine returns a scaled value, while at temperature 1 the variable makes no difference, as the two rows show. What actually happened The gap jumped because the engine and the trainer no longer meant the same log probability. The trainer scored every token over the whole vocabulary, and the engine returned the value after top-p renormalized the kept set, which is higher by minus the log of the kept mass, 0.0527 at the median on these tokens. Nothing changed in the kernels: the raw mode of the second engine matched the reference with a median absolute difference of 0.005. Choose one of two consistent pairs. Either set the engine to its raw mode, so that both sides use the full vocabulary, or turn on replay in Miles with both --rollout-top-p and --rollout-top-k , so that both sides use the kept set. The proof is the step-0 gap: back inside 0.0148 to 0.0157 with the raw mode, or near 0.0136 with replay, which is the step-0 value the manual recorded for the top-p run. Then keep reading the gap at every step, because a gap that grows later means the weights did not reach the engine, which is a different fault. Wrong turns "The new engine's kernels are worse, switch back." In raw mode the new engine matched the float32 reference with a median absolute difference of 0.005, about the same as the old engine's 0.0066. The jump came from the value the flag selected. "Turn on deterministic inference." It makes the engine repeat its own output and costs rollout time. It does not change the definition of the returned value, so the shift stays. "The gap is a constant, subtract it in the trainer." The shift is minus the log of the kept mass of each token, which spread over the tokens and sat below 0.99 for 74 to 79 percent of them. A constant correction leaves a bias on every token, in the same direction. "Lower top-p so that sampling gets sharper and the gap settles." A smaller kept mass makes minus its log larger. The shift grows. "Set the original-logprob variable on the first engine and the problem is solved everywhere." At temperature 1 that variable changed nothing in the probe. It matters when you sample at another temperature and the trainer scores at 1, which is a different mismatch. The lesson to carry Two systems that compare a number must agree on its definition before they compare its value. A sampler that truncates and renormalizes changes the definition of a log probability, and the change is a one-sided bias per token, not noise. Before you read a gap between two sides, probe each side against one reference you compute yourself, and keep the two sides on the same side of the sampler, both before the cut or both after it. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual derives the shift and measures replay in the logprob gap page and gives the step-0 ranges in the first step page , the vLLM manual explains the two modes in its RL rollout page , and the SGLang manual explains the temperature-scaled value in its logprobs page . Recap What to keep from this case Check definitions before comparing numbers. Know whether probabilities are before or after sampling filters. Use a healthy baseline gap to spot changes. Set the engine to return what the trainer expects.
