a2152: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Two Benchmark Clients, Two Numbers, One Server Lesson 21.52 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.22 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0, measured by the SGLang 0.5.22 client and by vllm bench serve Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : the shared second L4 of a two-GPU node, throttled but steady at 420 to 495 MHz The situation In plain words first Two engineers measured one server with two benchmark clients and two temperatures, and got numbers that looked like a regression. Neither was wrong: different clients count time differently, and temperature changes the work per token. The case trains comparing only like with like, and naming the method alongside every number. Two engineers evaluate one vLLM server that serves Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B on a shared L4, for a report that decides whether the team keeps the engine. The first uses the SGLang benchmark client at temperature 0.7, the temperature of the product, and files a median wait of 1,212 ms for the first token at 16 users and 331 output tokens each second at 64 users. The second uses vllm bench serve at temperature 0 and files 1,027 ms and 379 output tokens each second on that server. The first engineer concludes that the server regressed between the two sessions and asks for a rollback of the last image. The second says the first client is broken. A third teammate ran all three clients, the SGLang client and the two versions of the vLLM client, against one server in interleaved rounds, and hands you the output. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. One server, three clients, and the rules of the run Copy Median TTFT in ms from three clients at two temperatures Copy Output tokens per second from three clients Copy The four findings written under the tables Copy How the SGLang manual reads the same table Copy The four mistakes that make two runs disagree Copy Questions to answer first Before you read any table, list what differed between the two filings besides the server. Which cells of the TTFT table isolate the client, and what is the size of the client effect? Which cells isolate the temperature, and which metric does temperature move most? Why does one round at one user not count against the throughput finding? The two clients send different prompts. Why is that a confound here and not a cause? Write the benchmark rule that would have prevented this dispute, in four lines. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Two benchmark clients can report different numbers for the same server. ✗ The lower numbers show a regression in the engine. The gap matched client and temperature differences, not a change in the server. ✓ A report should state the client, temperature and prompt set with each number. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers List the variables first. The two filings differ in the client, the dataset the client draws from, the temperature and the session, and so in the clock and the cache state. The server is the one thing they share. A disagreement of this size has four candidate causes before the server is one of them. Read the setup. The third teammate's run holds four of those variables fixed. One server. The clock sat between 420 and 495 MHz for every run, throttled but steady, so the clock cannot separate the clients. The prefix cache was flushed before every run. Two rounds, interleaved by client, so drift over the session hits every client alike. Every run sent 512 tokens in and 128 out with seed 1 and ignored the end token. Isolate the client in the TTFT table. Compare cells at the same temperature across the columns. At one user and temperature 0, the SGLang client read 154 and 164 ms, vllm bench 149 and 150, and its Rust version 144 and 144. At 16 users: 1,077 and 1,045 against 1,033 and 1,027. At 64 users: 1,688 and 1,838 against 1,624 and 1,667. The SGLang client reads a higher first token in every cell. The two vLLM clients agree with each other within the noise, which puts the noise floor at a few milliseconds at one user and tens at 64. Isolate the temperature. Compare rows at the same client. For the SGLang client at 16 users, temperature 0.7 read 1,212 and 1,089 ms against 1,077 and 1,045 at 0. The notes under the tables give the metric that temperature moves most: the median TPOT was about 10 to 13 percent higher at one user, 34 ms against 30, and 3 to 6 percent higher at 16 and 64 users. Throughput was 3 to 10 percent lower. Sampling costs the server a kernel per token, and the client pays nothing for it, so the server is slower at 0.7 by that much on this card. Read the throughput table with its outlier. At 16 users the SGLang client read 218 and 216 tokens per second against 222 and 222. At 64 users, 359 and 348 against 379 and 377. At one user, one SGLang round read 39.9 against about 32 for every other round. One round out of two cannot stand as a finding, so the notes give no throughput gap at one user. The gap at 16 and 64 users is 2 to 8 percent, and the TTFT gap is 3 to 10 percent. Name the confound. The SGLang client drew its prompts from random-ids , and vllm bench from random . The two clients therefore sent different token sets, and part of a gap of a few percent can be the prompts, not the client code. The run cannot split those two, so it reports the combined client effect and names the confound. A cause would need the same prompts through both clients. Put the two filings together. The first filing is the SGLang client at 0.7. The second is vllm bench at 0. The gap between them is the client effect plus the temperature effect, measured on different days with no shared clock record. Nothing in it points at the image. What actually happened No regression and no broken client. The two reports measured two methods. On this server, the SGLang client reads a median TTFT 3 to 10 percent higher and an output 2 to 8 percent lower than vllm bench serve at 16 and 64 users, with a prompt confound inside that gap, and temperature 0.7 adds 10 to 13 percent to the time per token at one user against temperature 0. The two vLLM clients agreed within noise, which is the size of a real difference on this card. The rollback is cancelled. The team's rule has four lines: one client, one dataset and one temperature, written next to every number; interleaved rounds, at least two; a cache flush before each run; and the SM clock recorded, because the only reason this comparison held is that the clock stayed at 420 to 495 MHz throughout. A future report that uses a different client or temperature is a new baseline, not a comparison. Wrong turns "The server regressed, roll back the image." The two filings changed the client and the temperature at the same time, in different sessions. The controlled run shows that those two alone account for a gap of this size. "The SGLang client is broken, because it reads a slower server." Both vLLM clients also read a slower server at 0.7 than at 0, and the SGLang client's offset is 3 to 10 percent with a prompt confound inside it. A client that reads a few percent higher is a different ruler, not a wrong one. "Average the two filings." They measure different things. A mean of a run at 0.7 and a run at 0 is a number for a temperature nobody serves. "Run at one user, where the numbers are tightest." At one user one SGLang round read 39.9 tokens per second against about 32 for every other round. Small loads are not immune to outliers, and a single outlier flips a two-round cell. The lesson to carry A benchmark number is a property of the whole method, not of the server. Two numbers are comparable only when every part of the method that is not the thing under test stays fixed: the client, the dataset, the sampling settings, the cache state, the clock and the order of the runs. When two reports disagree, list what differed before you blame the system, and measure the size of each difference with a run that changes one thing at a time. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual compares the three clients in the benchmark page , the SGLang manual reads the same table in its benchmark page , and the load testing lesson explains why the harness changes the number. Recap What to keep from this case Compare numbers from one method only. Record the client, temperature and prompts. Measure the method gap directly. Use the product's temperature for the decision. a2153: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Failed Evals That Never Ran: a Model Gateway Unreachable from CI Lesson 21.53 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : AI evaluation reliability engineer, agentic AI engineer. Version : docker-agent v1.149.0 and sbx v0.47.0 Model : ai/qwen3:4b through the local model runner, as the subject and as the judge Hardware : one Mac, no GPU The situation In plain words first A nightly eval printed "2/2 evaluations failed" with a cost of zero and blocked a pull request. Zero cost meant no model was ever called: the eval containers could not reach the model runner. The case trains reading what a failure's own numbers say, and separating infrastructure failures from quality regressions. A nightly job scores the files agent against two saved eval sessions, with a local model as the judge. Last night the job printed Errors: 2/2 evaluations failed and a total cost of zero, and it blocked a pull request. The author of the pull request was told that the agent regressed. The author replied that the change was one word in the instruction and asked for the sessions, and there were none. The on-call engineer tried again with the models gateway flag on the command, pointed at the address that containers use for the model runner. That attempt exited 1 before it ran anything, with an HTTP 403 in the last line. A third attempt, with the same address set in the environment of the eval containers, ran both evals. You review the three runs and the two scores that came out of the third one. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The eval run that blocked the pull request Copy The summary block of the first run Copy The second attempt, with the models gateway on the command Copy The third attempt, with the gateway passed to the containers Copy The expected tool calls of the list-files eval Copy The second tool call the agent made in the list-files eval Copy The base URL of the model runner for each caller Copy Questions to answer first The first run says that two evaluations failed. What in its output tells you whether any evaluation ran? Why did the second attempt stop before the first eval, and what does the 403 name? The third attempt turned a flag into an environment variable. Who reads the variable, and who does not? Which number in the third run is a finding about the agent, and what did the agent do to earn it? Rewrite the gate so that an eval that did not run cannot block a pull request as a regression. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A cost of zero for a failed eval suggests nothing ran. ✗ The pull request made the agent worse. No session was scored; the containers could not find the model. ✓ Passing the gateway address into the containers fixed the run. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the line under each verdict. Both evals carry the same reason: the agent container failed with exit status 1, and its stderr says that it could not get models because the docker executable was not found in the path. The agent inside the eval image looks for the model runner through the docker command line, and the pinned release image has no docker command line. The agent never answered a prompt. Nothing was scored. Read the summary block. failed_evals is 2, and every other count is 0: total_cost , sizes_total , tools_count , relevance_total . sessions is null. A failed verdict with zero totals and no sessions is an eval that never started, not an agent that did badly. Read the gateway attempt. The flag moved the model address for the whole command. The judge is validated first, and the judge runs on the host, not in a container. The host cannot reach the container-only name, so the judge check failed with HTTP 403, and the command exited 1 before it built a container. The 403 names the judge request, not the agent. Read the container-variable attempt. -e DOCKER_AGENT_MODELS_GATEWAY=... sets the variable inside the eval containers only. The judge kept its host address. Both evals ran. Sizes passed 2 of 2, relevance passed 2 of 2, and tool calls averaged an F1 of 83.3 percent. One eval still failed, on tool calls score 0.67 . Read the expected calls and the extra call. The list-files eval expects one assistant turn with one list_directory call. The agent made that call, and then a second call to shell with wc -l README.md . One expected call, two actual calls, F1 of 0.67. This is the only number in the three runs that says something about the agent: it did one step more than the saved session. Read the base URL table. One model runner, and a different base URL for each caller: a host process uses localhost:12434 , a container uses model-runner.docker.internal , and a sandboxed agent goes through the sandbox proxy. The judge and the subject ran in two places, so they needed two addresses. What actually happened The blocked pull request was an infrastructure failure. The eval containers had no way to find the model runner, and the first run scored nothing. The fix is the third command: pass the gateway to the containers with -e , and leave the judge on the host with its own address. The proof is in that run: two evals ran, sizes 2 of 2, relevance 2 of 2, tool calls at an F1 of 83.3 percent, with cost still zero because a local model has no price. On a local runner the cost cannot tell a run from a non-run, so read the totals and the sessions. The gate changes in two ways. It fails the job as broken when the error count is above 0, and it reports a regression only from evals that ran. And the remaining 0.67 becomes a decision for a person: the agent added a line count with shell after the directory listing. If that extra call is wanted, the saved session gains a second expected call. If it is not, the instruction changes. Either way the eval did its job, which is to catch a call that the saved session did not ask for. Wrong turns "The agent regressed, revert the pull request." No eval ran. Both failures are container errors, every total in the summary is 0, and sessions is null. "Put the gateway flag on the command so the containers find the runner." The flag also moves the judge, which runs on the host and cannot reach a container-only name. The run fails with 403 before any eval starts. "Rebuild the eval image with the docker command line inside." The release image is pinned, and the containers lacked an address, not a binary. The eval command has -e to hand them that address. "Add the shell call to the expected list and move on." First decide whether the extra call is wanted. The eval exists to catch a call the saved session did not ask for. The lesson to carry An eval result has two layers: whether the eval ran, and what it scored. Zero totals and no sessions say the first layer failed, so read the error under the verdict before the verdict. Separate errors from failures in the gate. And remember that a judge and a subject can run in different places, with different addresses for the same service. How this connects Where this is taught The eval section records the three attempts, and the model runner section maps the base URL of each caller. Recap What to keep from this case Read cost and session counts as health checks. Separate infra failures from regressions. Never block on an eval that did not run. Prove the fix with a scored run. a2154: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Uniform Prompt Lengths That Hid a Tail Latency Stall Lesson 21.54 25 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.22 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 3 (Senior). Time : about 25 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 against SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory The situation In plain words first An engine evaluation used prompts that were all exactly the same length. That made requests move in waves, which flattered one engine and punished the other. With production's real mix of lengths the ranking reversed. The case trains testing with the shape of traffic you actually have. A team that serves Qwen/Qwen3-8B on L4 cards runs an engine evaluation before a contract renewal. The load test is the benchmark client's default shape: 64 prompts with 16 users at once, every prompt 512 tokens and every answer 128 tokens. Engine A reads a P99 inter-token gap of 502 ms and a median first-token wait of 1,499 ms. Engine B reads 81 ms and 1,775 ms. The output is the same, 181.7 against 182.3 tokens per second. The evaluation calls engine A's stream "unusable" and schedules a migration to engine B. A support engineer points out that production prompts run from a few tokens to several thousand, and that nobody has seen a 500 ms gap in production on engine A. The team repeats the test with the client's length ratio at 0.5 and at 0, where lengths vary, and the two engines change places on the stream metric. You are asked which result is the one to act on. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The waves workload on the L4 by length ratio, both engines Copy How the length ratio sets the prompt and output lengths Copy Total input tokens sent at each ratio, seed 1 Copy Five consecutive scheduler lines from a run at ratio 1.0 Copy How the SGLang manual reads the two traffic shapes Copy SGLang with the mixed chunk against vLLM, by ratio Copy The caveats of the ratio test and the rule for using it Copy Questions to answer first Explain, from the length ratio definition, what identical lengths at 16 users do to the arrival pattern. Read the five log lines. What happened in the second before the first line, and what did the scheduler do in the next two? Why does the engine that keeps the stream smooth in waves lose that advantage when lengths vary? The mixed-length runs sent fewer input tokens. What else differs between the two shapes, and what can you still compare? One SGLang flag cut its mixed-length tail almost in half. What did it cost, and when would you turn it on? Decide the renewal: which result, which flag, and which test you put into the contract. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Identical prompt lengths can synchronise requests into waves. ✗ Engine B has the better tail latency in general. With production lengths, engine A had the lower tail, 191 against 363 ms. ✓ A benchmark's default shape may not represent your traffic. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read what the ratio does. At a ratio of 1.0 every request has 512 prompt tokens and 128 output tokens. At 0, each length is drawn at random from 1 token up to that size. With identical lengths at a fixed user count, all 16 requests start together, finish together, and their replacements arrive together. The traffic comes in waves. With mixed lengths, requests end at different times and new prompts arrive one by one. See the wave in the log. In the first line only one request is running, so fifteen had just finished at once. The scheduler prefilled their replacements in two batches, 4096 and then 3583 new tokens, with no decode in between. Then all 16 decoded together: the generation throughput reads 2.62 tokens per second on the step that carried the prefill, then 231.07 and 229.85 on the steps after it. Prefill happened only between waves, so the decode steps had clean gaps and the first token of a whole wave waited for two full prefill batches. Read the table at ratio 1. The engines tie on output, 181.7 against 182.3. vLLM gives the first token sooner, 1,499 against 1,775 ms, and SGLang keeps the stream smooth, with a P99 ITL of 81 against 502 ms. That is the same choice the two engines make at a full pool: one admits the new prompts into the running steps, the other finishes the wave's prefill first. Read the table at ratios 0.5 and 0. With mixed lengths vLLM led. At 0.5 it gave 169.6 against 159.6 tokens per second, a median TPOT of 81.4 against 87.8 ms and a P99 ITL of 191 against 363 ms. At 0 the P99 ITL was 202 against 302 ms and the first token 284 against 283 ms. The SGLang manual's reading: when new prompts arrive one by one, each prefill shares a step with the running decodes, and vLLM split that work so the stream stalled less. The vLLM manual describes the mechanism as the batch token budget: in each step the running streams get their next token first, and a waiting prompt fills the rest. Account for the confounds. Mixed lengths sent fewer tokens: 32768 input tokens at 1.0 in seed 1, 24504 at 0.5 and 17870 at 0. The runs at 0.5 and 0 also came after the run at 1.0 on the same server, so part of their first-token gain can be the cache. The SGLang manual says that less work and the cache do not explain the stream: with mixed lengths its P99 ITL rose from 82 to 300 ms because each prefill stopped the running decodes. So compare the shape of each row and the ranking inside a row, not the absolute throughput across rows. Read the mixed-chunk test. With --enable-mixed-chunk , SGLang puts the running decodes into the prefill batch. On mixed lengths it then tied vLLM: the P99 ITL fell from 363 to 193 ms at 0.5 and from 302 to 196 ms at 0, with every seed range overlapping, and the output rose by about 8 percent. On fixed lengths the flag cost: the P99 ITL rose from 81 to 203 ms, with seeds from 83 to 349 ms, while vLLM stayed at 502. The log shows one prefill of 514 tokens with 15 requests decoding in the same batch. Decide what each setting measures. The SGLang manual states it: fixed lengths measure bursts, a slow first token and smooth tokens after it; mixed lengths measure steady traffic, a fast first token and stalls in the stream. Keep the ratio at 1.0 to compare two builds, because it repeats exactly. Run your real length distribution before you set a latency target. What actually happened The migration decision rested on a traffic shape that production never produces. Identical lengths at a fixed user count synchronize the requests into waves, and in waves engine A's choice to admit new prompts into running steps costs a 502 ms tail that engine B avoids by prefilling between waves. With the lengths production has, engine A had the lower tail, 191 against 363 ms at 0.5 and 202 against 302 at 0, the same or better first token, and more output. On the support engineer's evidence, the 500 ms gap belongs to the test. The renewal keeps engine A. If the team prefers engine B for other reasons, --enable-mixed-chunk removes its mixed-length disadvantage at a cost in bursts, 81 to 203 ms, so the choice depends on whether production arrives in bursts or steadily. The contract test changes: sample the real length distribution from production logs, run it as the acceptance test, and keep the fixed-length run only as the repeatable build-to-build check. Record the clock on both; every median clock in the mixed-length pairs was 1,410 MHz or higher, which is why those rows are comparable. Wrong turns "A 502 ms tail is a scheduler bug in engine A." The same engine read 202 ms at a ratio of 0 and 191 at 0.5. The tail came from 16 prefills landing in the same steps, which the test created and production does not. "Identical lengths are the fairest test, because nothing varies." They are the most repeatable, not the most realistic. They measure bursts, and the SGLang manual says to use them for build comparisons, not for latency targets. "Raise the token budget so prefills finish sooner." On the DGX Spark, a budget of 16,384 tokens raised the P99 ITL from 574 to 798 ms at a low rate, and the gain in the first token did not clear the seed spread. The budget trades the two latencies; it does not remove the stall. "Compare throughput, the engines tie, so it does not matter." The tie on output hid a 502 against 81 ms tail in one shape and a 363 against 191 ms tail in the other. Users feel the tail. "Turn on the mixed chunk everywhere on engine B." On fixed-length bursts it raised the P99 ITL from 81 to 203 ms with seeds up to 349. It fixes steady traffic and hurts bursts, so measure your traffic shape first. The lesson to carry A load test with one prompt length tests one point of the length distribution, and at a fixed user count it also synchronizes the requests, so it measures a burst that steady traffic never produces. The ranking of two schedulers can flip between those shapes. Sample the real distribution of lengths for every latency target, keep the fixed-length run for repeatability, and read the tail next to the median in both. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual holds the waves tables in the lab notes and the budget mechanism in the token budget page , the SGLang manual reads the pair on waves and tests the ratio in its benchmark page , and the load testing lesson names the prompt-uniformity trap. Recap What to keep from this case Benchmark with real length distributions. Watch for artefacts of synchronised load. Check tails, not only medians. Revisit decisions made on default shapes. a2155: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Conformance Testing: a 32.3 Percent Score Read Down to Requirements Lesson 21.55 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : design-review, debugging. Roles : agentic AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer, forward deployed AI engineer. Version : A2A 1.0.1 with the manual's capture kit (the test-runner, code-reviewer and deployer agents) Model : no model; the agents are deterministic fixtures Hardware : one machine, localhost, no network The situation In plain words first A conformance kit scored a server at 32 percent and a release was blocked. Most failures came from how the kit built a URL and how it counted skipped checks, not from broken requirements. One real defect remained. The case trains reading a score down to requirements: which MUSTs failed, which failures are the tool's, and what actually needs fixing. A team's A2A server is ready for its first release. The release gate runs the official conformance kit, a2a-tck at the tag 1.0.0.alpha2 , against the server and requires a passing score. The dashboard shows an overall compatibility of 32.3 percent, and the gate is red. The engineering lead opens a ticket with the title "fix the 63 failing JSON-RPC checks" and asks you for an estimate. The server under test is the kit's test-runner agent. Its card declares a JSON-RPC and an HTTP+JSON interface, streaming and push notifications, and no gRPC. You have the record of two runs against it on the same day: the first with the TCK as published, and the second after a two-line change to the TCK's own JSON-RPC client, repeated against the server after one fix. Your job is to say which failures belong to the server, which belong to the test kit, and what the gate should read. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The numbers of the two runs, from compatibility.json and pytest Copy Why there is a second run: where the TCK posted its JSON-RPC requests Copy Two accounting rules of the TCK that change how the numbers read Copy The ten requirements that fail on a real assertion, by class Copy The push requirements after the fix, verdict per binding Copy The one defect the run found in the server, and its fix Copy Where the TCK departs from the specification, in order of effect Copy Questions to answer first Which single cause explains most of the first run, and whose defect is it? After the second run, why do most of the remaining failed requirements still say nothing about the server? Of the requirements that fail on a real assertion, how many are the server's, and at which level? The push requirements pass on one binding and fail on the other. What does the TCK record for each one, and why? What was the one real defect, which rule does it break, and how was the fix verified? Write the release rule: what does the gate read, and what does it do with a failure that the test kit owns? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A tool's score can measure the tool's own assumptions. ✗ 63 failing checks mean 63 things to fix. The server broke no MUST; one real defect was found. ✓ Release rules should be written in terms of requirements. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the two runs. Run 1 scored 32.3 percent: 30 requirements passed, 63 failed, 11 were skipped and 25 were not tested, of 129. On the JSON-RPC transport 12 records passed, 63 failed and 10 were skipped, of 85. Run 2 scored 66.7 percent: 62 passed, 31 failed, 11 skipped, 25 not tested, and the JSON-RPC transport read 66, 29 and 7 of 102 records. All 72 gRPC records were skipped in both runs, because the card declares no gRPC interface. The server did not change between the two scores, apart from the push fix, and that fix moved no verdict. Read why run 2 exists. The TCK's JSON-RPC client posts to / on an HTTP client whose base is the interface URL. The library appends a slash to the base, so every request went to the card's URL plus a trailing slash. The server routes JSON-RPC at the exact URL and answers 404 with "No such path". 63 of the 85 JSON-RPC records in run 1 fail or skip for this one reason. The TCK's own reference server declares its interface at the host root, where the two URLs are the same, so the kit never meets its own defect. The specification requires an interface to declare its URL, and nothing requires a server to also answer at the URL with a slash. The two-line change replaces / with the base URL, and every one of those records passes. Read the accounting. The tag records a skip raised inside a test body as a failure. The main branch of the TCK fixed that and wrote why: recording it as a failure would misrepresent it. In run 2, 21 of the 31 failed requirements are such skips, most of them from a prerequisite that expects an agent that parks a task in an input-required state, which test-runner never does. With the main rule the run reads 62 passed, 10 failed, 32 skipped, 25 not tested: 86.1 percent overall and 89.4 percent on MUST requirements. The second rule: the per-transport entry is the last record written, so a requirement can show a pass on a transport beside a failed verdict. Read the ten. None fails on the server's account at MUST level. Seven are the TCK's: a required content-type error counted as a failure, two content-type substring checks that want application/json where the specification prefers application/a2a+json , a test that sends a non-JSON body and expects -32005 where the specification gives -32700, the snake_case task_id on push creation, and a MAY that the test asserts. Two come from the TCK's sample agent story, which expects fixed outputs that this agent does not produce. Two are SHOULD omissions the server documents: no Cache-Control and no ETag on the card. Read the push rows. Six push requirements show http_json=PASS , jsonrpc=FAIL , and the verdict FAIL, because a requirement fails when any transport fails. The JSON-RPC side fails because the TCK sends task_id where the specification's camelCase rule gives taskId . The server reads taskId , finds no task, and answers -32001. The HTTP+JSON client sends camelCase and passes. PUSH-GET-002 passed on JSON-RPC for the same wrong reason: the server answered not found for every config id, so the test never checked a real one. Read the defect. Before the fix, the HTTP+JSON binding served no route under tasks/{id}/pushNotificationConfigs , while the card declared both bindings with push notifications on. Section 5.1 of the specification says that all supported protocols must provide the same set of operations. The run recorded it as PUSH-CREATE-001 failing on HTTP+JSON with "404 Method not found" and five dependent skips. The fix added the four REST routes behind the same capability guard. The repeat of run 2 flipped six HTTP+JSON records to pass and raised the pytest count from 113 to 119, and eight hand checks covered create, get, list, a missing id, delete, get after delete, delete again, and an unknown task. Read the departures. Eight, in order of effect: the trailing slash, the snake_case parameters, the content-type substring, the missing expected error on one requirement, the non-JSON body, hard asserts on SHOULD and MAY tests, the skip recorded as a failure, and latent status codes of 409, 415 and 502 where the specification says 400, 400 and 500. Two of the eight are fixed on the main branch of the TCK. What actually happened The 32.3 percent measured how the TCK built a URL, and the 66.7 percent measured how it counted a skip. By requirement, the server breaks no MUST. Its one real defect, found by the second run, was the missing push routes on HTTP+JSON, and the fix is verified by six records and eight hand checks. Two SHOULD omissions remain and are documented. The release rule reads compatibility.json per requirement, never the percentage. It classifies every non-pass as the server's, the TCK's, the sample agent's, unsupported by design, or untested. It blocks only on a MUST failure that is the server's own, tracks the SHOULD omissions, and files each TCK defect upstream with the wire check that proves it. It also keeps a list of what the TCK does not test at this tag, among them binding equivalence, card signatures and owner scoping, and the team tests those itself. Wrong turns "Fix the 63 failures." 63 records fail for one reason that lives in the test client, and no rule requires a server to answer at the URL plus a slash. A two-line change in the TCK removes all of them. "Rename the JSON-RPC parameters to snake_case so the push checks pass." The specification requires camelCase, and the TCK's own HTTP+JSON client sends camelCase and passes. The server would break the specification to satisfy the kit. "Send application/json so the content-type checks pass." The specification prefers application/a2a+json , and the implementations split. Accept both when you read, and keep sending what the specification prefers. "Ship when the percentage reaches a threshold." The percentage counts PASS and FAIL only. The skip rule alone moves it from 66.7 to 86.1 with no change to the server, so a threshold measures the TCK version. "The push checks pass on HTTP+JSON, so binding equivalence is covered." The four equivalence requirements are not tested at this tag. The defect was caught by accident through a push test, and the next gap will not be. The lesson to carry A conformance score is a measurement, and the instrument has its own defects. Before you act on the number, read per requirement, separate the instrument's failures from the subject's, run again after the instrument is fixed, and ask what the instrument does not measure at all. The one real defect here sat in the gap between two bindings, a place the kit did not test. How this connects Where this is taught The conformance testing page of A2A 101 records these two runs and the table of departures, the errors page and the push notifications page give the rules behind the content-type and push rows, and the failure modes lesson warns that monitoring which tags only the headline misses the failures that matter. Recap What to keep from this case Read scores down to requirements. Separate tool artefacts from defects. Fix and verify the real defects. Write release rules on MUSTs, not percentages. a2156: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Memory Guard That Paused the Scheduler at Startup Lesson 21.56 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Hardware : one GB10 with unified memory, a desktop that other users share The situation In plain words first Server starts on a shared machine stalled silently for a while and then carried on. A memory guard watching the whole machine had paused the scheduler while it allocated its pool. Driver alerts on the same day looked related but the evidence did not link them. The case trains linking events only through evidence, not timing. A team gets time on a GB10 desktop that several people share, and starts an SGLang server for Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 . Three starts in one afternoon stall after the weights load. The server log stops, the scheduler process is alive but does nothing for a while, then the log continues as if nothing happened. Nobody sees an error. That afternoon the on-call channel also gets pages from a kernel-log alert. Nine bursts of an NVIDIA driver line that says Out of memory arrive between 13:52 and 16:46, up to 13 lines in one minute. The team puts the two things together: the driver is faulty, and the server leaks memory until the driver fails. They ask to move the model to a smaller, dedicated card. The owner of the desktop asks you to review before anyone changes hardware. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The guard log around the first pause Copy Two more pauses in the next hour Copy The weights and the pool of a default start that was kept Copy The driver line in the kernel log, counted by minute Copy What the manual can and cannot say about the three pauses Copy The driver bursts and the position of the manual Copy How to start on a shared machine with unified memory Copy Questions to answer first The scheduler stopped and later continued, and the server log shows no error. Which process stopped it, and on what rule? The guard saw one process grow by tens of GiB in five seconds. Which allocation is that likely to be, and how do you check it against a start whose log was kept? The three pauses report different growth. What can you conclude from the guard log alone, and what can you not? Nine bursts of the driver line fell on one day. What does the manual claim about them, and what would it take to tie one burst to one start? Which alert do you keep and which do you remove, and what is the start procedure for this machine from now on? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A guard watching the whole machine can pause a healthy process. ✗ The driver bursts caused the stalled starts. No capture linked a burst to a failed start. ✓ The server did not leak memory. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the guard log first. The desktop runs a memory guard daemon for its other users. It stops the process that grows fastest when free memory gets low. Its first entry reads Critical: 34.2 GiB left before the freeze zone , and the same second it paused sglang::schedul because it grew 36.7 GiB in 5s. Eight seconds later the guard logged Back to normal: 28.9 GiB available . The scheduler was the fastest-growing process on the machine, so the guard was correct by its own rule. That is the stall the team saw, and no server log records it, because the server was not told anything. Match the growth against a kept start. The default start that the manual kept shows what the scheduler allocates right after the weights: a KV pool that holds 227,243 tokens, with 10.40 GB for K and 10.40 GB for V, allocated in a few seconds, with 54.84 GB free before and 31.22 GB free after. The manual reads the 36.7 GiB as the size of a KV pool allocation. It also notes a field report of 25 to 40 GB of short-lived allocations outside the fraction, from the autotuner and the graph capture, and says plainly that the guard log does not separate the pool from those. So the growth is the startup allocation of a server on unified memory, and its exact split is not proven. Read the other two pauses with the same care. They report 9.4 GiB and 28.1 GiB of growth, and each time the guard reported normal within seconds. The server logs of those three starts were not kept, so nobody can say which allocation each pause caught. The manual's table of six kept starts shows why a single number would mislead anyway: the same weights measured between 54.78 and 57.92 GB, and the pools ran from 216,775 to 258,017 tokens, because the kernel's file cache changed during each load. What the guard log does prove is a process that grows by tens of GiB in seconds and then stops growing. A leak would keep the guard busy after the pool line, and no entry shows that. Read the driver bursts as a count, not a verdict. The kernel line is NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY from the driver's allocator. The bursts are dated 2026-10-16, the day of the first test and sweep starts, with 3 to 13 lines per minute. The manual kept no server logs from that day, so it cannot match a burst to a start and refuses to. What it can say is that every server in its later captures became healthy and finished its benchmarks. To tie a burst to a start you would need the server log with timestamps and the free-memory log of the machine for the same minute. Turn the reading into a procedure. The manual's position for a shared GB10 has four steps: start SGLang in a container with a memory limit, start below the fraction of 0.7 that its kit used, log the free memory of the machine once a second during startup, and raise the fraction only after you saw the peak. Add two more from the same page: pass --mem-fraction-static on purpose, and tell the other users of the machine before you start. For the guard, the manual agreed with the owner to stop it for the time of its runs. On the alert, the position is one sentence: do not alert on the driver line alone, alert when a server does not become healthy. What actually happened As far as the evidence shows, the server did not leak and the driver was not faulty. A guard that watches the whole machine paused the scheduler while it allocated its pool, three times, and resumed it each time within seconds. The driver bursts fell on the same day, and the captures hold no link from any burst to a failed start or to a user who saw an error. The team kept the model on the GB10 and changed how it starts: an explicit fraction, a container with a memory cap, a free-memory log during startup, and an agreement with the owner about the guard while the server runs. The kernel-line page was replaced with a health alert on the server's ready line and its health endpoint, which in the kept start returned 503 before the ready line and 200 after it. The measurement that supports the change is the set of later starts, which reached their pool lines and ran their benchmarks with no pause and no page. Two things stay open, and the write-up says so. No capture ties a driver burst to a start, and the field report of allocations outside the fraction is from before this version and was not measured here. Wrong turns "The server leaks memory until the driver fails." The guard logged normal within seconds of each pause, and no entry shows growth after the pool was in place. A pool of tens of GB allocated in seconds is the design, not a leak. "Replace the driver." The bursts carry no user-visible failure in the captures, and every later server became healthy. A line in the kernel log is not an incident until a user or a probe sees one. "Raise the fraction, so the pool is allocated once and the guard stops complaining." The fraction sets the pool size. A larger pool grows faster and leaves less for the other users. Lower it, cap the container, and watch the peak. "Match each burst to a start from the timestamps." Without the server logs of that day the match is a guess, and the manual refused to make it. Keep the logs that let you correlate before you correlate. "Move to a smaller dedicated card." That trades a shared machine for a smaller pool and gives up the result that the GB10 served every later run. Fix the start procedure first, then decide. The lesson to carry On unified memory, a KV pool is memory that the whole machine gives up in a few seconds, and every guard, daemon and user on that machine sees it go. Treat the start of a server as an event that you announce, cap and log, not as something that happens inside one process. When an alert fires, ask what it measured and who was harmed. Keep the logs that let you connect an event to a cause, and when they are missing, write down that the connection is not proven instead of asserting it. How this connects Where this is taught The memory page of SGLang 101 records the pauses and the driver bursts in a pool that other programs see and gives the start procedure in memory outside the fraction , and the incident index lists both with their status. Recap What to keep from this case Find who paused a process before blaming it. Link events through evidence, not coincidence. Know what shared-machine guards do. State what the evidence does not show. a2157: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Throughput vs Steady State: a Rate Sweep That Never Settled Lesson 21.57 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.8 , Lesson 17.22 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : system-design, debugging, ml-depth. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer, applied AI engineer. Version : vLLM 0.31.0 and SGLang 0.5.22 Model : Qwen/Qwen3-8B Hardware : one L4 with 24 GB of memory The situation In plain words first A capacity report said one card could serve 16 requests per second because every run completed. A fixed-rate run always completes: the client stops sending and the server drains the queue. The first-token times showed the queue growing to 94 seconds. The case trains telling completion from steady state. A platform team must size a fleet of L4 cards for a new chat API. They run a rate sweep against one card with Qwen/Qwen3-8B : requests arrive at a fixed rate from 0.5 to 16 per second, each request with a 512-token prompt and a 128-token answer. Every run completes and no request fails. The output rises to 286.6 tokens per second at 4 per second and is still 205.8 at 16. The capacity report concludes that one card can take 16 requests each second, so the fleet plan divides the expected peak by 16. You get the report the evening before the purchase order goes out. It shows throughput per rate and the median wait for the first token at each rate, and it labels that column "latency under load, expected". Nothing in the report says how long each run lasted or what the GPU clock did. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The L4 rate sweep from 0.5 to 16 requests per second Copy What a fixed request rate does that a closed loop cannot Copy The run length of the rate sweep Copy The SGLang pool and one decode line with requests waiting Copy The vLLM pool and one stats line with requests waiting Copy Which rates kept up, which met the target, and which row the manual refuses to compare Copy Completed requests per second as the offered rate rose past the peak Copy Questions to answer first Which column of the report proves that the card kept up with the arrivals, and at which rate does that proof stop? A closed loop at 64 users and an open loop at 16 per second both complete. What is different about the queue in the two cases? The median first token at 16 per second was 94,322 ms. What would that number be if the run had lasted twice as long, and why? Read the two log lines. How many requests ran and how many waited on each engine, and what set that limit? Define the capacity of this card for a target of one second and 100 ms, from the evidence. Write the rate test you would run instead, and the stopping rule that tells you a point is above capacity. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A growing first-token time across a run means the queue is growing. ✗ No failed requests means the card kept up. It finished by draining after arrivals stopped. ✓ Capacity is the rate at which latency stays flat over time. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the table as a time series, not as a list of points. Up to 2 per second the output grows with the rate: 70.6 at 0.5, 123.6 at 1 and 227.8 at 2 for vLLM, and the median TTFT stays between 180 and 317 ms. The server finishes work as fast as it arrives. At 4 per second the output is 286.6 and the median TTFT is 8,304 ms. At 8 the pair is 261.8 and 27,510 ms, and at 16 it is 205.8 and 94,322 ms. The output peaked at 4 and then fell, while each doubling of the rate multiplied the first token by more than three. The clock column falls from 1,245 MHz at 4 to 450 MHz at 16. Name the loop. The second listing separates the two kinds of load test. A closed loop with a fixed number of users never falls behind, because a user sends the next request only after the answer. A fixed rate keeps sending whether the server keeps up or not. Past the rate the server can serve, the queue grows, and the first token takes longer with every request. From 4 per second, the first-token column of the report measures queue time. Ask how long the run was. The third listing gives the run length: at least 32 prompts, or 30 seconds of arrivals. A median TTFT of 94,322 ms from a run with 30 seconds of arrivals means that the typical request waited longer than the whole arrival window. The queue was still growing when the last request arrived. Run the same rate for twice as long and the median grows, because every extra second of arrivals adds work that the server cannot drain. The number is a property of the run length, not of the card. That is what a point above capacity looks like: the latency never settles. Count who ran and who waited. SGLang ran 37 requests with 71 in its queue and the pool 93 percent full. vLLM ran 43 requests with 30 waiting and 99.7 percent of its pool in use. The pools hold 24,094 and 24,096 tokens, so about forty requests of 512 plus 128 tokens fit at once. Everything that arrives faster than those slots free up waits. The engines differ only in how many they admit before they queue. Define capacity from goodput. The manual set two limits, 1 s to the first token and 100 ms per token. At 2 per second, vLLM served a median of 1.36 requests per second within those limits and SGLang 0.88, with overlapping seed ranges. From 4 per second, no request met them on either engine. So the card sustains that target somewhere between 2 and 4 per second, and the number to plan with is 2. The row at 16 is not even comparable: every run of both engines stayed under 1,000 MHz after three tries, so the manual does not compare it. Count what overload cost. The last listing is the same card in the open loop of the SGLang manual. Past its peak, the BF16 server completed fewer requests as more were offered: 2.01 per second at 4 offered, 1.91 at 8 and 1.62 at 16. The median SM clock fell from 1,320 MHz at 4 offered to 465 MHz at 16, and 70 percent of the samples showed thermal slowdown. On this passively cooled card, overload is not free. It heats the GPU, the clock falls, and the server completes less than it did at a lower rate. What actually happened The report mistook completion for capacity. A fixed-rate run always completes, because the client stops sending at the end of its arrival window and the server drains the queue afterwards. The first-token column from 4 per second up is the length of that queue, and at 16 per second it reached 94,322 ms after 30 seconds of arrivals. The card never served 16 requests per second within any latency target. It served about 2 per second within the target of 1 s and 100 ms, with vLLM at 1.36 and SGLang at 0.88 requests per second of goodput at an offered 2. The peak is divided by 2, not by 16, before any headroom. The test changes in four ways. Run each rate long enough to see whether the first token settles; if the median TTFT rises when you extend the run, the rate is above capacity and the number is meaningless. Report goodput per offered rate against your own target, next to the throughput. Record the SM clock and the temperature, and repeat or discard any point that fell under the clock floor, as the manual did for the row at 16. Run the closed loop too, because the closed loop finds the knee by user count and the open loop finds the rate the card sustains, and a plan needs both. Wrong turns "Every run finished, so the card handles 16 per second." A fixed-rate client stops sending at the end of its window and the server drains the queue afterwards. Completion is guaranteed. The 94,322 ms median first token is the queue, not the service. "Output was still 205.8 tokens per second at 16, so throughput held." Output fell from 286.6 at 4 per second to 205.8 at 16 while the clock fell from 1,245 to 450 MHz. The server did less work at the higher rate, and the open loop of the SGLang manual shows the same fall in completed requests per second. "Take the TTFT at 16 as the worst case users will see." That value depends on how long the test ran. Extend the run and it grows. A number that grows with the run length describes the test, not the server. "Switch to the engine with the lower TTFT at 8 per second." At 8 per second both engines were far past capacity, 27,510 against 37,211 ms. Choosing between two overloaded servers by their queue length is not a capacity decision. The lesson to carry A system above its service rate has no steady state, so every latency you measure there is a function of how long you measured. Capacity is the highest offered rate at which the latency settles and the goodput holds, found with an open loop that runs long enough to prove the settling, and confirmed with a closed loop for the user count. Completion, throughput and a median taken from a growing queue are not capacity. How this connects Where this is taught The vLLM manual gives the sweep in the lab notes and the two loops in the benchmark page , the SGLang manual reads the same pair at a fixed arrival rate and runs its own open loop in the benchmark serving page , and the inference metrics lesson defines goodput while the load testing lesson names the four load patterns. Recap What to keep from this case Completion is not capacity. Look for steady latency over the run. Run long enough to see a trend. Size fleets on steady-state rates. a2158: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems A Rebuilt Function That Was Plausible, Not Equivalent Lesson 21.58 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, ml-depth, design-review. Roles : agentic AI engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : rea 6.7.0 at 27dc42d with the Ghidra provider Model : no model; the fixtures are the ledger binaries built at -O1 and -O2 Hardware : one aarch64 Mac The situation In plain words first An agent rebuilt two functions from decompiler output and they passed ten hand-written tests, but "passes naive tests" and "compiles" are not "behaves the same". The comparison tool it cited compared decompiler text, not behaviour. The case trains defining what "equal" means for a reconstruction and testing that, including edge cases. An agent is asked to rebuild two functions of the ledger fixture from Ghidra pseudocode, percent_change and grade , so that a team can drop the original object file. It writes percent_change with the long that the decompiler offered and grade as four threshold comparisons. It runs the ten hand-written tests of the lesson harness, and all ten pass. It then calls verify_reconstruction over two compare_functions records that cover the -O1 and -O2 builds, sees two claims pass and two fail, and reports: "percent_change is verified equal; total has changed between builds, so the compiler broke it." The team lead reads the report and asks two questions. What does a passed claim in that tool prove about a function, and what does a failed one prove? And which test decides whether the rebuilt functions are equal to the originals? You have the verification record, the harness notes, and the harness outputs for two candidate pairs. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The verification status, the summary, and the first claim Copy The total-assembly claim Copy What the harness is and what it ran Copy The agent's pair over the grid, head and first mismatch Copy The two grade cells that the threshold rebuild got wrong Copy The equal pair over the same grid Copy A rebuild with one wrong table entry in the byte comparison Copy Questions to answer first A claim passed with observed_status: "unchanged" . What was compared, and what does unchanged mean here? The total claims failed although both builds come from one source line. Does a failed claim say that the function changed its behaviour? All ten naive tests passed for the agent's pair. How many of the 92 grid cells did it get wrong, and which hazard classes do the failures belong to? Which pair agrees on every cell, and what else must that pair pass before you call it equal? A candidate with one wrong table entry has equal masked bytes and matching relocations. What check catches it? Write the acceptance rule for a rebuilt function, in order. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Matching decompiler text says nothing about behaviour. ✗ Ten passing tests prove the rebuilt functions are equivalent. Plausible code can pass naive tests and differ on edge cases. ✓ Equivalence needs tests that target edge cases and types. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read what the verifier compares. The verification record has status: "fail" with two passed and two failed structural claims. The first claim, percent-change-assembly , reads pass with an observed status of unchanged . A structural claim takes its status from one dimension of one compare_functions record, and that dimension is a line diff of the text that Ghidra printed. So a pass says that the two assembly texts matched line for line, and nothing more. The record's own limitation says that a pass is no proof that the whole implementation is equivalent. Read the failed claim. total-assembly reads fail with an observed status of changed . The -O2 build of total has different Ghidra text from the -O1 build, because the optimizer unrolled the loop. The manual counts 62 instructions where -O1 had 13. One source line, two texts. A failed text claim does not say that behaviour changed, and the agent's sentence about a broken total has no support. Read what the harness does. The harness notes describe two legs. Leg one compiles the original source and each candidate into one program and runs both over 92 cells. Leg two compiles each candidate for the original target and compares it with the original object after relocation masking. rea 6.7.0 has neither leg; this is the part that the agent had to run and did not. Read the agent's pair on the grid. The plausible pair is the long rebuild of percent_change with the threshold rebuild of grade . naive_passed is true and the mismatch list starts at once: at before 3 and after 2147483647 the original returns -133 and the candidate returns -1431655899. The manual's count over the file is 28 of the 92 cells, 26 of them overflow cells of percent_change where the original wraps the product to 32 bits before it divides and the long rebuild does not. Read the two grade cells. The threshold rebuild returns 4 for a score of 110 and for INT_MAX , where the original switch has no case and returns 0. The hazard class is "beyond the switch". Ten naive tests never reached either hazard, which is why they all passed. Read the equal pair. The pair that multiplies first and keeps the switch has an empty mismatch list and an empty oracle disagreement list on the same 92 cells. That is leg one passed. It is still not a proof of equal bytes. Read leg two on the wrong constant. The candidate grade_case10_wrong has 46 code bytes equal to the original after masking, one relocation of the same offset, type and section, and the status fail . Its table reads 1, 2, 3, 4, 3 against the original's 1, 2, 3, 4, 4. Only the read through the relocation catches it. A rebuild can pass a text claim, pass the masked byte compare, and still compute a different grade. What actually happened The report is withdrawn and rewritten. The percent_change claims that passed say that Ghidra printed the same text for both builds, and the total claims that failed say that it printed different text; neither says anything about behaviour, and nothing in the -O2 build is broken. The agent's two candidates are plausible: they compile, they pass the ten naive tests, and they fail 28 of the 92 grid cells. The accepted candidates are the multiply-first percent_change and the switch grade . They agree with the original on all 92 cells, their masked bytes equal the original's, their relocation records have the same shape, and the table they reference reads 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 on both sides. The acceptance rule the team writes down has four steps, and nothing weaker than a pass at any step adds up to a pass: the structural claims pass in rea, leg one agrees on every grid cell on a named host, leg two matches the masked bytes and the relocation records, and the bytes that each relocation points at are read and compared. The host and the compiler are recorded with the proof, because the trap cell returns a value on this arm64 host and traps on x86-64. Wrong turns "verify_reconstruction passed for percent_change, so the rebuild is verified." The claims compared two Ghidra texts of two builds of the original. They never saw the rebuild, and a pass means same text. "The total claims failed, so the compiler changed what total computes." Different text from one source line. The failure says the texts differ and stops there. "Ten tests pass, including a zero divisor and a negative score, so the rebuild is right." None of the ten reaches an overflow cell or a score beyond the last case. The grid has 92 cells for that reason. "The masked bytes are equal and the relocation matches, so skip the table read." That is the one check that fails the wrong-constant candidate. Read the bytes each relocation points at. The lesson to carry A verifier can only grade the claims it was built to grade, and its pass carries the limitation it prints. Before you accept a verdict, ask what was compared and against what, and whether the artifact you care about was ever an input. For a rebuilt function, equality is a chain of checks, each one catching a defect the one before lets through: text, behaviour over a grid that reaches every hazard the listing shows, masked bytes, and the data those bytes point at. Tests that pass without reaching a hazard measure nothing about it. How this connects Where this is taught The verification page of Reverse Engineering 101 reads the four claims, the harness page runs both legs over these candidates, lesson 36 builds the harness, and the failure modes lesson names a success claim that no state check supports. Recap What to keep from this case Define equal before claiming it. Know what each comparison tool compares. Test edge cases and integer types. Withdraw claims that rest on the wrong evidence. a2159: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems An Eval That Stopped RL Training before Step 0 Lesson 21.59 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory The situation In plain words first A smoke test that added evaluation to a training run failed before step 0, twice, with thousands of 503 errors. The cause is not known, and the case trains saying so: the smoke test did its job by failing early, and the long run should use a different eval mode instead of guessing a fix. An RL team wants an accuracy score on a held-out math set during its long GRPO runs. Before they touch the long run, they do the right thing and add the eval flags to a 2-step smoke test, with the interval set to every step. The job stops before it finishes step 0, with a Ray task error from the eval task after thousands of HTTP 503 lines. They run it again. It stops the same way. In the review, one engineer says the rollout engine died, as in the dead-engine incident, and wants the watchdog tuned. Another says the test set is too large for one GPU. The lead asks for a design that puts an eval score next to each step of the long run without this risk, and asks what the two failed tries prove and what they do not. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. Two tries of eval on the training engines, both before step 0 Copy Two 2-step runs of the same day without eval, which reached step 0 and step 1 Copy The flags that run eval on the training engines Copy How eval on the training engines works, and what happened on the GB10 Copy The three places where eval can run, and the limits of the fleet Copy What the router is and what a 503 from it means Copy Questions to answer first Compare this failure with a run whose engine died. Which component raised, which component retried, and why did this job stop while that one hung for an hour? The same recipe ran twice that day without the eval flags. What do those two runs rule out? Name what the two failed tries prove about the router and the eval client, and name the one thing they do not prove. Which component in this layout answered 503, and why does the count of those lines not tell you the cause? Lay out the three places eval can run, with the cost and the limit of each, and pick one for a long run on this machine. Write the gate that every eval configuration passes before it joins a long run, and the signal that proves it passed. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A smoke test that fails early has done its job. ✗ The rollout engine crashed, so restarting it will fix the eval. The two tries show the failure, not its cause. ✓ Running eval from checkpoints avoids the failing mode. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the two tries. Both ran the 2-step recipe with --eval-interval 1 and the GSM8K test file. Both finished zero steps. The first wrote 5311 lines of 503 Service Unavailable , the second 4339, and each ended with ray.exceptions.RayTaskError raised inside RolloutExecutor.eval() , from an HTTPStatusError . The eval client raised on the status code. This job did not hang, it failed and stopped. In the run whose engine died, the training rollout path retried the same status for 63 minutes and never raised. Two paths, two behaviors on one status code. Read the runs without eval. The tracker checks of the same day ran the same 2-step recipe, on the same image and machine, and logged step 0 and step 1 . They differ from the failed tries only in the eval flags. So the recipe, the engine start and the trainer were healthy that day. The eval flags are the change that broke the job. Read what the eval sends. The documented command sets the interval in steps and names the test split that the launcher downloads. With the interval at 1, the first eval ran at once, and the manual's record says that it sent the 1,319 test questions and that the router answered 503 to them. That is the whole burst: one eval of 1,319 prompts, many of them refused, counted as 5311 and 4339 error lines. Separate what is proven from what is not. The router is the small service that forwards each rollout request to an engine, and 503 is what it returns when no engine can take the request. So the evidence proves that, at the moment of the eval, the router had no engine that would take those requests, and that the eval client treats that status as fatal. It does not prove why the engine was not available at that moment. The manual ran this twice and did not find the cause. A design that depends on the cause being known is not available. Read the three places. On the training engines, the default, rollout production stops while the eval runs, the engines already hold the current weights, and on this machine the path failed twice. On a dedicated fleet, --eval-num-gpus N takes N GPUs of the job for eval and training never stops for it, with eval/lag_steps telling how late each score arrives, but the fleet cannot be combined with a checkpoint eval function and rollout fault tolerance does not work with it. Through your own service, --eval-function-path runs a checkpoint eval function, and the cost is only the checkpoint export. Place the two proposals. The watchdog guards a run that never stops. This job stopped by itself, so a watchdog finds no container and exits. The size of the test set is a guess with no measurement behind it, because the manual did not isolate the cause, and the only way to test the guess is the same 2-step smoke test with a smaller set. What actually happened The two tries prove that eval on the training engines fails on this machine at the first eval, loudly and before step 0, and that the cause is open. The team should not add that mode to a long run, and the smoke test did its job by failing first. For the long run on one GB10, run eval through a checkpoint eval function with --eval-function-path , which costs only the checkpoint export and keeps the training engines out of the eval. When a second GPU is available, use a dedicated fleet with --eval-num-gpus 1 , give its engines their own memory share with --eval-sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.9 , read eval/lag_steps , and accept that rollout fault tolerance is off with that layout. The gate stays: each new eval setting runs on the 2-step recipe first, with the interval at 1, and passes only when the log shows step 0 , step 1 and an eval score, with no RayTaskError . Keep the watchdog for the engine-death case, which is a different failure with a different signature. Wrong turns "The engine died, tune the watchdog." The job raised and stopped within its first step. The watchdog exists for the opposite case, a job that keeps sending requests to a dead engine and never fails. "Cut the test set to a few hundred questions and start the long run." The cause is not known, so a smaller set is a guess. Test it on the 2-step recipe, and only a pass earns a place in the long run. "Set the interval to 10 so that eval runs less often." The failure happened at the first eval. A longer interval moves the first eval later into a long run, where the same stop costs the work of every step before it. "Use the fleet together with rollout fault tolerance." Rollout fault tolerance does not work with a dedicated fleet in this version. Pick one. "Eval on the training engines is free, because they already hold the weights." It stops rollout production for the whole eval, and on this machine it stopped the job. The lesson to carry A smoke test that fails is a result, not a delay. Record what the failure proves and what it leaves open, and design around the open part instead of guessing at it. When one dependency answers the same error to two clients, know how each client treats it, because a retry turns an outage into a hang and a raise turns it into a fast stop. Keep the work that must not stop, here training, on different engines from the work that may fail, here eval, and let every new configuration earn its place through the same short test. How this connects Where this is taught The Miles manual lays out the three places for eval and records the two failed tries in the eval fleet page , defines the router and the 503 in the watchdog page , and gives the fault tolerance limits in the failures page . Recap What to keep from this case Smoke-test new modes before long runs. Say plainly when a cause is unknown. Choose a working alternative over a guessed fix. Keep the failure documented for later.
