a2160: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Exit Code 0 Is Not a Pass: a Nightly Binary Compare Job Lesson 21.60 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 14.101 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review, system-design. Roles : AI evaluation reliability engineer, agentic AI engineer. Version : rea 6.7.0 at 27dc42d with the Ghidra provider Model : no model; the fixtures are the ledger binaries built at -O1 and -O2 Hardware : one aarch64 Mac The situation In plain words first A nightly job posted "no change" whenever a compare command exited 0, which it did whenever it ran at all. For three weeks it never read the result. The case trains reading a tool's actual status instead of its exit code, and treating "unknown" as not a pass. A team keeps Evidence bundles of a shipped binary in version control. A nightly job analyses the current build with rea, exports a bundle, runs rea compare against the bundle of the night before, and posts "no change" to the team channel when the command exits 0. It has posted "no change" every night for three weeks. Then a release went out with a different optimization level, and the job still posted "no change". A reviewer opened the two bundles by hand and found that not one record was shared between them. Two more things went wrong in the same week. The job also keeps a digest of each bundle file to detect edits, and a colleague's export of the same records produced a different digest. And after the upgrade from the 6.5.0 release, an archived bundle that nobody had touched was refused at import. You are asked to say what the job measured for three weeks and to redesign it. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The import and compare commands with their exit codes Copy The head of the compare result Copy The first of the ten changes Copy The limitation at the end of the result Copy The MCP export and the CLI export of the same records Copy The import counts of the bundle that this release wrote Copy The import of the bundle that the old release wrote Copy Questions to answer first The compare command exited 0 on two bundles with no record in common. What did the job read, and what should it have read? Every change is classified unknown with the kind unresolved_branch , and records_removed is 0. Why does rea not call a record that is on one side only a removal? Two exports of the same eight records have different digests and byte counts. Which digest belongs in the archive, and how do you check that two files hold the same evidence? The old bundle was refused with retryable: false . Which record failed, why that one, and what does the team do with evidence it saved under the old release? Write the aggregation rule for the nightly job, and say which tool answers the question it was trying to ask. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Exit code 0 can mean the tool ran, not that the result is good. ✗ Three weeks of "no change" mean the binary did not change. The job never read the compare status. ✓ A result with unresolved records is not a pass. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the exit codes against the results. The command record shows rea compare with exit 0. The import of the current bundle also exits 0. Only the import of the old bundle exits 1. A zero exit from rea compare means that the comparison ran, not that it found two equal sets. The job treated the process status as the verdict and never parsed the output. Read the status and the summary. The result says status: "unknown" . Every records_ counter is 0, and unresolved is 10. So the two bundles share no record, nothing was classified as unchanged, and nothing was classified as changed either. The job's "no change" message described a comparison that compared nothing. Read one change. The first change has a right-side id and an empty left side. Its classification is unknown and its conclusion kind is unresolved_branch . The limitation on the change says that a bundle has no inventory completeness marker, so one-sided membership may reflect incomplete capture. rea cannot tell a record that was removed from a record that was never captured on that side, because the bundle format does not say whether a capture was complete. Read the closing limitation. The same sentence closes the whole result: one-sided membership remains unknown. The two bundles were made from two builds. No evidence_id can match across them, because the id is a hash of the record's semantic content and the content describes a different file. rea compare answers "what changed in this evidence set" for two bundles of one build. For two builds the question goes to compare_functions , one function at a time. Read the two exports. The MCP export and the CLI export hold the same JSON content and different bytes: 178398 against 178397 bytes. The one byte is the newline that the capture kit added to its copy. The canonical digest is the one from rea evidence-export , and the compare result names that digest as its left bundle digest. A job that compares file digests must canonicalize both files first, or compare the JSON content. Read the two imports. The import of the current bundle reports 8 imported of 8. The import of the old bundle stops with evidence_integrity_mismatch at records.3.evidence_id and retryable: false . The bytes are the bytes that the old release wrote. The hash rule changed: the current release includes a null relationship_coverage in the identity of a record, and the old release left it out. Records 0 to 2 are dossiers with a coverage object, so their ids still verify. Record 3 is the first record without coverage, so it is the first id that fails. What actually happened For three weeks the job measured whether rea compare could start. It never read the status. The redesign reads the JSON and applies one rule: a result with status unknown , or with unresolved above 0, is not a pass, and the message names the count. A pass requires status unchanged with every record classified. The job compares bundles of one build only. When the build changes, it opens both builds and calls compare_functions for each function of interest, and it reads the eight dimensions of each record, as the manual shows for _percent_change and _total . The archive stores the canonical digest from rea evidence-export next to each bundle, and the rea version that wrote it. The team does not migrate saved evidence. For the old bundles it keeps the old release available to read them, and it regenerates the evidence it still needs with the current release. The first nightly run after the change posted a result with unresolved: 10 and a red mark, which is what the two builds deserved. Wrong turns "Exit 0 means the comparison passed." The exit code says that the command completed. The verdict is in status , and here it was unknown . "Ten unresolved records on the right and none on the left means ten records were added." A bundle carries no completeness marker, so rea cannot say whether the left side was captured completely. It says unknown, and so must you. "Fix the old bundle by recomputing the ids and importing it." The refusal is not retryable, and rea does not migrate evidence. An id you compute yourself is no longer evidence that the tool wrote. "Compare the file digests to detect a change." Two valid exports of the same records differed by one trailing newline. Compare canonical digests or JSON content. The lesson to carry A tool that can say "I do not know" needs a reader that can hear it. Any pipeline that turns a result into a pass or fail must read the field that carries the verdict and treat every value other than pass as not a pass, including unknown, unresolved and skipped. Record the version of the tool next to every artifact it wrote, because the identity rules of a format can change between releases, and compare canonical forms, never raw files. How this connects Where this is taught The compare page of Reverse Engineering 101 reads this result, the bundles page explains the two exports and the refused import, the errors reference lists the results that refuse a conclusion and exit 0, and the failure modes lesson shows why a pipeline that tags only crashes misses most failures. Recap What to keep from this case Read the result, not the exit code. Treat unknown as not a pass. Name counts in the message. Compare like with like builds. a2161: Course home / Phase 21 · Interview Case Files: Debugging AI Systems Unexplained Reboots under RL Load: an Honest Postmortem Lesson 21.61 30 min Case file Completed Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.24 , Lesson 17.23 Type : Interview case file, incident. Level 4 (Staff). Time : about 30 minutes. Interview rounds : debugging, design-review, system-design. Roles : inference engineer, AI evaluation reliability engineer. Version : Miles main 08752a12 with its own SGLang 0.5.22 build Model : Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B Hardware : one GB10 with 128 GB of unified memory, a desktop machine under a 48-step RL run The situation In plain words first A machine rebooted three times in a day under training load with nothing in the logs. The cause was never recorded, and the postmortem says so; the mitigation, a heat guard that pauses the job, worked. The case trains writing an honest postmortem: what is known, what is not, and a mitigation proven by uptime. A research team runs a 48-step GRPO run of Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B on a desktop machine with one GB10. On 2026-10-18 the machine reboots three times. The run dies with it each time, and so does every other job on the machine. The boot list shows that the three boots lasted 13, 26 and 74 minutes. The journal has no panic, no out-of-memory kill and no error line before any of the three ends. The team wants a cause and a fix before they start the next two seeds. Two proposals are on the table. One says the engine ran out of memory and asks for a lower engine memory fraction. The other says the machine is unfit for RL and asks for a cloud GPU. You have the boot list, a guard script that someone wrote that morning, its log, and the lab notes of the manual. The evidence Read one listing at a time, and write down what each one tells you before you open the next. The boot list of the machine, read four days later Copy What the manual records about the load of that day and the guard Copy The loop of the heat guard Copy The first pauses and the rule change Copy The guard four days later Copy The heat guard and the pause count in the lab notes Copy Questions to answer first Read the boot list. What do the three short boots have in common, and what does the last boot of that day show? The journal gives no cause. Name the candidate causes for a machine that stops without a log line, and say which ones the evidence rules out. Read the guard loop. What does it watch, what does it do, and what are its two timers for? The guard paused the container 1,005 times. What does that do to every measurement from those runs, and which numbers survive? The chaos lesson asks for a safety plane with a kill switch and blast-radius limits. Where does this guard sit in that design, and what does it lack? You must state the cause in the postmortem. What can you write, and what must you not write? Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A postmortem can state that the cause is unknown. ✗ No panic in the log means the reboots were not caused by the run. The run was the only load; logs simply did not record a cause. ✓ Uptime after the guard is evidence the mitigation helps. Walkthrough Solution Open the walkthrough once you have your own answers Read the boots. The boots of the two days before ran through the whole working day. On the day of the incident the machine came up at 04:22 and was gone within a quarter of an hour, came up at 04:44 and lasted half an hour, came up at 07:52 and lasted a bit over an hour. The boot that began at 10:44 ran until 03:00 the next morning, and the boot of 2026-10-21 ran into the next day. Every short boot ended without a shutdown record. The guard log begins at 10:57 on that same morning, inside the first boot that lasted. Rule out what you can. Four causes stop a whole machine and can leave the journal silent: a kernel panic, a memory kill, a power event and a thermal shutdown. A panic leaves a trace in the journal, and there is none. A memory kill on this machine is a logged event that stops one process: Ray writes the node memory line and kills a worker, and the machine stays up, as the Ray out-of-memory scenario shows. That rules out the proposal to lower the memory fraction of the engine, because the symptom does not match. Power and heat remain, and the evidence cannot separate them directly, because nobody recorded the GPU temperature at the moment of any stop. What the evidence can show is what happened once the heat was held down. Read the guard. Every 5 s the script reads the GPU temperature. When a Miles container is running and the temperature is at or above 84, it pauses the container and notes the time. While paused, it resumes when the temperature is at or below 74 and at least 45 s have passed, or after 120 s no matter what. If the container is gone, it forgets it, and on exit it resumes whatever it paused, so no run stays frozen. The two timers are a floor and a ceiling: the floor gives the GPU time to cool, and the ceiling bounds the cost of any one pause. Read the first hour. The first rule was 80 and 68. The log shows a pause at 80 C and a resume at 68 C fifteen seconds later, then pause after pause within a minute. The team changed the rule by hand twice that morning, and from 11:27 it ran at 84 and 74. Four days later the pattern is steady: pause at 84 or 85 C, resume at 72 or 73 C after 45 s, about once a minute under load. The lab notes count 1,005 pauses up to 2026-10-22. Read what the pauses cost. Over the 9.3 hours of seeds 2 and 3, the container was paused for about 58 percent of the time. A pause stops the process and does not change its arithmetic, so the manual reads the reward, the answer lengths, the share of cut answers and the log-probability gap as valid, and says that it did not test this with a paused and an unpaused run of the same seed. The rollout times are not valid, and the manual does not report them for those seeds. Every wall-clock number from a guarded run needs the clean-step rule of the lab notes: time only steps that overlap no pause, and compare step numbers. Place the guard in the safety plane. The chaos lesson names a safety plane of kill switch, suppression windows, blast-radius limits and error-budget gates. The guard is a blast-radius limit on one container, with a resume-on-exit that acts as a kill switch for the guard itself. It lacks an alert, a temperature log of its own beyond the pause and resume lines, a bound on the total paused share of a run, and a test that the pause leaves results unchanged. It is a mitigation, not a diagnosis. Write the postmortem. The honest statement is that the machine stopped three times under sustained RL load with no cause in the journal, that a guard which holds the GPU at or under 84 C was running during every later boot, and that no stop recurred under it. That is a correlation with a plausible mechanism. The sentence "thermal shutdown confirmed" needs a temperature reading across a stop or a hardware event log, and neither exists. What actually happened The cause is not recorded, and the postmortem says so. The mitigation is a guard that treats the machine's heat as a budget: pause the container at 84 C, resume at 74 C after at least 45 s, and never hold one pause longer than 120 s. With the guard on, the boot that began at 10:44 on 2026-10-18 ran until 03:00 the next day, the boot of 2026-10-21 ran into 2026-10-22 while the guard logged pauses through the afternoon, and the machine did not stop again across 1,005 pauses. The cost is measured too: 58 percent of the wall-clock time of seeds 2 and 3 was spent paused, so their rollout times are not reported, and every later timing follows the clean-step rule. The memory proposal is declined, because a memory kill is a logged event that stops a process and leaves the machine up. The cloud proposal is deferred, because the machine held for four days under the guard. The next steps are the ones that would turn the correlation into a cause: record the GPU temperature once a second to a file that survives a reboot, read the hardware event log after any stop, and run the same load once without the guard on a day when a stop costs nothing. Wrong turns "Lower the engine memory fraction, it must be out of memory." A memory kill writes a line and stops a process, and the journal has none while the whole machine stopped. A lower fraction also shrinks the pool for every rollout. "The journal is empty, so it was power, call facilities." Not excluded, and worth a check. But the stops came under sustained load on one day and did not recur once the GPU was held at or under 84 C. Record the correlation and keep both candidates open. "Set the guard to 80 C to be safe." The first rule ran at 80 and 68, and the log shows a pause every minute. The team raised it to 84 and 74 that morning. A tighter limit buys more pauses, and every pause enters a step time. "Keep the guard and trust the step times." Seeds 2 and 3 spent 58 percent of their time paused. Time only steps that overlap no pause, and compare step numbers, as the lab notes do. "Call it a thermal shutdown in the postmortem." No temperature was recorded at the moment of any stop. Write what was seen: three stops without a cause, and no stop since the guard. The lesson to carry When a machine stops without a log line, the honest postmortem names the candidates, the evidence that rules each one out, and the mitigation you applied with its cost. A guard that keeps a resource under a limit is a safety plane for one container: it buys uptime with wall-clock time, so the measurement rules change on the day you turn it on, and the postmortem says "did not recur under the guard", never "cause found". How this connects Where this is taught The Miles lab notes give the guard and the clean-step rule in the heat guard section , the SGLang manual records the three shutdowns and the paused share in the two more seeds part of the rollout engine page , and the chaos engineering lesson and the SRE for AI lesson give the safety plane and the runbook shape. Recap What to keep from this case Separate known facts from guesses. Mitigate when the cause is open. Prove the mitigation with uptime. Say what would identify the cause next time.
